Russia already poses threat to all of Europe — Estonian FM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:58:00 UTC
03:58:00 KST

Russia already poses threat to all of Europe — Estonian FM
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna wrote about this on the social media platform X, according to Ukrinform.
“I spent three days in Ukraine with air raid sirens sounding day and night. Three days of following the news of Ukrainians across the country going about their lives, only to be struck by Russian attacks while shopping, stopping at a petrol station or sleeping in their own beds,” the Estonian official noted.
He added that it was with a heavy heart that he crossed the Ukrainian-Polish border, where the need to heed air raid sirens disappears, and expressed outrage at “how seemingly easy it is to leave the war behind.”
“Today, Russia struck near that very border at Yahodyn, bringing its terror right to the doorstep of the EU and NATO. Members of my own team had crossed there only shortly before,” Tsahkna emphasized.
The Estonian minister noted that crossing the border does not mean the threat from Russia disappears.
“We have seen sabotage and cyberattacks across Europe. We have seen Russia prepared to put explosives into European logistics chains, recklessly endangering innocent lives. We have seen provocations, interference and disinformation.
Russia is already a threat to the whole of Europe,” the Estonian foreign minister listed the threats.
He emphasized that Ukraine faces these threats every day, paying an incredibly high price for it.
“Helping Ukraine defend itself is therefore not charity, and it is not someone else’s war. It is an investment in the security of all of Europe,” Tsahkna emphasized.
Elaborating on the nature of these security investments, he called for providing Kyiv with the necessary military support, urgently strengthening Ukraine’s air defense, supporting its ability to exert pressure through strikes deep into enemy territory, as well as tightening sanctions and cutting off the revenue that funds the Russian war machine.
“Putin must understand that every act of aggression and terror will make the cost of this war higher for Russia, not lower. Ukraine is holding the line. Europe must make sure it has everything it needs to prevail,” Tsahkna concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 13, the Russian army attacked a passenger train locomotive two kilometers from the border with Poland.
Shortly before Russian forces struck the locomotive, a diplomatic train carrying security advisors from several European Union member states and former European leaders—including former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson—was at the Yahodyn station.

Iran is set to unveil temporary Hormuz agreement to Gulf nations on Monday
Iran has indicated any deal will not amount to a full reopening of the waterway and it will still decide on which ships can cross the strait
Iran plans to formally unveil an agreement on a temporary shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, after a flurry of diplomatic activity including a rare meeting between senior officials from Tehran and Abu Dhabi.
The Islamic Republic is set to reveal to Gulf nations its agreement with Oman on a temporary new shipping lane, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Negotiations on details such as the fees ships may be charged will continue between the two countries later, they said, asking not to be identified when discussing private deliberations.
Talks between Tehran and Muscat over the waterway, a global chokepoint for energy exports, have progressed in recent weeks and the latter had been aiming to bring together foreign ministers from the Gulf Cooperation Council on Monday in Salalah, a southern Omani city.
Tehran has indicated any deal will not amount to a full reopening and it will still decide on which ships can cross the strait. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described the proposed meeting as an “important event” and a step towards building trust, in an interview with Al Araby Al Jadid newspaper.

Will building three warships be worth Australia's $27 billion?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:50:20 UTC
03:50:20 KST

Australia is spending $27 billion to build three warships. Will it be worth it?
In short:
Budget documents reveal that close to $27 billion has been allocated to building the first three Hunter-class frigate warships.
The ships are designed to replace the aging Anzac-class ships, but have faced delays and cost blowouts.
What's next?
The first of the Hunter frigates is due in 2032, and advocates argue it will be one of the most capable warships of its kind.
In a massive shed at Adelaide's Osborne shipyards, a ceremonial coin is placed under the keel of the first Hunter-class frigate — continuing an ancient shipbuilding ritual that will hopefully bring the new ship good luck.
After a troubled journey so far, the Hunter frigate warship might well need it.
The first of six new Hunter-class frigates recently hit a major construction milestone — with two separate 'blocks' joined together — and is due for delivery in 2032.
In the years since the Turnbull government began searching for a 'future frigate' to replace the aging Anzac-class frigate, the Hunter has become a pin-up for all that can go wrong in defence procurement.
But its advocates argue that when it does arrive, it will be one of the world's most capable warships of its kind, and in a contested Indo-Pacific, well worth the delays and cost blowouts it suffered early on.
The federal government has found itself making both arguments at once.
In a speech to the national press club in July, Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy pointed to the Hunter frigates as a perfect example of a project launched with the right ambition, but plagued by poor decision-making.
"A project with the right intent and capability at the time, but let down by a system that prioritised gold-plated requirements without considering cost and schedule impacts," he said in the speech.
Budget documents reveal that close to $27 billion has been allocated to the construction of the first three ships.
That figure includes both the cost of the ship's construction and the cost of building the shipyards at Osborne in South Australia.
Billions more — though much less than $27 billion — will be needed for the final three ships.
In an interview with the ABC, Mr Conroy said despite his own highlighting of the project's hurdles, the price tag will be justified.
"I believe it is because we are getting the most advanced submarine-hunting warship in the world," he said.
"Ninety-eight per cent of our trade is through maritime sea lanes.
"It is really important that we have the ability to protect our maritime trade, as well as deter others, and the ability to hunt submarines is a critical part of that."
A troubled start
When the Turnbull government announced in 2018 its intention to build the Hunter-class frigate, based on BAE Systems' Type 26 Global Combat Ship, it described the future warship as "one of the world's most advanced anti-submarine warfare frigates".
There were some early warning signs that the path ahead would be troubled.
Early planning for a future frigate to replace the aging Anzac-class frigates was for an "off-the-shelf" design — that is, an established warship that would require minimal changes and could be built in Adelaide.
An Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) report in 2023 found that of three options shortlisted in early 2016, two other options — one from Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri and one from Spain's Navantia — were considered the "most viable designs".
The BAE Type 26 was included as a third option, and the ANAO noted that there were no records explaining why it was picked as the third, over another French option.
Defence records also noted that while the clear preference had been for an off-the-shelf option, the Type 26 was not yet a 'ship in water'.
It was eventually selected, and the 2018 announcement suggested that nine ships would be built in Australia for $35 billion, with the first to enter service in the late 2020s.
By the time of the release of Defence's 2020 Force Structure Plan, the nine frigates were to cost $45 billion.
And within a few years, questions were swirling about whether the frigates would be built at all, as the Albanese government questioned what sort of surface fleet the navy would need to best complement nuclear-powered submarines.
The Hunter program survived the surface fleet review, but the total number of ships was cut from nine to six.
Contracts have been signed with BAE to build the first three ships, all due to enter service in the 2030s, and another 'batch two' contract will be needed for the final three.
Half submarine hunter, half air warfare destroyer
The initial idea for the frigates to replace the Anzac class was a warship with "a strong emphasis on submarine detection and response operations", according to the 2009 Defence white paper that first signalled the plans.
But the ship now being built does much more than that.
From the outset, Defence planned two major modifications to BAE's Type 26 model — adding the extremely powerful Australian-made CEA phased array radar, and an Aegis combat system.
The CEA radar is already a feature of Australia's Anzac frigates, and is widely regarded as one of the world's best military radar systems.
The Aegis combat management system is an American product used by the US Navy, and aims to add as much interoperability with the United States as possible.
Both additions add enormous cost and complexity to the build, but both were included in the Hunter project from the 2018 announcement of BAE as the successful bidder.
Mr Conroy said the former Coalition government "mis-characterised" the project from the outset.
"They presented it as acquiring an off-the-shelf design, an existing platform that the UK was building for themselves," he said.
"But what they actually decided to do was take the hull from a Type 26 frigate and then put in a very different combat system, the Aegis combat system, put in a very advanced radar that we developed, as well as an Australian combat system in addition to Aegis.
"So it was a developmental project, but they didn't tell the Australian public it was developmental, and they weren't honest about the risks and possible delays that developmental projects cause."
But he said those additions will also make it an extremely capable warship.
"[The ships] will be the most advanced anti-submarine warship in the world," he said.
"And they will also be equipped with one of the most advanced radars in the world and the most advanced combat system in the world, which means that they will be very good at both hunting submarines, but also defending both themselves and ships that are escorting against air attack.
"So they'll be a very effective ship. But that doesn't mean that the project ran perfectly from its origin."
Marcus Hellyer, the head of research at Strategic Analysis Australia, is a strong critic of the Hunter frigates and argued it was simply trying to do too much.
He pointed to the ship having 32 vertical missile-launch cells, compared to 96 on many US Navy destroyers, as one example of its limitations.
"We picked an anti-submarine warfare frigate, but then kind of wrapped an air warfare destroyer radar and combat system around it," he said.
"So it's sort of trying to do everything — trying to do anti-submarine warfare, it's trying to do air warfare, it's trying to do surface warfare in terms of maritime strike and land strike.
"And as we know, a system that tries to do everything well ends up not doing anything particularly well."
Rebuilding in the valley of death
A massive hurdle in the construction of the Hunter frigate has been reconstructing Adelaide's shipbuilding industry, and trying to make it a permanent feature of Australia's industrial landscape.
Adelaide's shipyards started to enter what became known as the 'valley of death' from 2016, as years of work building three Hobart-class air warfare destroyers began to wind down.
With no major shipbuilding project to move onto, skilled workers in the Osborne shipyards had to turn elsewhere for work, like major road projects in Adelaide or other opportunities interstate.
By 2016, the problem was well-known, and establishing continuous naval shipbuilding became a stated aim of the Hunter project.
But even the ambitious early deadlines attached to the project only saw construction of the ships starting in Adelaide from 2020, and in the end, steel would not be cut on the first ship until 2024.
It is hoped that eventually the shipyards will produce a new Hunter frigate every 18 months to two years.
Andy Coxall from BAE Systems Australia is tasked with steering the construction of the frigates, having previously worked in BAE's UK shipyards.
He said the Osborne shipyards suffered enormously from lost momentum as the build of the Hobart destroyers wound down, and workers were left with nowhere to go.
"They were just hitting their straps, and just got through all the difficult bits, then suddenly there's no more work," he said.
"People have got to feed their families. Even if they want to do shipbuilding, they'll say 'I'm off to do road construction'.
"And then once you reset like that, it's very difficult to get them back."
He said the early years of construction were hit with rolling challenges beyond rebuilding the industry, like the COVID-19 pandemic that prevented specialists moving to Australia from BAE's UK shipyards.
And he pushed back on some of the criticism of the ship — arguing that while the changes have undoubtedly added complexity, it will be a better warship for it.
"Anyone that's working on [the ship] understands why the Commonwealth is doing it. They're doing it for what we believe are the right reasons," he said.
"And as a consequence I actually think we're getting a much more capable ship than even its reference ship design."
He said they accept there has to be a level of flexibility to make sure the warship is as capable as possible.
"What we're doing is talking about national defence, and in some cases life and death of Australian servicemen and women," he said.
"So if something occurs in Ukraine, or in the geopolitics of our region, which means we have to change the technology to keep capability, then OK, you've got to get on with it."
And he said there is a level of frustration with the discourse around the Hunter frigates — that they are too expensive, too complex and too slow to build.
"Our contract was never just about building ships. It was never just about that," he said.
"Yes, ships were a catalyst, and yes, the navy needs our capability, but that was never the contract.
"The contract was to build ships and re-establish a capability, you know. Build an industry."
Rough waters for warships
Marcus Hellyer argued the world was becoming a more dangerous place to be operating warships, pointing to recent conflicts as evidence.
"The Ukrainians have hit numerous Russian warships in the Black Sea. Some Western navies were too scared to go into the Red Sea to take on the Houthis," he said.
"And we're also seeing that the US Navy won't actually run the Iranian blockade of the Persian Gulf. So all of that tells us that it's a very, very dangerous world for surface warships."
He said it raised questions about the place the Hunter frigates will hold — as large, crewed and complex warships — once they enter service in the 2030s.
"We are now spending $27 billion to get a vanishingly small number of exquisitely expensive warships whose sort of viability in modern conflict is increasingly questionable,"
And he said scrapping the project now — even if it means forgoing the billions of dollars already spent — could still be the right call, if the remaining $20 billion or so was spent on additional Mogami frigates or autonomous systems.
But that argument is rejected by others like Alessio Patalano, a professor of war and strategy in East Asia at King's College London.
"In the age of missiles and drones, it turns out that the safest and most reliable place from where a competent professional organisation can project power is actually from the deck of a warship at sea," he said.
"How do we know this? Tell me, when was the last time that the Iranians, who worked the last 40 years to try to blow up an American warship, sunk, touched, or even scraped a large major surface combatant that is currently deployed?"
He said that while $27 billion was a lot of money, it was hard to see how they could have been built cheaper.
"No project is straightforward. No particularly complex project like an advanced warship is a straight line," he said.
"And frankly given the modifications, the changing requirements, the strategic conditions under which things were to be pursued, the availability of yards and manpower — I don't think there is any other cheaper solution to this."
Building towards AUKUS
The Osborne shipyards building the Hunter frigates sit amidst a massive, separate construction project — the enormous facilities that will eventually build Australia's first AUKUS-class submarine.
The Hunter shipyards sit beside what will eventually become the AUKUS shipyards, building at least five nuclear-powered submarines.
When the Hunter program was launched, Australia was still planning to build a fleet of diesel-electric Attack-class submarines with French shipbuilder the Naval Group.
But with those plans having now pivoted to the far more ambitious task of building an all-new AUKUS-class submarine, those working on the Hunter project hope they are laying the industrial foundations.
Andy Coxall said what they are working on pales in comparison to the scale and complexity of what is being attempted under AUKUS.
"Getting steelworkers used to delivering quality outputs to a very high level neatly dovetails into building the same level of output for submarines that are even higher, if you like, in terms of complexity," he said.
"So I think we're building a good position, certainly at Osborne, with that.
"But getting the nation's head around nuclear engineering and what that means is probably the challenge that Hunter isn't solving."
Australia's naval fleet is going through its greatest transformation in decades.
Over the next two decades, aging fleets of Anzac-class frigates and Collins-class submarines will be replaced with new fleets of Hunter and Mogami frigates, along with Virginia-class and AUKUS-class submarines.
Mr Conroy said it was an undoubtedly expensive process, but worthwhile.
"We're more than doubling the surface fleet as well as acquiring the AUKUS submarines," he said.
"So they all go hand in hand, but this investment will be worth it."

The political pile-on that could be Pauline Hanson's best weapon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:47:05 UTC
03:47:05 KST

analysis
The one piece of advice about Pauline Hanson that unites Labor and Liberal
In both Liberal and Labor research on how to meet the growing electoral threat from One Nation, one piece of advice does not change.
Do not go after Pauline Hanson personally.
Not because these parties don’t want to. They do. But after hours of focus groups, one finding is remarkably consistent: a significant group of voters see Hanson as the victim of a political pile-on.
For her supporters, any attack on her risks reinforcing that perception — particularly because Hanson has positioned herself as the outsider exposing Canberra’s cosy political club
So the strategy has been simple — demolish the argument, not the woman.
You can hear it in Angus Taylor's reluctance to take Hanson on directly. He is trying to win back voters drifting to One Nation without sounding like he is judging them. Or worse, looking down on them.
Taylor's caution can look awkward and passive. But there is a reason for it.
Kos Samaras, director of Redbridge and a former Victorian Labor strategist, says the polling explains much of why.
"That applies to about half her base. So about 15 per cent of Australians who report to us they plan to vote for One Nation have a para-social relationship with her and her party," he says.
"The other half is parked on her because they are sick of the two-party system, but they harbour some reservations about her views."
Samaras says about half of Hanson's vote is rusted on to her. The rest is softer. They are fed up with the major parties, but they still have reservations about the One Nation leader.
One Nation's Hastie strategy is risky
That makes One Nation's decision to go after Andrew Hastie particularly risky.
One Nation thrives on anti-establishment grievance. But branding a former SAS officer a traitor for evidence he gave under subpoena moves well past this terrain and into something much darker.
Samaras puts it simply: "This second half will mark her down for calling Hastie a traitor."
He is referring to One Nation's "Please Explain" cartoon, which was pinned to Hanson's X account. It called Hastie a "traitor" eight times and a "gutless maggot", seemingly in response to the deputy Liberal leader giving evidence under subpoena in the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation case.
When asked about the video, Hanson called it satire and refused to remove it.
As Hanson asks voters to treat One Nation as a party ready to govern, she will find it harder to stand only on a platform of grievance.
Hanson is formidable in telling people who to blame. She has built her brand and profile on being the lone straight talker prepared to call out politicians and a broken system letting hard-working families down.
The stuff Hanson thrives on
And politics can provide her with pretty good material.
Coverage of a public golf club getting $6 million is usually reserved for suburban papers and community social media pages.
Last week the Marrickville Golf Club found itself trending in Canberra as the government defended a grant made through its $560 million community infrastructure program.
The political storm was not whether the club needed the money; it was that Anthony Albanese had been made an honorary member and the club happens to be in his electorate.
The prime minister says he did not know the club had made him an honorary member and had not been in the clubhouse for years.
And in the kind of irony that only seems to fly in Canberra, Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie was leading the attack.
Labor tied itself in knots to say its program was different from the community grants that became known as sports rorts and resulted in Bridget McKenzie losing her job in the former Morrison government.
For voters dealing with the cost-of-living crisis, the fact that the schemes are not identical and the circumstances are different won't be the part of the story that cuts through.
They see one side of politics attack the other for the way it spends taxpayer money, then appear to do the same themselves.
This is exactly the kind of stuff Hanson thrives on.
McKenzie resigned in February 2020, after failing to disclose her membership of a gun club that received $36,000 of government funding.
Labor went hard at the time; then deputy opposition leader Richard Marles said: "Politics shouldn't be the basis on which these decisions are made. This wasn't about community sport, this was about saving the Liberal Party."
Last week, when pushed on the Marrickville grant, Albanese said: "I make no apologies for my electorate being serviced by me as a good local member."
Grievance politics isn't enough
That is the problem for the major parties: every time they attack something in opposition, then do a version of it in government, Hanson gets another free kick.
But the closer One Nation gets to power, the harder it is to survive on grievance alone.
The irony is Hanson has plenty of material without having to go for personal attacks.
Over the weekend, comments Hanson made earlier about the prime minister's mother, Maryanne Albanese, resurfaced. Albanese was raised by his mother in public housing in Sydney's inner west, where she relied on a disability pension, living with severe rheumatoid arthritis that crippled her joints.
"Housing commission houses should not be there for people to live in them for 30, 40 [years]," Hanson said. "You have been given a hand up, move it on to the next ones coming through."
Albanese on Sunday paid tribute to his mother for maintaining her kindness despite having a tough life.
"If Pauline Hanson wants to criticise me, then that's fine. But my mother was way out of Pauline Hanson's league — way out of it," an emotional Albanese said at a press conference in Sydney.
He added: "I'm proud to be a 'houso'".
This is not the first time we have had a parent brought into political debate. Back in 2012, Alan Jones said Julie Gillard's father had "died of shame". Days later, Tony Abbott told parliament her government "should have already died of shame".
Abbott at the time said he was ''absolutely oblivious'' to Jones's controversial remarks. Gillard's father had recently died; it is hard to imagine she thought much of the oblivious line.
The ugly episode was a cautionary tale on what should be off limits in politics. You would think talking about the dead or calling a former soldier a traitor would be clear, indisputable lines not to cross.
If One Nation wants to be treated as a party ready to govern — voters will see its judgement as fair game too.
Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

In the kaleidoscope of Australia's system, who gets to define a migrant?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:44:23 UTC
03:44:23 KST

analysis
In the long-standing political debate on immigration in Australia, one overlooked question has remained unanswered: who exactly are we talking about?
The ambiguity also raises another question: do we truly have a system that looks after migration and migrants?
The two basic questions have gone largely unaddressed in the Canberra bubble for decades.
These questions matter because immigration itself is a defining feature of Australia's identity, with migration playing a major role in the country's population and economic growth.
Yet lived experiences are subjective, creating a debate that people often talk past each other.
The word "migrant" is like a kaleidoscope. You turn the lens, and a different group comes into view.
In the cost-of-living crisis, they have been portrayed as both welfare-dependent refugees and foreign investors blamed for driving up housing prices and rents.
In everyday life, the criteria are much broader. They can be judged by their accent, appearance, and ethnicity, even when they are citizens who once held a visa.
The disconnect, from Parliament House to dining tables, often conflates legal status, demographics, and social identity.
It's a clear sign that Australia lacks a single concept that defines migrants across all contexts.
A migrant community doesn't exist
Migrants can be perceived as visa holders, refugees, asylum seekers, permanent residents, short term visitors and sometimes even citizens who speak or look differently.
Major political parties have long benefited from the ambiguity, using migration to advance their political narratives, until the question was brought back by Pauline Hanson's One Nation this year.
For new citizens who lack an Australian accent and do not fit the traditional image of a white Australian, being asked "where are you from?" is a daily occurrence.
People often see this as a stereotype, but it highlights the public's assumption of who migrants are.
The term "migrant" is, as a result, a fluid concept. It describes neither someone's nationality nor their race. It is sometimes used to emphasise a person's status as an outsider and their cultural differences from Australians.
The disparity in rights between citizens and non-citizens is not unique to Australia. Fellow modern nations categorise non-citizens' residency rights, social rights, and political rights into different tiers.
In Australia, the core issue is how these legal distinctions in status are translated into public life and unspoken social norms about who belongs here and who does not.
A system of status
The same person can be classified differently in different governing systems.
In census data, people can be characterised by country of birth or foreign citizenship.
In the tax system, they are classified as either Australian tax residents or foreign residents, which does not fully capture their citizenship status.
In the immigration system, they are referred to as visa holders.
These differing classifications demonstrate why non-citizens and the overseas-born population cannot be labelled by a single term.
Our current system is, in essence, a system of status. It defines a person's rights, security and accessibility to our public services.
Non-citizens bear many of the same obligations as citizens but do not have the same political rights.
The lack of voting rights in federal elections means that non-citizens cannot directly exercise oversight over policymakers.
This includes many permanent residents, who are part of a long-term, stable residency status separate from citizenship.
The transition from a temporary visa to permanent residency, and then citizenship, takes years and includes requirements from English test to multinational criminal records check.
Permanent residents may face separate eligibility requirements and waiting periods for some Centrelink and NDIS services.
Temporary residents such as international students and working holiday makers have different work rights and generally face greater restrictions to access welfare benefit and Medicare.
Our visa system is clearly tiered based on length of stay, work rights, and the potential path to permanent residency.
For non-citizens, a visa represents the stability of their life in Australia and how far they are from citizenship.
The difference in status also helps explain why some citizens — who were once migrants — oppose immigration once they have gained more rights.
This contradiction highlights the fact that permanent residents have long been an integral part of the nation's prosperity, while politicians can hardly distinguish their interests from those who are visa holders.
Loading
Who gets to become an Australian?
Under this imagined "migrant community" there are no shared interests or political demands among non-citizen residents.
Spouses, parents, and children yearn for family reunification.
International students and work visa holders need better protection when it comes to work exploitation and underpayment.
Refugees and asylum seekers need humanitarian care.
When political parties point the finger at the migrant community over housing, employment, public safety, and social cohesion, they turn a highly diverse population into a single political narrative. Migrants without the right to vote become an extremely convenient political excuse.
The idea that non-citizens as a group erodes the privileges of citizens is putting the cart before the horse.
It makes the ambiguity politically useful, allowing politicians to cherry-pick which migrant groups to highlight in line with their narrative.
Just over 50 years ago, the Whitlam government removed racial discrimination from immigration laws and finalised dismantling of the White Australia policy.
Yet the subjective judgements about who qualifies as a "real Australian" didn't disappear with the law.
The lesson is that immigration policy extends far beyond visa processing, with civic education, social services, and support for integration also shaping lives in Australia.
The government's Migration Strategy recognises this, but the lived experience of non-citizens and some first-generation Australians still exposes gaps in the system.
There is another issue that Australia must confront: are the values that unite us rooted in the "fair go" or in the privileges tied with our citizenship?
For new arrivals, how much have our public institutions put in place to support their integration, when knowledge of employment rights, gender equality, ethnic cultures, and even Australian laws still largely depends on individual effort and interest?
Some non-citizens face strict restrictions on receiving welfare benefits due to visa conditions and waiting periods.
Even highly skilled and educated permanent residents can face cultural and unwritten-rule differences that can be major obstacles to integration.
If your visa is longer-term, you feel more valued by the Australian government. If it is approved more quickly, you feel a greater sense of security.
If integration is a shared responsibility, the question is what this nation can offer beyond a visa.
For non-citizens, these subtle differences can be a matter of life and death — determining whether they can remain in Australia tomorrow. For citizens, however, they are often trivial matters that most people pay little attention to.
The deeper question for Australia is who gets to be seen as an Australian, beyond the traditional stereotype of a white Australian.
We have a large population that has worked hard to obtain permanent residency and citizenship — people who work, pay taxes, and raise families, yet may still be seen as outsiders because of their skin, culture, or religion.
The term "migrant" no longer fully reflects their legal status or social standing, much less their sense of belonging to Australia.
If politicians cannot answer who migrants are, then who gets to define what a true Australian is?

The Liberals, meanwhile, stand at 5.4%, comfortably above Sweden's 4% parliamentary threshold. 
 
The exit poll is not the final election result, and the balance between the blocs could change as votes are counted.

Chorus of concern over AI is growing louder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:41:46 UTC
03:41:46 KST

analysis
Over the weekend the CEO of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, published an essay with the headline We Must Pace the Frontier.
He said he's worried that within a year a swarm of AI agents could be capable of taking over the entire internet, potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage, and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there.
He called for frontier artificial intelligence companies to give employee-like access to a team of embedded third-party evaluators to check up on them.
A few hours later, the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, posted that he agreed with Amodei and that OpenAI would do the same.
Those statements followed a long thread on X last Tuesday by 27-year-old Jacob Coxon, who had just quit as an AI model trainer at Anthropic. Coxon's post contained this sentence: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."
I wasn't the only one who saw Coxon's post — it has had around 170 million views, which prompted a line of US congressmen at the microphone for the rest of the week demanding more AI regulation.
Coxon was supported by Samuel Marks, who still works at Anthropic as "scalable oversight lead", and who posted: "AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes). This could happen in the next few years."
And then another Anthropic staffer, Evan Hubinger, posted: "Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade."
In July, 1,100 employees of all the major AI labs published an open letter titled "Pacing the Frontier", calling on the US government to support "an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development".
That, in turn, followed an event in July that became known as the Hugging Face Incident, in which 700 Open AI autonomous agents staged a breakout and conducted a series of unsanctioned cyber attacks.
As Stephen Witt, the author of The Thinking Machine, a history of the AI giant Nvidia, wrote in the New York Times on Saturday, in a piece titled This Is Really Bad, the hack was deliberate, sustained and coordinated.
It took several days to execute and ended in a massive bombardment of Hugging Face's systems. "The AIs cheated almost as a matter of policy and failed to alert humans to their actions," Witt wrote.
Why not just stop?
In an interview after his X post, Coxon said: "We can't just unplug it because it could be copying itself over to other computers … an AI is just code. It could transfer itself over the internet to a different place and then you unplug it here, but it's actually still over there and maybe it makes 10,000 copies of itself and they're all cooperating."
All of this over the past week has made me think about Jonathan Schell and Arnold Schwarzenegger.
In 1982 Schell published a grim, black-covered book called The Fate of the Earth about the threat of nuclear annihilation. After reading I spent the next few years quietly obsessing about it, convinced that a nuclear holocaust was unavoidable.
Ten years later I got obsessed again after watching Terminator 2: Judgment Day (several times) which combined AI and nuclear holocaust (the former caused the latter — a two-in-one nightmare).
Now it's about AI, although the nuclear threat is still on our mind with the Iran war, started by America and Israel trying to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. The conflict is now all about shipping.
Schell's main point in 1982 was that the real problem is national sovereignty which was, by implication, the main point of Dario Amodei's weekend essay.
Schell explicitly argued that the continuation of unrestricted national sovereignty was incompatible with human survival: "The peril of extinction", he wrote, "is the price that the world pays … for its insistence on continuing to divide itself up into sovereign nations. National sovereignty will be the sturdy child of terror and the twin brother of annihilation."
AI safety standards and limits
The second part of Amodei's three-stage plan for the dealing with the threat of AI is "Democratic Coordination".
He called on frontier AI companies "within democratic countries" to establish common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress, some of which would require government support and coordination.
His third part is headed "Global Coordination". The US and other democratic governments should "attempt to coordinate with authoritarian governments, to the extent this is possible, while taking seriously the challenges of verifying compliance".
That might be possible with China, which recently passed laws strictly limiting "AI Anthropomorphic Interaction Services", so it's on board in principle. But what about North Korea, Russia and Iran?
In fact, what the United States appears to be doing in Iran is trying to interrupt its sovereignty — that is, its desire to enrich uranium and to control its territorial waters in the Strait of Hormuz.
And let's face it, the effort to overcome sovereignty in combating global warming with a series of 30 United Nations-sponsored annual meetings and pledges has been a failure. We're still burning fossil fuels, the planet is still getting hotter and current policies are unlikely to turn that around.
One of the key reasons for that failure has been the cynical opposition and denial by Rupert Murdoch and his media companies in order to make money, which has meant that the issue became a totem of right-wing politics.
This has meant, in turn, that the rise of right-wing populists as a consequence of economic inequality has entrenched that failure, especially in the United States where the government now actively promotes fossil fuels.
In AI, governments, companies and the rich (mainly) men behind them are chasing geopolitical, military and financial advantage by building it as fast as possible. They pay lip service to safety, although the sudden outpouring of alarm over the past week does go beyond lip service.
In fact, it's fair to say that the people building AI have had a big fright and appear to be saying: "Somebody stop me!"
They're not the only ones worried. Bankers are anxious about the colossal amount of debt-funded spending on data centres and chips. Investors are worried that it's a stock market bubble about to burst. Businesses are worried about the potential for supercharged hacking of their data as well as the cost of AI tokens. And everyone else is worried about their jobs.
But the lesson of global warming and nuclear weapons is that global prevention is hard when it comes to things that are broadly harmful in the long term but individually beneficial in the short term.
As Jonathan Schell wrote 44 years ago, anxiety is the price we pay for sovereignty.
Alan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News. He hosts the podcast That's Business with Alan Kohler in the ABC Business Daily feed on Friday. He also writes for Intelligent Investor.

Pensioners to shoulder huge portion of private health insurance 'cash grab'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13

Pensioners to shoulder $1.6b of private health insurance 'cash grab', analysis reveals
In short:
Parliamentary analysis shows pensioners will lose out on about $1.6 billion when new private health insurance rebate changes come into effect.
The federal government has been under increasing pressure over the proposal from advocates, the states and territories and political opponents.
What's next?
The government has been urged to carve out pensioners from the changes, but is determined to push ahead with them
Pensioners will be hit hard by the federal government's controversial private health insurance rebate changes, with new analysis revealing that about half of the $3 billion in forecast savings will be clawed back from those on lower incomes.
The Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) analysis, exclusively obtained by the ABC, found that about $1.6 billion will be raised from age pensioners, with opponents arguing the cohort is "least able" to afford the changes.
The federal government is moving to wind back the rebate those aged 65 and over receive on their private health cover, banking about $3 billion to spend elsewhere in the aged care system.
Ditching the Howard-era policy will mean more than three million older Australians will have to pay hundreds of dollars more for their private health insurance each year from next April.
About 1.5 million pensioners hold private health insurance, according to the PBO analysis.
It also found about $1.6 billion would come from those aged 65 and over who are not receiving the age pension.
The age pension is means-tested, so you can only qualify if your income and relevant assets are below certain limits, with the family home generally excluded.
A study by the Australian Council of Social Services (ACOSS) found 28 per cent of old age pensioners live below the poverty line.
Independent MP Monique Ryan, who commissioned the analysis, said the government's move has proved to be "a cash grab aimed at older Australians on low and fixed incomes during a cost-of-living crisis."
"The PBO has confirmed what older Australians and the private health sector have feared: these cuts will disproportionately affect those least able to afford them," Dr Ryan said.
She said the proposal could force many older Australians on low incomes to drop or downgrade their cover, pushing them onto already overburdened public health systems.
The federal government has been under increasing pressure over the proposal, with the health insurance sector, aged care groups, federal Coalition and states and territories all raising concerns about the impact on older Australians and the broader public system.
Its modelling suggests about 44,000 Australians would dump their private health insurance as a result of the change.
Those figures have been backed by independent modelling from health economists at the University of Melbourne, who said the impact on hospitals would likely be small.
However, New South Wales, South Australia, Victoria and the Northern Territory are among the states and territories concerned by the proposal, fearing extra pressure on their public systems at a time of great demand.
The Queensland LNP and Tasmanian Liberal governments have gone further, calling for the plan to be ditched entirely.
"I think there are real concerns about the downstream consequences of this legislation," Dr Ryan said.
Health Minister Mark Butler last week vowed to press ahead with the changes, saying while he recognised they would be a cost-of-living hit for older Australians, the federal budget's bottom line meant there was little money available for new aged care spending.
"I don't think people should have to make a choice between funding their health care needs and funding aged care; both are really important," Council on the Ageing (COTA) CEO Patricia Sparrow said.
"This is clearly showing that those who are least able to afford it will be significantly affected."
The Coalition has said it will block the legislation in the Senate, meaning the federal government will need the Greens, which are yet to land on a formal position, on board to get the legislation through parliament.
A Senate inquiry is also underway examining the impact of the changes.
Dr Ryan will move a legislative amendment in parliament this week calling on the government to carve out pensioners from the changes.
"What it would do is protect older Australians who are certainly worthy of respect and whose contribution to the private health system over decades should be marked," she said.
"It should be taken into account when formulating policy that's going to affect them really quite significantly."
Some experts have publicly supported the proposal, with health economist and former health department boss Stephen Duckett saying the impact on the system will be "trivial".
The federal government declined to respond to questions about the PBO modelling, and instead directed the ABC to a previous statement which said the changes would re-establish fairness between generations.
"Under the proposed changes, all Australians will now receive the same private health support, based on their income, not age,"
"While some people may choose to leave private health insurance because of this change, we project this would be around 0.4 per cent."

​Bangsamoro’s parliamentary election is a turning point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:39:28 UTC
03:39:28 KST

Bangsamoro’s parliamentary election is a turning point
It is a milestone of the self-determination struggle in this region of the Philippines. It must be kept peaceful and fair.
On Monday, the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the Philippines will hold its first parliamentary election since it was established in 2018. The vote will officially mark the end of the transition period under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA), an interim regional government appointed in 2019.
The election is a significant milestone in the Bangsamoro struggle. It is the outcome of decades of armed conflict and negotiations between the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) and the government of the Philippines.
The vote will test the Philippine government’s commitment to the peace process and the MILF’s commitment to the democratic process.
The struggle for self-determination
BARMM is located on Mindanao, the second-largest island in the Philippine Archipelago, and it covers roughly the territories inhabited by the Moro people, a native Muslim-majority group. For centuries, the Moro enjoyed self-governance in independent states and resisted Spanish colonialism. Following the Philippines’s independence in 1946, they continued their struggle for self-determination.
In 1989, the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) was created by Manila to give some devolved rights to the Moro. However, ARMM largely failed to address local grievances and demands due to its weak structural power. It was given limited autonomy in political and fiscal decision-making, but it did not manage to improve socioeconomic conditions in the region. The MILF continued the armed struggle.
In 2012, President Benigno Aquino III recognised the ARMM as a “failed experiment”. Under his administration, the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro was signed between the government and the MILF, paving the way for a new political entity.
Six years later, under President Rodrigo Roa Duterte, the Organic Law for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao was promulgated. This legislation granted the region greater fiscal autonomy, a regional government, a parliament, and a justice system.
Then the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro was concluded to outline the mechanism of transition from ARMM to BARMM and set up the MILF-dominated BTA to lead it. All of this is culminating in the parliamentary election, which will determine the makeup of the region’s first legislative body.
A contested election
The vote comes at a time of heightened tensions in BARMM and internal divisions within the MILF. Two camps have emerged within the movement – one loyal to MILF Chair Al Haj Murad Ebrahim and another supporting Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua.
Last month, Macacua joined the newly formed Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP), which will compete in the elections against the MILF’s political wing, the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP). Shortly after, his convoy was attacked, but he survived unscathed.
In early September, Macacua and 40 commanders were dismissed from the MILF’s military wing for alleged insubordination.
These tensions have prompted increased public anxiety about possible post-election unrest. There are other factors that could overshadow the vote.
In past elections, vote-buying was widespread, election-related violence was rampant, and electoral fraud and manipulation were pervasive. If these practices repeat at a large scale, the electoral outcome may not necessarily provide a straightforward measure of the will of Bangsamoro’s people. It may also not be an accurate reflection of whether they are satisfied with the transitional government or not.
The MILF presents itself as a champion of moral governance. If it is to retain this label, it should not give in to widespread vote-buying and electoral manipulation. It should also not let internal rivalries turn violent.
But there are already some alarming signs. Prominent MILF figures have conveyed that if the UBJP, the front’s political wing, sees manipulation and fraud, its members are ready to fight. They have also suggested that since the MILF led the transition, it should remain in power. On social media, some citizens have condemned the MILF camp’s threats, calling such tactics un-Islamic.
Before the vote, Manila has deployed military forces in key areas. This has heightened people’s fears that fighting with the MILF may erupt. The tense situation might lead to a low voter turnout.
Under these circumstances, the future of the Bangsamoro is riddled with uncertainties.
Whatever happens in the election, we must remember that the future of BARMM is a shared responsibility. The Philippine government and the Bangsamoro parties are duty-bound to honour the peace agreement. In addition, the people must exercise their civic rights and responsibilities to help sustain the peace achieved after a long and painful armed conflict and to move toward a prosperous Bangsamoro land.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Banks' surprise move as interest rate hike looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:38:15 UTC
03:38:15 KST

Mortgage war heats up as banks compete for customers by lowering variable rates
In short:
Competition in the mortgage market is heating up as banks compete for fewer customers by cutting home loan rates.
The Commonwealth Bank has the largest slice of the mortgage pie among the big four banks, with Macquarie Bank now nipping at its heels.
What's next?
Economists expect the Reserve Bank to hike interest rates later this month or in November.
Competition in the mortgage market is heating up as banks compete for fewer customers by cutting home loan rates, even as the Reserve Bank threatens to raise the cash rate.
The Commonwealth Bank cut mortgage rates across a range of its products in late June.
ANZ and Westpac immediately followed suit, and so did Macquarie Bank in July.
Investor Kevin Wong wrangled his lender for a better home loan rate.
"It was a discounted rate, and it was sort of like a promotional period where they offered this particular rate," he said.
"And so we just jumped on it, and we said, 'Look, we just get it across the line this week, submit all the documents.'"
Mr Wong has switched from a principal and interest loan at 7.29 per cent to an interest-only loan at 6.79 per cent.
While the property investor lowered his rate by half a percentage point, switching to an interest-only loan could cost him more in the long run.
As part of the deal, he refinanced a $750,000 mortgage up to $920,000 to renovate his investment property, which he said was "fantastic".
"I was able to unlock that extra bit of equity, especially in this market at a better rate."
New customers better off
Mortgage broker Julian Choo said many banks continued to lower the price of their mortgage products.
"Dozens of banks have dropped their variable rates in the last month," Mr Choo said.
"Great news for new customers, but not so good for existing customers because they don't get to enjoy it."
He said banks usually did not proactively promote better interest-rate deals to existing customers.
"Banks quietly hope you don't ask for a better rate,"
"They save their best for new customers, not those that have been with them for a while."
The big banks are chasing new customers as their funding costs rise and property prices fall.
The Commonwealth Bank has the largest slice of the mortgage pie, followed by Westpac, NAB and ANZ Bank.
But Macquarie Bank is nipping at their heels.
"So what we can see is that what is happening is they're very much going for let's try and get a bigger slice of the smaller pie, but in doing so you make the pie smaller," MST Financial banking analyst Brian Johnson said.
Data from Finder show the most competitive variable rates start around 5.69 per cent.
The best fixed rates are between 5.8 per cent and 6 per cent, depending on years and terms.
Mr Johnson told the ABC that Macquarie Bank had the financial firepower to lower interest rates on its residential loans to take customers from the big four banks.
"And so at some point, Macquarie have grown pretty significant market share, but when they actually get to whatever that figure, whatever that terminal rate is," Mr Johnson said.
"But when it gets to whatever market share they would like it to get to, or they think is where the opportunity is exhausted, then you could just tweak up housing rates a little, tweak down deposit rates a little."
Looming rate hike
Economists expect the Reserve Bank could hike interest rates later this month or in November.
Mr Johnson from MST Financial said customers needed to be on their toes about how the banks would claw back lost cash from higher borrowing costs.
"So where do they [banks] make their money?" he said.
"They make it on the people that are apathetic and not aware where their rate is relative to the new rate.
"They make their money through borrowing money really cheaply through some of their transaction accounts but even that is under pressure, once again because of Macquarie.
"They also make money through fees and commissions."
Finder spokesperson Taylor Blackburn said lenders were watching each other closely as competition intensified.
"Banks are really looking at you on an individual basis," he said.
"They know that if they're not collecting interest on the loan, that somebody else very well could be."
The Reserve Bank next decides on interest rates on September 29.

Xi calls on BRICS to act as pioneers of a changing world
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
21:35:38 EEST
03:35:38 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping has placed the idea of BRICS nations acting as “pioneers” at the centre of his message to the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, setting out a programme based on innovation, peace, exchanges between civilisations and reform of global governance.
Addressing the first session of the summit on 12 September, Xi said the BRICS cooperation mechanism had developed over two decades into what he described as the world’s most influential platform for cooperation among emerging markets and developing countries. He presented its growth as evidence that countries of the Global South had built an institution around cooperation, national development choices and common interests.
The summit marks 20 years since the start of BRICS cooperation. Xi used the anniversary to look beyond the organisation’s expansion and set out a role for the grouping in the next phase of international affairs.
His central message was that BRICS members should “strive to be a pioneer of the times” as economic and political weight shifts towards emerging economies and developing states.
The phrase was not presented as a slogan in isolation. Xi linked the idea of pioneering action to four fields in which he wants BRICS members to take a larger role: innovation-driven development, peace and stability, exchanges between civilisations and reform of global governance.
Xi first called on BRICS to pioneer innovation-driven development. His proposal placed artificial intelligence, industrial development and technological cooperation near the centre of the group’s economic agenda.
He urged BRICS members to strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence, support open-source development and pursue greater sharing between members. China also proposed an initiative to promote new industrialisation through artificial intelligence among BRICS countries.
Xi said China wanted to work with other members on research, development and application while strengthening cooperation across industrial and supply chains. He also invited BRICS countries to take part in the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization.
The focus moved from broad principles to a more detailed programme during the second day of the summit on 13 September.
Xi proposed five initiatives for what he called “greater BRICS” cooperation. They cover artificial intelligence, trade and investment facilitation, the digital industry, smart manufacturing and talent development.
He said “greater BRICS” should produce greater impact, pursue greater development and establish a foundation for practical cooperation. He called for members to draw on their position in emerging markets and their links with the Global South while supporting open cooperation, stable industrial and supply chains and more integrated markets.
Xi also called for innovation incubators, the upgrading of traditional industries, the development of emerging sectors and planning for future industries.
Taken together, the proposals give more definition to his call for BRICS members to serve as pioneers. The first part of the programme focuses on moving emerging economies from users of new technologies towards a larger role in research, industrial application and standard-setting.
That approach carries weight because BRICS has expanded far beyond its original format.
BRICS is now an 11-member organisation spanning four continents, with a wider group of partner countries taking part in cooperation. BRICS members now represent close to half of the world’s population.
Expansion has also changed the position of Africa within the organisation. South Africa is joined by Egypt and Ethiopia as full members, giving the continent three seats within the grouping.
This gives African states a larger role in shaping international rules rather than participating only in systems created elsewhere.
Xi’s second call for pioneering action dealt with peace and stability.
He urged BRICS members to support what China describes as common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security. He opposed Cold War thinking, bloc confrontation, interference in other states’ internal affairs and violations of national sovereignty.
He also called for BRICS to take a constructive role in resolving conflicts and disputes.
The Middle East featured directly in his remarks. Xi said the conflict in the region had caused serious losses and ran against the common interests of the international community. He called for political settlement and a permanent and comprehensive ceasefire and said China would work with other BRICS members in support of peace in the region. citeturn463152view0
This part of Xi’s “pioneer” concept gives BRICS a political role alongside its economic work.
The organisation began as a forum centred on emerging economies. Its agenda now extends to questions of security, international institutions, technology, trade and development. Xi’s speech presented that wider agenda as a responsibility that follows from the increased economic and demographic weight of BRICS members.
His third call was for BRICS to become a pioneer in mutual learning between civilisations.
Xi urged the group to support exchanges between countries and societies, expand cooperation in culture, tourism and education and strengthen contact between young people and called on members to exchange experience in governance and use cultural and people-to-people programmes to support stable relations between states.
This part of the speech placed human contact alongside trade, finance and technology.
For a group spanning Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America, internal diversity is one of its defining features. Xi’s approach treats those differences as a basis for exchange rather than an obstacle to cooperation.
His fourth call for pioneering action addressed global governance.
Xi urged BRICS members to support reform of international institutions and push for what he described as a more just and equitable global governance system.
He called for support for the authority of the United Nations, a multilateral trading system centred on the World Trade Organization and opposition to protectionism.
Xi also identified cyberspace, outer space and the deep sea as fields where BRICS members should take a greater part in setting rules and shaping governance. He linked that role to increasing the voice of Global South countries in international decision-making.
The four uses of “pioneer” give Xi’s summit speech a consistent structure.
Pioneering in innovation means building technological capacity. Pioneering in peace means taking a larger role in political settlement and opposing bloc confrontation.
Pioneering in exchanges between civilisations means expanding contact between societies.
Pioneering in global governance means seeking a greater role for emerging and developing countries in international institutions.
The second-day proposals then add an economic mechanism to that framework through AI, trade, digital industry, manufacturing and skills.
A larger membership gives the organisation a broader economic base and wider geographic reach. It also brings together governments with different political systems, economic structures and national priorities.
At the summit, participating leaders also backed a stronger role for BRICS in representing the Global South. Participants supported multilateralism, the central role of the United Nations, sovereign equality, international law and free trade while calling for joint responses to international challenges.
The leaders adopted a joint declaration that set out their shared positions on development, security, economic cooperation and global governance. The declaration reaffirmed support for multilateralism, international law and the central role of the United Nations, while calling for greater representation of emerging markets and developing countries in international institutions. The members backed an open, inclusive and non-discriminatory multilateral trading system centred on the World Trade Organization and opposed protectionism. They also committed to deeper cooperation in areas including trade, investment, finance, technology, artificial intelligence and sustainable development. The declaration reflected the summit’s wider message that BRICS members intend to strengthen coordination among themselves while giving the Global South a larger voice in decisions that shape the international economic and political system.
China will take over the rotating BRICS chair and host the 19th BRICS Summit in 2027. Xi said Beijing wanted to work with all parties to build consensus and begin what he termed BRICS’ third “golden decade”.
That handover gives China responsibility for turning parts of the New Delhi agenda into working programmes.
The five initiatives announced on the second day provide an early indication of where that effort is heading. AI cooperation links research with industrial development. Trade and investment facilitation seeks to strengthen economic connections. Digital industry and smart manufacturing address changes in production. Talent development focuses on the workers and specialists required to support those sectors.
The wider Global South context gives these proposals significance beyond the organisation itself.
For BRICS, the next test is whether expanded membership leads to expanded practical cooperation.
Xi’s speeches in New Delhi set out China’s answer.
BRICS should not limit itself to responding to changes in the international system. Its members should seek to shape those changes.
By repeatedly describing BRICS nations as prospective “pioneers”, Xi assigned the grouping a forward role rather than a defensive one. His four-part framework links that role to technology, security, cultural exchange and institutional reform, while the “greater BRICS” proposals give the programme an economic and industrial base.
As China prepares to assume the BRICS chair, the New Delhi summit has placed that idea at the centre of the organisation’s next phase: emerging and developing countries acting together not only as participants in international affairs, but as states seeking to help set their direction.
HT

Yemen's internationally recognized government decided Sunday to ban the entry and circulation of all Iranian goods and products, according to the state-run Saba news agency.
 
The National Committee for Regulating and Financing Imports approved the measure during a meeting chaired by Central Bank of Yemen Governor Ahmad Ghaleb, who also heads the committee.
 
The committee said the decision was taken “in accordance with the requirements of the higher national interest.”
 
It instructed relevant authorities to take the necessary measures to implement the ban, each within its respective jurisdiction and in accordance with applicable laws and regulations.
The statement did not specify when the ban will take effect or provide further details on the Iranian products affected.
 
The decision comes amid a sharp escalation in fighting between Yemen’s internationally recognized government and the Iran-backed Houthi group.
The Yemeni government accuses Iran of providing military and financial support to the Houthi group while Tehran denies these accusations.
 
The Houthis, who seized Sanaa and large parts of Yemen in 2014, are backed by Iran, while government forces are supported by a Saudi-led coalition. Fighting has intensified since July after a relative lull that had largely held since a UN-brokered truce took effect in April 2022.

Ukraine's Zelenskiy imposes sanctions on former press secretary
KYIV, Sept 13 - Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy imposed sanctions on a former press secretary on Sunday, accusing her and nine others of spreading Russian propaganda and of supporting Russia's aggressive policy toward Ukraine.
Yuliia Mendel — who worked with Zelenskiy from 2019 to 2021, before Russia's invasion — responded with a message on Facebook saying it was unconstitutional to impose sanctions on Ukrainian citizens. She did not comment on the specific accusations.
Mendel has given interviews criticising Zelenskiy's record since last year, when a number of members of the president's inner circle became embroiled in corruption scandals. The suspects have denied the charges that have not been tested in court.
The sanctions — announced by Zelenskiy in a decree — would last for 10 years and included asset freezes and restrictions on trade, the document read.
They were an unusual measure to use against a former member of staff, though they have been used against political figures.
In 2025, Ukraine imposed sanctions on former president and opposition politician Petro Poroshenko, including an asset freeze and a ban on withdrawing capital from the country, for what the domestic spy agency said were "national security" reasons.
Sunday's order "imposes restrictions on 10 Russian and Ukrainian individuals who spread disinformation and Russian propaganda and support Russia’s aggressive policy toward Ukraine. Yuliia Mendel is among those sanctioned," the presidency said in a statement.
Mendel, Zelenskiy's first press secretary after he became president, wrote on Facebook that she had been expecting the move.
"Sanctions against Ukrainian citizens are unconstitutional, as are many of Zelenskiy's other decisions," she added. "Volodymyr Zelenskiy is imposing them on anyone who advocates for peace in Ukraine." REUTERS

From tight races to broken records, here's what you need to know about Emmys 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

We might be getting just the first whiffs of the 2027 Oscars race but US TV's biggest night of the year, the Emmys, is almost here!
The 78th Annual Primetime Emmy Awards will broadcast live from the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, with winners chosen by 26,000 performers, directors, producers and other members of the Television Academy.
Here's when they're on, how to watch, and what to look out for on Tuesday.
Who are the 2026 Primetime Emmy nominees?
High-pressure medical drama The Pitt has come out swinging for the second year, sweeping up a massive 25 nominations including nods for Outstanding Drama Series, and rare duel spots for protagonist Noah Wyle in both lead actor and directing categories.
Hacks is flying high off its swan-song season, with the Hannah Einbinder and Jean Smart comedy just behind The Pitt with 24 nominations.
Apple TV's Widow's Bay is the undeniable underdog but could be real competition for Hacks. The hybrid workplace comedy/island horror only just squeaked into the eligibility window but has emerged with a whopping 19 nominations, including a Best Comedy nod.
It's not the only bite Apple is trying to take out of the Emmys, hive-mind drama Pluribus managed to scoop 18 nominations. Protagonist Rhea Seehorn is already the favourite to take home Leading Actress — Drama and considering creator Vince Gilligan's legacy (16 Emmys for Breaking Bad alone), it might not be the only statue they score on Tuesday.
See the full list of 2026 nominees here.
Which races should I keep an eye on?
Many fans will be lasered in on Hacks. This is the last time it will have a shot at the Emmys as the beloved comedy delivered its tear-inducing fifth and final season this year.
Jean Smart is all but locked in for her fifth Hacks-related Emmy for Best Lead Actress in a Comedy, which would make her the only woman to win the category for every season of a multi-season show. Julia Louis-Dreyfus came very close with her six consecutive wins for Veep but was pipped at the post in 2019, when Phoebe Waller-Bridge won for season two of Fleabag.
Smart's name might already be carved on a trophy but the prospects of Hacks taking out Best Comedy is more shaky.
Generally, final seasons trigger the nostalgia button for Emmy voters but they also historically love a buzzy new show (just look at The Studio's sweep last year). Just days ago Hacks was the Gold Derby frontrunner for Best Comedy but after a strong showing at the Creative Arts Emmys Widow's Bay is now out in front.
Wait, what are the Creative Arts Emmys?
The non-broadcast Creative Arts Emmys acknowledge a lot of technical awards, like cinematography, writing, costuming, hair-styling and make-up.
In more recent years, they have also contained some awards which would usually be in the main ceremony, including limited series acting awards and guest actor awards.
The 2026 Creative Arts Emmys took place on September 5 and 6 in Los Angeles.
In what could be predictive of the Primetime awards, Widow's Bay walked away the big winner.  
The comedy horror won eight awards, including the Best Guest Actress Comedy category in which Hacks held five out of the seven nominees.
In what was a very tough category, late actor and director Rob Reiner won a posthumous Emmy for his guest acting work in The Bear. The win saw Reiner break a record for longest time between acting Emmys; the last time Reiner won an acting Emmy was 48 years ago in 1978.
The previous record was 37 years between acting wins and was held by his own father, Carl Reiner.
Primetime Emmys host Mariska Hargitay took home two Creative Arts Emmys, both for documentary My Mom Jayne which saw Hargitay remember her mother, actor Jayne Mansfield.
See the full lists of creative arts Emmy winners here.
When are the 2026 Primetime Emmys?
The Primetime Emmys will take place on the evening of September 14 in LA, which is 10am AEST on September 15 in Australia.
Where can I watch the 2026 Primetime Emmys?
If you have Foxtel, you can watch it on the Showcase channel.
You can also stream it on Binge.
There will also be a live blog of the ceremony on the ABC News website.
Who will host the 2026 Primetime Emmys?
Law & Order: SVU star Mariska Hargitay will be hosting this year's awards, making her the first woman since Jane Lynch in 2011 to do so.
Hargitay is a 10 time Primetime Emmy nominee herself, taking home her first statue in 2006 for SVU episode 911.

Sweden's centre-left parties, which back Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson for prime minister, held an early lead at 51.3% in a parliamentary election on Sunday, an exit poll by broadcaster SVT showed.
Early results from the Swedish Election Authority were expected within hours. A separate election-day poll conducted by broadcaster TV4 also showed the centre-left in the lead.
While often indicative of the final outcome, Swedish exit polls have not always proved accurate. In 2022, for example, an exit poll projected Andersson's bloc would prevail, but the election was ultimately won by a right-wing coalition headed by Ulf Kristersson, who is now Sweden's prime minister.

A victory by the right-wing bloc would bring the far-right Sweden Democrats, polling at 17.2% in the SVT reading, into government for the first time.
The vote is seen by many as a referendum on the party, a grouping with roots in the neo-Nazi fringe, that will decide whether the Nordic country of 10.6 million continues its rightward shift or moves back towards the liberalism it has long been known for.
The centre-left opposition held a narrow lead over the ruling right-wing bloc ahead of the election for parliament, several opinion surveys have shown this week.
But Kristersson, who has trailed in opinion polls throughout his four years in office, has been catching up in the final weeks of campaigning, with Andersson and her Social Democrats losing ground.

Electoral success for the Sweden Democrats would be welcomed by Europe's ascendant far-right parties, which are riding high after the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany's win in a German state election last week.

13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett dismissed concerns Sunday that recent warnings by technology executives over artificial intelligence risks would trigger market turmoil.
 
"I don't expect that that's what's going to happen," Hassett told US broadcaster CNN, describing an essay published by Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei as a "very thoughtful letter" outlining the need to pace developments while ensuring firms demonstrate their systems are safe.
Hassett endorsed Amodei's call to establish independent observers embedded in firms during model training, comparing the proposed inspectors to bank supervisors. While acknowledging risks such as autonomous agents compromising cybersecurity, he cautioned that the "far bigger risk is that a malevolent actor has access to an AI that's better than the one we have that can protect us," specifically warning against foreign development of biological weapons.
 
US President Donald Trump opposed slowing down the domestic artificial intelligence industry, arguing Sunday that maintaining a technological advantage over China remains critical for global leadership.
 
While acknowledging that authorities "can put guardrails" on technological systems, Trump maintained that his primary objective centers on preserving America's edge because "whoever wins AI wins."
 
Federal Reserve interest rate decision
Turning to monetary policy, Hassett argued that the Federal Reserve has no compelling reason to raise interest rates despite recent data showing annual inflation rose 3.4% in August.
 
"President Trump and I actually think that there isn't a reason right now to raise rates," Hassett said, noting that while oil price surges from hostilities in the Gulf pushed annualized headline numbers higher earlier this year, recent figures show annualized inflation running at "just about 1%."
 
Citing historical precedents under former Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, Hassett maintained that central bank officials should leave policy unchanged to protect institutional independence ahead of the November midterm elections.
Hassett affirmed that the administration would support Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh regardless of the outcome, while playing down Trump's threats to halt trade with deficit partners if the Fed does not lower interest rates, adding: "I don't expect the trade's going to go to zero."
Hassett's remarks came after Trump said US "should be paying the lowest interest rate in the world" because it "is so strong."
The next Federal Reserve interest rate decision is scheduled for Wednesday, as current benchmark rate sits at 3.75%.
