STOCKHOLM — Former center-left Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson is on course to retake power in Sweden as exit polling suggests a rightwing alliance that includes the far right is falling short.
Andersson, the leader of the Social Democrats, spent much of the election campaign warning voters against handing ministerial posts to what she called an “extremist” party with “neo-Nazi” roots — the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats.
If the survey proves accurate, it would mean rejection for incumbent PM Ulf Kristersson. The conservative Moderate party leader had decided to work closely with the Sweden Democrats and promised to give them seats in cabinet for the first time if he won.
Advertisement
According to Sweden’s SVT public broadcaster, Andersson’s left bloc is on track to take 51.3% of the vote.(Sweden’s electoral system is based on proportional representation.) Kristersson’s alliance on the right is projected to win 46.8%.
Exit polls have not always been accurate in the past, but the picture should become clearer later on Sunday night when broadcasters are expected to announce updated forecasts after a critical mass of districts declare results. Whoever ends up winning, party leaders will take weeks to finalize a new coalition agreement.
“Swedish elections are always close,” Andersson told POLITICO earlier on Sunday as she toured the suburbs of Stockholm in her dark red campaign bus. “When I’ve been around Sweden, a lot of people I’ve spoken to said they see things that the government has done that they like but there are also lots of things that they don’t like. And many people say to me that it’s enough now.”

“The hate that they have spread through this election, and if they would become ministers and use their platforms as ministers to spread hate? Well, we’ll see if the Swedish people are very tempted on that,” she said.

US deports Afghan woman in first-ever case before special terrorism court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:16:46 UTC
03:16:46 KST

In a first, the US Department of Justice brought a case before a previously unused special court and deported an Afghan woman legally residing in the US after she conceded to being an “alien terrorist,” according to court records.
Prosecutors in the DOJ alleged that Nazira Haji Zada, a 47-year-old mother originally from Afghanistan, supported a plan by her son and son-in-law to commit an ISIS-style mass shooting on America's Election Day in 2024.
Both Haji Zada’s son and son-in-law were charged in the plot and will be deported following their release from prison.
Haji Zada was arrested in July at her home in Fort Worth, Texas. She was tried in the never-before-used Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC), which Congress created in 1996.
The court’s initial purpose was to make it easier for the DOJ to use classified evidence during prosecutions that posed a risk to national security, according to an analysis by NPR.
Afghani woman's deportation not an 'endorsement of this court's legitimacy'
Court records dated August 20 state that Haji Zada waived her right to challenge the detention and agreed to the deportation order; the presiding judge ordered her removal the same day.
Attorney General Todd Blanche stated, “This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law. Those who support and condone terrorism should not be living in the United States, and this first-ever case before the ATRC shows how the Department will use every tool at its disposal to protect our country.”
Haji Zada’s public defenders contested the legality of the case, arguing they were not permitted to review the evidence because it remained classified.
A statement from the DOJ noted that Haji Zada and her lawyers were provided with almost half a terabyte of evidence supporting the government’s case against her.
Haji Zada’s lawyers stated that their client’s consent to the deportation order “should not be seen as an endorsement of this court’s legitimacy.”
“Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process,” they said.
“We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue.”
The DOJ statement on the case alleged that Haji Zada worked to “radicalize” her family and “formally pledged loyalty to ISIS.”
Assistant Attorney-General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said: "Zada supported her sons’ terrorist plot to attack the United States while she enjoyed the privilege of residing here as a resident alien.”

'Death of a Democracy': Exploring the rise and fall of Weimar Germany - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:16:44 UTC
03:16:44 KST

"Berlin has been defiled – shame on a people that considers itself among the world’s civilized.” This was the editorial in the social democratic daily Vorwärts, commenting on a pogrom enacted in the city against the poor emigrant Ostjuden (Galician Jews). This attack took place 10 years before Hitler rose to power.
Victor Sebestyen’s Weimar Germany: Death of a Democracy paints a graphic picture of a liberating republic after the fall of the Hohenzollern monarchy at the end of World War I.
This interesting book tells a familiar story of Berlin, plagued with hyperinflation, antisemitic nationalists, and blinded Stalinists. A place where famous downtown thoroughfares were lined with prostitutes, and cocaine and opium were easy to obtain.
In 1922, a quarter of all German Jews lived in Berlin. A city where homosexuality was quietly accepted despite its legal ban, where literature, films, and music flourished, and where many Jews felt at home.
The period before the machtergreifung – Hitler’s takeover – was known as the “golden years,” when the currency had finally been stabilized in the Weimar Republic under Germany’s first president (1919-1925), the Catholic-born atheist Friedrich Ebert.
It was a Jewish physician, Magnus Hirschfeld, who established here the first LGBT organization in the world.
The Jewish academic Hugo Preuss drafted the constitution for the new republic.
Weimar created a system of democratic representation that had not existed under Kaiser Wilhelm II.
The Wall Street crash of 1929 hit Germany much harder than other countries – and the rest is a history that no Jew can forget.
Hitler's rise to power was not inevitable
The author argues astutely that Hitler was not inevitable. A combination of unprecedented circumstances, moral weakness, political opportunism, and bad luck all played a part.
He tells how Germany by 1916 had become “a silent dictatorship” – a military regime, overseen by Paul von Hindenburg and Erich Friedrich Wilhelm Ludendorff, that preached “final and total victory” in the war against the Allies.
No one – least of all the kaiser – expected a sudden end to the conflict. He blamed the Jews for his eventual abdication.
The war had cost $1.45 trillion in 2025 values. In the summer of 1917, the three democratic parties in the Reichstag had called for a ceasefire in the war.
The generals reacted by forming “the Fatherland Party” and began deflecting responsibility away from themselves. The Jews were blamed for “the stab in the back.”
Already by 1916, Hindenburg and Ludendorff had initiated an inquiry to demonstrate that Jews were underrepresented in the German armed forces. Yet the inquiry proved the opposite: 12,500 German Jews perished in the trenches.
Within weeks of the kaiser’s departure, there was a botched attempt by the Spartacus League to overthrow the republic, led by the Polish-born Jewish revolutionary Rosa Luxemburg.
This was followed by other attempts in which Jews played a prominent part to create a different type of society: Politician, journalist, and revolutionary Kurt Eisner declared a Bavarian Workers and Soldiers Council. The anarchist Gustav Landauer, whose writings influenced Martin Buber, was murdered in Stadelheim prison. German-Russian Communist revolutionary Eugen Leviné headed the second Bavarian Soviet republic.
ALL MET untimely deaths at the hands of the Freikorps, embittered antisemitic nationalists who could not understand why the war had ended so abruptly, why the monarchy had disappeared, and why there had been a challenge to traditional Prussian norms.
Ebert willingly used the Freikorps as well as the army to crush any challenge to the Weimar Republic.
The exhausted returning soldiers proved willing recruits for the Freikorps. The author writes: “Their eyes were hidden in the shadow, thrown by the peaks of their caps, sunk in dark hollows, gray and sharp.”
The Bolsheviks in Soviet Russia desperately hoped that revolution would also break out in industrialized Germany and save them from isolation.
Lenin, however, was in despair at all these failed attempts and berated the German revolutionaries, noting: “when the moment may come to storm the railway stations, they would line up in a queue and buy platform tickets.”
Weimar labeled as 'the Jew republic'
The nationalists called Weimar “the Jew republic” and celebrated when the Jewish foreign minister, Walter Rathenau, was assassinated in 1922. He was accused of being one of 300 “Elders of Zion” bent on world domination.
The author argues that the repeated attempts by the Left to gain power by undemocratic means diverted attention from the threat of the Right.
While Berliners had little sympathy for the attempts to establish a Soviet republic in Germany, they were appalled at the violence and thuggery of the Freikorps.
Albert Einstein was on a Freikorps hit list and, like Rathenau, feared assassination. Nationalists demonstrated outside his home and outside his office at the Prussian Academy of Science.
The Nobel Prize winner Philipp Leonard and his colleague Johannes Stark were brilliant thinkers but devout antisemites. They railed against Einstein and “the Jewish style of physics.”
The Bauhaus ideas of Walter Gropius were regarded as “Bolshevist architecture.” Braided hair was “Aryan”; bobbed hair was “Jewish.”
A DISQUIETING conclusion from this work is that if events had taken another course, any mention of Adolf Hitler would today have gained a mere footnote in a history book.
During the Beer Hall putsch in 1923, Hitler and his followers marched to the center of Munich. They refused to obey police warnings and were then fired on. Max Scheuber-Richter, who had linked arms with Hitler, fell dead.
At Hitler’s subsequent trial, the judge, well-known for his hardline nationalism, allowed the future fuhrer full rein to theatrically perform in the courtroom. He received a six-month jail sentence instead of deportation to his home in Austria.
Stalin directed the German Communists to challenge the social democrats and thereby split the vote at every turn. The split allowed Hindenburg to win the presidency on the second vote in 1925. As a committed monarchist, he was determined to destroy the republic.
Hitler's electoral breakthrough
In the early days, the Nazis could not have advanced without generous financial donations to the party coffers. Hitler was funded by the piano manufacturer Carl Bechstein and the Ruhr steel magnate Fritz Thyssen.
All this allowed Hitler to make an electoral breakthrough due to soaring unemployment. Six million were unemployed by mid-1932. Hitler stood against Hindenburg in the presidential election that year and lost. He claimed that the election had been stolen and continued to do so even after a German court ruled that Hindenburg was indeed the victor.
The Berlin correspondent of the British Daily Mail wrote that he saw Hitler as “a man whose power lies not... in his eloquence and his ability to hold the attention of the crowd but in his convictions.”
The aged Hindenburg similarly came around to “understanding” Hitler. He was egged on by his son, Oskar, by Franz von Papen (German chancellor in 1932 and vice chancellor 1933-1934), by the leader of the monarchist German National People’s Party Alfred Ernst Christian Alexander Hugenberg, and by many political notables, in the belief that they would easily be able to control the Nazi leader.
The story of Germany between 1918 and 1933 is painful to contemplate amid a plethora of what-ifs. What if the police bullet had hit Hitler during the Beer Hall putsch and not the man standing next to him?
Sebestyen has painted a vivid picture of the life and eventual death of Weimar Germany. It is an important and illustrative rendition of the events which defined this transient republic.
As the Austrian writer Peter Drucker noted before escaping to the US: “Fascist ideas spread when people refuse to believe in anything.”■
WEIMAR GERMANY: DEATH OF A DEMOCRACY
By Victor Sebestyen 
Pantheon
480 pages; $35

China Focus: China broadens tourism appeal with easier travel, richer experiences
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
02:16:04 CST
03:16:04 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- For an overseas visitor to Beijing, a day of sightseeing no longer has to end at the Forbidden City or the Great Wall.
The city's tourism map is expanding. In the outer districts, a countryside stay can be paired with a scenic train ride or a visit to a major scientific facility, while old towns and modern industries are making their way onto international visitors' itineraries.
"China offers not only inspiring historical landscapes but also innovative tourism products and services," said Australian tour operator Manuel Condoleon, adding that his clients are increasingly seeking personalized experiences and homestays. Safety, he noted, is another major advantage drawing international visitors to China.
That changing landscape was at the heart of the 2026 World Conference on Tourism Cooperation and Development, held during the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) in Beijing.
The conference released 121 detailed scoring criteria supporting ISO 11778 on tourism city brand evaluation. Led by the World Tourism Cities Federation (WTCF), ISO 11778 is the world's first international standard dedicated specifically to evaluating tourism city brands.
The new scoring rules build on eight top-level indicators and 53 secondary indicators in the standard, covering areas including tourism resources, infrastructure, service convenience, environmental sustainability, safety, stakeholder evaluation, visitor numbers and financial performance.
Dai Bin, president of the China Tourism Academy, said quantitative indicators such as visitor numbers and tourism revenue remain important, but greater weight should be given to how tourists actually experience a destination.
A report released during CIFTIS by the institute of international trade in services under the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation pointed to a similar challenge. It found that growing inbound visitor numbers have yet to be fully converted into tourism spending in China, and that among five dimensions examined, improvements in service quality and visitor experience had the strongest effect on unlocking further growth potential.
Across China, efforts are underway to make travel easier while offering visitors more reasons to stay longer and explore more deeply.
SMOOTHER JOURNEYS
For international visitors, planning a trip to Beijing can now start long before arrival.
A new digital platform, launched by China Daily and the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism during the conference, brings itinerary planning, flight and train bookings, accommodation, translation, transport, currency conversion and online payment services into one place. International visitors can access it either by visiting www.chinabound.cn/beijing or searching for "ChinaBound" in Alipay.
"Beijing is leveraging digital technologies to enhance tourism services and improve the experience of international visitors," said Zheng Fang, deputy director of the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism. The platform also features an AI assistant that answers questions and helps plan trips, serving as a digital guide for first-time visitors.
At CIFTIS, exhibitors showcased AI-powered multilingual guides and AR translation glasses designed to make on-the-go communication easier. One system used at the tourism conference displayed real-time translations directly in the wearer's field of vision, while other devices supported real-time translation in dozens of languages.
"Language used to be the biggest problem, but it is increasingly less of an issue," Condoleon said. "Technology, including AI, has made it much easier for today's travelers to get around China than it was ten or twenty years ago."
Chinese online travel platform Trip.com Group said inbound visitors still encounter difficulties with language, understanding tourism products, coordinating itineraries and dealing with unexpected situations, with problems during a trip particularly prominent.
The company has helped more than 170 scenic spots launch multilingual websites and deployed multilingual self-service ticket machines at nearly 300 attractions. Using AI, it also provides product information in up to 16 languages for more than 8,000 scenic spots and 450,000 hotels.
The demand keeps climbing. Latest data shows that foreign nationals made nearly 61.29 million border crossings in the first eight months this year, up 19.5 percent year on year. Visa-free entries by foreign nationals totaled 23.72 million, accounting for 77.6 percent of all inbound foreign visitors to China, up 26.8 percent year-on-year.
BEYOND THE LANDMARKS
The World Tourism Cities Development Report (2025-2026), also released at the conference, ranked Beijing fifth among 100 global tourism cities, behind New York, Tokyo, Paris and London. The remaining top 10 spots were rounded out by Shanghai, Hong Kong, Milan, Istanbul and Dubai.
For Beijing, expanding inbound tourism increasingly means giving visitors more choices beyond its best-known landmarks.
A scenic train route offers another way to explore Yanqing in the city's northwest. In Huairou, visitors can see major national scientific facilities and a science city, while Shunyi offers a look at modern logistics and service industries.
"Beijing has not only history and the past, but also the present and the future," Dai said.
He said inbound tourism in the new era should go beyond a single historical narrative and give overseas visitors greater access to contemporary life, technological innovation and popular culture, alongside traditional attractions.
Foreign visitors are already traveling farther from Beijing's urban core. Platform data show that overseas tourists have booked homestays in all 10 of Beijing's suburban districts this year, with bookings in Yanqing up more than 50 percent year-on-year and in Huairou up 14 percent. Courtyard homestays have proven especially popular, with bookings from foreign visitors rising 50 percent.
The trend extends well beyond the capital. First-tier and new-first-tier cities remain the main gateways for foreign visitors, but more travelers are now venturing inland to smaller destinations. Data from homestay platform Tujia showed that Gansu, Xinjiang, Ningxia, Qinghai and Shanxi were among the provincial-level regions recording the fastest growth in homestay bookings by foreign tourists in the first half of the year.
"The travel footprint of inbound visitors is expanding, and their pace is slowing down, as they take time to seek out more authentic cultural experiences, like browsing local markets, trying street food, exploring ancient architecture or trying their hand at intangible cultural heritage crafts," said Ma Yiliang, vice president of the China Tourism Academy.
China's tourism development plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) calls for further improving services for inbound travelers, building tourism networks around major gateway cities and developing products centered on areas ranging from traditional crafts and historical culture to technology, study tours, festivals and shopping.
Joseph Lema, an expert with the WTCF, said competition among tourism cities has moved beyond attractions and visitor numbers. What matters now, he said, is the ability to deliver quality experiences, effective governance and sustainable development. ■

Trump tells Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian diesel supplies
A global surge in diesel prices is being driven by the Russia-Ukraine war, the US president says.
United States President Donald Trump has urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure, saying they were to blame for a global fuel shortage that was driving up prices, and not the war with Iran.
“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing: he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump said on Sunday, speaking to reporters during a trip to the Republic of Ireland. “We spoke to Mr Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel. That’s hurting the world.”
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Saudi Arabia shuts critical oil pipeline after drone attack: What it means
- list 2 of 3Diesel price hits all-time high in US amid Iran war woes
- list 3 of 3Iran and Ukraine wars: Why ship fuel is running short, and why it matters
A wave of long-distance Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries in recent months has reduced that country’s fuel production, triggering petrol shortages across the country.
Ukraine, which faces regular Russian attacks on its own energy infrastructure, says refineries are legitimate military targets. Kyiv says Russia’s oil industry both funds and directly fuels Moscow’s more-than-four-year-old invasion of its neighbour.
Fuel prices are weighing on Americans as they prepare to vote in midterm US elections in November.
The price of diesel hit an all-time high in the US on Friday, reaching a national average of $6.06 a gallon ($1.60 per litre) according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily prices. The price of diesel a year ago, according to AAA, was $3.71 a gallon ($0.98 per litre).
The fuel has a significant impact on the cost of transportation, and is used by ships, trains, and trucks to move international goods, many of which are now more expensive, as those costs are passed on to consumers.
On Sunday, Trump said the increase in the price of diesel “isn’t done by the Middle East, this is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine”.
Oil prices globally have gone up since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran in February, disrupting the flow of oil from the region, including through the Strait of Hormuz, and causing a global energy crisis. Around one-fifth of the world’s oil passes through the strait in peacetime.
Crude oil prices crossed the $100-per-barrel mark last week for the first time since July. Brent crude, the global benchmark, climbed as high as $109 at one point.
The war in Ukraine is, along with the Iran conflict, having an impact on diesel prices too, according to the International Energy Agency.
A monthly report from the agency published on September 11 said the war between the US and Iran was hampering efforts to normalise flow through the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, but the Russia-Ukraine conflict also was having an influence, particularly on diesel supplies.
“The disruptions to Russia’s refining system and a near-halt to product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks have compounded these losses,” the agency said.

Weidel also called for Syrians living in Germany to return to Syria once the grounds for their protection no longer exist.
“For Syrian citizens who came to us, as soon as the reason for fleeing no longer exists in their country of origin, these people have to go back,” she said.
She argued that asylum is a temporary right and that people should return to their countries when the grounds for asylum cease to exist rather than be naturalized.
Weidel said that under an AfD-led government, Syrian citizens would be expected to return to Syria rather than remain permanently in Germany.
She also said an AfD government would review the naturalization of Syrians to determine whether the criteria had been properly met, saying the party had “considerable doubts” about some cases.

Andrei Rublev’s 15th-century ‘Trinity’ icon is reportedly warping after its climate-control chamber broke. A German specialist fixed it once but couldn’t return when it failed again.
The special climate-controlled chamber housing the Trinity icon, which was transferred to the Russian Orthodox Church in 2023, broke down several months ago, Ekho and religious affairs researcher Ksenia Luchenko said, citing sources.
Ekho’s source said a specialist from Germany was called in to repair the chamber. He fixed it, but it broke down again immediately after he left — and they were unable to bring him back “because of difficulties in international relations.”
The icon is now being kept at 80% humidity, although experts insist it should be stored at 50% to 55% humidity.
Ekho said Trinity was painted on three wooden panels. High humidity causes the panels to absorb moisture and swell, narrowing the gaps between them. This warps the icon, effectively “curling into a tube.”
Luchenko’s source said the leadership of the Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius “was afraid for some time to tell the Tretyakov Gallery after realizing that the icon was in bad shape.” Luchenko said the icon is now in the monastery’s restoration workshop.
Trinity was housed at the Tretyakov Gallery for nearly 100 years. Russian President Vladimir Putin transferred it to the Russian Orthodox Church by decree in the spring of 2023, after which it was taken to the Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius.
Art historians opposed the transfer from the outset, warning that improper storage conditions could damage or destroy the icon.

Unintentional mind wandering disrupts attention in ADHD through two different mechanisms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:00:36 UTC
03:00:36 KST

New research suggests that unintentionally losing focus, known as spontaneous mind wandering, predicts distinct aspects of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in adults. The findings indicate that both a general tendency to experience unintentional mind wandering and real-time performance drops during these episodes are linked to higher levels of inattentive and hyperactive traits. The study was published in Journal of Attention Disorders.
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsive behaviors that interfere with daily functioning. To understand how attention lapses happen, scientists often look at the default mode network. This is a network of brain regions that typically becomes active during rest or internal thought and tends to decrease in activity when a person engages in a demanding task requiring focus on the outside world.
Mind wandering occurs when a person’s attention shifts away from the task at hand and turns toward internal, unrelated thoughts. Historically, mind wandering was treated as a single concept, but recent evidence suggests it is multidimensional. Deliberate mind wandering is an intentional shift of thought, which can be adaptive for planning, recalling past experiences, or creative problem-solving. Spontaneous mind wandering is an intrusive, unintentional drift of thought that frequently disrupts a person’s ability to complete ongoing tasks.
The distinction between intentional and unintentional focus loss is a growing area of psychological research. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2016 demonstrated that people tend to engage in intentional mind wandering during easy tasks but experience higher levels of unintentional mind wandering during difficult tasks. Another study covered by PsyPost in 2016 proposed that spontaneous thought is linked to reduced activity in cognitive control networks. This provides a theoretical framework for viewing conditions like ADHD as natural extensions of standard variations in spontaneous thinking.
In addition, a 2026 study of adults with ADHD found that a subjective feeling that one’s attention has drifted off task, even without remembering the specific thoughts, is associated with poorer attention and lower well-being. This highlights the complex ways off-task thoughts interfere with daily life.
“Executive function deficits have long been considered a core mechanism underlying the symptoms of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), including inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity,” Takehiro Minamoto, an associate professor of psychology at Shimane University, told PsyPost. “However, emerging evidence suggests that spontaneous mind wandering, the unintentional intrusion of task-unrelated thoughts, may also play a critical role in ADHD symptomatology.”
“This raised an important question about how spontaneous mind wandering contributes to ADHD symptoms, prompting us to investigate the underlying mechanisms using methods developed in psychological research,” Minamoto explained. Building on this background, the research team sought to examine how intentional and unintentional mind wandering relate to ADHD symptoms by directly measuring people’s performance during these specific mental states.
The research team recruited 67 university students. Several days before the main experiment, the participants completed self-report questionnaires to measure their ADHD symptoms and their general tendencies to engage in both deliberate and spontaneous mind wandering in daily life. The participants also completed a working memory test to ensure general intellectual ability was accounted for and did not skew the results.
During a later session, the participants completed a modified counting Stroop task on a computer. In this test, participants saw groups of Japanese words that spelled out numbers, but the meaning of the word never matched the actual number of words shown on the screen. For example, the word “four” might be written two times. Participants had to press a keyboard key corresponding to the number of words, ignoring what the text actually said. The task was long and demanding, consisting of 1,152 trials. To prevent participants from guessing or falling into a physical rhythm, the correct response key changed on every single trial.
To track mind wandering, the researchers randomly paused the task 40 times. During these pauses, they presented a prompt asking participants to classify their attention at that exact moment. Participants could report being fully concentrated, engaging in deliberate mind wandering, experiencing spontaneous mind wandering, or dealing with other distractions.
Deliberate mind wandering was defined as thinking of a strategy or intentionally thinking about unrelated things without affecting performance. Spontaneous mind wandering was defined as unintentional thoughts that affected performance or the mind simply wandering off. Eight participants were excluded for various reasons, such as not reporting any mind wandering at all, leaving 59 participants in the final analysis.
The researchers found that participants engaged in deliberate mind wandering more frequently than spontaneous mind wandering. Despite being less frequent, spontaneous mind wandering had a much more negative impact on task performance. When participants reported spontaneous mind wandering, their accuracy was lower, their response times were slower, and their reaction times varied more wildly compared to periods when they reported deliberate mind wandering. The drop in accuracy during spontaneous mind wandering showed a moderate effect size, highlighting a distinct behavioral difference between intentional and unintentional attention shifts.
When looking at ADHD traits, the data indicated that two different measures of spontaneous mind wandering independently predicted higher ADHD symptom scores. First, participants who scored higher on the self-report scale for spontaneous mind wandering in daily life tended to have higher ADHD symptom scores. Second, participants who had poorer real-time accuracy specifically during spontaneous mind wandering episodes in the counting task also tended to have higher ADHD symptom scores. The deliberate mind wandering scale and accuracy during deliberate mind wandering did not predict ADHD scores at all.
Because the self-report scale and the real-time accuracy metric did not overlap in their predictive power, the authors propose that people with ADHD traits might suffer from two different types of interference. The self-report scale captures macroscopic interference, where individuals struggle generally in daily life because they are frequently distracted by unrelated thoughts. The task accuracy metric captures microscopic interference, meaning that when these individuals do experience a spontaneous thought, they have a much harder time coping with the immediate distraction and making the correct decision in the moment.
“Our findings suggest that spontaneous mind wandering may contribute to ADHD symptoms through at least two distinct mechanisms,” Minamoto noted. “One appears to reflect a persistent tendency for task-unrelated thoughts to interfere with attention and self-regulation, while the other reflects momentary disruptions in the ability to switch between mental states and maintain focus.”
“This highlights that attentional difficulties in ADHD may not arise from a single underlying process, but from multiple forms of cognitive interference that affect everyday functioning,” he added.
These results align with research covered by PsyPost in 2022, which found that mind wandering heavily disrupts attention and productivity in children with ADHD, though the new study specifically utilized adult self-reports and real-time cognitive testing rather than childhood classroom observations. The findings are also in line with a 2024 study covered by PsyPost indicating that excessive mind wandering is linked to ADHD symptoms in adults. It is worth noting that the earlier research focused on clinically diagnosed patients rather than a general student sample.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The sample consisted entirely of university students, none of whom had a formal clinical diagnosis of ADHD. While a portion of the participants scored high enough on the symptom scale to warrant clinical evaluation, the results might look different in a formally diagnosed population.
Additionally, the structure of the counting Stroop task required participants to use different fingers to press alternating keys. The physical distance between these keys varied randomly on the keyboard, which might have obscured deeper connections between mind wandering and the raw speed of response times. Future studies could use tasks with simpler motor requirements to better capture how reaction speeds relate to attention lapses. Because the study measured traits at a single point in time, it cannot determine whether spontaneous mind wandering directly causes ADHD symptoms or if the condition leads to a higher frequency of mind wandering.
“Our next step is to conduct further studies to confirm the two potential forms of interference associated with spontaneous mind wandering and to better understand their underlying neural mechanisms,” Minamoto said. “In the long term, we hope this line of research will inform the development of more targeted behavioral, cognitive, and pharmacological interventions to help alleviate the challenges experienced by people with ADHD.”
The study, “Behavioral and Self-Report Measures of Spontaneous Mind Wandering Predict Different Aspects of ADHD in Adults,” was authored by Takehiro Minamoto, Takuma Hayashi, and Md Abdullah Al-Mamun.

Ukraine's missile gap — Kyiv's struggle to close the ballistic divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
17:51:12 UTC
02:51:12 KST

Ukraine's missile gap — Kyiv's struggle to close the ballistic divide
Screenshot from a video showing a test launch of the FP-7 ballistic missile, published on Feb. 27, 2026. (Denys Shtilierman / X)
Incredibly fast and destructive, ballistic missiles have become a key feature of Russia's continuing long-range assault against Ukrainian cities. And while Kyiv has built world-leading drone technology, when it comes to producing ballistic missiles, a key capability in modern warfare, Ukraine still decisively lags behind Russia.
This could soon change, as Kyiv seeks to close the gap by mass-producing its own ballistic missiles, two of which are scheduled to enter service in the coming months.
Fire Point's new FP-7 short-range ballistic missile is due to enter service with the Ukrainian military within "weeks," with the longer-ranged FP-9 "currently undergoing flight tests," according to Fire Point's CEO, Iryna Terekh, speaking at a defense conference in Poland on Sept. 10.
"Ukraine’s new ballistic missiles could have a significant impact on the outcome of the war if they enter service in meaningful numbers," Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent.
A battle of ballistics
Hoffmann said a ballistic missiles would give Ukraine the ability to quickly launch devastating missile strikes against valuable, time-sensitive military targets, such as Russian ballistic missile launchers — a capability Ukraine currently lacks, though one it desperately needs.
Broadly speaking, ballistic missiles fly in high arcs at hypersonic speeds and only a handful of air defense systems can intercept them. Cruise missiles fly significantly slower and lower to the ground, and are generally easier to intercept.
Ukraine relies on American-made Patriot PAC-3 air defense systems to defend itself against ballistic missiles and a chronic shortage of Patriot interceptors has left cities highly vulnerable ahead of winter.
Russia currently produces the munitions at a rate of "about 120 ballistic missiles every month."
Russia currently produces the munitions at a rate of "about 120 ballistic missiles every month", Ukrainian President Zelensky told a NATO-Ukraine Council meeting in Kyiv on June 3, a tempo of production that allows for sustained and deadly missile barrages against Ukrainian cities.
Unfortunately for Ukraine, Russian production of ballistic missiles far outpaces Western production of Patriot ballistic missile interceptors — which Lockheed Martin currently produces at a rate of around 50 per month — let alone Ukraine's ability to acquire the costly and in-demand missiles.
When Russia’s full-scale invasion began in February 2022, Ukraine possessed around 500 OTR-21 Tochka short-range ballistic missiles for around 90 launchers, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), with no ability to produce more. These Soviet-legacy missiles were both limited by range of a maximum of 120 kilometers (75 miles) and were relatively inaccurate compared to modern precision weapons.
In comparison, Russia fielded 900 modern and longer-ranged Iskander-M ballistic missiles in February 2022, according to the IISS, along with significant numbers of Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles, 3M22 Zircon quasiballistic missiles, and a large number of S-300 and S-400 surface-to-air missiles with a secondary land attack role.
By ramping up domestic production, as well as by sourcing supplies of munitions from North Korea, Russia has been able to maintain a stockpile of ballistic missiles while routinely subjecting Ukrainian cities to mass barrages.
Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) assessed that by mid-2026, Russian stockpiles still held 130 Iskander ballistic missiles, 400 RM-48U ballistic missiles for the S-400 system, 120 Zircon quasiballistic missiles, 50 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles, and 50 North Korean ballistic missiles of various types.
In comparison, Ukraine currently has little to no serial domestic ballistic missile production. While President Zelensky claimed Ukraine had "begun using" the 1KR1 Sapsan short-range ballistic missile on Dec. 9, 2025, evidence of it entering widespread production has remained elusive. If the weapon system had indeed entered Ukrainian service, it did so in extremely small numbers.
read also
Limited supplies
With such limited domestic production, Ukraine has relied on foreign allies for an extremely limited supply of replacement ballistic missiles — the American-made ATACMS. Ukraine officially received its first consignment of these older American missiles in October 2023. Unofficial reports suggested Ukraine received between 40 to 50 of the missiles.
Upon arrival, Ukraine immediately put them to use. On Oct. 17, 2023, Ukraine used M39 ATACMS to strike two helicopter forward operating bases in occupied Luhansk and Berdyansk, destroying 14 Russian helicopters, according to a British Defence Intelligence assessment — including eight Ka-52 attack helicopters — approximately 11% of Russia's entire fleet of that type.
Ukraine had to use its small stockpile of ATACMS sparingly, as opportunities to replenish stocks were extremely limited. The most significant replenishment came in August 2026, when Ukraine signed an agreement to purchase 70 M39 ATACMS missiles from Turkey as part of a wider arms deal.
This reliance on external supply from often unreliable foreign partners has created a key strategic vulnerability Ukraine has sought to address with domestic ballistic missile production. As part of this, leading Ukrainian defense company Fire Point spent 150 million euros to construct a solid rocket fuel plant in Denmark to support the development of Ukraine's new FP-7 and FP-9 missiles.
Ukraine's ballistic hopefuls
Fire Point has become an important domestic defense manufacturer since its founding in 2022, manufacturing a series of highly effective long-range drones, yet corruption allegations and questions about the ultimate ownership of the company have accompanied its rise.
Despite the allegations, Fire Point's FP-1 long-range drone has become a key part of Ukraine's deep strike campaign, while the FP-2 medium-range drone — which sacrifices range for a larger warhead — has become a mainstay of Ukraine's increasingly successful mid-range strike campaign.
"The development of Ukraine's drone program has demonstrated that, with sufficient funding and prioritization, significant results can be achieved in the production of long-range weapons," Nazarii Barchuk, an analyst at the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, told the Kyiv Independent, while noting that "ballistic missiles are a more complex type of weapon to manufacture."
Barchuk believes the critical factor will be ensuring "adequate funding for the program," including investment from foreign partners, as well as the "preservation and expansion of component production chains."
Although Ukraine's various domestic long-range drone programs have matured into a successful capability that frequently inflicts severe damage on Russian military and economic infrastructure, they have been less able to deal with more mobile military targets. Russian forces have frequently mitigated the damage of Ukrainian drone raids against military airfields by flying valuable aircraft away from incoming slow-flying drones.
read also
A learning curve
Fire Point also manufactures the FP-5 Flamingo heavy cruise missile, and while the first few operational uses saw the missiles fall short of their intended targets, recent Flamingo launches have been far more successful. In June 2026, three of the large cruise missiles struck the Titan-Barrikady manufacturing plant in Volgograd, damaging the facility.
"The Flamingo was fairly inaccurate in the beginning," Hoffmann told the Kyiv Independent, explaining that Fire Point has since modified and upgraded its missile.
"The FP-5 Flamingo is now operationally more useful and I could see the same process taking place with the FP-7 and the FP-9," Hoffmann said.
The new FP-7 ballistic missile is designed with a claimed range of 200 kilometers (124 miles), a top speed of 1,500 meters per second (3,355 mph), and a 150-kilogram warhead. The missile is based on the Soviet-era 48N6 interceptor used in the S-300 and S-400 air defense systems, but uses modern components and manufacturing techniques.
"This will be an analog of ATACMS, probably even with a larger warhead. But it will cost at least twice as little," Denys Shtilerman, chief designer and co-founder of Fire Point, said in an interview in March. Shtilerman emphasized the goal was to produce the system en masse. "If you produce two or three ballistic missiles a month, it makes no sense. It will not affect the front," he said.
read also
Likely targets
"There will be different targets for each type of missile," Barchuk told the Kyiv Independent. "The FP-7 is designed for targets at the front line and in the immediate rear, such as headquarters and command posts, weapons storage facilities, military equipment (radar stations, electronic warfare systems, air defense systems, and missile launchers), drone launch sites and military infrastructure, including airfields within the missile’s range," he said.
The larger and more complex FP-9 is due to enter service "by the end of the year," according to Terekh.
The FP-9 is a significantly larger, faster, and longer-ranged missile, with a range of 855 kilometers (531 miles), a top speed of 2,200 meters per second (4,920 mph), and the ability to carry an 800-kilogram warhead.
Besides enabling strikes on a huge number of military facilities and important industrial sites, the missile also puts Moscow, as well as other Russian cities, within range.
"If Ukraine is able to mass produce around 50 FP-9 missiles per month, and if they're reasonably accurate so they can go after high-value military assets, as well as larger infrastructure targets, then it's going to get much more uncomfortable for the Russians," Hoffmann told the Kyiv Independent. "That would be really significant, I would say, but we have to get there first."
"The FP-9 has a longer range and a larger warhead," Barchuk said. "This missile is intended to strike targets deep in the rear, specifically on Russian territory. Their targets may vary, but priority is likely to be given to military-industrial facilities, protected weapons arsenals, critical communications nodes (including satellite communications), military installations and airfields from which Russian tactical aircraft take off to carry out strikes against Ukraine," he said.
The successful introduction of the FP-9 could be a significant upgrade of Ukraine's capabilities, Hoffmann said. "Within minutes you could strike, 600, 700, 800 kilometers deep into Russia, which could make ballistic missile launcher hunting or air defense suppression and destruction a lot more successful."

Nearly 100,000 displaced in Sudan’s Blue Nile state since January amid fighting: UN agency
Unknown

Adel Abdelrheem and Mohammad Sio

Nearly 100,000 people have been displaced in Sudan’s southeastern Blue Nile state since January amid escalating fighting between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the UN International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Sunday.
The IOM said an estimated 99,277 people, representing 19,497 families, were displaced from different parts of Blue Nile state between Jan. 11 and Aug. 23, 2026.
The figure represents a 66% increase from the agency’s previous update on May 21, when 59,742 displaced people were recorded.
Nearly half of those displaced, or 47%, are children under the age of 18, the agency said.
The IOM said 39,570 people were displaced from Geissan locality, 32,515 from Kurmuk and 27,192 from Bau.
The displaced population moved to seven locations across Blue Nile state, including Damazin, which received 45,740 people, and Geissan, which received 15,735.
The agency said 58% of the displaced are staying at informal gathering sites, while 9% are living with host families and 33% are sheltering in schools and other public buildings.
Blue Nile state has seen intensified fighting in recent days amid attacks by the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, on several areas.
Sudan’s humanitarian crisis has continued to worsen since fighting erupted between the army and the RSF in April 2023 over disagreements related to the integration of the paramilitary force into the military.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

‘Escalation is becoming a fact’: Tusk says Russia may target Ukrainian border crossings after drones hit a Kyiv–Warsaw train and nearby gas station

Polish PM warns of possibility of more serious Russian attacks in Poland
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said the coming weeks and months will see very intense Russian activity and that more serious attacks on Polish territory cannot be ruled out.
Source: RMF24, citing Tusk at a meeting at the Government Centre for Security, as reported by European Pravda
Details: At 17:00, Tusk began a meeting at the Government Centre for Security headquarters with the interior and defence ministers and the heads of the individual services. The meeting follows Russian attacks in the immediate vicinity of Poland on the night of 12-13 September and on the morning of 13 September.
Tusk noted that "the escalation of Russia's actions is becoming a fact, and its manifestations are increasingly approaching our border".
"An attempt to paralyse border crossings is not the first such incident," the prime minister said.
"We must be aware that from today we will be operating in a significantly heightened mode. Because we know, and can also expect, that the coming weeks and months will be a period of very intense Russian activity. Unfortunately, we cannot rule out that the escalation will also affect our territory," Tusk said.
He said he hopes that the worst-case scenario would not materialise. "Unfortunately, the events that have occurred so far confirm the information we have been receiving for many months: that more serious scenarios are also possible," he added.
Tusk stressed that he does not want to give in to the tense atmosphere, but said there is no doubt that "we must be ready for a joint response if the need arises".
"The attacks this night demonstrate that the Russians are willing to use more dangerous technology than before. I mean jet-powered drones. Their range and accuracy are concerning. Of course, even Ukraine, which is very well-prepared to defend against drones, is unable to counter them 100% effectively, to put it mildly," the prime minister noted.
Deputy Defence Minister Cezary Tomczyk said that 13 strikes were recorded during Russia's drone attack on Ukraine's west on 13 September.
"So we must be aware that Russia has such capabilities. Therefore, I will also expect information on how prepared we are for the possible use of drones and related attempts to disrupt our work – whether on the railways or at businesses. I do not rule out similar situations occurring here as well," the prime minister said.
Background:
- Dariusz Sinecki, spokesperson for the Nadbużański Border Guard Unit in Poland, said that a drone hit a lorry near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing on the night of 12-13 September.
- Earlier, Andrii Demchenko, spokesperson for Ukraine's State Border Guard Service, said that the Yahodyn border crossing itself on the border with Poland had not been hit.

UN Security Council Resolution 1244 of June 10, 1999 recognizes the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija is part of Serbia. It also authorized international civilian and military presence in the province. However, Kosovo’s authorities unilaterally proclaimed its independence in February 2008. Sixteen world nations, including Russia, India, and China, as well as five European Union countries, are refusing to recognize Kosovo’s independence.

French must come first, far-right leader Marine Le Pen says at presidential campaign launch
HENIN-BEAUMONT, France - Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, a frontrunner in the French presidency race, signalled on Sept 13 that she would favour French citizens over foreigners, defending her long-held principle of “national priority”.
Speaking seven months before France’s presidential polls, Le Pen, 58, said that under her presidency French people would “have priority in their own country”, regardless of their skin colour, religion, or origin.
“We will guarantee all French citizens a natural and fair right, as is done in every country in the world,” she said in the first major campaign speech of her fourth presidential bid, speaking in the northern town of Henin-Beaumont, the far-right’s stronghold.
French nationals would enjoy “more rights in France than others,” Le Pen said to around 2,000 supporters, with Jordan Bardella, head of her far-right National Rally party, seated in the front row.
Le Pen has her best-ever chance in 2027 to win the Elysee, with polls showing her well ahead in a first round of voting and posing at least a major threat to any rival in the second round.
The policy of “national priority” would apply to housing, Le Pen said, adding that French citizens should receive preferential access to social housing.
One of her priorities would be to increase housing supply, Le Pen said, adding that she wanted various environmental regulations scrapped.
“There is nothing, my friends, more rewarding than the feeling of harmony in one’s home and being able to say: ‘I am at home’,” she said.
“This presidential election will decide everything: either we allow our country to sink deeper into the quicksand of old habits and wrongdoing, or we choose the surge of renewal that we want and that will lead to France’s rebirth,” she added.
The far-right leader did not address a series of controversies that have dogged her party in recent weeks, including claims of policy differences with 31-year-old Bardella, Le Pen’s choice for prime minister in the event of victory.
Le Pen is running despite an appeals court in July upholding a graft conviction, a verdict she is seeking to overturn with the country’s highest court. AFP

The new strategic power of the Resistance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
17:26:08 UTC
02:26:08 KST

The new strategic power of the Resistance
Kayhan, in a note discussing recent developments in the Middle East, argues that a new strategic power structure has emerged within the Resistance axis. This new power is the result of several interconnected factors: Iran’s ability to overcome and outmaneuver the United States, Israel, and their regional allies, Yemen’s offensive military capabilities, and the steadfastness of Lebanon and Palestine.
These elements have combined to create a coherent and consolidated strategic force that has “broken through all barriers” and established a new regional equation stretching from the Mediterranean Sea to the Indian Ocean. This new equation has taken shape over nearly three decades of conflict, and despite the severity of ongoing events, it is now entering a phase of final stabilization. When, in the midst of Yemen’s successful operations and Iran’s repeated strikes, certain Arab governments ask Iran to reduce tensions with the United States, Israel, and themselves, it reveals that all previous options against the Resistance have become obsolete. The current moment is one of consolidating the Resistance’s major achievements, and that such consolidation requires a cleansing of the region, meaning the removal of destabilizing or hostile elements.
Sobh-e-No: BRICS; from potential cooperation to operational implementation
Sobh-e-No analyzed President Pezeshkian’s trip to New Delhi for the BRICS summit. The visit has two main dimensions. First, bilateral relations between Iran and India. The meeting between Pezeshkian and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted the importance of Tehran–New Delhi ties. Both sides emphasized expanding cooperation and continuing strategic agreements. Second, turning BRICS cooperation into practical mechanisms. Tehran’s focus during this trip was on ensuring that BRICS membership does not remain at the level of political dialogue. Instead, Iran wants BRICS capacities to be transformed into operational frameworks in areas such as trade, financial systems, use of national currencies, and broader economic cooperation. The simultaneous presence of both leaders at the BRICS summit created an opportunity to pursue bilateral and multilateral diplomacy at the same time.
Javan: The Strait of Hormuz will not be reopened
Javan discussed the recent understanding reached between Tehran and Muscat, with Persian Gulf foreign ministers present. According to the paper, the agreement is strictly technical, concerning the details of new entry and exit routes in the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman. Other Persian Gulf states are attending the meeting only to signal their implicit non‑objection to the international community. Javan emphasizes that this understanding does not mean the Strait of Hormuz will reopen. Iran has delivered seven conditions to the United States through intermediaries. These conditions have been approved by Iran’s highest authorities, and until they are fully implemented, the strait will remain closed. Thus, the Iran–Oman agreement does not signify reopening; rather, it establishes that if the strait is eventually reopened, it will be done under this specific framework, which the paper describes as a major step in asserting Iran’s sovereignty. Any reopening depends entirely on US compliance with Iran’s conditions.
Ham‑Mihan: Why has Iran’s nuclear file returned to the UN Security Council?
Ham‑Mihan explains that Western governments are trying to move Iran’s nuclear issue from the IAEA Board of Governors back to the UN Security Council to create a “two‑track process.” Track One is the JCPOA & Snapback Mechanism. This track is based on alleged Iranian violations of the JCPOA. However, China and Russia opposed this path in the Security Council, preventing it from gaining full legal legitimacy. Track Two is Safeguards Non‑Compliance Referral. This new track focuses on alleged Iranian non‑compliance with its IAEA safeguards agreement. The key difference of the second track is that because in the Board of Governors, there is no veto, so a resolution can be passed and the case referred to the Security Council. Once referred, China and Russia cannot easily dismiss the IAEA’s findings and will face a more difficult diplomatic position. Ham‑Mihan argues that the Western goal is for these two tracks to reinforce each other, increasing pressure on Iran.
Farhikhtegan: Dynamite in the oil market
Farhikhtegan analyzed the reasons behind the surge in oil prices above $100 per barrel. The paper says that although analysts cite various factors, they all agree on one central issue: geopolitical developments in Yemen and around the Bab al‑Mandab Strait. Energy experts argue that the main issue is not just reduced supply but the shrinking security margin of the global oil market. Key factors include: ongoing restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz, increased control by Yemen’s Ansarallah around Bab al‑Mandab, reduced Russian supply and refining capacity, declining global inventories, and changes in China’s oil purchasing patterns. However, the $109 price recorded on Thursday night was clearly the result of Ansarallah’s dramatic and rapid territorial advances, which sharply intensified geopolitical risk and pushed prices beyond the $100 threshold.

The arithmetic of US decline
TEHRAN — The myth of American military omnipotence is dying not on a grand battlefield but in the quiet statistics of empty warehouses and the weary eyes of exhausted sailors. The United States projects an image of infinite power, yet closer inspection reveals a superpower suffocating under the weight of its own hubris. The numbers are devastating. The strategic calculus is broken. For the Islamic Republic, the path to regional dominance is now paved with the debris of American logistical failures.
Consider the missile arsenal. Before the current conflicts, Washington boasted roughly 2,300 Patriot Advanced Capability interceptors. Today, CSIS puts the remaining stock at about one third. America is down to its last 36 percent of Patriot missiles, a reality forcing its allies to the back of the line. The Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system functions at barely half capacity, with stockpiles between 52 and 62 percent. The Precision Strike Missile, hyped as the future of American long-range fires, is effectively nonexistent, with stocks down to 10 to 22 percent.
This is not a supply chain hiccup but an industrial failure of epic proportions. Even the Tomahawk cruise missile holds at roughly two thirds of its prewar stockpile. That scarcity explains why Japan’s order for 400 missiles has been delayed and why the acting Navy secretary confirmed a freeze on sales to Taiwan. Representative Michael McCaul, who signs off on foreign arms sales, admitted that when Washington cannot deliver, it hurts alliances because the promise cannot be kept. But admission does not solve the arithmetic. If American defense industry can produce 600 interceptors a year, rebuilding the pile takes four years, assuming no one fires another shot. Wars do not pause for factory schedules.
The math against current reality is fatal. In a single night, during a single strike on a single base, Jordanian forces reportedly fired enough interceptors to stop 18 of 20 incoming missiles. That was one base on one night in a war where Iran has already launched more than 1,500 ballistic missiles. The consumption rate renders American stockpiles useless within weeks. Pentagon planners know this. They are trapped in a cycle of depletion that their economic base cannot sustain. The United States cannot outproduce the resolve of the Axis of Resistance.
While arsenals dwindle, the human machinery of empire is grinding to a halt. For months, the Pentagon paraded the USS Abraham Lincoln as the crowning jewel of American might. Yet the carrier’s recent deployment told a story of exhaustion. After 286 consecutive days at sea, a record the Western press breathlessly celebrated, the Lincoln limped into Pattaya, Thailand, for what was essentially a morale rescue. Five thousand sailors and Marines disembarked into a port where Thai authorities braced for incidents involving American personnel. When American families and even their own lawmakers raise concerns about deployment lengths, it reveals a military machine running on fumes. The stopover was not a victory lap but an admission of human limitation.
The United States can project force, but it cannot project endurance. The Lincoln’s extended deployment consumed fuel, parts, and psychological resilience that America cannot indefinitely replenish. When a carrier strike group’s port call becomes a liability rather than a strategic maneuver, the empire is running on empty.
The deepest humiliation came beneath the waves. The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps executed a flawless operation near the Strait of Hormuz, capturing an intact American unmanned underwater vehicle, the Anduril Dive LD. This is not scrap metal. The Dive LD is a sophisticated autonomous system, measuring nearly six meters, capable of operating for 10 days at depths of 6,000 meters. Its modular design allows intelligence gathering, mine warfare, and seabed mapping. Now it sits in Iranian hands, a treasure trove of physical architecture, sensor arrays, and propulsion secrets.
Washington pretends reverse engineering is impossible, but they know better. Even partial analysis of this machine gives the Islamic Republic an unprecedented window into American autonomous warfare. The United States sent its most sophisticated underwater spy into waters Iran has studied and dominated for decades. The spy came home in an Iranian net. That is the bitter truth of asymmetric warfare: every tool of aggression becomes a source of intelligence when captured intact. The humiliation is not that American technology failed. It is that technological superiority cannot guarantee strategic success.
Geography remains the eternal enemy of empire. The Strait of Hormuz sits beside Iranian territory, a chokepoint we control with layered defenses of missiles, drones, mines, and coastal artillery. America may possess global reach, but reach is not control. The United States cannot sustain its presence against Iranian resistance. The carrier exposes the burden of endurance. The captured drone exposes the vulnerability of technology. The empty missile warehouses expose the bankruptcy of strategy. For Washington, the lesson is inescapable: global military reach is not unlimited power. In today’s security environment, especially in the Persian Gulf, outcomes depend on what a military can sustain, protect, and convert into durable political results.
The United States is a paper tiger, capable of impressive parades but unable to translate technological superiority into strategic victory. Each round of this conflict leaves Iran stronger, holding the chokepoints, absorbing the technology of its enemies, and watching the American war machine suffocate on its own logistics. The superpower is bleeding out, not from a single blow, but from a thousand cuts delivered by geography, economics, and the unyielding will of a determined nation. The math is done. Washington has lost.
The question is no longer whether Washington can project power into the region. It can. The question is whether it can sustain that power long enough to impose its will. That is the question Iran has forced America to answer and the answer is becoming increasingly uncomfortable.
Washington still has the missiles, the carriers and the money. But it is discovering that none of them guarantees endurance. Iran has turned geography into a weapon, time into an advantage and American consumption into a strategic vulnerability. That is the real arithmetic of decline: Washington has the arsenal, but Tehran holds the map.

Is Israel winning?
MADRID — Israel finds itself in a situation entirely different from the one it occupied before October 7, 2023. Its strategic calculations, regional projection, and capacity to impose its political will are being strongly questioned, and nothing suggests this will be reversed in the future.
First, it must be clear that Israel does not have a foreign policy in any conventional sense; it has only a security-driven policy. That is, its entire policy serves almost exclusively to guarantee its own security. This has been so since the very moment of Israel's founding, precisely because of the manner in which it was carried out.
Israel was born as a settler-colonial state in Palestine and, therefore, cannot erase that inaugural violence. Nor can it forget that colonial violence permanently haunts the colonial occupier until the end of its days. From this arises Israel's security imperative: an attempt to secure regional domination through expansion and territorial control, giving it guarantees no colonial settlement has ever enjoyed.
The regional military domination that takes shape after 1967, always with the explicit support of the United States, is the materialization of that very strategy.
Since 1967, Israel has not suffered any serious threat to its colonial sovereignty. This includes what occurred in 1973, when Egypt attacked Israeli troops to recover the Sinai Peninsula. Despite the war, Egypt's principal objective was not to destroy Israel or liberate the Palestinians; it was simply to recover territory occupied by the colonial state in one of its multiple territorial expansions.
All of this changed on October 7. With the Hamas attack, the first major crisis since 1967, the Israeli colonial state set in motion two distinct strategies. One was directed at the Palestinians, consisting of unleashing a genocide to eliminate the native population; the other had a regional vocation. The latter sought to create a unipolar region where Israel would be the undisputed central pole, with a "domesticated" Iran — through regime change or civil war — and Arab countries completely aligned with its project. Furthermore, Israel continued counting on absolute United States support at all levels — political, economic, diplomatic — because Israel functions as a domestic issue in American politics, not a mere foreign policy matter.
The genocide had a clear worldwide repercussion. More and more countries see Israel as a pariah state, similar to apartheid South Africa, completely delegitimized. It is true that United States protection prevented economic sanctions, but that protection could not shape the perception the colonial state currently holds among Americans themselves. A poll published last week caused commotion in much of the United States foreign policy establishment that follows the Middle East closely. The poll showed that 60% of American adults hold an unfavorable opinion of Israel. In both political parties, more than half of people under 50 evaluate Israel negatively. Although this trend had already become evident in recent years, an additional marked deterioration of support for Israel among Americans across the political spectrum is now observable.
The additional data paint an even more concerning picture. The general downward trend conceals a collapse in Israel's valuation among younger Americans, even among groups many in Israel consider reliable bastions of support.
The war against Iran confirmed Israel's worst strategic nightmares. Despite the assassination of senior military officials and Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, Iran did not collapse — precisely what the Israelis had expected.
They assured Trump that three or four days of bombing would bring down the Islamic Republic. They expected either regime change or civil war — surely Tel Aviv's preferred option. But that did not happen. The institutions survived and went on the offensive. Iranian missiles repeatedly penetrated Israel's celebrated air defense system, reaching the heart of Israel and targets across the country, paralyzing it and causing unprecedented casualties plus massive destruction. This, together with the failure to achieve any objectives, constituted another victory for Iran.
The missiles reached their targets; Iran's image was not tarnished, most of the world saw it as a victim of an Israeli and American attack, and Iran's options for responding were not limited.
Beyond its military defeat, Israel faces a regional political reconfiguration different from the one it designed just a few years ago. The clearest example is the current posture of the Persian Gulf monarchies toward the so-called Abraham Accords. The strategic objective was for the two pillars of American policy in the region — the Arab countries and Israel — to come together in a single bloc against a common enemy: Iran.
Saudi Arabia, the most coveted piece, stepped back from normalization with Israel, and not only that. The war against Iran, and Iran's subsequent response against American bases in the region, exposed the weakness of the protection Washington had deployed to safeguard its allies. This explains the security pact among Saudis, Turks, and Pakistanis.
Israel's attempt to rewrite the regional balance by defeating or weakening Iran has failed. Israel depends even more on the United States; the Abraham Accords are dead, Hezbollah remains, and Iran was not defeated; instead, it has become a force setting the tone in the region. The Persian Gulf countries have recognized that their alliance with the United States and their possible agreements with Israel expose them to greater risks than those they seek protection from.

Rescuers in Indonesia said at least six people were killed and 129 others were missing after a ferry capsized in rough seas on Sunday, with one survivor recounting scenes of panic as passengers scrambled for life jackets.
The Virgo Transport 8 -- which authorities said carried 213 passengers and 30 crew -- lost contact with its shipping company early Sunday after departing from Surabaya in East Java.
Basarnas, Indonesia's national search and rescue agency, said six people were killed and 129 others were missing.
Another 108 people were rescued.
"People were panicking. Some climbed onto tables, some were pushing each other," survivor Rinto Arahap, 33, told AFP.
He said many passengers were asleep when the vessel began listing at around 2:00 am on Sunday (1800 GMT Saturday), adding that he heard what sounded like metal breaking about five hours into the journey.
With waves more than two metres (6.6 feet) high, people began shouting and fighting for life jackets as the vessel tilted, Arahap said.
"There was no warning from the ship's crew. Basically, it was just someone taking the initiative, shouting, 'Oh, the ship is listing, listing, listing,'" he said from a stretcher at a health facility in Banjarmasin, where survivors were taken.
'Didn't save anything'
The first rescue ship carrying survivors arrived before nightfall at a pier in Banjarmasin, on the southern coast of Borneo island. Some of the survivors were carried on stretchers into waiting ambulances. Others were put into wheelchairs or needed help walking.
Indonesian Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said the ship had capsized.
Local search and rescue chief I Putu Sudayana earlier told AFP that the ship's captain had reported to its owners before losing contact that the vessel was "tilting".
Rescuers battled waves of up to 2.5 metres to reach the ferry, Sudayana told reporters. Two helicopters were involved in the search, as well as other vessels from the navy, police, the rescue agency and the ferry company.
The vessel's last position had been detected in the Java Sea, around 150 kilometres (93 miles) from its destination.
Heri Purwanto, head of Banjarmasin Sea Port Authority, said the ship lost contact at 2:00 am. "We responded quickly to the incident report," he said.
Arahap told AFP he grabbed a life jacket before the ship overturned, saying he and others were adrift for about four hours before they were rescued.
"I didn't save anything, just myself," said Arahap, who was travelling to Samarinda in East Kalimantan to start work on a palm oil plantation. My wallet, everything... was lost. Things like my school diploma were gone. All my clothes were swept away."
'Very shocked'
Rescue authorities have established a command centre at the Banjarmasin port, with paramedics and ambulances on standby, an AFP reporter saw.
Dozens of relatives and friends of the passengers checked a whiteboard where the names of people rescued were being updated.
Jenah, 26, told AFP she came to the command post for information about her older brother.
"I am saddened and very shocked. Until now, I haven't received any more information," said Jenah, who like many Indonesians has only one name.
"He was travelling alone. I hope he survives. I couldn't contact him since last night."
Marine accidents are a regular occurrence in Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands that relies heavily on boat connections for daily transport and tourism.
