The baby who lost his mother in an enemy strike on the capital celebrated his first birthday
Kyiv • UNN
Little Nazar was born by emergency C-section after his mother was injured in a Shahed drone strike.
Nazarчик, whose parents came under Russian shelling in Kyiv in September 2025, celebrated his first birthday, UNN writes, citing the capital's Perinatal Center, where the baby was born.
On September 7, 2025, an enemy "Shahed" struck a building, and both of Nazarчик's parents — Vadym and Tetiana — were injured.
Tetiana was 34 weeks pregnant. As a result of the enemy strike, she suffered blast trauma, burns covering almost the entire surface of her body, burns to her respiratory tract, and was in a state of shock.
Doctors decided to perform an emergency cesarean section. That was how Nazarчик was born.
Unfortunately, several weeks later, the baby's mother died from the injuries she had sustained, while the infant himself remained in extremely serious condition.
Hanna Antoniuk, Deputy Medical Director of the Municipal Nonprofit Enterprise "Perinatal Center of Kyiv," said: "This is a child who was born amid severe stress. His mother suffered burns, and the child, given his condition, was not ready to be born."
The infant spent a month and a half in intensive care on a ventilator. Nazarчик underwent four brain surgeries, and a shunt system was installed.
Only in November was he transferred to a regular ward, and in December 2025 he was discharged.
The boy was taken in by his paternal aunt, Oksana, his father's sister, who lives in Ivano-Frankivsk with her husband and son.
"So little, but so strong. What he has achieved this year is simply incredible. Thank you for being with us, Nazarчик. There is only light ahead," the boy's aunt wrote.

CCP and China becoming one and the same: experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:42:25 UTC
01:42:25 KST

The Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) tighter control has made it difficult to separate China from the party, a former Taiwanese defense academic said on Saturday, urging the public to recognize their growing overlap.
Former Fu Hsing Kang College at National Defense University dean Yu Tsung-Chi (余宗基) made the remarks at a forum in Taipei titled “Anti-Communism 2.0: Rethinking Communism in the 21st Century — Completely Eradicating Communism” hosted by the Formosa Republican Association.
Yu said that in the 1958 book The Naked Communist, W. Cleon Skousen wrote that people can persuade Chinese to change China if they distinguish the country from the CCP. A similar belief was also held by US officials during the first term of US President Donald Trump, Yu added.
Photo: Hsu Yung-ching, Taipei Times
However, with the advancement in technology and CCP enforcing stricter domestic control by enacting Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law and revising the National Defense Education Law, the party effectively makes the country one where nearly everyone is mobilized for national defense, Yu said.
Any hope of dividing and sabotaging Chinese nationalism is an illusion, he said.
“We should gradually equate China with CCP,” Yu said. “Rather than hoping for change to happen with the CCP, we should be prepared for war by building the capacity and resolve to deter China.”
Political commentator Chin Heng-wei (金恆煒), who also attended the forum, similarly refuted the argument that CCP is not China.
China has never experienced democracy, and even if the CCP and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) were to fall, any new force that emerged would be unlikely to steer the country toward democracy, as “power corrupts, and power breeds authoritarianism,” he said.
Taiwanese human rights activist Lee Ming-che (李明哲), who was imprisoned in China for five years after being convicted of “subverting state power,” was in the audience at the forum. He said that democratization in China does not guarantee Taiwan’s safety.
“Taiwan is not obligated to support China’s transition to democracy. China under the communists’ rule still considers taking Taiwan by force. If China becomes a democratic country, people there could organize a referendum on whether China should overtake Taiwan by force,” Lee said.
Seasoned journalist and Taipei Times adviser Sean Lu (盧世祥) told the forum that the US’ National Security Strategy released last year shows that Washington has come to recognize the nature of China and no longer believes Beijing can be integrated into the rules-based international order.
Taiwan should avoid repeating the mistakes of its “boldly going west” policy that advocated for unfettered investment in China, he said, adding that China’s economy has already fallen into deflation.
Escaping deflation is no easy task, Lu said, adding that China also faces challenges including the middle-income trap and the disappearance of its demographic dividend.
Lu added that this does not mean opposing any exchanges between Taiwan and China, but Taiwan should instead focus on its role in global supply chains and deepen its connections with the rest of the world, he said.
Meanwhile, Yu said that during the US’ 250th anniversary celebrations, Trump devoted 12 minutes of a 30-minute speech in July to discussing the threat posed by communism. Yu quoted Trump as warning that communism was making a comeback and threatening the US, and that it had not only deepened divisions within US society but posed a threat greater than those of World War I and World War II combined.
Yu also cited Taiwan’s national security agencies as saying that nearly 40 schools in Taiwan have “communist groups” on campus. This underscored the need to speak out and remind the public of the threat posed by communism, he said.
Taiwan must not allow communism to threaten the country, he added.
Yu went said that more than 2 million Taiwanese traveled in China during the first six months of this year, showing that many have dropped their guard against communism.
“The extent of the harm we suffer would depend on the degree of our ignorance,” he said, adding that politics should be listed as a required course, in which communism should be listed as a key subject on the curriculum. He said Taiwan should also follow the international trend of tightening laws and impose harsher penalties for assisting China’s transnational repression, as the threat facing Taiwan is inevitably more serious than that faced by other countries.

Mastro said she was impressed by Taiwan’s increased defense spending, emphasis on asymmetric capabilities and efforts to prepare society for conflict, but questioned whom those initiatives were influencing. China seeks leverage before US summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:42:22 UTC
01:42:22 KST

Recent Chinese diplomatic and military moves are aimed at creating pressure ahead of a planned meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) and US President Donald Trump, National Security Council adviser Huang Chung-yen (黃重諺) said.
Trump when visiting China in May extended an invitation to Xi to visit Washington on Sept. 24.
China is yet to officially announce plans for Xi’s visit to the US.
Photo: Bloomberg
In an interview with the Liberty Times (sister paper of the Taipei Times) on Thursday, Huang said Xi’s overseas visits, China’s “gray zone” activities along the First Island Chain and efforts to expand its trade surplus with the US through low-priced exports are intended to create “final pressure” ahead of the meeting.
The moves are aimed at securing leverage in negotiations abroad while creating the impression at home that China is doing well despite its economic downturn, Huang said.
Xi began a series of overseas visits late last month, including attending a Shanghai Cooperation Organization meeting in Kyrgyzstan, where he met Russian President Vladimir Putin, visiting Egypt, the first country to join the Belt and Road Initiative, and attending the BRICS summit in India, Huang said.
China has also stepped up “gray zone” incursions in the East China Sea, South China Sea and waters around Taiwan, particularly in Taiwan’s eastern waters and waters near Japan and the Philippines, using increased geopolitical pressure as a bargaining chip, he said.
Economically, China’s overcapacity and low-priced exports have spilled over into G20 and other countries. Beijing is seeking to use its growing trade surplus with the US as leverage to negotiate increased purchases, Huang said.
The issues are growing concerns for other countries, which must protect domestic industries from low-priced Chinese exports and address geopolitical pressure from Beijing.
The US must protect its trade interests while ensuring regional security, he said.
Regarding a possible US-China dialogue on artificial intelligence (AI) security before the summit, Huang said AI encompasses computing capacity, energy infrastructure, chips and semiconductors, and downstream applications, making it extremely resource intensive.
Countries must establish security safeguards while maintaining technological competition, preventing authoritarian countries from gaining control of critical technologies, he said.
Huang said that during the administrations of former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) and President William Lai (賴清德), Taiwan’s core objective has been to remain “indispensable” to the geopolitical landscape and global supply chains.
Taiwan’s indispensability is also reflected in the US National Security Strategy and National Defense Strategy, which establish Taiwan as a core element of security along the First Island Chain and in global supply chains, Huang said.
Separately, regarding a Kyodo News report on Saturday saying that China has asked the US not to approve new arms sales to Taiwan before the summit and that Xi could consider canceling his visit if Washington approves such sales, Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗), an assistant professor at the University of Taipei’s Center for General Education, said yesterday that even an agreement between the US and China would be unlikely to alter their strategic competition.
The meeting would involve negotiations over major strategic interests, and Taiwan must understand how Washington and Beijing handle the Taiwan issue to prevent its interests from being affected by their negotiations, Hung said.
If the two sides reach partial agreements, the key question would be whether US-China relations enter a period of short-term easing or merely adjust the way they compete, he said.
The outcome would affect security in the Taiwan Strait, the US-Japan alliance and the broader Indo-Pacific region’s security framework, Hung said.

BOOKMAN BILINGUAL 雙語書林 Chinglish or Natural English? 中式英語或道地英語？
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:42:18 UTC
01:42:18 KST

1. 他太太勸他戒酒，但沒有成功。
ˇ His wife advised him to give up drinking, but in vain.
ˇ His wife tried to persuade him to give up drinking, but in vain.
Photo: AdobeStock l 照片：AdobeStock
χ His wife persuaded him to give up drinking, but in vain.
註︰persuade 是「說服」，沒有說服成功，就不能用 persuade，應用 advise 或 try to persuade，錯句中上下文顯然有矛盾。
2. 他們難道不準備在會議上說些什麼嗎？
ˇ Aren’t they planning to say something at the meeting?
χ Aren’t they planning to speak something at the meeting?
註︰speak 指「講」的發聲；say 指「講」的達意。孩子牙牙學語，可以說 The baby is learning to speak, but he is unable to say anything.。啞巴不能 speak，而瘋子能 speak，但不能 say anything sensible。可以說 speak English ( / Chinese / the Shanghai dialect / a foreign language), speak at the meeting, speak to/with someone, speak about / of something, speak on some subject；不可以說 *speak something，應說 say something（或nothing）。
3. 我寫那篇報告只花一個鐘頭。
ˇ I only spent one hour writing the report.
ˇ It only took me one hour to write the report.
ˇ Writing the report only took me one hour.
χ I only took one hour writing the report.
註︰「用掉了多少時間」，如主詞是人，用 spend... ＋ 動名詞，但如果主詞是事物，則必須用 take... ＋ 不定詞，而不用 spend。
4. 醫生將在三點給他動手術。
ˇ The doctor will perform the operation on him at three o’clock.
χ The doctor will make an operation on him at three o’clock.
註︰「動手術」是 to perform an operation 或 to operate，不說 *to make an operation 或 *to do an operation。「為某人動手術治療某種疾病」，應說 perform an operation on someone for some disease。
5. 我說服她改變主意。
ˇ I persuaded her to change her mind.
χ I convinced her to change her mind.
註︰convince 是「使（人）信服」，即 make one believe；persuade 的第一意義等於 convince，第二意義是「說服（人）」、「勸服（人）」，即 make one act。要使別人有所行動，往往要先使他信服。例如：
We convinced (/persuaded) him that we were right and he was wrong.
We convinced him that it was his duty and persuaded him to do it at once.
Exercises
A. 我花了半個月的時間才使他相信天然飲食有助於他康復。
It took me half a month to __________ him that a natural diet can help him recover from his illness.
1. convince 2. persuading 3. advise 4. suggest
B. 我能佔用你幾分鐘嗎？我有一些話要對你說。
Could you spare me a few minutes? I have something to __________ to you.
1. say 2. speak 3. tell 4. declare
Answers: A. 1 B. 1
文章由書林出版公司提供：
www.bookman.com.tw
蘇正隆 — 台灣翻譯學學會前理事長、師大翻譯研究所兼任副教授; 編著《走讀自然.花言樹語》，《英語的對與錯》，《世紀病毒：必讀防疫英文知識與詞彙》...等。國家教育研究院中英雙語詞彙審議委員；研究領域為翻譯、術語及詞典編譯，從事植物與人文導覽數十年，亦曾應邀遠赴國外大學做植物人文導覽。
“OK.” You say it dozens of times a day without giving it a second thought. It slips effortlessly into text messages, office meetings and casual chats alike. Yet behind this surprisingly simple expression lies one of the most entertaining origin stories in the history of language. The story begins in 1839, when a craze for creative abbreviations had swept through New England’s educated classes. Editors at the Boston Morning Post led the trend, though nearly all their inventions faded within months. One, however, proved far more enduring. On March 23, editor Charles Gordon Greene coined “OK” as a humorous abbreviation for

Unknown Publisher

State-owned oil supplier CPC Corp, Taiwan (CPC, 台灣中油) on Saturday announced that it would raise domestic gasoline prices by NT$0.7 (US$0.02) per liter and diesel prices by NT$0.6 per liter this week after international crude oil prices rose above US$100 per barrel last week.
Formosa Petrochemical Corp (台塑石化) yesterday said that it matched CPC’s price adjustments for this week.
The decisions end a six-week period during which CPC and Formosa kept fuel prices in Taiwan unchanged.
Photo: CNA
Retail gasoline prices this week would rise to NT$31.2, NT$32.7 and NT$34.7 per liter for 92, 95 and 98-octane unleaded gasoline respectively at CPC and Formosa stations, the companies said.
Premium diesel prices would also rise to NT$29.9 per liter at CPC stations and NT$29.7 per liter at Formosa pumps, they said.
Amid escalating military conflicts in the Middle East that have increased risks to crude oil supplies and transportation, CPC said its floating price mechanism, based on a weighted average of 70 percent Dubai and 30 percent Brent crude, showed that the average international crude oil price rose to US$115.61 last week from US$99.82 per barrel in the previous week.
A stronger New Taiwan dollar, which averaged NT$31.556 against the US dollar last week, compared with NT$31.682 a week earlier, helped CPC mitigate the impact from higher crude prices to some extent, the company said.
Overall, CPC’s crude oil price costs rose 12.29 percent last week, it said.
Despite the hike in domestic fuel prices, CPC said it still expected to absorb a loss of NT$6.8 per liter on gasoline sales and NT$8.7 per liter on diesel sales this week, as the company aims to help the government ease domestic inflationary pressure and maintain Taiwan’s competitive edge by keeping local fuel prices lower than in neighboring markets.
The company estimated that by Sunday it would have absorbed NT$19.85 billion in cumulative losses since the war in the Middle East began, by not fully passing on higher crude oil costs to consumers and businesses under the government’s price stabilization measures.
Separately, the Ministry of Economic Affairs yesterday urged the Legislative Yuan to support the Executive Yuan’s supplementary budget for state-owned energy companies, such as CPC and Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電).
The Cabinet on Sept. 3 finalized a supplementary budget that includes a NT$234 billion capital injection and a further NT$101.43 billion in subsidies for CPC to pare its losses from absorbing part of cost increases in fuel and natural gas prices.
The proposal — which is conditional on approval by the opposition-controlled legislature — also includes NT$71.1 billion in subsidies for Taipower to help the loss-making utility offset rising fuel costs arising from the war in the Middle East.

Ukraine’s economy hobbled by Russian strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:42:15 UTC
01:42:15 KST

Ukraine’s economy is being crippled by intensifying Russian strikes hitting key sectors, and its GDP could slump by 1.5 points in 2026, Kyiv officials said on Saturday, warning of a “very difficult” winter ahead.
Russia, which devastated Ukraine’s energy sector during the course of 4.5 years of war, has since this summer stepped up a campaign of missiles and drones that Kyiv is struggling to intercept. These have severely restricted grain exports in the Black Sea — a crucial source of Kyiv’s revenue. The strikes have also targeted steel companies, another key sector, as well as supply chains — notably in the rail sector — and major warehouses.
“The economy is in the most difficult situation,” Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said during the annual Yalta European Strategy forum in Kyiv.
Photo: AFP
He said the intensity of the strikes and the level of destruction have increased.
“We anticipate a very difficult winter in terms of both critical infrastructure, which is being destroyed every day by Russian attacks, but also in terms of overall economic conditions in the country,” Ukrainian Minister of Economy and Environment Oleksandr Kravchenko said.
Kyiv estimates that “the total destruction of infrastructure and assets are likely to be close to US$10 billion” this year.
This destruction and the blockage of seaports are likely to reduce national GDP by 1.5 points, Kravchenko added, with some Western experts calling the situation “catastrophic.”
Roksolana Pidlasa, the head of the budget committee in Ukraine’s parliament, described a bleak outlook.
“It can get worse, but it’s already bad now,” she told the same forum.
“Russia specifically targets revenue-generating industries by attacking grain corridors, by attacking seaports and metallurgical plants,” she said at the same forum. “It is not something that you could reconstruct quickly.”
Ukraine’s largest steelworks, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rig, on Saturday said that a Russian missile strike killed two of its workers and damaged facilities.
Kyiv has also upped its retaliatory strikes on Russia, targeting oil facilities, factories and warehouses. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy hopes his US counterpart Donald Trump would pressure Russia to ensure Black Sea ports reopen and for a mutual suspension of strikes on energy sites. He warned of the risk of food crises in African and Asian countries, saying that Moscow was also unable to export its grain through the Black Sea. Both countries are key global suppliers of grain.
“At the very least, again, if peace is impossible from today ... we can at least resolve the issue of an energy truce, a food truce, food security; such decisions can be made,” he told the Kyiv forum this weekend.
Zelenskiy called on resolving these “now” and “not in winter.”
At the same time, Kyiv’s military spending is rising. In 2024 “one day of war costs 140 million US dollars per day, this year it costs 190 million dollars a day,” Pidlasa said.
Kyiv has had to start using international aid this year to even pay its soldiers’ wages, she said.
The release of about US$30 billion in international aid intended to finance this year’s budget deficit is conditional upon parliament passing draft laws demanded by Western countries, Koretsky said.
These include anti-corruption measures after Ukraine was hit by several large-scale graft scandals during the war with Russia. However, the Ukrainian parliament is struggling to approve suggested laws, which include unpopular measures such as imposing duties on parcels from abroad, intended to boost revenues.

Green-collar exam sees pass rate hit 60% in second test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:42:15 UTC
01:42:15 KST

The National Environmental Research Academy on Friday announced results of the Ministry of Environment’s green-collar training exam, saying the exam had a 60 percent pass rate, with an average score of 60.
The course’s second exam of the year was held earlier this month with more than 900 people taking the exam after they completed the 48-hour training course, the academy said.
The average score of all test-takers was 60 points, and the highest score was 90 points, it said.
Photo: CNA
Data from the academy showed that of the examinees, 52 percent were women, with an average score of 61, slightly higher than their male counterparts’ average score of 59.
In terms of age, examinees aged from 31 to 45 scored the highest at an average of 62 points, followed in order by those aged 46 or older (60 points) and the others aged 30 or younger (58 points), it showed.
Working people scored an average of 62, higher than students’ average score of 57, the data showed.
That reflected that course trainees with work experience had better learning outcomes, likely because they could integrate net zero course content into real-world work contexts, the academy said.
The second exam tested memory and required examinees to make decisions based on knowledge of carbon emission calculation, carbon inventory, carbon reduction regulations and product carbon footprints, it said.
Examinees must integrate concepts across different course modules to answer correctly, the academy said.
Such an exam was more challenging but better assessed examinees’ understanding of carbon management, it said.
Academy director-general Chang Shun-chin (張順欽) encouraged course trainees who failed the exam to keep studying, as each trainee has up to two retest opportunities.
They can sign up directly with their original training school for this year’s last exam, scheduled for Nov. 21, he said.
Those who pass the exam can download their digital certificate from the academy’s green-collar talent information platform, Chang said.
The certificate demonstrates its holder’s carbon management knowledge, he said, adding that no paper copies of the certificate would be provided given the digital certification policy.
The academy said college students aged 30 or younger and the approximately 12,000 environmental educators nationwide are eligible for a 50 percent discount on the NT$12,000 tuition.
People with disabilities or of low-income households are eligible to fully waive the tuition, it said.

Central bank pressured to raise rates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:42:14 UTC
01:42:14 KST

With domestic inflation topping the 2 percent alert level for a fourth consecutive month last month and several major central banks around the world raising their key interest rates, Taiwan’s central bank is facing growing pressure to raise rates at its quarterly policymaking meeting on Thursday, economists said.
At its June meeting, the central bank left interest rates unchanged for the ninth consecutive quarter, with the discount rate at 2 percent.
Central Bank Governor Yang Chin-long (楊金龍) had said that the bank maintained a somewhat hawkish stance, with two board directors voicing support for a rate hike at the meeting.
Photo: Tyrone Siu, Reuters
Cathay United Bank Co (國泰世華銀行) chief economist Lin Chi-chao (林啟超) last week said that the central bank had forecast in June that the consumer price index (CPI) would rise by less than 2 percent this year.
However, the situation has since changed, as international crude oil prices have risen amid escalating tensions in the Middle East, he said.
“Inflationary pressure has been on the rise,” Lin said, citing a forecast by the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics last month that CPI would increase 2.07 percent this year.
The central bank must also take into account the monetary policy moves of other major central banks when deciding whether to adjust interest rates, he said.
The Bank of Korea hiked its benchmark interest rates for a second consecutive time last month to 3 percent, Lin said.
The European Central Bank raised its key interest rates by 25 basis points last week, marking its second rate hike this year, he said, adding that there was a high possibility that the Bank of Japan would raise rates this week.
More importantly, the US Federal Reserve could raise rates this week, with the odds rising to nearly 90 percent after last month’s CPI data showed persistent inflationary pressure, Lin said.
“Whether considering domestic conditions or the international situation, the interest rate hike checklist has been fully checked,” Lin added.
With GDP growth forecast to top 11 percent this year, the economy is expected to be able to absorb the impact of a rate hike, Lin said.
Taiwan Institute of Economic Research Economic Forecasting Center director Gordon Sun (孫明德) said he expects the Fed to raise rates this week, which could serve as an indication for Taiwan’s central bank to follow suit.
If Taiwan’s rates remain unchanged, there would be a wider interest rate spread between Taiwan and the US, which is an important factor to consider, Sun said.
A central bank rate hike would not primarily be aimed at curbing inflation, but at addressing tightening liquidity in the local market, Sun added.
Fund demand has increased as companies step up investments amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, while high-flying stocks have boosted demand for funds, further tightening liquidity, he said.
Tight liquidity has pushed up market interest rates, so the central bank needs to respond by raising its key interest rates, he added.
However, Sun also raised concerns about a rate hike, saying Taiwan’s strong economic growth is largely driven by AI development, while the traditional economy has lagged behind, so higher interest rates could place a heavier financial burden on traditional industries.

Hojjatoleslam Qomi visits “Minab School” exhibition, calls for international presentation of artwork
TEHRAN- Hojjatoleslam Mohammad Qomi, the head of Iran’s Islamic Ideology Dissemination Organization, paid a visit to the group exhibition “Minab School” at the Art Bureau in Tehran on Saturday, calling for the international presentation of artworks addressing the Minab tragedy.
During his visit, he also met with a number of the participating artists and discussed their works and perspectives on the events surrounding Minab.
The artists explained the approaches behind their works and spoke about their needs and requirements for more effective production and presentation of artworks dealing with the subject.
Hojjatoleslam Qomi expressed his appreciation to those who had contributed to organizing the exhibition and to artists who have produced works focusing on Minab.
 
  
 
 “I appreciate those who made efforts to organize this exhibition and those who are working for Minab,” he said, adding that committed artists are expected to continue producing works on the subject.
He also stressed the importance of following up on and supporting such artistic productions.
He described artistic approaches to war crimes as an effective means of raising awareness and influencing international public opinion.
He said the Art Bureau has a responsibility to support artworks addressing such issues, while emphasizing that his main concern is ensuring the effective and appropriate international presentation of works related to Minab.
“These works should certainly be presented in venues such as the United Nations and institutions that are the source of important international decisions.”
He added that the Islamic Ideology Dissemination Organization would do everything within its capacity to facilitate the international presentation of the artworks and would pursue the matter seriously.
The “Minab School” exhibition brings together works by a group of Iranian artists who have approached the Minab tragedy through different artistic forms and perspectives.
Among the artists featured in the exhibition are Behzad Shishegaran, Sirous Moqaddam, Gholam-Ali Taheri, Morteza Asadi, Kazem Chalipa, Ali Nedai, Hassan Yaqouti, Abdolhamid Ghadirian, Mostafa Goudarzi, Nasser Seifi, Jamshid Haqiqatshenas, Seyyed Masoud Shojai Tabatabai, Kamyar Sadeqi, Seyyed Ali Mirfattah, Mahyar Charmchi, Mostafa Qorbani, Hossein Einibakhsh and Mohammad-Ali Naderi.
The exhibition is currently underway at the Art Bureau’s gallery and will continue through September 22. It is open to visitors daily from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.
On February 28, the Shajareh Tayyebeh girls' elementary school in Minab, Hormozgan province, became the site of a devastating massacre as the United States and Israel initiated their strikes against Iran.
While dozens of girls and boys aged between 7 and 12 were beginning their lessons, the school was targeted by a missile strike that caused the building to collapse, trapping children and teachers beneath the rubble. Iranian authorities confirmed a final death toll of 168 people, with at least 95 others wounded, marking one of the most harrowing incidents of the conflict's opening day.
Despite attempts by US and Israeli authorities to distance themselves from the carnage as images of the tragedy spread across social media, detailed forensic and digital investigations have painted a starkly different picture.
An analysis by Al Jazeera’s digital investigations unit, utilizing over a decade of satellite imagery and recent video clips, revealed that the school was a clearly distinct civilian facility, separated from any adjacent military sites for at least ten years. Furthermore, witness accounts and satellite-based analyses confirmed that the school was triple tapped by three separate, deliberate strikes, leaving no doubt about the nature of the attack.
The international community has faced mounting evidence regarding the responsibility for this atrocity, with investigations from major global outlets including The New York Times, BBC Verify, CBC, and NPR all concluding that the United States was responsible for the strike.
These findings have raised fundamental questions about the intelligence used to justify the bombing, as the patterns of the strike suggest a direct targeting of a civilian educational institution. The Minab school tragedy now stands as a somber testament to the immense human cost of the aggression and a focal point for those demanding international accountability.

OpenAI will not go public this year: CEO Sam Altman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:42:13 UTC
01:42:13 KST

OpenAI will not go public this year, CEO Sam Altman said in remarks published on Saturday, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) that render “unacceptable” even a 10 percent risk that AI could cause human extinction by decade’s end.
The comments come as more US lawmakers urge new rules to govern AI systems after dire warnings from two researchers from OpenAI rival Anthropic PBC that rapidly progressing AI could lead to the extinction of the human race in the not-too-distant future.
“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman said.
Photo: AFP
Asked if there was a 10 percent chance of AI-driven extinction, Altman said he did not know how such an estimate could be made, but that the risk was serious enough that AI companies and governments should act as though it could not be tolerated.
“Whether it’s 10 or eight or six, the point is, we all have a tremendous amount of responsibility, and cannot let egos or incentives for profit or anything else get in the way,” Altman added. “We need to act such that we are not taking any of those numbers of risk, and I believe we can.”
Politicians have responded with alarm and calls for more action after cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI safety researchers quitting their companies out of concern at the technology risks.
Asked if an initial public offering this year was off the table in favor of next year, Altman said: “I would say not 2026. We got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together.”

After taking 10 years to win his first world championship, Ryan Garcia on Saturday night needed only 4 minutes, 25 seconds to finish off Conor Benn in the first defense of his WBC welterweight title.
“I kind of figured he would just come at me crazy,” Garcia said. “Second round, I said I’m tired of him coming forward; I’m gonna stand my ground a little bit ... and then he got caught with a hellacious one.”
Garcia’s sharp right hand to the jaw put Benn on the canvas early in the second round. Moments later, with the Englishman on the ropes, Garcia (26-2, 21 KOs) served a flurry of punches that prompted referee Thomas Taylor to step in and end the contest at the 1:25 mark and send the announced sold-out crowd of 18,855 into a frenzy.
Photo: AP
“He’s exactly what I thought he was; he went in and tried to fight me. I think he needs to be a little bit more patient,” Garcia added. “I don’t think he has enough experience. I think he will be back. I have a new level of respect for him.”
The bout was more than another high-profile main event, as it marked a career-defining crossroads for both fighters.
For Garcia, he solidified himself in the 147-pound (67kg) weight class as a durable, legitimate titleholder rather than a gifted attraction whose career has often been defined by controversy, inconsistency and unrealized potential.
The convincing victory positioned Garcia for a lucrative welterweight fight against the division’s other leading names, including Teofimo Lopez, who was ringside, or another major showdown with Devin Haney, who was also in attendance.
Garcia called out both of them.

For the 29-year-old Benn (25-2), it is likely back to the middleweight division after failing in his first world-title opportunity and a chance to escape the considerable shadow of his father, former two-division champion Nigel Benn.
Benn was transported to a hospital after the fight for observation.

Amorous sheep get fined
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:42:13 UTC
01:42:13 KST

A livestock farmer in Changhua County was fined NT$1,000 after his flock of about 95 meat sheep made noises in the night, disturbing nearby residents.
According to the final ruling delivered on Tuesday last week by the Changhua District Court, the man surnamed Chen (陳) began raising meat sheep in the residential area in 2023, with his flock now grown to almost 100 sheep.
Neighbors said that the sheep frequently made high-pitched noises of varying volume and frequency, particularly at night, disrupting their sleep, the ruling said.
Photo: Taipei Times
Police visited the farm in January and issued a citation ordering Chen to address the noise problem, the ruling said.
However, the sheep again began bleating collectively late at night in mid-May, prompting neighbors to call police again, it said, adding police subsequently fined Chen NT$1,000 under the Social Order Maintenance Act (社會秩序維護法).
Chen said the bleating was not a persistent problem and mainly occurred during the spring and autumn mating seasons, when rams and young male sheep would call out, the ruling said.
It quoted Chen as saying he had since taken measures to address the problem, including separating the rams and castrating young males that matured early.
Chen said the sheep’s calls were only brief sounds and were “quieter than birdsong,” making them acceptable, and said the authorities had failed to properly investigate the matter.
The judge ruled that noise covered by the Social Order Maintenance Act does not have to exceed a specified decibel level or continue for an extended period, and that noise that is sufficient to disturb others’ peace and quiet can constitute an offense.
Although the sheep’s calls were brief, they were particularly noticeable and piercing at night, and could disturb nearby residents’ sleep, the judge said.
Although Chen had separated and castrated some of the sheep, the measures displayed limited effectiveness and had failed to prevent the flock from disturbing neighbors, the ruling said.
The court rejected Chen’s appeal and upheld the NT$1,000 fine.

In the second inning of the five-inning mercy-rule victory, with 14 plate appearances by Taiwan’s nine batters, who combined for eight hits and four walks.
Chen Yao-chieh and Bunun player Pasula Takislinian each had two hits.
Photo: CNA
Taiwan added a run in the bottom of the fourth inning and two more in the fifth before the game ended under the five-inning mercy rule. Under the rule, a game ends early if one team leads by 10 or more runs after five complete innings.
Taiwan’s three pitchers — Yang Yao-cheng, Tsai Cheng-lung and Chen Yu-hsun — combined to allow just two hits throughout the game. Tsai, who struck out two in two innings, was awarded the game. Starter Yang struck out three and Chen Yu-hsun struck out three in the fifth.
Taiwan on Friday similarly defeated the Philippines 10-0 in five innings.
Taiwan has finished third six times in the tournament, which has been held every two years since 1994.
Taiwan, who won the previous edition in 2024, were seeking their first back-to-back titles and fourth overall championship win, but a 2-1 loss to Japan on Saturday ended those hopes.
The hosts were relegated to the third-place playoffs after losing 2-1 to Japan in the Super Round on Saturday.
All three runs were scored in the first inning, when Taiwan briefly took the lead before Japan immediately responded.
Hu Chen-jui drew a leadoff walk, moved to second on Chang Yi-an’s sacrifice bunt and reached third on a wild pitch before scoring on a groundout from Liu Huan-yu.
Yusei Ishida reached on an infield single before Ritora Yamada hit an RBI double and Kenshin Manya followed with a run-scoring single, giving Japan a 2-1 lead.
Neither team scored again over the remaining six innings.
Japanese starter Shoki Oda allowed one run on three hits over six innings, striking out seven while issuing five walks. Manya pitched a scoreless seventh to secure the win.
Taiwan starter Liu Jen-yu surrendered two runs on six hits over 4-2/3 innings, recording seven strikeouts without issuing a walk.
Wu Hao-siang held Japan hitless over the final 1-1/3 innings, but Taiwan could not erase the deficit despite finishing with four hits and drawing five walks.
South Korea last night blanked Japan 2-0 for their sixth tournament title and their first since besting Taiwan 7-5 in 2018.
Japan have won five titles, the most recent being a 1-0 victory over Taiwan in 2016.

US President Donald Trump on Saturday said that he would “love to see” a united Ireland, wading into a politically sensitive subject as he embarked on a two-day Irish visit that blurs the lines between his presidency and personal business interests.
After meeting Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin, Trump said reunification of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland — split for more than a century — would be “a fantastic thing.”
“It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now,” he told reporters, adding that “the UK will have something to say about it, obviously.”
Photo: AP
The island of Ireland has been split between the Irish republic in the south and Northern Ireland, which is part of the UK, since 1921.
Under the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, which ended three decades of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland that killed about 3,000 people, a referendum can be held if the British government determines a majority there is likely to favor joining the Republic of Ireland.
Republic of Ireland voters would also have to endorse reunification in a poll for it to happen.
Photo: Reuters
The US has previously adopted a neutral position on the issue.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham last month said that a unity referendum was “off the table,” drawing a sharp response from the pro-unity party Sinn Fein.
Asked about Trump’s comments, a spokesperson for his Downing Street office referred reporters to comments Burnham made in parliament on Wednesday last week when he vowed to “stick to the Good Friday Agreement 100 percent.”
However, Gavin Robinson, leader of the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, said on social media that “as unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish Republic.”
Trump had touched down at Dublin airport shortly before 8:25am under a security operation dubbed one of the largest ever mounted in Ireland and reportedly costing 20 million euros (US$23.2 million).
At least 4,000 police and other personnel, including snipers, have been mobilized.

One small group of demonstrators — dressed in black and wearing masks and dark glasses — set a US flag on fire, according to The Irish Times.
In Dublin, Trump appeared to receive a frostier reception from left-wing Irish President Catherine Connolly, an outspoken critic of the US leader.

Notes from Central Taiwan: The ‘Wall Street Journal’s’ Taiwan blind spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:42:10 UTC
01:42:10 KST

The comical bit of parachute journalism by Simon Shuster in the Atlantic last week under the title “Will Taiwan Just Give Up?”, drew much attention for its numerous minor errors, largely forgivable, its total lack of understanding of Taiwan and its history and its strange, pro-China interpretations, including taking Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) seriously. The laughter and indignation that essay generated among Taiwan aficionados is an indicator of how far Western journalism on Taiwan has come. Twenty years ago, it would have been another piece for the pile. Today, it is an obvious outlier.
Shuster’s piece was a one-off. Lost in the hilarity around it, however, was a truly obnoxious piece of parachute journalism last week that gave us an example of how the soft power of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and its framings continue to shape media presentations: Wei Lingling’s (魏玲靈) “At Taiwan’s Temples, a Glimpse of What China Could Have Been” in the Wall Street Journal. WSJ’s editors should be ashamed of this one.
Wei’s Taipei-centric piece artfully uses the temples of Chinese folk religion to present Taiwan as an “alternative China.” That approach has been out of place for two decades, with good reason: it’s nonsense. Taiwan is not “what China could have been.” To claim so is an attempt, in prose, to annex Taiwan to China, appealing to a “preserver” trope that frames Taiwan as a “preserver” of “Chinese tradition” when it is a settler culture that has a completely different history and traditions of its own. In reality, temples carry local social meanings that resonate with the lived experience of locals, as a sharp friend of mine remarked when he read this piece. Those meanings date back centuries.
Photo: Michael Turton
LONGSHAN TEMPLE AND TAIWAN’S DEMOCRACY
The story for Wei begins at Taipei’s Longshan Temple, an ironic choice. The temple has been the site of numerous historical events over its nearly three centuries of existence, but all that is gone from Wei’s piece. Most notably, it sits in one of the oldest areas of Taipei, long a hotbed of Taiwanese nationalism.
Democracy activists in 1986 held a famous sit-in to protest decades of martial law, earning the temple the sobriquet “sacred ground for the opposition movement.” When democracy and free speech activist Deng Nan-jung (鄭南榕) killed himself in 1989 as the police closed in, supporters erected a shrine to him in Longshan Temple and mourned him for a month.
Photo: Wang I-sheng, Taipei Times
The particular local and social identity of Longshan Temple — its long association with Taiwan democracy — vanishes in Wei’s hands. In fact, “democracy” itself is deep-sixed. The word is never used in the piece despite its centrality to modern Taiwanese religious experience. The source of all this difference is thus withheld from the reader’s purview.
A large, rich body of scholarship on the interplay of religion, democracy and identity tells this story (see Ting Guo’s paper “Religion and Official Politics in Contemporary China, Hong Kong and Taiwan,” Religion Compass, March, 2026, for an excellent round up of the research). All that is swallowed up by the China-centric concept of “separation.”
In fact, the KMT controlled and shaped religion in Taiwan in the same way as the Communist Party in China, because — as in China — religion is an important source of local identity and site of resistance to the murderous Leninist authoritarians running things (hint: what was the purpose of the old KMT Committee for the Revival for Chinese Culture?). The rich, critical local history of Longshan Temple instead resolves as pious images of people praying.
“More than seven decades of separation between [China] and Taiwan have not only produced different governments, but also populations with different inner lives,” Wei writes.
The idea of “separation” is a tell that the writer is pro-PRC, as are the silence on democracy and on the 50 years of Japanese colonial rule. Just flip the “separation” claim. Assuming they were under the same government, would the lived and practiced religious experience be the same? Would they have the same inner lives? We have over 200 years of Manchu rule of the western settler part of Taiwan to comprehensively disprove that.
TELLING OMISSIONS
Because the piece is China-centered, it simply omits things that are not Han Chinese, as if they never existed. Christianity appears only in a quoted remark to Wei. Where are the Muslims and Mormons, the True Jesus Church and Yi Guan Dao?
The syncretic and creative religious traditions of Taiwan’s indigenous communities, especially in border areas, is also unexamined. It would strongly complicate the idea of “separation” and “alternative China” if Wei had posted a picture of the fabulous Catholic mural in Wanluan Township (萬巒) in Pingtung County with its melange of local religious elements, or the temple in Tainan with the skulls of dead animals hung by its altar I stopped at several years ago.
One wonders what Wei would made of the famous Shinto shrine in Taichung where Japanese war dead are interred, with a dedication from former president Lee Teng-hui (李登輝). Indeed, Shinto shrines are tucked away in the hills of southern and eastern Taiwan, and are still treated with reverence by indigenous people. The choice of China-centrism also forecloses the possibility of situating Taiwanese religious experience as one expression of local religion in the vast Chinese settler diaspora across southeast Asia.
Missing too are the rich exchanges between religious groups in the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and Taiwan since the end of martial law and the advent of democracy in the late 1980s. The seven decades of “separation” in the WSJ piece is entirely an artifact of Wei’s invention. In the real world, it is more like a four-decade interregnum. The lack of convergence between religion in Taiwan and PRC religion since 1987, despite a wealth of exchanges, should have given Wei much food for thought. That lack shows how “separation” for Wei means political control, not communications. Rich, regular exchange networks simply don’t matter.
MAZU WORSHIP
Another element gone rogue from Wei’s presentation is the PRC’s use of religion as a vector of influence in Taiwan. Scholarly and pundit commentary on the use of Mazu worship by the PRC to infiltrate and influence Taiwan is entirely missing, nor is there any comment on the role of local temples as critical nexuses of organized crime, business and local politics. Tourism, a major shaper of religious facilities, practice and display in Taiwan, is absent. Where are the strippers, shamans speaking in tongues and men slashing each other with watermelon knives? Were they just the wrong social class for “separation”?
Clearly, a key move of Wei’s presentation is to avoid localizing Taiwanese religion. Even when she writes about local earth god shrines, she reminds the reader that these are the same gods and rituals on the other side of the Strait, thus claiming a uniformity of religious experience (and of Chineseness!) in the PRC that exists only as a propaganda dream of the Chinese Communist Party.
The insistence on “separation” and the presentation of Taiwan as “separated Chinese” are components of the unsubtle Han ethnonationalism and expansionism that colors this piece. The fact that Wei was able to put this story about Taiwan in a major US paper of record shows how PRC propaganda continues to shape stories about Taiwan and China in the US media, a critical aspect of PRC soft power.
“In Taipei’s crowded temples, a Chinese-born reporter witnesses what was lost” says the piece. Alas, nothing was lost, because there was never a moment when it existed.
Taiwan isn’t China, and it never was.
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.
Drones are widely recognized as a critical weapons technology of the future. Because of this, the pro-China Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) appear to be obstructing their development. One approach to handling this obstruction is to circumvent it by building robust drone capabilities across a wide swathe of the population. Taiwan is doing just that, but more is needed. The Penghu County Government on Monday said it was testing flying drones on routes from Magong City (馬公), the county seat, to Jibei Island (吉貝嶼). Because all of the inhabited islands lie within 40km of Magong,
For a time, it became popular to describe the tactics of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) in encroaching on sovereignty and militarizing islands in the South China Sea as “salami slicing.” Those slices have been getting chunkier. The People’s Liberation Army has been increasing its navy and air force activities in the region. NTUH releases simplified medical care guidelines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:42:10 UTC
01:42:10 KST

The National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH) yesterday released the Healthy Taiwan Guidelines for Appropriate Use of Healthcare Services, providing healthcare recommendations for 1,067 common symptoms.
The NTUH Referral Management Center released the guidelines with the aim of addressing the phenomenon of seeking treatment at large hospitals for mild illnesses and at medical centers for non-emergency conditions.
The center’s deputy director Jan Chyi-feng (詹其峰) said the center invited 256 medical experts from different levels of care for conducting a comprehensive review and held an in-person consensus meeting attended by 80 experts to finalize its conclusions.
Photo: CNA
The 1,067 symptoms are categorized into four levels of recommended care — about 13.8 percent can be managed by self-care and observation, 31.9 percent should seek treatment at community primary care clinics, 7.9 percent at hospitals’ outpatient departments and 46.5 percent require emergency medical attention, he said.
Overall, 45.7 percent of the symptoms can initially be managed through self-care, observation, or community-based primary care, and do not require a visit to a major hospital or medical center, Jan said.
The hospital announced that it would launch a public healthcare consultation hotline at (02) 2356-2891 on Oct. 1, to assist the public in finding appropriate healthcare.
The hotline would operate from 8am to 5pm daily and the service would be staffed by nurses and healthcare professionals, who would assess callers’ symptoms and urgency and provide guidance on the appropriate course of action, including the four levels of medical attention, it said.
NTUH deputy superintendent Huang Kuo-chin (黃國晉) said the hospital is promoting five practices for intelligent healthcare use.
They include encouraging everyone to have a long-term and trusted family physician who can provide ongoing and comprehensive healthcare, and to check with the hotline when unsure if they need medical attention or which department to visit, he said.
The other three are: Turn to primary care clinics for minor illnesses, recognize red flag emergency conditions, and follow the healthcare workers’ referral recommendations for appropriate healthcare institutions for evaluation and treatment, he said.
Red flags include symptoms such as severe chest pain, difficulty breathing, altered consciousness, sudden weakness of a limb or sudden speech abnormalities, Huang said, adding that people should seek immediate medical attention if they experience these.
He said the goal is to ensure efficient allocation of healthcare resources through a tiered medical system, preventing patients with mild conditions from overcrowding emergency rooms, while ensuring timely emergency care for those who need it.

====================================================================================================

You are never too old to learn new things
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:42:08 UTC
01:42:08 KST

The faster technology advances, the easier it is for many retired people to mistakenly think that tech is only for young people and that they are too old to learn it. After using artificial intelligence (AI) and smart-home technology, I have become convinced that age is not the real obstacle. What matters more is how we learn and whether we are willing to take the first step.
Smart cameras, plugs and locks might seem quite complicated, but once set up, everyday use involves little more than a few taps on a smartphone. Smart cameras can allow people to check on their homes and talk to family members, smart plugs allow people to turn off appliances while they are away and sensors can send alerts when doors or windows are opened or a water leaks occur.
AI is similar. Upon first encountering ChatGPT, Gemini and other generative AI systems, many feel intimidated. However, ordinary users do not need to understand the technical principles behind AI; they can simply treat it as a personal assistant that can chat and answer questions.
If users do not understand English, they can ask the chatbot to translate. If they want to write an article, they can tell it their ideas. When traveling abroad, they can ask it to organize information. If they have questions about a news report, they can ask it to fact-check and analyze the issue. If they encounter a tech product they do not understand, they can take a photo, send it to the chatbot and start asking questions.
The key is not how much a person understands, but if they are willing to try.
Learning to use technology does not require fully understanding it. A person should use it first, then gradually understand. It is OK to make a mistake, and it is OK if the user does not get the desired results at first. Ask again, rephrase the prompt, identify what went wrong and try again. Trial and error is learning in itself.
This is where a good teacher makes all the difference. Good teachers do not do everything for their students; instead, they point them in the right direction when they get stuck and allow them to complete the task themselves. Try, make a mistake, receive guidance from a teacher, try again, succeed and build confidence.
When someone successfully completes an AI conversation for the first time, sets up a smart-home system or uses a camera to check on their home from afar, the most important thing they gain might not be a new technological skill, but the belief that they can do it. Once that confidence takes hold, technology no longer seems so intimidating, and learning shifts from a passive activity to something self-directed.
Retirement is not the end of all learning. It can be the perfect time to start anew. In the past, many people learned how to use technology for work. After retirement, people can learn how to use it for life — to make themselves more independent, make life safer and more convenient, and stay connected with family and the wider world.
What is truly important about using AI and smart-home technology has never been how many technical terms you know, but whether you are willing to start.
Do not wait until you know how before you try. Start and you learn along the way.
Be willing to try, willing to make mistakes and have a good teacher provide guidance when needed.
Technology is not as difficult as it might seem.
True wisdom is not about chasing after technology, but about using it to serve us, and allow for more comfortable and fulfilling lives.
Hsiao Hsi-huei is a freelancer.

College costs are due a correction, not a crash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:42:02 UTC
01:42:02 KST

A lot of people used to think about college the way a lot of people now think about protein: good for you in any quantity, and the more the better. How times have changed.
Not only is the share of people who see college as a worthwhile investment in decline, but some smaller schools are digging into their endowments to stay afloat. Even popular and established schools such as Syracuse are falling short of enrollment goals and facing a budget crisis. It is all leading to speculation that higher education is a bubble that is about to pop.
That is unlikely. College is less like an overvalued stock about to crash than an expensive bond due for a repricing. In the meantime, it would still make payments.
American universities face many challenges. First, the numbers are not in their favor. In the postwar era, each generation was larger than the previous, and more people from each generation wanted to go to college. International students were also willing to come to the US at almost any price. Now those sources of growth are exhausted. Enrollment in a four-year college has been steady, about 40 percent, for more than a decade. Future generations are smaller, and there are fewer foreign students.
Universities are not without blame. They have let themselves be seen as more political or even promoted views many Americans do not share. They offer some degrees of dubious value that have become a source of embarrassment. Grade inflation, opaque admissions and other ways to cheat the system have undermined the academic worth of a college degree. And now the value of knowledge jobs is less certain. Amid all these sins, tuition for four years of university is now pushing US$400,000.
And yet, none of this means education is a bubble about to pop. A growing share of Americans went to college over the past few decades because they were responding to an unambiguous economic incentive to do so. For most areas of study, there still exists a significant college wage premium (although it has shrunk a bit). The odds are excellent, if you graduate, that you would earn almost US$1 million more over your lifetime and experience less unemployment.
And while it might sometimes seem like college is full of people getting useless degrees, most students major in career-oriented subjects such as business or health-related fields. Humanities enrollment has been on the decline, and very few people major in niche fields that are often the subject of controversy or ridicule.
Most people still want to go to college to have some fun, learn some useful things and get a good job when they graduate — and many of them get that. Many parents, especially those who are also college graduates, want that for their children, and raise them with the expectation that college is something they should do.
That expectation is part of where things go wrong. As obscenely expensive as it is, college is still one of the best investments you can make. For a long time, that made it seem like a risk-free asset — one for which any price could be justified (sort of like low-risk longer-term bonds the past 20 years). This was especially true at prestigious private schools where prices rose the most. And like the bond market, there was plenty of government interference in the form of loan subsidies, which made prices insensitive to market forces: Universities could charge almost any price without paying attention to the service they were providing.
What is happening in higher education is a lot like what is happening in the bond market. Bonds were overpriced for a while, but they still make payments. There is just less certainty of the value of those payments right now, so prices are adjusting.
Prices would take longer to fall at universities, in part because they have taken on debt and have lots of infrastructure to pay for, but the market has already started to speak. More students are seeking out state schools in the South that are cheaper and less politically fraught. One reason some private schools got so expensive was they conveyed a sheen of prestige that signaled exceptional intelligence and connections. However, as more people go to a greater variety of schools that sheen would dull, and the value of different schools would equalize. The upshot is that elite private schools would need to reform the most — in cutting costs and demonstrating their academic merit.
It is not an impossible task. Universities have changed before: Once only for elites, they learned to serve more people. Now they would need to demonstrate their value to price-sensitive customers. Ideally, the result would be more accountable universities — and less emphasis on elite institutions, which never offered a better education, but still charged a premium. And a little market discipline, as any business school class will teach you, is never a bad thing.
Allison Schrager is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering economics. A senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, she is author of An Economist Walks Into a Brothel: And Other Unexpected Places to Understand Risk. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

When the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary cataloged “Taiwanese,” it dated the word’s entry into written English to the mid-20th century, recording five distinct meanings: a native or inhabitant of Taiwan, the primary local language and the adjectives describing the place, its people and its speech. Equivalent multilayered entries appear in Random House Webster’s Unabridged Dictionary, The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language and Wiktionary. Taiwan key for a China-free drone supply: source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:41:59 UTC
01:41:59 KST

Taiwan cannot be overlooked in building a drone supply chain independent of China, US-based Shield AI’s Taiwan representative Chen Yi-ju (陳奕儒) said in an interview.
Two years ago, less than 1 percent of the materials used in Shield AI products came from Taiwan, Chen said. That figure had risen to 16 percent in May and June this year, and the company expects that Taiwanese suppliers could soon account for as much as 25 percent of the value of an individual drone.
Founded in 2015, Shield AI develops artificial intelligence (AI)-powered autonomous systems and military uncrewed vehicles. Its core products include the Hivemind AI pilot and V-BAT uncrewed aircraft, which enable military platforms to fly autonomously, operate cooperatively and carry out missions in environments subject to electronic interference.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
In an interview with the Liberty Times (sister paper of the Taipei Times), Chen said that Shield AI’s presence in Taiwan was a long-term investment, citing the nation’s mature drone, electronics, software and hardware industries.
Taiwan has considerable potential to contribute to physical AI, including through academic researchers involved in AI model training, while its hardware industry has strengths in making drones lighter, extending flight times and improving heat dissipation, he said.
Beyond procuring components, Shield AI wants to develop more capabilities locally. Chen said the company hopes to establish local capabilities in logistics, maintenance, training and some assembly, so products introduced to Taiwan would not have to be sent to the US for support during special or wartime circumstances.
The widespread use of uncrewed vehicles in the Russia-Ukraine war has highlighted their military importance, but Taiwan’s operational environment differs significantly from Europe’s, Chen said.
A key challenge for Taiwan is withstanding severe electronic warfare interference, he said, adding that Hivemind enables uncrewed vehicles to continue carrying out missions under intense interference.
Shield AI has learned from Ukraine that it must be physically present in a country to fully understand customers’ needs, Chen said. The company works with Taiwanese users and policymakers to understand military requirements and help partners develop sovereign AI capabilities tailored to Taiwan.
Shield AI also hopes to provide software development kits that allow Taiwanese engineers to design software models and mission functions themselves, rather than simply importing a fixed foreign system, he said.
Shield AI cofounder and president Brandon Tseng said in a written statement that the company is firmly committed to expanding its presence in Taiwan. It has established an office at Taipei 101 and plans to double its local staff next year.
The company is building a cooperation ecosystem with Taiwanese partners, including the National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology, Aerospace Industrial Development Corp (漢翔航空工業) and Thunder Tiger Group (雷虎科技), he said.
Tseng, a former US Navy SEAL, said his frontline experience showed him the gap between advanced military equipment and technological integration, prompting him to pursue autonomous technology.
“Victory without war is the greatest victory,” he said, explaining that Shield AI aims to develop technology that gives military forces the ability to deter conflict before it breaks out.
The US Air Force has awarded Shield AI a contract for autonomous mission system software for Collaborative Combat Aircraft. Tseng said the program is designed to enable AI-piloted wingmen to operate alongside human pilots, reducing the risk to personnel.
Shield AI has integrated Hivemind into Anduril’s YFQ-44A Fury uncrewed aircraft. Following flight tests, it demonstrated that two different mission autonomy systems could alternate during a single mission, achieve the same objective and safely return to base.
Hivemind has been used on more than 40 different platforms, Tseng said, demonstrating its flexibility for use with other collaborative combat aircraft.

Russian strikes on Saturday killed at least seven people and wounded almost 60 across Ukraine, Kyiv said, as Moscow steps up attacks ahead of another winter of war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy called for an adequate response from allies as Russia intensified attacks in a fifth year of war.
US envoys visited both Moscow and Kyiv last week, but announced no breakthrough in talks to end fighting.
Photo: AFP
Ukrainian officials said two people were killed in the southern Zaporizhzhia region and another two in the central Zhytomyr region.
Steelmaker ArcelorMittal said two others were also killed by a missile strike on its plant in the central city of Kryvyi Rig.
“We emphasize our plant is a civilian facility in the mining and metallurgical industry, and we strongly condemn these insidious enemy attacks,” the company said, reporting damage at its production facilities.
The two victims in the Zhytomyr region were killed when Russia struck a “grocery store” in the city of Zvyagel, about 230km west of Kyiv, regional leader Vitaliy Bunechko said.
He said two petrol stations were also hit in Korosten, in the same region further north toward the Belarus border, but there were no casualties.
Russia had increased strikes on petrol stations in the past few days in Kyiv and on motorways, Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said.
A Russian strike on an apartment building in Odesa also wounded 37 people, where rescue teams were searching for two missing people, Zelenskiy said, adding that another 11 were wounded in Chornomorsk, in the Odesa region.
Others were wounded in the Kryvyi Rig and the Kyiv regions, Zelensky said.
He called on allies to call out Russia’s intensifying campaign, with fears of what another winter of war would look like.
“When the Russians so blatantly turn ordinary people into targets of their terrorist attacks, it is frustrating that the response from the world’s strongest powers does not match the level of Russia’s escalation,” Zelensky said.

More delegations visit Taiwan: MOFA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:41:48 UTC
01:41:48 KST

Foreign diplomatic and business visits to Taiwan are reaching new highs, with landmark firsts and large-scale delegations, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) said, pledging to deepen mutual trust and substantive cooperation.
Italian Senate Vice President Gian Marco Centinaio led the largest-ever delegation of Italian lawmakers to Taiwan from Aug. 31 to Sept. 5, where he met with President William Lai (賴清德), Deputy Legislative Speaker Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) and other dignitaries, and attended Semicon Taiwan.
Yves-Francois Blanchet, leader of Canada’s Bloc Quebecois, led a delegation to Taiwan earlier this month, marking the first trip by a party member to Taiwan since the party’s founding in 1991, and the first time a sitting leader of a major Canadian political party led a delegation to the nation, the ministry said.
Photo: Yang Cheng-yu, Taipei Times
On the industry front, Arizona Commerce Authority president and CEO Sandra Watson led a delegation of more than 100 representatives from industry, government and academia — including five mayors and several key political figures — to Taiwan during Semicon Taiwan earlier this month.
Former commander of the US Army Pacific Charles A. Flynn led a 41-member delegation to Taiwan to attend the Taiwan-US Defense Industry Forum in May, focusing on the transformation of the Taiwan-US defense supply chain and technological research and development (R&D), the largest delegation for such an event.
In addition, several Japanese lawmakers visited Taiwan recently, including former Japanese minister of agriculture, forestry and fisheries Yasuhiro Ozato, who visited earlier this month, the ministry said.
Nobuyuki Baba, chair of the Japan Innovation Party’s Taiwan friendship discussion group, led a parliamentary delegation to Taiwan from Monday to Wednesday last week, marking the party’s first major visit since joining the ruling coalition with Japan’s Liberal Democratic Party, it added.
Japanese Senator Haruo Kitamura also led a seven-member cross-party parliamentary delegation from the Diet Members’ Association for Peace and Stability in the Taiwan Strait to Taiwan on Tuesday last week, it said.
Ministry spokesman Hsiao Kuang-wei (蕭光偉) said the exchanges highlight Taiwan’s deepening interactions with its international partners, built on shared values of democracy, freedom, human rights and the rule of law, while reflecting growing global concern and support for the nation.
International support for Taiwan is not only about the number or size of visiting delegations, and greater importance lies in further transforming these exchanges into sustained, mutually beneficial and concrete cooperation, he said.
The ministry will continue to leverage “integrated diplomacy” — combining forces across government, legislature, local authorities, business, academia and civil society — to deepen Taiwan’s partnerships with like-minded nations, Hsiao said.
The ministry will continue deepening bilateral mutual trust and exchanges at all levels, and leverage Taiwan’s strengths in technology, industry, healthcare, disaster prevention and democratic resilience to align mutual interests with partners and push forward practical cooperation, he said.
Taiwan aims to make meaningful contributions to key global issues through bilateral and multilateral engagements, and it would continue to work with like-minded partners to serve as a reliable ally, upholding a rules-based international order and promoting peace, stability and prosperity in the region, he said.
Kuo Kuo-wen (郭國文), a Democratic Progressive Party legislator and chair of the Taiwan-East Asia Parliamentary Friendship Association and the Taiwan Semiconductor Strategy Parliamentary Coalition, yesterday said that the international community not only focuses only on Taiwan’s security, but increasingly values its semiconductor industry and its role in global supply chains.
Amid exchanges with the foreign delegations, the next step for Taiwan should be turning these short visits into lasting relationships and institutionalized cooperation, he said.
Kuo said the ruling parties in Taiwan and Japan have evolved from holding virtual meetings during the COVID-19 pandemic to in-person exchanges, expanding from “2+2” talks to “4+4” talks, and will further scale up to “5+5” talks during the seventh policy dialogue in Tokyo today.
The transition marks a shift from the “a Taiwan contingency is a Japan contingency” strategic concept to concrete tactical execution aimed at solving practical issues, he said.
Kuo said after he led a delegation to Japan for official talks with Japan’s Parliamentary League for Semiconductor Strategy Promotion in April, he hopes future exchanges can be institutionalized.
Taiwan should expand its international space by establishing long-term cooperation across semiconductors, talent, R&D and supply chain resilience, and turning the visits into a stable mechanism and concrete outcomes, he said.

Elena Rybakina is on top of the tennis world, celebrating her first US Open title and her rise to No. 1 barely more than three weeks after she feared injury would force her out of the final Grand Slam of the year.
Kazakhstan’s Rybakina on Saturday beat two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 to claim her third Grand Slam title.
She had already assured herself of toppling Sabalenka from the No. 1 spot just by reaching the semi-finals.
Photo: AFP
“I can’t find words right now, honestly,” Rybakina said. “I don’t expect nothing like this coming to this tournament. I’ve been dealing with a little bit with an injury, but somehow everything aligned together on my side.”
The “little bit of an injury” saw Rybakina hobble out of her Cincinnati quarter-final on Aug. 20 — 10 days before the start of the US Open — unable to put weight on her left heel.
“It wasn’t the best time, for sure, because I was so upset,” she said. “I didn’t know actually how it’s going to be day by day.”
“We arrive to New York. We did MRI. It didn’t look that great. We had to talk with a lot of doctors to get opinion what we should do,” she added.
With a doctor in Australia providing valuable long-distance advice, Rybakina and her team came up with a plan to manage her training, rest and treatment and give her a chance at her second major title of the year, after her victory over Sabalenka at the Australian Open.
Her run to the final included an impressive fourth-round victory over two-time champion Naomi Osaka before come-from-behind wins over resurgent Olympic gold medalist Zheng Qinwen and former champion Coco Gauff.
It all led to her 18th showdown with Sabalenka in a rivalry that has emerged as the most dynamic on the WTA tour.
Having narrowed Sabalenka’s lead in their head to 10-8, Rybakina is looking forward to more chances to take on her fiery rival, whose on-court personality is the perfect foil to her own cool approach.
“I don’t know what the future will bring, but it’s always very difficult matches against Aryna,” she said. “I feel like we push each other to be better after such tough battles.”
The two seem destined to tussle for the top spot for some time. Other players — Gauff and Jessica Pegula — also had a chance to seize the number one ranking in New York, so Rybakina knows that Sabalenka is not the only rival she must be wary of.
“I feel like not only with her, with also other players, top players, you always want to try something new, to change in your game, to be better,” she said. “I don’t know what future is going to bring, but I hope success and some more wins.”

Anthropic CEO Amodei calls for AI slowdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:41:46 UTC
01:41:46 KST

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Saturday called on artificial intelligence (AI) firms to slow down the development of the powerful technology, amid mounting worries over the risks of “superintelligent” computer systems.
His comments came a few days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who left OpenAI to join Anthropic, decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of “gambling with our lives” in the race to develop models capable of self-improvement.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns xAI, quickly chimed in to say they agreed with Amodei’s assessment as pressure builds for improved oversight.
Photo: AFP
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote on his personal Web site.
“Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. We have sought a middle way,” Amodei said.
“But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence,” he said.
Amodei’s statement echoed another call by Anthropic in early June to slow or suspend development.
Altman in late July said developers might need to voluntarily tap the brakes.
More than 1,000 employees at cutting-edge AI companies including Amodei signed a petition calling on the US government to help “deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”
OpenAI had revealed that during testing, AI models broke out of their confined environment, connected to the Internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a site developers use to store and share code. In that incident and others, the blame was placed on AI agents, which are software programs that can carry out tasks without constant supervision by humans.
“Dario is right,” Musk wrote on social media, as Altman said: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.”
Last week, Coxon, 27, sounded the alarm after spending the past three years pretraining AI models — first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach. Pretraining is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data.
“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said on Tuesday last week.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he said in a social media post.
Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI’s capabilities exceed human intelligence.
Amodei cautioned that the Hugging Face incident should not be dismissed as a one-off.
“A swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack and that were unrelated to the task at hand,” he said.
“Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in six-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire Internet,” potentially generating hundreds of billions of dollars in damage, he added.
