Chinese microdrama distorts history: academic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:41:43 UTC
01:41:43 KST

A Taiwanese academic yesterday slammed Chinese drama Emperor Jiaqing and the Journey to Taiwan (嘉慶君遊臺灣), saying it distorted history and promoted a cross-strait unification narrative.
The microdrama is funded and presented by Jingcai Taiwan, a Chinese state-run media platform of the Beijing Municipal Taiwan Affairs Office, with its premiere held in Beijing on Friday last week.
The Taiwanese academic, specializing in Qing and Taiwan history, said on condition of anonymity that historical records clearly show that during the more than 200 years of Qing rule over Taiwan, no Qing emperor, including Emperor Jiaqing (嘉慶), ever set foot in the nation.
Photo: Screen grab from Pekingimage’s X account
The folktale, which circulated in Taiwan in the 19th century, was similar to Chinese legends such as “Emperor Zhengde’s Tour of Jiangnan” (正德皇帝遊江南) and “Qianlong’s Tour of Jiangnan” (乾隆下江南). At their core, the stories were fictional fantasies and a form of psychological compensation born out of authoritarian rule, repression and the frustrations of the era, they said.
Taiwanese in the 19th century created the story of Emperor Jiaqing traveling secretly to Taiwan mainly because the Beijing-based Qing Dynasty adopted a repressive policy that prioritized guarding against Taiwan over governing Taiwan, the academic said.
At the time, the Qing court regarded Taiwan as a hotspot of rebellion and strictly restricted cross-strait travel with a ban on bringing family to Taiwan, as the nation was primarily populated by remnants of the previous dynasty, they said.
That resulted in severe gender imbalance and many displaced people, the academic said.
The situation was compounded by exorbitant taxation for Taiwan, exclusion of Taiwanese from official positions and the deployment of garrison forces using only troops from China’s Fujian or Guangdong provinces, they said.
The populace had no choice but to pin their hopes on the imaginary arrival of a savior monarch, they said, adding that the folktale was not only a psychological compensation during years of hardships, but a silent indictment and satire of the local officials’ tyranny.
It is not a story that sings the glory of the ruler, they said.
The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) misrepresented the folktale out of the historical context and framed it as “Taiwanese longing for the grace of the Chinese emperor,” the academic said.
That reflects China’s feudal patriarchal mindset and “celestial empire” arrogance, they added.
The CCP is naive to believe that such a soap opera would evoke the feeling of “shared ancestry” among Taiwanese, the academic said.
China’s attempt to use the micro drama to bring the two sides of the Strait closer would only backfire, the scholar said.
The political stunt not only reopens the wounds of discriminatory treatment and unequal policies imposed on Taiwan by China’s central authorities throughout history, but also demonstrates to the international community and the Taiwanese public that Beijing neither understands Taiwan’s history nor the mindset and democratic values of modern Taiwanese society, they said.
Taiwan’s growing defense preparations might be sending a stronger signal to the US than to Beijing, highlighting the need for Taipei to tailor its deterrence efforts to different audiences, a US security academic said yesterday. Stanford University Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies fellow Oriana Skylar Mastro made the comment during a Taipei Security Dialogue panel examining lessons Taiwan could draw from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. Mastro said she was impressed by Taiwan’s increased defense spending, emphasis on asymmetric capabilities and efforts to prepare society for conflict, but questioned whom those initiatives were influencing. She said when she asked

Taiwan does not need a fleet capable of competing with the Chinese navy for traditional control of the Taiwan Strait, but rather “sea denial” capabilities that would prevent China from freely using the waterway, Taiwanese aerospace and security expert Holmes Liao

NexCOBOT Co (創博) expects robust growth in its artificial intelligence (AI) controller business this year and next year, as partnerships across a range of robotics applications begin to bear fruit, chairman Clement Lin (林茂昌) said in an interview with the Taipei Times on Monday last week.
NexCOBOT is a robotics subsidiary of industrial PC maker Nexcom International Co (新漢), where Lin also serves as chairman.
AI controller shipments are expected to exceed 1,000 units and account for about 20 percent of NexCOBOT’s controller sales next year, as the company has received orders for AI controllers for wheeled robots with humanoid upper bodies, he said, adding that the company plans to ship hundreds of units from the second half of this year through early next year.
Photo: Meryl Kao, Taipei Times
Controller sales — including those for computer numerical control equipment, industrial robotic arms, collaborative robots and AI robotics — are expected to account for more than 20 percent of NexCOBOT’s total revenue next year, he said.
The company’s AI controllers made with higher-end Nvidia Corp computing modules could cost US$5,000 to US$8,000 per unit, significantly higher than standard controllers, which are priced at about US$1,000 each, Lin said.
NexCOBOT expects to ship about 500 advanced AI controllers based on Nvidia’s IGX Thor platform next year, up from several hundred units this year, he said.
Quadruped robot dogs and wheeled robots with humanoid upper bodies are likely to begin volume production earlier than fully bipedal humanoid robots, Lin said.
Nexcom, the Industrial Technology Research Institute and Compal Electronics Inc (仁寶) demonstrated a robot dog solution in July, drawing the interest of firefighting agencies, while wheeled robots are generally more practical than bipedal humanoids in factories, he said.
Fully bipedal humanoid robots still require major advances in vision-language-action models and multimodal AI, Lin said, adding that meaningful progress was unlikely for at least another three years.
To address the complexity of humanoid robots’ more than 20 joints, as well as the demands that heat dissipation, wiring and real-time synchronization place on AI controllers, NexCOBOT earlier this year introduced a “four-in-one” AI control platform that combines motion control, functional safety, AI computing and cybersecurity, Lin said.
With the four-in-one platform, NexCOBOT adds its own I/O baseboards, communications, and control hardware and software to computing modules from Nvidia and Intel Corp, enabling components such as joints, vision modules, dexterous hands, thermal-imaging systems and predictive maintenance tools to be directly integrated and operated together, he said.
“While industrial PC suppliers typically provide only graphics cards or hardware baseboards, NexCOBOT aims to offer a more complete ‘last-mile’ solution to help system makers develop and deploy robots faster,” Lin said.
Last month, NexCOBOT unveiled its “RoboWIZ AI Robot Open Platform” to bring together dozens of robotics ecosystem partners and support the development of humanoid, quadruped and dual-arm robots, while allowing customers to focus on robot design, dynamic balancing, application development and commercialization, thereby shrinking the time to market, Lin said.
Taiwanese robotics partners mainly supply cameras, thermal-imaging and predictive maintenance technologies, while functional safety joints, complete 3D vision modules and advanced dexterous hands still require the support of European and US partners, he said.
NexCOBOT works with motion control supplier Synapticon GmbH on developing functional safety joints, he added.
Nexcom plans to establish RoboWiz hubs in Taipei, Taichung and at the Curiosity Lab in Atlanta, Georgia, to serve robot system makers and engage with local ecosystem partners, Lin said.
The company also aims to leverage Taiwan’s information and communications technology integration capabilities to expand AI robotics supply chain cooperation and position the country as a key partner for US robotics development and non-China supply chains, he said.

All eyes on US Fed to tackle high inflation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:41:39 UTC
01:41:39 KST

The US Federal Reserve goes into a key rate-setting meeting this week with markets expecting policymakers to pull the trigger on a rate hike to tackle persistently high inflation — and analysts said central bank chief Kevin Warsh’s credibility is on the line.
The world’s largest economy has been dealing with years of higher-than-target inflation, and prices have surged in the wake of US President Donald Trump’s war on Iran, his signature tariff policies and the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
The Fed has held rates steady since January, choosing to wait to gauge the effects of energy price shocks and let the tariffs’ effects on prices ripple through the economy.
Photo: Reuters
However, over the past few weeks, several Fed policymakers — including Warsh — have hinted that if inflation does not show clear signs of slowing, the central bank would have to act by raising interest rates.
On Friday, new data on consumer inflation for last month showed it remaining steady at 3.4 percent — no change from the month before, but still well above the Fed’s long-term two percent target.
Market expectations of a 25-basis-point rate hike on Wednesday surged in the wake of the data, with the probability at more than 85 percent, the FedWatch said.
The Fed last raised rates three years ago, when it was fighting surging inflation in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. They stand at between 3.50 and 3.75 percent.
Warsh was appointed by Trump and analysts say this is his first real test since taking office: Would the Fed raise rates to combat inflation, or hold steady in line with what the White House prefers?
“This is the test. This is what comes with that job, and now he has to decide how to handle it,” Brookings Institution senior fellow David Wessel said. “He’s either going to completely disappoint the markets, or he runs the risk that he’s going to start to anger Donald Trump.”
The Fed’s Federal Open Market Committee, with its 12 voting members, would announce its decision after a two-day meeting on Wednesday at 2pm.
“It’s quite likely that the Fed will raise interest rates next week,” New Century Advisors chief economist Claudia Sahm said.
“It’s not a done deal,” she said. “This is a difficult decision for them to make.”
The Fed could hold rates steady rather than raise them, but it would have to explain its decision clearly to markets, Sahm said.
“If they surprise markets and they can’t explain why they’re surprising markets, then Wednesday afternoon will be pretty messy,” she said.
Warsh has advocated in the past for lower interest rates due to expected productivity gains from AI technology, but in recent weeks he has doubled down on the Fed’s mandate to bring inflation down.
“There’s always been this doubt about whether Kevin Warsh is going to be like his predecessors and do what’s right for the economy, even if it’s politically inconvenient,” Wessel said. “If he raises rates now and Trump goes ballistic, he will have established his credibility as an independent Fed chair for the rest of his term.”

ESG as corporate responsibility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:41:37 UTC
01:41:37 KST

Over the past year, many friends of mine who are responsible for sustainability at listed and over-the-counter companies have been extremely busy. They have shouldered a major responsibility: preparing sustainability reports and compiling materials for related assessments. The Taiwan Stock Exchange and Taipei Exchange have established a mechanism to evaluate companies’ environmental, social and governance (ESG) commitments, with the results expected to be announced by the end of April next year.
The heavy rains that have caused flooding and other damage in central and southern Taiwan in the past few days and weeks have prompted me to think about what companies can do. Specifically, how they can put their profits and resources to good use and support disaster relief efforts, thereby fulfilling their social responsibilities. ESG assessments generally assign different weights to each of its three evaluating principles; many frameworks heavily weight governance, followed by social factors, with environmental risks coming in last. There has also been a shift away from institutional questions and toward focusing on results.
There is good reason for governance to carry the greatest weight, as it is the foundation of sound corporate management.
However, what I would suggest is that when disasters occur as a result of extreme weather under climate change, the weightings for the environmental and social metrics could be adjusted upward. This would give companies greater incentives to contribute to disaster relief and have their efforts to be reflected in ESG assessment scores.
The purpose of ESG assessments is to encourage companies to improve their governance, fulfill their social responsibilities and do more to protect the environment. Dynamically adjusting the weightings of the three dimensions in response to changing circumstances, is practical and worthwhile. Such flexibility could be a boon for corporate performance and social wellbeing.
Cheng Ming-te is a professor at the Taipei City University of Science and Technology’s department of business administration.

EDITORIAL: Puma Shen’s waves gaining size
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:41:36 UTC
01:41:36 KST

With candidate registration for this year’s local elections closed on Sept. 4 and the elections less than 80 days away, Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) rapidly growing popularity has become the focus of political talk shows and online discussions over the past week, heating up the mayoral election race in Taipei.
Local media headlines and political pundits have picked up his supporters’ slogan “ocean current” (洋流) — a play on the last character of Shen’s name, which literally means “ocean” (洋), and the character (流), which can mean “current,” “flow” or “trend” — to describe the nationwide attention Shen has been attracting recently.
Shen on Wednesday last week launched a Taipei residents’ participation platform on Line called “Mayor, listen to me” (市長，你給我聽好了), which allows users to leave messages regarding their municipal concerns and see other users’ messages. In just two days, the platform received more than 30,000 messages, which Shen’s team are analyzing and would respond to with policy proposals next month.
The platform is a stark contrast with the style of Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安), who often evades questions or gives vague or deflective answers, not only toward questions by reporters or scrutiny from DPP city councilors. Taipei City Councilor Chin Huei-chu (秦慧珠) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) last week said Chiang had ignored her messages for two months after she publicly criticized a city official in July.
During Shen’s near-daily campaigning, visiting parks and traditional markets in the morning and occasionally night markets and shopping districts in the evening, his visit to Shihpai Hub, a shopping area in Beitou District (北投), on Thursday last week was described by local media as a political “sensation,” because the street was teeming with supporters as if it were the eve of the election.
The same day, Shen did a radio interview with prolific television producer Wang Wei-chung (王偉忠), who is widely seen as “pan-blue,” during which they had a relaxed and fluid conversation about municipal issues and various topics. The interview drew more than 1.3 million views in less than three days. Shen’s fluent and confident responses earned him praise from viewers, especially compared with Chiang’s interview with Wang four years ago when he was running for mayor. Chiang’s video has only garnered about 220,000 views after four years.
The interview was seen as a successful breakthrough for Shen in reaching out to non-DPP supporters. It gained even more attention after pan-blue supporters questioned why Wang did not interview Chiang, and the radio station responded that it had reached out to the mayor several times, but received no reply — reinforcing the impression that he often dodges questions.
Several political commentators said they saw a critical turning point in the Taipei mayoral election through Shen’s performance last week, indicating that he has genuinely become a “challenger” that poses a real threat to incumbent Chiang.
Taipei’s voter structure has long been characterized as a pan-blue stronghold, typically leaning toward the conservative KMT, so for the first half of the year, Chiang was expected to easily win re-election even without putting in extra campaigning effort. He was confident enough to travel outside of Taipei to stump for other KMT candidates and refused to endorse the party’s allied Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) city councilor candidates, prompting complaints from TPP supporters about the mayor’s “arrogant” attitude.
However, in the face of the “ocean current,” and with Chiang knee-deep in controversies — construction safety issues, an unsolved rat problem (which regained attention after a rat interrupted a baseball game at Taipei Dome on Wednesday last week), child abuse cases and reports of students with stomach problems after eating school lunches, as well as allegations of special treatment for his son in securing a US exchange program slot — and his apparent inability to respond to the city’s problems, people are seeing an opportunity for change in Shen.
Local media reported that the DPP’s internal polls have shown Shen’s approval rating is catching up with Chiang’s, with a gap of less than 10 percentage points left. Chiang might be feeling the pressure, as he appeared on stage at TPP Taipei City Councilor Chang Chih-hao’s (張志豪) event on Saturday, hinting that he needs to secure TPP supporters’ votes.
With about two months until election day, whether Shen’s approval rate can continue to grow depends on whether he can continue to find ways to make his ideas reach independent voters and even pan-blue voters, and if he can accurately grasp residents’ main concerns through his Line platform and canvassing events and come up with convincing and actionable solutions.

Hsiao visited Italy to attend the Second Ventotene European Conference for Freedom and Democracy on the Italian island of Ventotene at the invitation of event organizers, despite strong protests from Beijing.
In an interview with the Central News Agency on the sidelines of the event on Saturday, Picierno, the conference’s main initiator, described Hsiao as a role model.
Photo: CNA
“I believe the world needs the courage of women; and throughout history, many women have changed the course of history through their determination,” Picierno said.
“As authoritarian regimes threaten our democracies, we have an even greater need for courageous women like Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim,” she added.
Hsiao fights for human rights and women’s rights, and is a “staunch pro-democracy activist who inspires freedom-loving women across the world,” Picierno said.
“We must recognize this and send a clear message: Women who cherish freedom and democracy are determined to stand united,” she said.
It is rare for Taiwan’s senior leaders, including the president or vice president, to visit countries with which Taipei does not have official diplomatic ties.
The trip was Hsiao’s second visit to a European country that recognizes Beijing instead of Taipei since she took office in May 2024. Her first visit was in November last year to Brussels to address a meeting of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China.
The Italy trip once again infuriated the Chinese government, prompting Beijing to lodge protests with Italy and the EU.
Asked if she was concerned about her personal safety from China, Picierno said she had already been under the protection of Italian security details for more than a year due to threats against her from Russia and other authoritarian regimes.
“I do not fear threats from autocratic regimes; I will face them unwaveringly, because I know that every generation has its own battles to fight,” Picierno said.
Picierno said the history of the EU was made possible “by courageous and wise statesmen-predecessors who paid a price for it.”
“Defending democracy is not always easy or a given, nor is it something one can do while keeping one’s hands clean; it always requires courage and determination,” she said. “The clear message we are sending from Ventotene is that we do not fear threats or intimidation; the European Parliament’s agenda is determined neither in Moscow nor in Beijing.”
Picierno said she believes there is absolutely “no room for compromise with authoritarian regimes that violate human rights.”
As authoritarian regimes such as Russia, China and North Korea have aligned, freedom-loving people around the globe must unite to “champion the language of freedom and democracy,” she said.
Picierno announced on Friday that she had accepted Hsiao’s invitation to visit Taiwan in the near future.
She said on Saturday that planning for the visit would begin in the coming weeks.
“Our collaboration — between myself and the vice president of Taiwan — is just beginning; there is much to be done and much to be discussed in the future,” she added.

Israeli-made Gaza film wins Venice jury prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:41:33 UTC
01:41:33 KST

A chilling new documentary about Israel’s artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted killing of civilians in Gaza by two Israeli directors on Saturday won a special jury prize at the Venice Film Festival.
NAZA, by Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, had been tipped by some critics for the top Golden Lion prize for best film after a record-breaking 25-minute ovation at its premiere on Thursday.
Receiving the award, Abraham said that in the 10 days since the festival began, “Israel killed six Palestinian children in Gaza at least.”
Photo: AFP
“The Israeli intelligence officers we spoke with talked to us how this mass killing is systemic: not by accident, but by design, actions of murder and policies that are based on the total dehumanization of Palestinians,” he told the audience.
The special jury prize is given out each year by the jury to recognize an outstanding work, but it is below the Golden and Silver Lions in the pecking order.
Abraham and Szor last year won an Oscar for their film No Other Land about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
In their Gaza film, the directing pair used conversations with 24 different Israeli military or intelligence whistle-blowers who spoke on condition that their identities be protected.
The 80-minute film left many audience members stunned, with interviewees describing how they felt like they worked in a killing “factory” or a lethal video game while using Israel’s AI-powered targeting systems to bombard Gaza.
It was described as an “urgent, gut-punch” by film magazine Screen, while The Hollywood Reporter said it inspired “outrage” and “most certainly disgust, on a profound level, for the current Israeli regime.”
The film was the only documentary in Venice’s main competition.
Abraham called it “really, really, especially important for us that Israelis watch this film.”
“It’s our country that is doing these crimes,” he said.
Israel’s bombardment of Gaza has left about 73,500 Palestinians dead and 174,500 wounded since October 2023, according to Gaza’s Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the UN deems reliable.
The pounding of the territory followed an attack on Israel by Hamas militants on Oct. 7, 2023, that resulted in the death of 1,219 people, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official figures.
The Israeli military has criticized the use of anonymous testimonies in the film, saying on Friday the identities of the whistle-blowers “cannot be verified.”
Israel denies deliberately targeting civilians.
Asked by a journalist following the awards ceremony about the military’s reaction, Abraham responded that “it seems like an attempt to not face reality.”
Abraham defended the film’s reporting, done in partnership with Britain’s The Guardian newspaper, calling it “rigorous” and its findings reported by other mainstream journalists as well. He added that the filmmakers had received threats, but did not go into more detail.

Falling birthrates: cash cannot buy belonging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:41:32 UTC
01:41:32 KST

Why are people in one of the world’s richest, safest countries having so few children? Singapore is asking that question. In 2000, its fertility rate matched the US’ at 1.6 children per woman. By last year, it had dropped to 0.87 — almost half the US rate. Singapore’s leaders, worried about population collapse, have reached for the checkbook. Each child, including those born to unmarried parents, would get US$55,000 in government support by the time they turn 17. Yet a quarter of Singaporeans say they do not intend to have children. Wealth and security, clearly, do not guarantee more babies.
UN data shows that global fertility fell from 5.3 births per woman in 1963 to 2.2 in 2023 — but this masks a growing divide. In some poor sub-Saharan African countries there are around six births per woman. Compare this with England and Wales, where the figure is just 1.39. More than half of the world — including a billion women in India and China — have a fertility rate below the global 2.1 “replacement level” needed to sustain populations without migration.
However, even in poor countries with high mortality rates and consequently higher replacement rates, births outpace deaths. In Nigeria, for example, the fertility rate of 4.4 exceeds its replacement rate of 2.6 children per woman.
To understand this phenomenon, the UN asked 100,000 18 to 39-year-olds from 73 nations their views on relationships and having children. The results, released in July, were striking: Two-thirds said they want to marry or live with a partner. Those who did not have children overwhelmingly wanted them. Yet about a quarter of those aged 25 to 39 said they wanted a partner, but were single and not dating — a status reported more by men than women. More than half said the biggest barriers to a durable relationship were economic constraints. Young people want partnership and parenthood, but questioned achieving the “emotional and financial” stability needed for a shared life.
The Nordic region — consisting of five states and three territories — is viewed as a good place to have children thanks to generous parental leave and subsidized childcare. Yet fertility rates have fallen by up to third since 2010, against 12 percent across the EU. The Polish sociologist Anna Gromada wrote that despite her country’s economic success, its fertility rate was 1.05. While the state transfers cash worth 10 percent of the median wage for every child born each month, Poland’s population is shrinking. Gromada argues that people are not just deciding against children; many never form lasting relationships in which the question arises. Almost half of under-30s are single. Cash paid after a family exists cannot create the togetherness needed for a family in the first place.
The world is not running out of people. The UN expects today’s 8.2 billion people to become 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s. What is emerging is a demographic divide between ageing, shrinking rich societies and population growth in poorer ones. Getting richer seems to mean lower fertility. The baby bust might indicate a wealthy country’s failure to reproduce itself socially as well as biologically. People ask not only whether they can afford children, but whether they fit in, can trust each other and believe in a future. This loss of confident belonging poses questions that politics across the rich world has yet to tackle.

Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) yesterday encouraged newlyweds to have children while attending a mass wedding held by Chunghwa Telecom in Taipei, where 72 couples were married.
Cho, who served as a witness at the ceremony at the Grand Hotel, thanked the newlyweds for taking a step that could help Taiwan “address its demographic challenges,” referring to the country’s low birthrate.
Ministry of the Interior data showed that Taiwan’s fertility rate fell to 0.695 last year — one of the lowest in the world — while the number of births dropped for a 10th consecutive year to a record-low 107,812.
Photo: CNA
While encouraging the couples to have children, Cho added that childbirth remains a personal choice.
“Marriage is everyone’s right, and having children is everyone’s choice. It is definitely not a responsibility or obligation,” he said.
Cho urged couples planning to start families to use government support, highlighting plans for a NT$5,000 monthly child-rearing allowance starting next year, expanded childcare services and measures aimed at easing housing and education costs.
Cho said he hoped state-owned enterprises would organize more large-scale mass weddings, adding that Taiwan Power Co is planning to hold one as well.
At least one person in each of the 72 newlywed couples works for Chunghwa Telecom, and in five cases, both spouses were employees of Taiwan’s largest telecom.
Chunghwa Telecom chairman Alex Chien (簡志誠) said the company began holding mass weddings in 1963 and has held them almost every year since, with about 800 couples taking part since 2010.
Chien said he hoped the couples would “have children soon.”
He highlighted company measures to support employees starting families, including an NT$80,000 childbirth subsidy, a seven-hour workday with eight hours’ pay for employees with children younger than six, and 18 workplace childcare facilities nationwide.
Among the newlyweds was 44-year-old senior engineer Lin Kuan-nan (林冠男), who said he and his wife plan to have a child.
A 19-year Chunghwa Telecom employee, Lin said the planned NT$5,000 monthly allowance had “some appeal,” but added that the amount would “definitely not be enough” amid rising living costs.
“Of course, the more the better,” he said, adding that he hoped the government could provide additional subsidies.
Dino Chen, a senior engineer who has worked at Chunghwa Telecom for five years, said he and his wife plan to have a child in a year or two, but added that while the government’s available support showed “sincerity,” it remained insufficient.
“Once you take on a mortgage, you might have to pay NT$20,000 to NT$30,000 a month,” the 30-year-old said, identifying housing as their “main” concern.
While Chen said that “there is definitely pressure,” he said his wife works too and that they share the mortgage payments, easing the financial burden.

====================================================================================================

AfD victory in Germany  is great news for Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:41:29 UTC
01:41:29 KST

To understand the geopolitical importance of last weekend’s election breakthrough for Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the small state of Saxony-Anhalt, pay attention to the apparently unrelated commentary from the Kremlin that emerged around it.
On Sept. 6, Germany’s hard-right populist party won with 44 percent of the vote, just shy of the majority needed to run the state on its own. Like many of its ideological counterparts across Europe, the AfD is pro-Russia, believing it shares a common enemy with Moscow in Europe’s liberal establishment. These parties are natural allies for Moscow as it tries to secure its best hope for winning the Ukraine war: persuading Europeans to halt the military and financial support that sustains Kyiv’s defense.
The most compelling argument to achieve this goal involves stoke fears among European voters that their governments, far from halting a threat from the east by backing Ukraine, are instead inviting war with a nuclear superpower.
Illustration: Yusha
Consider Russia’s take on the armed drone discovered at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle airport. As my colleague Andreas Kluth pointed out, it took about a month for the German government to finger Moscow for planning the attack and hit back — with a feather. It closed a Russian consulate and cultural center and, along with several other European countries, called in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s ambassadors for a chat.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov called this milquetoast response “kind of the beginning of a real war,” in remarks that the Russian state-run Vesti TV station posted on Telegram the day of the Saxony-Anhalt vote. Denying Russian involvement with the drone, he said Berlin’s response reminded him of World War II, when Nazi Germany pulled its diplomats out of Russia just before invading. “They want a war once again,” he said.
They do not — and Lavrov is well aware of that. Germany has no nuclear weapons and little air defense, artillery, drones or deployable combat troops, so it would never choose to fight Russia. He understands that Adolf Hitler’s emptying of diplomatic missions in a country he was about to invade has the polar opposite implications to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s shuttering of offices on his own territory.
In reality, the failed drone plot was just one part of a wide-ranging Russian sabotage offensive, while the German response was symbolic, designed to avoid escalation. Lavrov’s hyperbole is disinformation aimed at fueling German fears of war and amplifying the messaging of Kremlin-friendly parties such as the AfD.
This campaign is systemic and not limited to Lavrov. So, when the US flew launch systems capable of firing Tomahawk cruise missiles to Norway for exercises last month, Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia would have to respond in kind to this new security threat. Sure enough, a few days later Ukrainian intelligence reported that a Russian unit armed with Oreshnik missiles was on its way to eastern Belarus, close to NATO borders.
The Oreshnik is a nuclear-capable, hypersonic ballistic missile with a range up to around 5,500km that can put much of Europe at risk. Tomahawks are a much slower, non-nuclear-capable cruise missile that would have limited reach inside Russia from where the exercise took place between the Norwegian coast and an island halfway to Greenland. No Tomahawks were used — this was a 10-day experiment to establish whether the launchers could be flown to Europe for use, if needed.
The irony here is that Russia’s security situation has indeed worsened, but entirely as a result of its own actions. In 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea, citing the threat from an expanding NATO, no such threat existed. NATO had agreed in 1996 not to station bases on the territories of its new Eastern European members, and did not until 2017, in response to Russia’s actions. Likewise, at the time of Crimea’s annexation and for nine months of the war that followed, Ukraine’s constitution banned NATO membership; Ukrainians did not want it. Europe’s defense budgets were still declining. Only a year earlier, the US had pulled its last active-duty tanks from the continent.
However, while there was no buildup of capabilities for Russian generals to interpret as a potential threat in 2014, today there is. Following Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Finland and Sweden joined NATO. European — and in particular, German — defense budgets reversed their declines. US tanks are back in Europe and there are permanent NATO military bases on the territory of eastern alliance members, NATO membership being a key goal of the Ukrainian state that has wide popular support.
At home, Putin treats this reversal as proof of NATO’s aggression, allowing him to argue to Russian parents that they are sending their children to die in Ukraine not to capture a few depressed mining towns, but in defense of the Motherland against yet another existential threat from the West, akin to the Napoleonic and Nazi invasions. In Europe, Russia and its (sometimes paid) friends in populist parties such as the AfD portray support for Ukraine and efforts to rebuild lost NATO defenses as provocations that risk World War III and potential nuclear annihilation.
No one in NATO has any interest in attacking Russia, but these fabrications make for powerful messages and they are paying dividends for the Kremlin. The AfD’s success in Saxony-Anhalt would not be its last. Other European populist parties could also succeed at the polls over the coming year, undermining support for financing Ukraine and sanctioning Russia. France, where the far-right National Rally’s Marine Le Pen leads the field ahead of presidential elections next spring, offers the biggest potential prize. This week, her party’s president Jordan Bardella said it was time to stop paying for Kyiv’s defense.
This kind of stance and the AfD’s weekend victory explain Putin’s continued unwillingness to compromise in peace talks, despite the growing economic and political costs of the war at home. They encourage his belief that he is winning the information war in Europe and that, if he waits a little longer, a new political configuration would hand him Ukraine, together with a divided West and a broken NATO alliance. It brings a whole new meaning to the Soviet-era name given to Moscow’s fans in the West: useful idiots.
Marc Champion is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Europe, Russia and the Middle East. He was previously Istanbul bureau chief for the Wall Street Journal. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Ryan Hass On Taiwan: Taiwan’s Inside-Out Paradox
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:41:28 UTC
01:41:28 KST

Taiwan’s domestic political situation is following recognizable political rhythms, while the international environment surrounding Taiwan is undergoing a major transformation.
Within Taiwan, there are ongoing battles between the legislative and executive branches over the budget, and between cities and the central government over resources. Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved.
Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It is one of the world’s strongest-performing advanced economies and occupies a central position in critical technology supply chains. In fact, Taiwan’s economic performance is so strong that the government is planning to return some of the wealth to its people. This is a powerful contrast with virtually every other major economy in the world today, all of which face fiscal constraints.
There are, of course, continuing challenges inside Taiwan. The benefits of the AI boom are not being felt evenly across society, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises and the employees who power them. Partisan gridlock continues to constrain progress in strengthening Taiwan’s self-defense. And prices are rising faster than wages for many people, causing frustration and pessimism about the future.
At the same time, Taiwan’s civil society remains vibrant, its independent media serves as a check on government, and public opinion remains solidly in favor of preserving the cross-Strait status quo. In other words, Taiwan’s political system is engaged in familiar debates. The world around Taiwan is not.
The scale and speed of change in the international system today are probably greater than during any period since the immediate aftermath of World War II. During that moment, the United States organized international efforts to establish the United Nations, rebuild Europe and Japan, and forge a trade order that began in the free half of the world and later spread to cover the globe.
Now, many global trendlines are moving in the opposite direction.
The United Nations is losing relevance, America’s global alliance network is losing cohesion, and America itself is acting more like a 19th-century imperialist than a 20th-century leader of the free world. The United States retains extraordinary power — militarily, technologically, financially — but it is losing followership on the world stage.
Now that the American people have elected President Donald Trump twice, countries around the world are increasingly concluding that Trump is not a strange passing phenomenon in America, but rather a part of America’s political establishment. In other words, some version of America First will likely guide American foreign policy periodically for the foreseeable future, as power shifts back and forth between Democratic and Republican administrations. Even among Democrats, former President Joe Biden likely was the last of his kind. Future American leaders will not win elections by vowing to restore America to its former role in a world that no longer exists.
It now is broadly accepted that the post-World War II era of American global dominance, Pax Americana, is over. A debate is underway about what type of international order will come next. American foreign policy expert Hal Brands has presented three potential scenarios. The first is a revival of Cold War-style blocs, anchored by the United States and its partners on one side and China and its partners on the other. A second scenario is the emergence of spheres of influence, in which major powers dominate their respective neighborhoods and global rules give way to bargaining between great powers. A third scenario would be a more fragmented and fluid multipolar order, whereby middle powers exercise greater flexibility to build issue-based coalitions to address specific challenges, as opposed to fixed blocs.
Each of these futures would present Taiwan with different diplomatic, economic, and security challenges. Bloc competition would push Taiwan toward aligning with democratic partners and likely would shrink policy space for new approaches to cross-Strait relations. Spheres of influence would raise the risk of great power bargaining over Taiwan without Taiwan’s involvement. Multipolarity could create more opportunities for Taiwan to participate in different issue-based coalitions, but it also could lead to greater fragmentation and disorder.
Of these scenarios, spheres of influence hold the greatest risk for Taiwan. I view this as the least likely scenario, at least in Asia. China faces the least hospitable geography of any major power to assert dominance over its periphery. ASEAN exists to prevent such an outcome in Southeast Asia. In Northeast Asia, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan all have formidable capacity and will to protect their ability to pursue their respective interests.
Moreover, the world is on the cusp of being transformed by the AI revolution. As the world’s leading producer of advanced semiconductors, Taiwan will not simply be affected by the AI revolution; it will be shaping it. As AI diffuses and gains adoption around the world, it will transform how power is conceptualized and exercised. AI will not be confined by national boundaries. Embodied AI and related technologies will lower the cost of military technologies and make them more accessible to a wider array of actors. Already in Ukraine and Iran, significantly overmatched militaries are using AI-enabled drones and other technologies to hold off larger militaries. As AI-enabled weapons systems become more affordable and accessible, it could become costlier and riskier for countries to seek to militarily conquer others.
My point is not to suggest that I have a special window into the future. Nobody does. Rather, it is to observe that the world is undergoing a profound transformation before our eyes. This transformation will likely not play much of a role in the 9-in-1 elections this November, which understandably and appropriately will be centered around local issues. But it should spur a serious debate going forward. A central question for Taiwan’s leaders in 2028 and beyond is not merely how to win partisan battles or manage cross-Strait relations. It is how to make Taiwan more secure and prosperous in a transforming world.
Ryan Hass is a senior fellow, the Chen-Fu and Cecilia Yen Koo Chair in Taiwan Studies, and director of the China Center at the Brookings Institution.

GUIYANG, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- China broke the world record in the men's speed relay at the World Climbing Series Guiyang here on Sunday, taking gold medals in both men's and women's competitions on the final day.
With the two relay titles, China finished the three-day event with three golds, three silvers and one bronze across the men's and women's speed individual, mixed relay, and men's and women's speed relay events.
In the men's speed relay, China's first team of Zhao Yicheng and Ling Yongzhi clocked 9.91, 9.75, 9.58 and 9.67 seconds across four rounds. They matched the previous world record of 9.75 seconds, set by Zhao and Long Jianguo, before breaking it with 9.58 seconds in the semifinal.
China's second team of Shi Zechuan and Li Xu also improved round by round, recording 10.77, 10.56 and 10.18 seconds in the first three rounds to reach the final. Facing their strong compatriots in the final, Shi and Li posted their best time of 9.87 seconds.
"Actually, I am still very happy," Zhao said after the race. He noted that he had not performed well in the individual speed event earlier, but on Sunday night, despite some pressure, he was more focused and relaxed. "Eventually, everything fell into place naturally."
In the women's speed relay, eight teams competed in the final round. China's second team of Qin Yumei and Wang Shengyan was eliminated by South Korea's first team in the first round due to a mistake.
China's first team, composed of Fan Jingyue and Guizhou native Zhang Shaoqin, clocked 13.94, 14.81 and 13.18 seconds in three rounds, defeating Japan's first team, South Korea's first team and Spain's first team in succession.
Although they won the title, their road to victory was far from smooth. In the semifinal, they made mistakes and fell behind, but fought back to reach the final and seal the championship.
"Trust your teammates, do your best, and climb every try well," Fan said of the key to victory. Zhang attributed the win to local fans who came to support her. "I am extremely happy to have won a precious relay gold medal as a local athlete in my hometown. Thank you, fellow villagers for your encouragement and support." Zhang said. ■

Antonelli wins F1 Spanish GP after Norris setback

By F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
BEIJING, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli claimed his eighth Formula 1 victory of the season in Sunday's Spanish Grand Prix, capitalizing on a virtual safety car that cost Lando Norris the chance to become the first winner at Madrid's new Madring circuit.
Antonelli finished 4.3 seconds ahead of Red Bull's Max Verstappen, with Norris third after a badly timed virtual safety car and a slow pit stop transformed a race the McLaren driver had controlled from the start.
Norris had built a lead of more than six seconds by lap 13, with Antonelli struggling with front-left tyre graining, but the race changed when Lance Stroll crashed into the wall on lap 15.
The VSC was deployed moments after Norris had passed the pit entry, allowing several of his rivals to stop at reduced time cost. Norris had to complete another lap before pitting, and his problems were compounded by a seven-second stop that dropped him to fifth.
Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, who had started on hard tyres and did not stop under the VSC, inherited the lead ahead of Antonelli and Verstappen.
Leclerc's long first stint kept him at the front until lap 48, when he finally pitted and emerged fourth. That handed Antonelli the lead, and the Italian controlled the remaining laps to seal his eighth win of the campaign and extend his points lead over second-placed George Russell to 81.
"It was a very difficult race - not straightforward at all, especially trying to manage tyres," said Antonelli.
"I think today it's good to win but it doesn't feel as good because I think Lando today deserved the win but overall, we take it."
"Other than that, it was a very strong race, especially on the hard we had good pace. Now we have to keep pushing."
Behind him, Verstappen held off Norris in a late battle for second, although the Red Bull driver attracted the attention of race control after cutting the track while defending his position.
The outcome was particularly frustrating for Norris after an impressive recovery from a difficult buildup to the race.
The world champion had missed much of Friday's second practice because of a gearbox problem, forcing him to rely heavily on data gathered by teammate Oscar Piastri.
Despite that lack of track time, Norris took a surprise pole position by just 0.011 seconds from Antonelli, with Verstappen third.
Antonelli twice went off the track while attempting to pass Norris on the opening lap, briefly allowing Verstappen into second. The Dutchman was subsequently told to surrender positions after gaining an advantage off the circuit, before repassing Lewis Hamilton for third on lap five.
Hamilton's race quickly unraveled after he reported that his brake pedal was going long. He fell from fourth to 10th before retiring on lap seven, telling Ferrari he had no brakes.
Despite pre-race predictions of an incident-filled Grand Prix, prompted by driver concerns over the Madring's difficult corner entries, close walls and limited overtaking opportunities, the race's only intervention came as a result of Stroll's accident.
Leclerc finished fourth ahead of Russell and Liam Lawson, while Franco Colapinto took seventh. Piastri took eighth, with Arvid Lindblad and Nico Hulkenberg completing the top 10.
The next round of the 2026 Formula 1 season is the Azerbaijan Grand Prix around the streets of Baku on September 26. ■

South Africa confirms herpesvirus most likely cause of 2,600km sardine die-off
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
00:35:07 CST
01:35:07 KST

CAPE TOWN, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- South Africa's environment department said Sunday that a herpesvirus was the most likely cause of widespread sardine mortality spanning 2,600 km of coastline, as investigations into the event continue.
In a statement, the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE) said laboratory testing had confirmed pilchard herpesvirus (PHV) in affected sardines from both the Western Cape and the Gqeberha area, supporting a link between the mortality events.
The deaths were first reported in the Western Cape in late July and later extended eastward along the coast. Similar strandings have been reported in Namibia, although laboratory comparisons are still needed to determine whether they are linked.
The department said the reported locations span about 2,600 km, but mortality was not recorded continuously along the entire stretch. It has received no further reports of dead or dying sardines since Sept. 3, and no strandings have been reported along the KwaZulu-Natal coast.
"Taken together, the consistent detection of high levels of PHV in affected sardines, its confirmation in Western and Eastern Cape samples, and the observed mortality pattern indicate that PHV is the most likely primary cause," the DFFE said.
Investigations have not supported harmful algae or the marine biotoxins screened for as the primary cause, although oceanographic and other environmental conditions cannot yet be excluded as contributing stressors.
"The event cannot yet be regarded as concluded," the department said.
The scale of the mortality remains uncertain. Preliminary estimates depend on assumptions about fish density, the extent of affected coastal areas and the degree to which local observations can be extrapolated.
The DFFE's Small Pelagic Scientific Working Group found no evidence that the mortality had reduced the sardine population enough to warrant a complete closure of the fishery, but recommended a temporary precautionary limitation on catches.
The department said there was also no evidence showing when or how PHV reached South African waters, and no basis for attributing its origin to any particular country, company or product.
A hydroacoustic survey scheduled for October and November is expected to provide the first post-event estimate of sardine biomass and distribution.
PHV is not known to infect people, but the DFFE advised the public not to collect, eat, feed to animals or use as bait dead or dying sardines found near the shore.
It also said the mortality event does not provide a basis for discontinuing commercially produced canned sardines processed under regulatory oversight. ■

Russian athletes have appealed to international sporting and human rights bodies to help end World Athletics' ban on Russian competitors, arguing that more than four years of exclusion has deprived a generation of athletes of their careers.
In an open letter dated Sept. 10, seen by Reuters and addressed to the International Olympic Committee (IOC) Athletes' Commission, the IOC Advisory Committee on Human Rights and the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, the athletes said the continued ban was having a devastating impact.
“For us, this is not an abstract legal or political issue. Athletics is our life,” the letter said. “Four years is a long time in any life. In an athlete's life, it can be the most significant years.”
The World Athletics Council reaffirmed its decision to exclude Russian and Belarusian athletes from international competition on July 3, maintaining sanctions first imposed following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russian Athletics filed an appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport on July 9 challenging the decision and lodged a further appeal last month.
While World Athletics have been contacted for comment, federation president Sebastian Coe reiterated earlier on Sunday that the governing body's position had not changed ahead of the arbitration proceedings.
“This isn't about politics or passports. It's about the integrity of competition,” Coe told reporters at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest.
Coe said he recognized the importance of ultimately restoring full global participation in the sport.
“We want a full complement of people on a global level competing in our sport, and that has to be our overall objective,” he said. “Of course, it does.”
The Russian athletes argued that the federation's stance amounted to collective punishment and was out of step with other international sports federations, many of which have gradually reintroduced Russian and Belarusian athletes under neutral status.
The IOC provisionally lifted their suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee on July 8, marking a significant step toward the nation's reintegration into the Olympic fold ahead of the Los Angeles 2028 Games.
“Athletics remains one of the very limited exceptions where Russian athletes continue to face a full blanket exclusion,” the letter said.
The athletes said they had separately asked the Court of Arbitration for Sport on July 17 for permission to participate in the appeal proceedings, but had yet to receive a response.
They added the prolonged uncertainty was taking a personal toll.
“A legal or institutional process can continue for years. An athlete's career cannot,” they wrote.

The Guardian view on the government’s corporate reforms: entrenching neoliberalism, not ending it | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:30:07 UTC
01:30:07 KST

The question of what corporations are for is deeply political. In a 1970 article for the New York Times, Milton Friedman argued that the “social responsibility of business is to increase its profits”. The idea that CEOs should worry about providing good jobs was “pure and unadulterated socialism”, he wrote. Friedman and his fellow neoliberals saw companies as vehicles for enforcing their politics. Their ideas endured: UK bosses are now paid 130 times more than average workers.
Despite Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism, a 12-week consultation recently launched by his government risks entrenching it. The consultation was first announced as part of the Starmer government’s crusade against “red tape”. The average annual report for some businesses now runs to 98,000 words, and no doubt there are areas that could be simplified. But the consultation proposes removing vital information and presumes that company reports primarily serve shareholders, rather than other stakeholders. Both are steps in the wrong direction.
The consultation proposes scrapping information about the ratio between CEO and worker pay, removing a vital benchmark for inequality. British CEOs already earn 95% more on average than their European equivalents, and opaque pay ratios only serve their interests. There is scant evidence that higher-paid CEOs create more productive firms. As one Harvard Law School paper observed, pay ratios show how much a company invests in its “human capital”, and matter to workers and investors alike. Consumers who are made aware of this information are more likely to choose products from firms where the ratio is lower, encouraging those firms to address glaring pay disparities.
The consultation reflects the idea that inequality within a company is immaterial, a perplexing stance for a government concerned with fairness. It suggests removing annual shareholder votes on director pay, on the basis that votes are still required every three years. Annual votes were a modest attempt from Theresa May’s Tory government to tame the “unacceptable face of capitalism”, and the GC100 lobby group of corporate leaders has called to scrap them. By giving way, Labour would be removing a Tory policy designed to rein in boardroom greed.
It also proposes allowing companies to shift towards fully virtual annual general meetings. Companies have been holding online AGMs since Covid, and the government suggests these can improve “accessibility”. This is misguided: such meetings tend to be shorter, and prevent shareholders from asking as many questions. In-person AGMs are an imperfect form of accountability, but confrontation is easier to avoid when people aren’t in the room. Earlier this year, more than 50% of BP shareholders voted against a resolution to replace in-person AGMs with online meetings. Shareholders and climate groups argued these were a threat to accountability.
If reporting is too onerous, it would be better to start afresh with a new regime that recognised the interests of workers and society at large. Some voluntary initiatives, such as B Corporations, already take a more holistic approach to the information they disclose. Even better would be a requirement to include workers on company boards and provide greater transparency on pay levels, including that of all executives and workers paid less than the living wage. As the legal professor Katharina Pistor observes, corporate law is a tool that creates inequality. If the government wants to end neoliberalism, it should scrap this consultation and start again.

Libya: Haftar's military courts threaten dozens with execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:29:48 UTC
01:29:48 KST

Breadcrumb
Libya: Haftar's military courts threaten dozens with execution
At least 50 men sentenced to death in eastern Libya face imminent risk of execution following a series of firing squad killings carried out by military authorities, Amnesty International warned this week, raising renewed concerns over the use of military courts and the future of Libya's divided justice system.
The rights group said that military commander Khalifa Haftar's self-styled Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), which controls much of eastern and southern Libya, had resumed executions for the first time in the country since 2010.
According to Amnesty, at least 30 people have been executed since 23 August after what it described as grossly unfair, secretive and torture-tainted military trials, while dozens more remain under sentence of death.
Some of those convicted were accused of terrorism-related offences and assassinations linked to Libya's armed conflict between 2014 and 2018. Amnesty said several defendants alleged they had been tortured into making confessions later used as evidence against them.
The executions have drawn condemnation from Libyan and international human rights organisations, as well as Tripoli's internationally recognised Government of National Unity, which said trying civilians before military courts undermined due process and the rule of law.
"This isn't justice," Anas El-Gomati, founder and director of the Sadeq Institute, told The New Arab.
"Secret military trials, confessions taken under torture, and firing squads for a war that ended in 2018?"
El-Gomati said the executions highlighted the extent to which eastern Libya's military establishment had expanded beyond its traditional security role and into the judicial sphere.
"Libya's own Constitutional Court said civilians can't be tried this way. That ruling, of course, was ignored, which tells you where authority really sits," he said.
Libya's Constitutional Chamber has ruled that legislation allowing civilians to be prosecuted before military courts in terrorism and state security cases was unconstitutional, reaffirming that civilians should appear before ordinary civilian judges.
Despite that ruling, military prosecutions have continued in areas controlled by the LAAF.
For El-Gomati, the central issue is not simply whether military courts exist, but whether any meaningful separation remains between the institutions responsible for arrest, prosecution and judgment.
"Who arrests, who interrogates, who prosecutes, who judges, who fires? Same institution, every time. The LNA," he said, using another abbreviation for Haftar's forces.
"So perhaps think of it as expanding their influence into the justice sector, and gutting it of any neutrality, impartiality or independence. It literally serves the Haftars now."
The remarks come as international and Libyan officials continue efforts to reunify the country's fractured political and state institutions after more than a decade of division between rival administrations in the east and west.
Recent negotiations have focused on creating a single executive authority, unifying sovereign institutions and advancing preparations for long-delayed national elections.
However, El-Gomati argued that the existence of fundamentally different justice systems presented a deeper obstacle than disputes over ministries or government appointments.
"You can't merge two justice systems when one of them isn't one," he said.
"Budgets and ministries can be carved up or split between two families in a smoky room. Courts can't, because a court is a claim about whose law applies to whom."
He warned that reunification without meaningful judicial reform risked entrenching rather than dismantling the military justice apparatus operating in eastern Libya.
"Reunification on these terms wouldn't dissolve the military justice apparatus, it would nationalise it, so everyone lives under it."
Amnesty has called for an immediate halt to all planned executions and urged authorities in eastern Libya to quash death sentences issued after military proceedings that failed to meet international fair trial standards.
The organisation said Libya's return to executions marked a dangerous reversal after years in which the death penalty had remained largely suspended in practice, warning that irreversible punishments were being carried out amid continuing concerns over torture, secret trials and the absence of an independent judiciary.

Russian drones target Volyn, Rivne oblasts in rare mass attack in western Ukraine
Russian forces launched a mass drone attack on western Ukraine on Sept. 12, injuring at least five people in Volyn Oblast and causing power outages in neighboring Rivne Oblast, regional authorities said.
Both regions are located in Ukraine's northwest, far from the front lines, making them less frequent targets for Russian attacks.
The attack on Volyn Oblast lasted more than four hours, with more than 10 Russian unmanned aerial vehicles entering the region’s airspace, according to regional Governor Roman Romaniuk.
Most of the drones targeted the Kovel community, Romaniuk said. Five people were injured and received medical assistance. No deaths were reported.
Debris from one of the drones also struck a passenger train in Lutsk. Passengers had been evacuated before the impact, and no one aboard was injured, according to the governor.
In neighboring Rivne Oblast, Russian attacks caused power outages in parts of Dubno and in the Rivne district, according to regional Governor Oleksandr Koval. An unspecified enterprise in the Sarny district was also destroyed in the attack.
No casualties were reported, and energy crews were working to restore electricity, Koval said.
The attacks illustrate Russia's ability to strike deep into western Ukraine, far from the line of contact. Volyn borders Poland and Belarus, while Rivne lies immediately to its east.
Western Ukrainian regions have repeatedly come under long-range Russian drone and missile attacks targeting energy, transport, and other infrastructure. While these regions are targeted less frequently than Kyiv or Odesa — and far less frequently than front-line cities in Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts — they have increasingly been reached by Russian drones during large-scale nationwide attacks.
On Sept. 3, Russian drones hit several western regions during a nationwide attack that killed five people and injured dozens.
The attacks on Volyn and Rivne were part of a wider Russian drone assault across Ukraine on Sept. 12. According to President Volodymyr Zelensky, Russia launched nearly 500 strike drones at the country during the day.
"In essence, the Russians have expanded this war from the front lines, where they cannot achieve success, into the economic sphere, and their tactics are extremely primitive: to destroy every object that can help people endure the conditions of the war," Zelensky said.

Russian strikes hit 2 major Ukrainian steel plants, killing 2 and injuring 6
Russian missile strikes hit two major Ukrainian metallurgical plants overnight on Sept. 12, killing two people and injuring six others, according to statements from Zaporizhstal operator Metinvest and ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih.
In Zaporizhzhia, four ballistic missiles struck the Zaporizhstal steel plant, injuring four employees and causing what Metinvest described as critical damage.
The attack was the third ballistic missile strike on the plant in a month, following earlier attacks on Aug. 11 and Aug. 27. Zaporizhstal had still not resumed production following the previous strikes, according to Metinvest.
"Zaporizhstal produced pig iron and steel for civilian needs. The plant did not manufacture products for military purposes and did not host anything on its territory that could make it a military target," Metinvest Chief Operating Officer Oleksandr Myronenko said.
"Even this did not stop another attack," he added.
The strike damaged equipment in the plant's blast furnace and open-hearth shops, as well as its energy systems, internal networks, and logistics infrastructure, Metinvest said.
One of the four injured workers received treatment at the plant and declined hospitalization, while three others were taken to hospitals with moderate injuries.
"The scale of the destruction is increasing with every strike," Myronenko said. "It is not yet possible to fully assess it, but preliminarily we consider the damage critical."
Separately, a Russian missile strike hit the ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih steel plant, which is in the city of Kryvyi Rih in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, overnight — killing two employees of contractor companies and injuring two plant workers, the company said.
Production and auxiliary facilities were damaged, while search and rescue operations continued at the site. The company said specialists were assessing the extent of the damage and possible timelines for recovery.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih noted that the facility is a civilian mining and metallurgical enterprise.
The plant has been hit repeatedly during Russia's full-scale war. A December 2022 strike killed one employee and destroyed a rolling mill, while another attack in August 2026 killed two plant employees and one contractor and injured 18 others, damaging key energy and blast-furnace facilities and partially halting production.
The attacks on the two plants were part of a broader wave of Russian strikes across Ukraine overnight on Sept. 12 that killed at least 11 people and injured 96 others. Odesa Oblast was the main target of the overnight missile and drone attack, while deadly strikes were also reported in Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy, and Kharkiv oblasts, among others.

At least 11 people were killed and 96 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, as Moscow launched a mass overnight missile and drone attack targeting Odesa Oblast, local authorities said on Sept. 12.
In Odesa Oblast, at least 35 people were injured, including a five-month-old infant and a 17-year-old, local Governor Oleh Kiper said.
"The enemy attacked the city. A multi-story residential building was damaged," Kiper said as the first consequences of the strike emerged.
Russia launched 129 attack drones of various types overnight, including Shahed-type and jet-powered drones, as well as eight Kalibr cruise missiles, six Kh-59/69 guided missiles, and Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, the Air Force said. Ukrainian forces shot down 110 targets, with hits recorded at 20 locations and debris from intercepted targets falling at four additional sites.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, two people were killed and at least 22 others injured, including a child, local Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. In Dnipro, one person was killed and 19 injured as Russian drones, artillery, and aerial bombs damaged an enterprise, apartment buildings, garages, and vehicles.
Overnight, another person was killed and three injured in Kryvyi Rih after Russian forces struck an industrial enterprise. A 54-year-old man was hospitalized in serious condition, Hanzha added.
In Donetsk Oblast, four people were killed and five injured in Russian attacks over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Two people were killed in Sloviansk, while one person was killed in Kramatorsk and another in Yasnohirka.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, two people were killed and 11 injured in Russian attacks, Governor Ivan Fedorov said. Russian forces carried out 1,001 strikes against 45 settlements in the region over the past day, including five missile strikes on the city of Zaporizhzhia, according to Fedorov.
In Kyiv Oblast, one person was killed and three others injured, including a child, as Russian strike drones hit five districts over the past day, local authorities said. Damage was recorded in the Brovary, Obukhiv, Bucha, Boryspil, and Vyshhorod districts. Fifteen sites were damaged, including seven homes, vehicles, warehouses, hangars, and a power line.
In Sumy Oblast, a 68-year-old man was killed in a Russian drone strike on the Myropillia community, while a 64-year-old man was injured in a separate drone attack on the Novoslobidska community, local authorities said. Russian forces carried out more than 50 attacks against 25 settlements in Sumy Oblast over the past day, using artillery, mortars, FPV drones, other unmanned aircraft, and guided aerial bombs.
In Kharkiv Oblast, a 32-year-old man was killed in an attack on Kharkiv, while a 19-year-old man was injured elsewhere in the region, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Russian forces attacked Kharkiv and seven other settlements using guided aerial bombs and multiple types of drones.
In Kherson Oblast, 18 people were injured in Russian attacks targeting residential areas as well as critical and social infrastructure, local authorities said. Fifteen apartment buildings were damaged, along with shops, a gas station, a service station, an ambulance, and vehicles.
Russian Shahed-type drones also struck railway infrastructure in Lutsk, Volyn Oblast, and Fastiv in Kyiv Oblast, Ukrzaliznytsia said. No passengers were injured after monitoring teams detected the threat in time and evacuated them, according to the state railway operator.

Ukrainian naval drone destroys Russian unmanned boat in Black Sea, Navy says
A Ukrainian unmanned surface vessel destroyed a Russian naval drone in the Black Sea in what Ukraine's Navy described as the "first-ever naval battle" between unmanned boats.
The operation was carried out jointly with Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR), whose units detected the unmanned Russian vessel, the Navy said on Sept. 12.
The Russian drone was destroyed by a Ukrainian Sargan-3000 unmanned boat, equipped with a 12.7-mm Protector remote weapons station, according to the Navy. The drone-on-drone encounter marked a historic first.
"This is the first-ever battle between unmanned naval boats," the Navy said.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the Navy's report at the time of publication.
The joint operation represents a shift from naval drones attacking conventional ships to drone-on-drone maritime combat. Both Ukraine and Russia are increasingly moving toward unmanned warfare at sea.
Ukraine has dramatically expanded maritime-drone operations in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, hitting dozens of Russian vessels and maritime logistics targets this summer, striking 105 Russian vessels in the Sea of Azov campaign alone.
Russia is also developing and deploying more unmanned surface systems. Recent satellite imagery indicated Moscow was building what appeared to be its first dedicated naval-drone port in occupied Crimea.
Ukraine's Sargan-3000 is a naval unmanned system that passed combat testing in April 2026. The multi-purpose platform is "highly maneuverable" and capable of executing strike missions, according to the Navy.

Kushner reveals how failed Doha strike helped Washington pressure Israel on Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:28:10 UTC
01:28:10 KST

Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and special adviser and one of the administration’s key figures in diplomacy surrounding the Gaza Strip, delivered sharp criticism over the weekend of Israel’s strikes in Doha, Qatar, last year, while also acknowledging that Washington used the international fallout from the attack to increase pressure on Israel and push it toward an agreement.
Speaking by video at a conference in Kyiv, Kushner described the Israeli operation bluntly.
“Israel did the strike in Doha, which was a terrible thing,” Kushner said. “And obviously, it was unsuccessful as a military operation. And that led to Israel being globally isolated.”
Kushner went further, saying the Trump administration saw a diplomatic opportunity in the crisis and used the new dynamic to push Israel toward a deal.
“We used that dynamic in order to push them into a deal that now today they’re quite happy with,” he said. “At the time, they were a little uncomfortable with kind of what we were pushing them to do," Kushner said.
In Kushner’s telling, the pressure ultimately paid off.
“Ultimately, it turned out to be great for them,” he said of Israel. “And it turned out to be great for the people of Gaza, because now we have a new government there.”
Trump administration regards Israel's Doha strike as a failure, Kushner says
He added that the new governing structure is expected to take over as demilitarization progresses.
“That’s obviously looking to take over soon once we advance on the demilitarization,” Kushner said.
Kushner’s account offers a rare public glimpse into how the Trump team views the path that led to the Gaza agreement. What at the time appeared to be one of Israel’s most serious diplomatic setbacks became, from Washington’s perspective, an opening that could move the parties toward a broader arrangement.
He stressed, however, that such an opening would not have been enough on its own without extensive preparatory work carried out beforehand.
“We had to both find the opening in order to put in place,” Kushner said. “But had we not done all the pre-work before, when the opening came, nothing would have occurred.”
The remarks shed unusual light on the Trump administration’s internal view of the Gaza diplomacy: not as a purely linear or predetermined process, but as a combination of months of groundwork and the ability to capitalize on an unexpected crisis created by an Israeli military action.
Kushner’s language was also strikingly direct. Describing the Doha strike as “a terrible thing” and “unsuccessful as a military operation” amounts to a relatively rare public acknowledgment from a senior figure close to Trump that the administration regarded the operation not merely as a tactical failure, but as an event that inflicted broader strategic damage on Israel by leaving it internationally isolated.
Until now, assessments along those lines had largely surfaced in private conversations and background briefings rather than in such explicit public language.
At the same time, Kushner made clear that, in his view, the damage eventually became part of the route to a better outcome. Israel may have been uncomfortable with some of the pressure applied by Washington at the time, he said, but is now “quite happy” with the resulting agreement.
His message was therefore twofold: the Doha strike weakened Israel diplomatically, but that weakness gave Washington leverage — leverage the Trump administration says it then used to push forward a broader restructuring of Gaza and the postwar arrangement.
