Carney reportedly seeks ‘associate’ EU membership as Ottawa-Washington ties hit fresh low. He will address the European Parliament next week.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is exploring closer ties with the European Union, including becoming an “associate member” of the bloc, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.
The status does not currently exist, but the EU could be open to creating special membership arrangements, the newspaper said, citing unnamed EU and Canadian officials. The European Commission did not respond to a request for comment.
The report comes ahead of a speech by Carney to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday, where he is expected to set out his vision for Canada-EU ties in a challenging geopolitical environment.
Ottawa is locked in a historic trade war with the United States, with steep tariffs in place and no signs of de-escalation.
The EU and Canada want to bolster trade ties of goods, services and workers, particularly in areas including energy, artificial intelligence, defence and critical minerals, according to the report.
The two are also said to be discussing major joint projects, including undersea cables, data centres, cloud infrastructure and satellite networks. Canada also wants to expand energy exports to Europe, the WSJ said.
Still, securing any form of “associate member” status could prove difficult. The EU has strict rules on membership and a lengthy process for making changes to its existing arrangements.
Yet the impact of Trump's presidency, marked by tariffs and threats on both sides of the Atlantic, could encourage a more flexible approach.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz earlier this year outlined his own vision for an “associate member” status, originally intended for Ukraine but potentially applicable to Canada. The model would deepen ties with the EU without requiring full membership.
Macron and Carney in joint visit
French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will visit the French territory of Saint-Pierre-and-Miquelon next week, about 20 km off Canada’s Atlantic coast, in a show of support for their close ties amid tensions with US President Donald Trump, Paris said on Sunday.
Trump posted an image on his Truth Social account on Monday showing a map of North America with the US flag over several French overseas territories, including Saint-Pierre-and-Miquelon, as well as Guadeloupe and Martinique. The map also included Iceland, Greenland, Mexico, Canada, much of Central America and the Caribbean.
The visit will highlight the shared values of France and Canada, including “freedom, democracy, the rule of law and respect for the sovereignty of nations”, the Elysee Palace said.
“In a world marked by the return of power politics, geopolitical tensions and new forms of dependency, France and Canada share a common ambition” to strengthen their ability to act independently, it added.
The visit will be the first by a Canadian prime minister to the archipelago, the French presidency said. The last French president to visit was Francois Hollande in 2014.

The far right’s rise is a wake-up call for Europe | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
15:58:00 UTC
00:58:00 KST

Rafael Behr is right to warn that far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin influence threaten Europe’s liberal democracies (European democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyss, 9 September). But he overlooks the role of the liberal centre itself in creating the conditions for their rise.
While Thatcher, Reagan and their successors weakened trade unions and workers’ bargaining power, subsequent centre-left governments largely accepted these changes rather than reversing them. Under the banner of the “third way”, they expanded labour market insecurity, embraced financialisation and allowed private interests to penetrate ever deeper into public services. Social and economic inequality soared.
From the anti-globalisation movement and post-2008 anti-austerity protests to more recent pro-Palestinian mobilisations, the liberal centre has relied increasingly on policing, surveillance and legal restrictions to contain political opposition.
Decades of economic insecurity, shrinking democratic participation and declining faith in established institutions have created fertile ground for the far right. Kremlin money and Maga-style politics can only thrive because the centre has hollowed out the social and political foundations of liberal democracy. The Alternative für Deutschland’s success should be a wake-up call. History suggests the centre will hit the snooze button.
Benjamin Selwyn
Professor of international relations and international development, University of Sussex
Jörg Lau rightly identifies the shattering of Germany’s postwar consensus in Saxony-Anhalt, but framing this as a sudden rupture obliterates decades of the political establishment’s structural rot (Friedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismic, theguardian.com, 8 September).
Germany’s crisis began with suppressing authentic reckoning. In the immediate postwar era, former Nazi party members were allowed to dominate state institutions. This continued until the 1970s. Willy Brandt, the “Historikerstreit”, the countrywide discussion of the series Holocaust and Goldhagen’s book Hitler’s Willing Executioners were short glimmers of real change. Then the institutionalised remembrance culture emerged. It was top-down – a state-directed ritual to appease European partners that reinforced the German “nanny state” mentality.
In eastern states like Saxony-Anhalt, this top-down moral framework was forced on a population thrust into the post-1989 market shock. Now, with an ageing demographic and economic stagnation straining the social safety net, this abandonment is coming due. The AfD feeds on these unhealed wounds, exploiting anger over stale ritualised politics and, once again, channelling economic angst into xenophobic nationalism.
Merz is a product of decades of missed opportunities. But the AfD is not an alien shock to the system. Mainstream parties built the void the far right now occupies. If mainstream political Berlin continues to ignore their systemic neglect, the collapse will be complete.
Dr Michael Esser
Los Angeles, California, US
 The Public Order Act 1936 put a stop to the quasi-military demonstrations by Oswald Mosley’s blackshirts. Is there any reason why it cannot be used to put an end to thuggish demonstrations by intimidating, black-clothed and balaclava-wearing protesters on the streets of Dover and Portsmouth?
William Ward
London

A painful truth about post-Brexit immigration | Letters

Your report (Wife of British man at risk of deportation from Sweden calls on Burnham to intervene, 3 September) highlights a painful truth about post-Brexit immigration: families are being treated as administrative burdens rather than human beings. However, this harsh treatment cuts both ways.
I am a 71-year-old German-American citizen, married to my British husband for 38 years. We have only ever been apart for work. We bought property in the UK in 2023 so my husband could retire there. After retiring from my job in Germany, I applied for a UK family visa on 1 April 2026, expecting to settle down with him and my two adult sons within six weeks. The lawyer was rather optimistic.
Five months later, and over £7,000 on costs, I am still waiting. My application remains “under consideration”. I have hired a lawyer, involved an MP, filed official complaints, and paid for priority services, yet the Home Office remains an impenetrable wall.
While British media rightly highlights the harsh treatment of UK citizens abroad, the UK Home Office is quietly inflicting the exact same cruelty on older spouses from allied nations. At 71, my husband and I are losing precious time together to bureaucratic inertia. If we expect European countries to show humanity to British citizens, the UK must show the same decency to the families of its own people.
Vera-Lynn Watson
Birkenfeld, Germany

Israel 'striving to destabilise Syria', Fidan says in Damascus
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan accused Israel on Sunday of trying to destabilise Syria through its repeated strikes on the country.
He spoke while on a visit to Damascus, where his Syrian counterpart Asaad al-Shaibani said his country remained committed to diplomacy as it knew the consequenecs of war.

He was toppled by rebel forces led by now President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who relies on support from Turkey.
Israel has sent troops to occupy a UN-patrolled buffer zone that had long separated Israeli and Syrian forces on the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights.
It also carries out regular raids deep into Syrian territory, with Israeli officials saying they intend to keep troops in the country.
Israel and Syria have held several rounds of direct talks, most recently last month in Jordan after the Abu Duhur attack.
Shaibani said the attack "conveyed a destructive message aimed at undermining the path of building the Syrian state".
The attack "has no legitimate or legal justification", Shaibani added, emphasising that it "does not affect Syrian-Turkish relations".
Shaibani said Damascus's position on Israel's escalation was "firm and unwavering" and insisted on the need for Israel to withdraw from areas it invaded after Assad's fall.
Turkey is a strong backer of Syria's authorities.
Fidan said that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan was expected to visit Syria soon, without specifying a date.

You wait years for one party donation of £36m and then two come along at once. Reform can hardly believe its luck. All hail the crypto billionaires. Tacky pale turquoise suits all round. And Nigel Farage won’t have to worry about spending any of his own money – if you can call the £5m freebie his own money – on his security. Nor do those champagne and oyster lunches to discuss loose change donations of £500k from people living overseas pay for themselves. From now on Reform won’t need to bother getting out of bed for anything less than eight figures.
Fair to say that if it had been Labour or the Tories trousering £72m from Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo then Reform would be on full outrage rampage. How the political system was rigged against it and how the two main parties are hotwired cash machines. In bed with the super-rich. But since the money is heading towards its own bank account, everyone in the party is totally chilled. This is just the way life ought to be. Who wouldn’t want a country where two billionaires can attempt to buy the democratic process?
So it was a joy to find that Reform had sent out Robert Jenrick to gloat about its unexpected cash windfall on the Laura Kuenssberg show. Who better to speak about the party’s incorruptibility than the man, who as a junior minister in the Tory government, unlawfully overruled the government’s own planning inspector and just happened to save the Tory donor cum pornographer, Richard “Dirty” Desmond, the best part of £45m in tax. And what did the Tories get in return? A gift of about £12k. You’d have hoped the lesson Honest Bob had learned from that was not to sell his soul – if he has one – so cheaply.
“Everything was totally above board,” he insisted. Though forgive us all for asking the question. Reform is currently the subject of at least two – or is it three? it’s so easy to lose count – police investigations into alleged financial wrongdoing, and the party has acquired a reputation for being at the sleazier end of British politics. A place where Dicky Tice shuffles money from Posh George into and out of his accounts and Nige is so blase he can’t even be bothered to listen when two potential donors talk at length on how they are planning to break the law. Remarkable stuff. Nige can even not listen while maintaining a conversation.
Laura did suggest that Reform might have to give some of the money back if the government were to retrospectively implement the findings of the Rycroft review into party funding. But Honest Bob wasn’t having any of it. There was no way he would be handing back a penny. Finders keepers. Possession nine-tenths of the law. You’d be amazed how Reform can make money disappear when it feels like it. Though, of course, everything would be done in a totally legitimate way.
What we all had to understand was that this was a huge vote of confidence in Reform. Far from being an indication that the party’s funding had become exponentially more murky, this was proof that it was being totally transparent. Think of it this way. When he had been a Conservative MP, Honest Bob had been more than happy for his party to shower peerages on donors. Some only had to hand over less than £100k to end up in the Lords. But Delo and Harborne weren’t asking for anything like that. All they wanted was for the laws around crypto currencies to be relaxed a little. Where was the conflict of interest in that?
Ben and Christopher were just regular guys who just happened to be billionaires. And yes, it was unfortunate that Ben had been convicted in the US for failing to comply with anti-money-laundering legislation – somehow the fact he had been pardoned by Donald Trump made him sound doubly guilty – but this had just been an oversight. He was a very busy man and it had been the sort of mistake anyone could make.
“They are both just patriots,” Honest Bob continued. So patriotic that Delo had spent much of the last few years based in Hong Kong while Harborne lived in Thailand. We should try to feel their pain. They were both just run-of-the-mill billionaires who happened to have been priced out of Mayfair. Rather than indulge in the politics of envy, we should applaud them for their philanthropy. Two guys just trying to make a difference. Making Britain better.
Now and again, Honest Bob found himself getting a little confused. For example, when he came to think about it, Delo and Harborne giving £72m from their crypto empires was much the same as tens of thousands of ordinary workers donating to Labour through their union subscriptions. Because what Ben and Chris wanted most was for the income tax threshold to be raised to £15k. That £500 they would get back could make the difference between them remaining tax exiles and returning to this country.
The money would be spent on the professionalisation of Reform. When all welfare payments – those that were left – would be paid in crypto. When Reform would rise above the ashes of sleaze. When all bus sites and billboards would be covered with adverts for Reform. When all TV stations promoted Reform without question. It wasn’t enough to have GB News doing that for nothing. There would be no rest until the BBC had also been captured. Make no mistake. This £72m was only the start.

Pregnant woman among more than 10 killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza

2026-09-13
15:51:33 UTC
00:51:33 KST

A pregnant Palestinian woman died on Saturday from injuries sustained after being shot in the head by Israeli forces south of Khan Younis, according to her family and medical workers, as strikes across Gaza killed at least 10 people in 48 hours.
The woman, named as Iman Shalouf, 27, who was nearly eight months pregnant, was sitting inside her family’s tent in the al-Mawasi area when Israeli gunfire struck her, according to paramedics and witnesses.
‘‘We heard the sound of gunfire while I was praying,’’ Wathfa abu Mashi, Shalouf’s mother-in-law, said in a video interview with Anadolu. “My daughter asked me, ‘Where is Iman?’ I told her she was in her tent. She went to check on her and found her covered in blood after she was hit by a bullet.”
Shalouf’s husband, Ismail abu Mashi, said “Where is the ceasefire they keep talking about? There is no such thing. There is killing every day. People are dying here every day.”
Shalouf was rushed to Nasser hospital, where doctors initially detected her unborn baby’s heartbeat, but she and her unborn baby died a few hours later.
According to relatives, Shalouf had already chosen the name Ayoub for the baby, who was due in November.
Relatives and community members gathered at the hospital to hold funeral prayers for Shalouf and her child before carrying their bodies for burial in Khan Younis. They were buried side by side.
Contacted by the Guardian, the Israel Defense Forces said they were looking into the incident.
Despite the ceasefire agreement reached in October 2025, violence and the killing of Palestinians continue on a daily basis.
The health ministry in Gaza said 10 Palestinians had been killed and 56 wounded in Israeli attacks over the previous 48 hours, amid artillery shelling and gunfire in several areas of northern, central and southern Gaza.
Four members of the same family – Momen Ahmed, his wife, Haneen Saleh, and their daughters Lana, 12, and Bana, eight – were killed when their home in Beit Lahiya was struck on Thursday night, according to the ministry. Six other Palestinians were reported killed in Khan Younis and Gaza City on Friday, including a man who died of wounds sustained in an earlier attack.
Several other Palestinians were injured in attacks across Gaza. On Friday, two people were reportedly seriously injured in an attack in Beit Lahiya, while three people including a woman six months pregnant and a child were wounded by gunfire in the same city.
 On Saturday, nine people were injured when a displaced people’s tent in al-Mawasi was shelled, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent.
On Sunday, two Palestinians were killed and several others injured when a vehicle was struck in Tel al-Hawa in Gaza City, according to the health ministry. The attack also injured people on a passing bus carrying women and children.
On 28 August, Unicef said at least four children had been reported killed in the preceding five days and many others wounded, including children who sustained life-changing injuries. On 2 September, it said three other children had reportedly been killed and at least five others injured in the preceding 24 hours, bringing the number of children reportedly killed between 23 August and 2 September to seven.
“Airstrikes by Israeli forces continue killing and wounding Palestinians,” Médecins Sans Frontières said. “Between September 6 and 9, Israeli forces issued 18 so-called evacuation orders and struck a building less than 250ft from an MSF clinic.”
The humanitarian situation remains severe. According to the UN’s humanitarian office, “most of Gaza’s 2.1 million are approaching the rainy season in overcrowded displacement sites, at risk of flooding and disease, while efforts to help them prepare are constrained by funding shortfalls and access restrictions”.
On 31 August, a temporary halt to desalination in Israel reduced the water available to about a million people in Gaza who rely on the Israeli grid.
Several electricity generators at hospitals across the Gaza Strip have stopped working because of shortages of spare parts and fuel, the territory’s health ministry has said.
According to the ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025. Since Israel’s war in Gaza began on 7 October 2023, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the ministry.

Unknown Publisher

18:49:50 EEST

Iran to present Gulf countries with a temporary route through the Strait of Hormuz — media
Kyiv • UNN
Tehran will propose a temporary maritime route through the Strait of Hormuz without fully reopening it. The plan will be discussed in Salalah; the agreement will not be signed immediately.
On Monday, Iran plans to present the Gulf countries with a plan for a temporary maritime route through the Strait of Hormuz. According to Bloomberg, it is based on an agreement Tehran previously reached with Oman, UNN reports.
Details
Oman is trying to bring together the foreign ministers of the Gulf countries and Iran in Salalah for talks.
According to Bild, the plan does not envisage the full reopening of the strait. Iran intends, as before, to participate in decisions on which vessels will be allowed to pass through the strategic waterway.
The talks are taking place amid disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran insists on retaining control over passage, while the Gulf countries are discussing how to respond to Tehran’s proposal. At the same time, no agreement is likely to be reached on Monday: an Iranian official said the meeting is intended to mark the beginning of negotiations, rather than result in the signing of a finalized treaty.
In addition
Before the start of the current crisis, around 20% of the world’s seaborne oil trade passed through the Strait of Hormuz. Therefore, even a partial resumption of shipping could affect global energy prices.

Carney pushes idea of making Canada 'associate member' of EU, WSJ reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
15:47:12 UTC
00:47:12 KST

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney wants closer links with the European Union and is exploring whether his country could become an "associate member" of the bloc, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.
The EU, which has not been flexible about membership rules in the past, is open to the idea of granting Canada a yet-to-be-created status of associate membership, the newspaper reported, citing unnamed officials both from the EU and Canada.
The Canadian embassy in Brussels and spokespeople at the European Commission did not respond to separate requests for comment.
Canada's escalating trade war with the United States has added urgency to its strategic pivot towards other trading partners.
Canada's relations with Washington have deteriorated sharply since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in early 2025, with disagreements on trade and other issues. The trade spat has led to tariffs on tens of billions of dollars in cross-border trade.
What would associate membership of the EU mean for Canada?
Canada and the EU are discussing ways to let Canada's goods, services, and workers involved in strategic supply chains such as energy, AI, defense, and critical minerals move freely, effectively shifting the EU border, The Wall Street Journal said.
Canada and the EU are also talking about laying underwater cables, jointly constructing data centers, cloud storage and new satellite networks and infrastructure to ship Canadian energy to the EU, the newspaper said.
Carney has spoken regularly with several EU leaders, most notably French President Emmanuel Macron, about the possibility of letting Canadians live and work visa-free in the EU, WSJ said, citing two unnamed officials familiar with the matter.
Both leaders are set to meet later this month.
Macron's press office did not respond to a request for comment.
The project to closely tie Canada and the EU together is not such an easy feat, as fierce opposition to a more modest trade deal showed.
More than a decade after the deal was struck and nine years since it provisionally entered into force, several EU countries still have not ratified it.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said seven police officers were injured and treated at the scene, while vehicles belonging to the Coastguard and Border Force were damaged.

The first person charged in connection with the demonstration in the city appeared in court on Saturday morning.

Anti-immigration activists returned to the streets of Portsmouth on Saturday afternoon, where they faced counter-protests from anti-racism groups.
Tony Rowlinson, assistant chief constable, said the scenes at Eastney Marina had gone beyond peaceful protest. “Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest,” he said. “Clearly events on Sunday evening were not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder.”
Rowlinson said officers had worked to protect people in the area and warned that police would pursue those responsible after reviewing footage.
“The reality of public order policing is that arrests at the time are not always possible, especially where evidence may need to be reviewed to clearly identify who is responsible for offences,” he said.
He added that none of the seven injured officers had been seriously hurt, but said they “did not deserve to be assaulted” while policing the demonstration.
Police also said they were investigating online threats and abuse directed at officers and staff from partner agencies after the disorder.
The force has appealed to anyone who recognises the six men to contact police on 101 or report information online, quoting reference 44260435943.
Rowlinson said: “If you break the law we will take action against you and where it is feasible to do so seek a prosecution.”

US ‘secretly flew diplomat out of UK’ after child abuse images found, reports say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
15:44:18 UTC
00:44:18 KST

U.S. authorities secretly flew an American diplomat out of Britain after images featuring sexual abuse of children were allegedly found during a raid on his London home, without fully informing British authorities beforehand, British media reported Sunday.
The Daily Mail and The Sun reported that British authorities were formally informed about the investigation only after the diplomat had already been removed from the country, angering officials over what they viewed as an operation carried out outside normal British legal channels.
According to the reports, the U.S. investigation began after suspicions arose that the diplomat’s brother, who lives in the United States, had sent him images depicting child sexual abuse.
American personnel reportedly raided the diplomat’s apartment in Putney, south London, on August 25. After allegedly finding child abuse images at the property, they took him to a U.S.-linked military facility in Britain and flew him to the United States.
U.S. Marine Security Guards, who protect the American Embassy in London, are believed to have been involved in the raid, The Sun reported.
Flight records cited in the British reports appeared to support the account of the diplomat’s removal. On August 24, Kalitta Air flight K49709, a Boeing 747-4R7F cargo aircraft, flew from Chicago to RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, where the U.S. Air Force maintains a significant presence.
The following day, the same aircraft, operating as flight K4529, departed Fairford at 5:33 p.m. and landed at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware at 7:44 p.m. local time after a flight lasting seven hours and 11 minutes.
‘They should have told Scotland Yard’
Britain’s Metropolitan Police confirmed that U.S. authorities informed them on August 25 about an investigation involving suspected offenses in London linked to indecent images of children.
“On August 25, U.S. authorities made us aware of an investigation they are conducting into suspected offenses in London relating to indecent images of children,” police said. “We continue to liaise with them regarding this matter.”
But the reported operation sparked anger because American personnel have no powers of arrest in Britain and there was reportedly no formal extradition request.
“They should have told Scotland Yard when they carried out the raid, and certainly when they found material,” a source told The Sun.
“Instead, we think they took him to a U.S. airbase and flew him more than 4,000 miles to where his brother was being investigated. We think it was a dawn raid before they then took him to the base in a U.S. military convoy.”
The source added that while the diplomat could ultimately face justice in the United States, the alleged offenses may also fall within British jurisdiction.
British officials are understood to have held high-level discussions over the incident, including meetings involving Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley and senior government ministers, among them Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood.
One possibility being examined in Britain is that U.S. authorities obtained an American court order connected to the investigation of the diplomat’s brother, who is in the United States. But British legal experts questioned whether such an order could authorize American personnel to exercise law enforcement powers on British soil.
The British government offered a measured public response. “We expect all foreign diplomats in the UK to abide by our laws,” it said. “As a U.S. investigation is ongoing, it would not be appropriate to comment further.”
U.S. officials have not publicly detailed the operation or denied the reports. A spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy in London said: “We are aware of allegations concerning an individual assigned to the Embassy. The United States government expects all personnel to adhere to the highest standards of conduct, and we take these allegations seriously.”
The reported August 25 Fairford-Dover flight and the quoted statements from British police, the British government and the U.S. Embassy are also reflected in the original British reporting.

00:43:38 KST

Layan Bsharat and Mohammad Sio
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
 Israel is holding 37 Palestinian journalists in its prisons, including 19 under administrative detention without charge or trial, the Palestinian Prisoner Society said Sunday.
The nongovernmental group said all 37 journalists were detained following the start of the Gaza genocide in October 2023.
It said Israel continues to target Palestinian journalists through arrests, prison sentences, solitary confinement and prosecution over their work and freedom of expression.
Among the latest detainees are journalists Muath Ammarna and Sabri Jibrin, who were arrested Thursday after Israeli forces raided their homes in Bethlehem in the southern West Bank.
The group said Ammarna has been repeatedly targeted by Israeli authorities and is now being detained for the third time over his journalistic work.
It also cited the case of journalist and writer Mahmoud Fatafta, who was sentenced to 48 months in prison over what Israel describes as “incitement,” one of the harshest sentences issued in such cases, according to the statement.
The society said Israeli authorities increasingly use “incitement” charges against journalists, alongside administrative detention based on what authorities describe as “secret files.”
Nineteen journalists from the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, are currently held under administrative detention, accounting for 51% of all detained journalists, it added.
The group also highlighted the case of journalist Bushra al-Tawil, 33, who was transferred from Damon Prison in northern Israel to solitary confinement at Ramla Prison in central Israel.
It accused Israeli authorities of intensifying isolation and other restrictive measures against female Palestinian prisoners, alongside food deprivation, denial of medical treatment and poor sanitation conditions.
The society said detained journalists face the same conditions as other Palestinian prisoners, including hunger, medical neglect, torture, abuse, solitary confinement and denial of basic rights.
Journalists are also targeted through killings, enforced disappearances and direct attacks while carrying out their work, it added, describing this as part of a systematic policy aimed at restricting Palestinian reporting and documentation of Israeli crimes and violations.
The occupied West Bank has seen daily Israeli army raids and escalating attacks by occupiers since the start of the Gaza genocide in October 2023. The attacks have included killings, arrests, demolitions, attacks on homes, vehicles and mosques, destruction of agricultural land, restrictions on farmers, displacement of Palestinians and expansion of illegal settlements.
On Thursday, the Palestinian Prisoner Society said Israeli forces detained more than 100 Palestinians across the West Bank over the previous week, bringing the number of West Bank detainees since October 2023 to more than 25,000, in addition to thousands detained from Gaza.

World Insights: Rubio tour lays bare U.S. push to tighten strategic grip on Latin America, analysts say
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
23:38:44 CST
00:38:44 KST

MEXICO CITY, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio came to South America on Sept. 8-10 talking mostly about drugs, crime and security. He left behind an agenda that reached much further.
Across Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, Rubio's tour touched on critical minerals, infrastructure and closer political ties, alongside an expanding U.S. "security role" in the region.
For analysts, the three-country trip offered a revealing look at Washington's broader strategy: using security cooperation to deepen its influence at a time of political change across South America.
The fight against organized crime was the most visible theme of Rubio's trip.
In Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, he called for closer cooperation against drug trafficking and groups Washington describes as "narcoterrorists."
Fernando Romero Wimer, a professor at Brazil's Federal University for Latin American Integration, said the language itself matters.
"The militarization is already underway," he said, arguing that recasting drug trafficking as terrorism could expand the legal and operational room for U.S. involvement in the region.
Cristina Pecequilo, a professor of international relations at the Federal University of Sao Paulo, said the approach has clear precedents, from Plan Colombia to the Merida Initiative.
Security cooperation can also create leverage beyond the fight against crime, said Luis Ricardo Delgado, a professor at Venezuela's University of Carabobo.
"Security cooperation does not automatically produce development," he said. "What it produces is strategic dependence. And that dependence then conditions the sovereign decisions of each country."
Rubio's agenda also extended into sectors with longer-term strategic importance. In Colombia, for example, the two sides discussed cooperation on strategic minerals.
"The United States does not care if emerging countries continue selling appliances, clothes, toys or even vehicles in the region," said Delgado. "They are focused on critical infrastructure, cutting-edge technologies and strategic natural resources."
He described the approach as part of the "Donroe Doctrine," a modified version of the Monroe Doctrine promoted by U.S. President Donald Trump to pursue U.S. primacy in the Western Hemisphere.
Romero Wimer made a similar argument, saying security cooperation can also become a tool for exerting pressure over ports, infrastructure and other strategic projects. ■

BERLIN, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Borussia Monchengladbach fired head coach Eugen Polanski on Sunday, a day after a crushing 5-0 defeat at Freiburg left the team without a point from its opening three Bundesliga matches.
Assistant coach Tobias Trulsen was also relieved of his duties alongside the 40-year-old Polanski. The decision came after sporting director Rouven Schroeder declined to publicly back the coach following Saturday's defeat, during which Gladbach captain Tim Kleindienst was sent off after receiving a second yellow card.
"Despite a good preparation and positive approaches, the team failed to achieve the desired results in the Bundesliga," Schroeder said. "The performances shown recently led to the decision to relieve Eugen of his duties effective immediately. Eugen is a true Borussia man through and through. We thank him, and Tobias Trulsen, for their commitment to Borussia."
Polanski said the departure was painful.
"Borussia Monchengladbach was and remains my club," he said. "That is why it hurts so much that things have turned out this way. After securing Bundesliga survival last season, we changed a number of things this season. We had big plans but failed to put them into practice. I am sorry for that.
"I very much hope Borussia turns things around quickly. I wish the club, the team and all the wonderful fans only the best."
Co-coach Jan-Moritz Lichte, who previously served as head coach of Mainz, will take interim charge with support from Markus Gellhaus until a permanent successor is appointed.
Polanski came through Gladbach's youth system and made his Bundesliga debut for the club in 2005. He played 54 competitive matches for the first team before spells with Getafe, Mainz and Hoffenheim.
After retiring in 2018, Polanski returned to Gladbach and later coached the club's under-17 and under-23 teams before taking interim charge of the first team in September 2025. He was appointed permanent head coach two months later on a contract through 2028.
Gladbach, which finished 12th last season, hosts Mainz on Saturday before a three-week international break. ■

Trump calls on Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries
The U.S. president denied that his war on Iran was responsible for surging diesel prices, but a senior European official said Trump was using Kyiv as a scapegoat.
DOONBEG, Ireland — U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukraine to stop targeting Russian oil refineries in light of the surging price of diesel fuel worldwide.
Trump, who is on a two-day visit to Ireland, made the remarks to reporters while walking around his golf course in County Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open tournament.
Asked about the current surge in global fuel prices, particularly diesel — which broke a record $6 per gallon in the U.S. on Friday — Trump insisted the spike was being caused by Ukraine rather than his own war with Iran, which has sharply restricted oil shipments from the Middle East.
Advertisement
Trump said officials from his administration had asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop drone and missile attacks on any Russian sites that produce diesel.
“Mr Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump said during a pause on his tour of his Doonbeg golf course on Ireland’s west coast. “Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel fuel.”
The U.S. leader maintained that the conflict Washington initiated with Iran more than six months ago is not to blame for the shortfall. “This isn’t done by the Middle East,” Trump said. “This is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine. So we spoke to Mr Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.”
Ukraine’s increasingly deep-range strikes on Russian energy infrastructure are seen as a key part of its strategy to make Russia’s 4-year full-scale invasion of the country prohibitively costly for Moscow.
But a senior European official familiar with U.S.-brokered mediation talks between Moscow and Kyiv told POLITICO that the Trump administration was searching for scapegoats ahead of crucial Nov. 3 midterm elections in the United States. The official was granted anonymity to comment on sensitive aspects of the three-way discussions.
“This administration is blaming Ukraine because they do not know what to do with their war [in Iran],” the official said. “Russian exports of diesel and oil have never been significant for U.S. consumption. The very idea is absurd. Moreover, we have all heard President Trump say that America itself can supply as much oil as anyone wants.”
Advertisement
Trump is not the first U.S. official to blame Ukrainian strikes for the price of diesel. Last week, Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CBS that “the diesel situation has been challenging because Russian refineries have suffered significant damage.” Days before that, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told the “Fox & Friends” program that America was experiencing “an energy shock” partly because “Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets and refined properties.”
The senior European official said that if Washington wanted Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries, it should get Moscow to stop hitting Ukraine’s energy grid. “An energy ceasefire must be mutual,” the official said. “Putin does not respect this [U.S.] administration. That is why a ceasefire hasn’t begun.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the Vesti news service on Saturday that Moscow would not pause its attacks during the talks with Kyiv. “We remain ready for negotiations, but the special military operation will not be halted for the duration of the talks. We have already been through this experience and drawn our own conclusions.”

BRICS must reject "occupation, settler colonialism," and "settler terrorism," as Israel's "aggression" in the Middle East has affected "far beyond" those directly involved, the Malaysian prime minister told the bloc's annual summit in New Delhi on Sunday.
"BRICS must say plainly and unequivocally that occupation, settler colonialism and, more pointedly, 'settler terrorism' cannot become destiny, and that no life weighs less for where it is lived," Anwar Ibrahim said, according to a statement on the US social media platform Facebook.
"We cannot speak of inclusive growth and prosperity while war drives energy prices higher and threatens the sea lanes on which our economies depend," he said.
Anwar said Israel's "aggression" in the Middle East has affected "far beyond" those directly involved, driving up inflation and uncertainty.
The US and Israel launched a war on Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to fire missiles and drones at Israel and regional countries hosting US assets.
Iran also announced the closure of the Strait of Hormuz to navigation, causing widespread disruption to global energy and trade flows.
Anwar explained Kuala Lumpur's position as respecting sovereignty, protecting civilians, and keeping global economic arteries out of the battlefield.
He also warned that while technology is advancing rapidly, economic gains remain out of reach for much of the developing world, with many countries facing debt distress or at serious risk of it.
Speaking at an open session titled "Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth," he said BRICS' combined market strength offers opportunities to diversify trade and reduce reliance on traditional Western markets.
BRICS must "act jointly through concrete measures to dismantle unfair trading practices, share our development experience and strengthen technical cooperation and training in emerging fields, including semiconductors and artificial intelligence (AI)," he said.
He said financing must meet basic needs without leaving countries with unsustainable debt, highlighting the need to advance initiatives through the New Development Bank, local-currency settlements, and Islamic capital markets.
The green transition must reflect countries' differing circumstances, development stages, and pace, Anwar added.
The expanded 11-member BRICS grouping includes Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.
Vietnam, as well as Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, and Uzbekistan, joined BRICS as partner countries in 2025.
On Saturday, the bloc adopted the New Delhi Declaration, pledging to deepen cooperation with emerging markets, developing countries, and BRICS partner nations.

====================================================================================================

As Chavez and Maduro images disappear, is Venezuela entering a new chapter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
15:22:59 UTC
00:22:59 KST

Caracas, Venezuela – In a small square in central Caracas, Victor Rodriguez pauses at a giant mural of a figure draped in teal green. It’s the man he credits with giving him the opportunity to become an artist: former President Hugo Chavez.
Rodriguez, who paints under the name Forastero, helped create the image for the late Venezuelan leader's birthday on July 28. He says Chavez opened up new spaces for art and culture, giving artists from poorer neighbourhoods opportunities they never had before.
But today, Forastero is dismayed. He worries about the future of such art.
“Chavez represents revolution. He is anti-imperialist,” Forastero told Al Jazeera. “But now Chavez murals are disappearing.”
In recent months, Caracas has seen a transformation. Monumental images of Chavez and other figures linked to his political movement, chavismo, used to be common.
But now, graffiti, murals and billboards are being painted over or taken down. The Palace of Justice, once flanked by twin portraits of Chavez and the 19th-century revolutionary Simon Bolivar, has seen both images covered up.
In their place, there are new blue banners, emblazoned with the slogan "Venezuela renace" or "Venezuela reborn".
The changes come as Venezuela undergoes a period of political change after nearly three decades of chavista rule.
Since the United States launched a military operation to abduct and imprison then-President Nicolas Maduro in January, the country has been under intense pressure to reimagine its socialist government.
For some Venezuelans, the cosmetic changes are happening faster than any substantial ones. Some don’t want any changes at all.
Forastero sees maintaining his murals as a way of pushing back against the US influence in his government. “Now, painting Chavez is resistance," he said.
'Venezuela reborn’
In parts of Caracas, the smell of fresh paint lingers on walls and buildings where the new government motto "Venezuela renace" now appears.
Bright blue and yellow billboards are plastered across government housing blocks and motorway roadsides, advertising the catchphrase.
The "Venezuela renace" campaign began in the weeks after the country was struck by twin earthquakes on June 24. At least 6,500 people were killed.
The government of interim President Delcy Rodriguez came under heavy criticism for its initial response to the disaster. It then moved to put reconstruction at the centre of its public messaging.
Orlando Perez, a political scientist at the University of North Texas at Dallas, sees the new imagery as part of Rodriguez's efforts to establish her own political identity, separate from chavismo.
After all, until January, Rodriguez was Maduro's vice president. Maduro himself was Chavez's handpicked successor.
“Rodriguez is asking to be judged on [Venezuela's] reconstruction rather than on revolutionary lineage or history,” Perez said. “What makes it interesting is that it is contested.”
Perez explained that chavistas are divided over the removal of the images. In June, the governor of one Venezuelan state, Freddy Bernal, criticised efforts to replace Chavez and Maduro portraits in government institutions.
But much of that internal tension predates the "Venezuela renace" campaign, according to Perez.
“The fight is about who owns chavismo, who owns the movement,” Perez told Al Jazeera.
Since 1999, Venezuela has been led by Chavez and his successors. But after almost three decades of political dominance, chavista leaders now are contending with a new factor: a US leader who seeks control over Venezuela's government.
US President Donald Trump has leveraged his influence since Maduro's abduction to push Venezuela to pursue economic reforms, including greater foreign access to the country's oil and mining sectors.
He has also exercised control over Venezuela's fuel exports and landed a deal last month that would give the US a majority stake in 65 billion barrels of oil reserves in the country.
Despite the US-led upheaval, many Venezuelans say they’ve noticed few changes in their everyday lives.
Change or rebranding?
Javier Hernandez is a retiree who receives a state pension equivalent to just $0.14 a month. This year, he said food prices have risen, and the electricity goes out several times a day.
But he welcomes the disappearance of the chavismo-themed images. He hopes political and economic changes will follow.
“These chavista figures have brought nothing but damage and hatred and bad things to our country. They don’t deserve for anyone to be looking at pictures of them,” Hernandez told Al Jazeera.
Still, their replacements leave him feeling ill at ease. Hernandez lives in La Guaira, the area hardest hit by the June earthquakes. Three of his nieces and nephews died, as well as other family members and friends.
Amid the destruction, he noticed the bright blue and yellow "Venezuela renace" signs starting to rise.
“When I see or hear that phrase, it angers me because those politicians don’t live here, and they haven’t suffered the impacts of the earthquakes like we have,” Hernandez said.
“People are still searching for bodies. They’re still taking people out of the rubble.”
The government has promised to rebuild La Guaira, one of Venezuela’s main tourist areas, known for its sandy beaches.
It has also launched the Gran Mision Venezuela Renace, promising temporary accommodation for those displaced, new housing before the end of 2026 and subsidies for affected families buying homes.
But Hernandez said La Guaira is far from being "reborn".
“Many people in La Guaira are now unemployed because the main source of jobs and activity is tourism, hotels, restaurants, businesses. We're having a very hard time here — very, very hard," he explained.
The ‘ghost’ of Chavez
Political imagery has often grown more prominent in Venezuela when residents are struggling, according to Irina Troconis, author of the book The Necromantic State, about Chavez's lingering influence.
Such imagery can serve as a counternarrative to real conditions on the ground, she explained.
“The imagery is used at certain times to represent supposed change that people are actually not living through at all," Troconis said
She pointed to government slogans like "Venezuela has been fixed", which were used in 2022 to project optimism despite hyperinflation and economic collapse.
Troconis also argues that the enduring presence of Chavez in public art allowed his influence to endure even after his death in 2013.
The pervasiveness of Chavez-themed imagery puts later leaders like Maduro constantly in dialogue with the late president's leadership. It also projects the image of continuity, from Chavez onward, according to Troconis.
“Chavez remained the president in this sort of ghostly figure, and Maduro was more like the vice president to that ghost,” she said.
But she cautions that Venezuela's changing imagery may not signal deeper political transformation.
"What makes chavismo unique in some ways is its capacity to mutate and adapt and change through a process of rebranding that doesn't always require real internal, inherent change," Troconis said.
Art as propaganda
Chavez’s eyes still gaze from walls across Caracas. So too do the eyes of other figures, like Maduro and independence leader Simon Bolivar. Some images are faded. Others are accompanied by slogans like "To doubt is treason".
Forastero has worked on government projects, including under Rodriguez. But he is critical of some of the newer images. He remembers a time when he painted murals of Chavez playing with children or riding a bicycle, not slogans.
“When Chavez was alive, people painted Chavez because we loved him very much. It’s as simple as that,” he said.
In recent decades, he argues that Venezuela's public art has fallen increasingly under government control, with murals commissioned to carry explicitly political messages.
“Muralism is a story told on a wall," Forastero said. "What we really see on the walls now are propaganda posters. I’m a chavista, and I’m disgusted by it."
Still, the removal of the artwork is another form of propaganda, in Forastero's eyes. He believes the Rodriguez government is seeking to project a more "neutral" appearance to better appeal to the US.
He also accuses Rodriguez of abandoning ideals key to the chavismo movement: namely, anti-imperialism and revolution. He pointed to the US's role in shaping Venezuelan policy.
“The United States is forcing our government to behave this way," Forastero said.
Rafael Araujo, a Venezuelan activist, has a different view of the changing landscape.
To him, there was something “jarring” about seeing chavista figures plastered across city walls, especially the leaders who have caused the country so much pain.
During their time in power, Chavez and Maduro both faced allegations of overseeing human rights abuses, including through the violent suppression of dissent. Venezuela's last two presidential elections have been widely denounced as illegitimate.
Known in Caracas as Senor Papagayo, Araujo has used colourful, handmade kites to protest against government violence and economic policy.
He sees the Chavez murals as a form of oppression, an ever-visible reminder of a repressive government apparatus.
His kites are a way of sending a different message. His favourite carries aloft a single word: "Freedom".
“Freedom is what all countries need. Democracy is the most balanced system a citizen can live under,” Araujo said.
Structural changes or cosmetic ones?
Under pressure from the US, the Rodriguez government began negotiations with certain opposition lawmakers, though critics argue some of the most prominent voices have not been included.
A first round of talks in August resulted in an agreement to overhaul the government-aligned Supreme Court (TSJ), housed in the Palace of Justice, where Chavez's portrait once hung from the facade.
But Perez, the political scientist, warns against mistaking the court's cosmetic changes for deeper institutional ones.
He pointed out that the chavista movement remains in power, and no new elections have been set.
“The iconography, the symbols have moved considerably faster than the institutional changes,” Perez said. “There’s still no electoral calendar.”
A second round of talks this month is expected to focus on the political, civil and electoral guarantees for such a vote.
But the perceived subservience of the Rodriguez government to the US might hasten the transformation of Venezuela's chavismo movement, according to Perez.
He pointed to the August oil deal, which transfers a significant share of Venezuelan oil reserves to a US-controlled public-private partnership.
“Handing 65 billion barrels to a private operator on 100-year terms — or 25, depending on which government you ask — does more damage to chavismo as a political project than the removal of every mural in Caracas,” Perez said.
For a certain group of chavistas like Forastero, such a deal is a “very open surrender” to the US.
“They kidnap our president and then we negotiate with them? No," Forastero said, shaking his head in disgust.
Protecting the images he believes in is his way of taking a stand. From the small Caracas plaza, Forastero walked towards another mural he recently painted, of Chavez in his signature red beret.
“Chavez’s images are being removed all over the place. But I’ve never allowed it to happen here,” he said. “This square here, this is my bastion of resistance.”

Portugal's scariest festival wrapped up with the Méliès d'Argent for best European feature going to a Danish film set in 19th-century Faroe Islands, and tributes to Solveig Nordlund and Julie Corman.
In a landmark year marking its twentieth edition, MOTELX once again gave Lisbon audiences a fright with the best and most diverse horror cinema from different latitudes and styles, bidding farewell on Saturday night to an already loyal public with the crowning of an imaginative short about Portugal's Estado Novo and two Nordic films.
The MOTELX Award – Best Portuguese Horror Short 2026, the largest cash prize for national short films, worth €5,000, was presented to "A Hora do Chico!", by João Severo and Rafael Sá Carneiro. The jury, made up of Fernando Vasquez (programmer), José Santiago (journalist and programmer) and Sandra Henriques (journalist and author), highlighted the "ambition and maturity" of the film, "a disturbing journey through a past that few miss, which merges, in the best possible way, with an alternative reality".
There was also a Special Mention for "Consumido", by [carrozo], for its "humour and visual care, combined with narrative economy that turns the roles of predator and prey on their head".
As for the Meliès d'Argent awards, which select a feature and a short of European production to go on to compete for the Meliès d'Or in Sitges, the jury opted for "Mancave", by Norwegian director Fredrik S. Hana, in the short film competition, and "No Rest for the Wicked", by Dane Kasper Kalle, for features. The film is set in the Faroe Islands in the 19th century and showcases breathtaking landscapes.
The film "weaves desire, religion, repression, beauty, love and death together with rare elegance", as underlined by the jury composed of Isilda Sanches (journalist and music broadcaster), Leone Niel (director) and Teresa Nicolau (cultural director and columnist).
The juries also handed awards to "Hóspede", by Miguel Monteiro Rico (MOTELX Award – Best Portuguese Horror Screenplay), "Lexi" (Spain), directed by Portuguese filmmaker Bruno Simões, in the "Lobo Mau" section, aimed at younger audiences and families, and "Gunman", written and directed by Argentine filmmaker Cris Tapia Marchiori, winner of the Audience Award.
The festival paid tribute to Portuguese-Swedish filmmaker Solveig Nordlund with the Noémia Delgado Award for outstanding women in horror cinema and to Julie Corman, widow of American director and producer Roger Corman, to mark the centenary of his birth. Julie Corman returned to MOTELX for a masterclass largely devoted to her husband's long career, having previously accompanied Roger Corman when he was a special guest at the 2017 edition.

How could Reform UK spend its £72m of new billionaire donations?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
15:17:38 UTC
00:17:38 KST

Nigel Farage once said he could spend his £5m gift from Christopher Harborne on Ferraris if he wanted to, given its unconditional nature.
With the new donations to his party from Harborne and his fellow crypto billionaire Ben Delo of £72m over the past weekend alone, Farage’s party now has nearly enough cash to buy a Reform UK branded Ferrari for a party organiser in each of Britain’s 632 constituencies (though that would certainly be a waste and a bit of a tax headache).
But what the cash can buy first and foremost for Reform is manpower. Already the party is seeking to recruit more than 60 local organisers in key areas of the country.
Though the donation is certainly enough to staff every constituency in England, Scotland and Wales with organisers, that would also be a massive waste of resources in seats Reform UK is never likely to win. Instead, experienced regional staff can build impeccable targeting data for the seats Reform UK needs to win a majority.
Reform has already invested heavily in improving its canvassing tools and its ReformPro software – but it is boots on the ground that ensure the data being fed into those tools is as accurate as it can be. That requires door-to-door canvassing to identify switching voters and non-voters who might be persuaded to turn out.
For most parties, those kinds of local resources are only really deployed far closer to an election. Beginning that level of organising and data collection this far out could give Reform UK a massive head start at the next election, though other parties have very valuable legacy data from previous elections of which Reform has much less available.
Local parties could also print and send a many more direct mail drops, which are uncapped outside of the election period, with voters receiving “local newspapers” which are in fact Reform UK campaigning mailouts.
As well as on the ground, the cash also gives Reform UK massive potential power in the air war, on social media in particular with paid ads that can be micro-targeted locally and professionally produced and filmed. It can spend large amounts of money buying social media advertising completely legally and without limit, including on YouTube and Facebook.
Again, there will be little competition in this space as many parties will not use their resources on this so early in the electoral cycle. Already Reform has professionally built broadcast studios, and splashes the cash liberally on major policy announcements at aircraft hangars, and stadiums for rallies.
Theo Bertram, the director of the Social Market Foundation thinktank, who was previously a Labour adviser and vice-president at TikTok, said in a post on X that he believed Reform would also wish to invest the money in getting in serious policy expertise and preparation for government.
Parties often rely on goodwill from expert supporters to help prepare for government or draft their manifesto. But Reform UK could recruit some of the best legal and constitutional experts to help it find ways of implementing some of its most radical and controversial policies, including mass deportations and evicting non-UK citizens from social housing. Bertram estimates that getting the best and most expensive consultants on the issues would cost the party about £25m.
Candidate vetting has also been a nightmare for Reform and cash could be used to considerably sharpen the process. There would be a vast war chest for legal challenges – Reform UK has often threatened or begun judicial reviews of government policies – which keep the party in the headlines.
There is one way that Reform UK may come a cropper if it spends the money like water over the coming months. Should Andy Burnham call a snap general election before next autumn, election spending rules are retrospective for the previous years.
That means the spending cap, roughly £34m across Great Britain, applies for the previous 12 months, leaving the party in a bit of a trap if it has already outspent that amount outside the six-week election campaign. Might that be one reason to tempt Burnham into an early poll?

Under heavy cloud cover, Russia fires massive drone barrage at western Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
15:15:49 UTC
00:15:49 KST

- Russia launched 863 Geran-2 and other drones at Ukraine in 24 hours, striking a train locomotive near the Polish border under heavy cloud cover.
- A separate chartered train carrying Boris Johnson was evacuated nearby, and Poland scrambled jets after drones struck within 5 kilometers of its border.
Under heavy cloud cover, Russia fired a massive barrage of Geran-2 attack drones, the Russian-built version of Iran’s Shahed-136, at western Ukraine early Sunday. The Ukrainian General Staff said Russia launched 863 drones at Ukraine over the previous 24 hours, one of the largest barrages of the war.
French open-source analyst Clément Molin wrote on X that Russian forces flew the drones in large groups along the Belarusian border before turning west, with some reaching the Polish frontier by morning. Molin said the poor-visibility conditions that day made it harder for Ukrainian air-defense crews to track and engage the drones visually, and he said Russia had been holding back a stockpile of Geran-2s for weeks before launching them in this attack.
The Kyiv-based open-source monitoring group CyberBoroshno separately said the drone routes it tracked ran almost entirely under the cloud cover blanketing northern and western Ukraine that day, entering through the Chernihiv region and cutting west toward Volyn while a second group flew around Kyiv from the south. The group said overcast conditions degrade optical and thermal tracking and make visual spotting by mobile air-defense teams difficult, forcing crews to rely on sound alone.
Ukraine’s Air Force said the overnight wave mixed Shahed/Geran-2 drones with Gerbera decoys, Parodiya decoys and S8000 Banderol missile-carrying drones, along with a newer jet-powered drone variant that flies faster and is harder to intercept. Air defenses shot down or jammed 409 of the drones tracked in the immediate overnight window, the Air Force said.
The heaviest confirmed impacts fell along the rail corridor near Ukraine’s border with Poland. A Russian drone struck the locomotive of a passenger train in the Volyn region, about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the border, early Sunday. Ukrzaliznytsia, the state rail operator, said its threat-monitoring teams detected the danger and warned the crew beforehand, and no casualties were reported. “The enemy struck the locomotive of a passenger train,” the operator said.
A separate chartered train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and senior European security officials was halted on the same route around 5 a.m. and partially evacuated as a precaution. The group, which included a top security adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and security advisers from the U.K., France and Italy, was returning to Poland from the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv. Former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, traveling in the same corridor, said his train was not the one struck. “This wasn’t our train, but the one just minutes after us,” he said.
Poland’s defense minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said Polish radar tracked drones striking within a few kilometers of the frontier overnight. “One of them struck 1 km from the border with Poland, another 5 km,” he said. Warsaw scrambled F-16 fighters, helicopters and a SAAB airborne early-warning aircraft, and officials said Polish airspace was not breached.
The Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing briefly closed after a drone destroyed a truck roughly 800 meters (2,600 feet) from the checkpoint, Polish border guards told Reuters. It reopened after inspections. Other crossings saw temporarily suspended checks before returning to normal.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the strikes near the border were meant to send a message to Kyiv’s Western partners. “This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO,” he wrote, calling for a full trade embargo and expanded sanctions on Russia’s defense sector.
At least nine people were injured in a separate overnight strike on Odesa, according to Serhiy Lysak, head of the city’s military administration. Across the wider 24-hour period, several civilians were killed nationwide and more than 20 others were wounded, Ukrainian officials said.
Molin said Russia is likely to rely increasingly on two tactics in the coming months: jet-powered Geran drones aimed at Kyiv and central Ukraine, and large nighttime groups of standard Geran-2s routed through bad weather along the Belarusian border or through Moldova to strike fixed targets further west. This remains his forecast and has not been independently confirmed.

Donald Trump on Sunday doubled down on his controversial pledge to give US adults a $5,000 “dividend” if his Republican party keeps control of Congress after November’s midterm elections.
The plan has been greeted with expressions of incredulity across the US political spectrum as well as outraged accusations of seeking to bribe voters. The plan – which would cost more than a trillion dollars – also comes amid huge concern over the US national debt, which topped $40tn for the first time in August.
“I don’t know but it’s easy if the Republicans win. $5,000 to all adults in the country and we can easily handle that because we’re taking in so much money,” Trump told reporters in Ireland where he is on a visit to a golf course.
Trump had been asked if Congress would need to approve the $5,000 pledge and continued: “The Democrats can’t make that pledge because it would all go to hell right away, we’d go into a depression … I made that pledge, I always keep my pledge.”
The US has roughly 240 million adult citizens, suggesting a cost of $1.2tn. The federal government spent about $7tn in fiscal year 2025, with about $2tn taken on as debt.
When the plan was first touted by Trump last week at a rally in Texas, Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget wrote on X: “The result would be a huge spike in the deficit, and almost certainly in the inflation rate.”
Democratic political leaders also reacted with a mix of outrage, disbelief and condemnation to the remarkable suggestion, which comes at a time when Trump is struggling with low poll numbers and a disastrous conflict in Iran, which is having an impact on the health of the US economy.
“After making you sicker and poorer with his war, Donald Trump now wants to buy your vote with $5,000 in taxpayer-funded blood money,” said California governor, Gavin Newsom. “The most corrupt man ever to occupy the Oval Office.”
But some Republicans have backed the idea.
“I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” said US senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, in a social media post on X.
Any such payment would need to be approved by Congress and on Sunday Mike Johnson, the House speaker and a Louisiana Republican, told CNN: “Of course, the devil’s in the details. We have to figure all that out.”
But Democratic politicians on Sunday morning talkshows in the US dismissed the idea. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, told ABC’s This Week that the plan is not a “serious proposal”.

What are the five pros and cons of artificial intelligence?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
15:03:48 UTC
00:03:48 KST

What are the five pros and cons of artificial intelligence?
AI creates new opportunities in programming and automation, but experts warn of the spread of harmful content and risks to early-career workers.
Artificial intelligence has rapidly become a tool used by hundreds of millions of people, but tech leaders are sounding alarms against the rapid advancement of AI that is being seen as a threat to humanity.
AI systems can now generate text and images, write computer code, and perform complex analyses that once required a significant amount of time and human input.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3China slams US claims of ‘industrial-scale’ AI theft
- list 2 of 3Anthropic claims Claude AI used for missile projects, global espionage
- list 3 of 3Anthropic warns of bids to use AI to build biological weapons
Supporters argue these tools could raise productivity and create new kinds of work.
However, their rapid development has also raised concerns about job losses, the spread of misinformation, and the resources needed to power AI infrastructure. Researchers have also warned that regulation and safeguards are struggling to keep pace with the technology.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, whose company created AI tool Claude, said on Saturday. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”
So, what are the pros and cons of artificial intelligence, and where is this rapidly growing technology headed?
Boosts productivity and makes tasks easier
One of the obvious benefits of AI is its ability to help people complete some tasks more quickly.
AI tools are already being used for education, writing and editing text, gathering information, and computer programming.
Almost one billion people use AI for a wide range of tasks, according to the 2026 International AI Safety Report published by the United Kingdom’s government.
The report found that the most frequent queries by users on AI giant OpenAI’s ChatGPT platform involved practical guidance on editing or generating text, researching medical health, and searching for information.
There is also evidence of significant productivity gains in particular tasks. In September 2025, the Bank for International Settlements found generative AI had “productivity gains of between 10 and 65 percent, and efficiency gains of roughly 20 to 50 percent in time savings”.
Gains were particularly evident in industries such as “coding, consulting tasks and professional writing”, it added.
Indian technology company Wipro, for example, said its use of AI had freed up capacity equivalent to 20,000 employees, who were reassigned to other roles.
Creates new opportunities and skills
While AI is certainly bound to eliminate or transform some jobs, it is also spurring the creation of others.
Demand is increasing for skills that include machine-learning programming and chatbot development. Software developers are also increasingly using AI to produce code before checking and debugging the results.
The changes mean workers may increasingly need to learn how to use AI alongside traditional professional skills.
Wipro Chief Technology Officer Sandhya Arun said the company was training more than 100,000 employees in advanced AI skills as it shifts towards what it calls a “human-AI operating model”.
Threatens jobs
AI’s groundbreaking ability to automate work is also one of the biggest risks to society, experts say.
While no concrete data exists, some 60 percent of jobs in advanced economies and 40 percent in emerging economies could be vulnerable to AI, depending on how employers and workers adopt the technology, the 2026 International AI Safety Report warned.
Earlier this year, a slew of tech giants announced cuts amid growing reliance on and shifts towards AI.
Amazon slashed 16,000 jobs in a second wave of layoffs at the e-commerce giant in three months, while social media site Pinterest announced it would cut 780 jobs as the company reallocated resources amid increased investment in AI.
There are also concerns about people starting their careers.
Stephen Clare, lead writer of the 2026 International AI Safety Report, said there is “suggestive evidence” that early-career workers in occupations highly exposed to AI may be finding it harder to get jobs.
Can be misused and spread harmful content
Generative AI – which creates content based on existing data – can create convincing text, voices, images and videos, capabilities that can also be exploited.
AI-generated deepfakes have been used to scam people, and AI systems have also been used in cyberattacks.
Deepfake technology has been used to impersonate senior US officials and corporate executives.
Criminals can use synthetic voices and videos to make people reveal sensitive information, providing access to computer systems, and transferring money.
Uses significant energy and resources
AI technology depends on physical data centres filled with powerful computer chips, which require large amounts of electricity and cooling.
The expansion of data centres is raising questions about electricity supply and whether governments have enough infrastructure to support large AI projects.
For example, a proposed data centre in the US state of Utah would use more electricity than the entire state.
Beyond electricity, environmental activists in the United States are ringing the alarm over the enormous amounts of water needed to cool down servers at data centres at a time when parts of the country are experiencing droughts.
Some residents living near US data centres have also complained of the constant hum they emit. A Gallup poll conducted in March suggested that 71 percent of Americans oppose establishing AI data centres in their areas.
The concerns around data centres extend beyond just the US and the developed world.
In Kenya, a proposed $1bn data centre involving Microsoft and Emirati technology company G42 has drawn considerable attention.
Kenyan President William Ruto highlighted the scale of the centre’s energy demands, warning that the infrastructure of that size would require substantial additional power generation.
