Physicists can’t agree on how the Universe works
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:15:56 UTC
22:15:56 KST

Physicists can’t agree on how the Universe works
- Date:
- September 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Waterloo and Perimeter Institute
- Summary:
- A massive worldwide survey of physicists has revealed surprisingly little agreement about some of the universe’s biggest mysteries. No majority backed the standard cosmological model, a leading explanation for dark matter, or any single theory of quantum gravity. One area of stronger agreement stood out: 68% said the Big Bang does not necessarily represent the beginning of time. Researchers say the divisions show just how alive and unsettled the frontiers of physics remain.
- Share:
The largest global survey of physicists ever conducted has revealed just how unsettled some of the biggest questions in modern physics remain. Researchers found surprisingly little agreement on topics ranging from black holes and dark matter to the long-running effort to reconcile Einstein's theory of gravity with quantum mechanics.
Even the standard model of cosmology, known as ΛCDM (Lambda Cold Dark Matter), failed to win support from a majority of respondents. That result may reflect recent findings from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), which suggested that dark energy could change over time. Such a possibility would conflict with the standard model, which assumes that dark energy remains constant.
And cosmology was far from the only area where physicists disagreed.
Standard Answers Fail To Win Broad Support
"The most striking result is how few of the 'standard answers' in fundamental physics command overwhelming support, with most falling short of a majority. The interesting point is not that physicists are confused. It is that the frontier is genuinely alive," says Niayesh Afshordi, associate faculty member at Perimeter Institute and professor at the University of Waterloo.
Afshordi led the study with coauthor Phil Harper and the American Physical Society's Physics Magazine.
Across the questions included in the survey, only two received majority agreement.
One concerned the Big Bang. Despite the way it is often portrayed in popular culture, 68% of the physicists surveyed said the Big Bang does not necessarily represent the beginning of time. Instead, the theory describes how the universe developed from an extremely hot and dense state. It does not, by itself, explain whether time had an absolute beginning.
The second point to cross the majority threshold was cosmic inflation. Just 51% agreed that the early universe experienced an extremely rapid period of expansion known as inflation.
Dark Matter Remains Wide Open
On many other major questions, the responses were much more divided.
Dark matter is one example. Only 17% favored the idea that dark matter is made of a yet undiscovered low-mass particle or particles. Another 12% supported modifications to the theory of gravity. The largest single group, at 21%, favored some combination of the many proposed explanations.
That spread of responses highlights how little consensus exists around one of the central mysteries of modern cosmology.
No Clear Winner for Quantum Gravity
Physicists were similarly divided over quantum gravity, the effort to develop a theory that can describe gravity within the framework of quantum mechanics.
String theory received the most support, but only 19% of respondents selected it as the most likely solution. Loop quantum gravity received 12%, while 18% favored the possibility that gravity cannot be quantized at all.
The result shows that even after decades of theoretical work, no single approach has emerged as the dominant answer.
Why Disagreement Could Be Good for Physics
So what does such widespread disagreement mean for the future of the field? Afshordi sees the lack of consensus as a sign of opportunity rather than failure.
"Scientific truth is not decided by a vote. But consensus, or its absence, tells us where the evidence feels settled and where researchers still see room for radically different ideas. In this sense, lack of consensus can be a clue. It marks places where better data, sharper theory, or new connections between subfields may be needed. In the eternal words of the Canadian singer and songwriter, Leonard Cohen: 'There is a crack in everything, that's how the light gets in.'"
Rather than suggesting that physicists have lost their way, the findings point to areas where major discoveries may still be possible. Some of the most fundamental questions about the universe remain open, leaving room for new observations, stronger theories, and unexpected ideas to reshape our understanding.
The survey results are described in an article published in Physics Magazine. An online dashboard also allows readers to explore the responses in greater detail.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Waterloo and Perimeter Institute. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Turkey: 162 arrested in LGBTQ+ raids

Unknown Publisher

Turkey: 162 arrested in LGBTQ+ raids
September 13, 2026
Turkish police have arrested at least 162 people and searched the offices of six LGBTQ+ associations in weekend raids designed to support the country's campaign to protect family values.
The Ankara-based LGBTQ+ rights group Kaos GL claimed that beyond arrests, the government had also cut access to dozens of websites and social media accounts belonging to associate groups and rights advocates.
Government says its fulfilling duty to 'protect families and children'
Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said investigations — prompted by accusations of prostitution and obscenity — were coordinated by prosecutors in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Aydin and Mersin and involved judicial proceedings against 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses across 15 provinces.
"As per the duty to protect families and children given to the state by the constitution, no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated!" Gurlek added in a social media post.
Authorities say they seized drugs, digital equipment, smuggled alcohol and a gun in weekend police operations targeting gay bars and night clubs as well as a hammam that was said to be a place of prostitution.
The Istanbul prosecutor's office added that it had found evidence indicating that children and minors were being inappropriately swayed on issues tied to sexual orientation and gender identity.
Rights groups say the government is unfairly targeting the LGBTQ+ community, with Kaos GL saying that it had been accused of making "posts containing obscenities" accessible to children.
Erdogan scapegoats LGBTQ+ 'perverts' for falling birthrates, avoiding actual contributing factors
The weekend police operation was dubbed "My Family is Safe" by the government and was part of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's "Decade of Family and Population" scheme, which is designed to reverse plummeting birthrates in the aging country.
Authorities say it was intended to make sure that society does not see LGBTQ+ activity as "normal" and that raids were carried out to "protect children, the institution of the family, and our shared moral values."
Although same-sex relations are not illegal in the country, homophobia is rife, with President Erdogan blaming LGBTQ "perverts" for Turkey's rapidly declining birthrates.
That would seem a rhetorical diversion from the actual complexity of reasons for the decline, which Erdogan — who has ruled as the country's authoritarian president since 2014 as well as serving as its influential prime minister for 10 years before that — has called "a disaster."
Though Turkey's statistical agency, TurkStat, tracked a sharp decline in the total fertility rate between 2013 and 2023 (from 2.11 to 1.51 ), the shift brings birthrates in the country closer to those in other developed nations.
Observers say the real reasons for the drop are more likely of a structural and institutional nature rather than one chalked up to lifestyle.
Turkey's chronically worsening financial crisis, inflation, skyrocketing housing prices, family unfriendly workplace environments, limited access to affordable childcare, and higher educational and employment rates for women are all considered reasons for Turks to postpone having children, as well as for having fewer when they finally do.

Russia strikes passenger train near Polish border as drone swarms reach deeper into western Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:10:51 UTC
22:10:51 KST

Russia struck a passenger train just two kilometers from Ukraine’s border with Poland on 13 September, as Moscow continued a second day of attacks on Ukraine’s railway network and expanded strikes against transport and logistics infrastructure far from the front line.
Russia is increasingly using its expanding drone fleet to reach transport, logistics, industrial and civilian infrastructure deep inside Ukraine. Western regions, long considered safer because of their distance from the front, are now seeing strikes on railways and border crossings, making even civilian travel and routes out of the country increasingly dangerous.
The latest attack took place in Ukraine’s north-western Volyn Oblast, near the Yahodyn border crossing with Poland. According to Ukraine’s state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia, a Russian drone struck the locomotive of a passenger train.
A monitoring team detected the threat in advance and warned the train crew, preventing casualties. The railway operator said trains to Warsaw and back were already running again after the strike, although with significant delays.
A gas station was also struck in a Russian drone strike near the Yahodyn crossing, causing a large fire, according to UNN, adding to the danger around a key transport route between Ukraine and Poland.
Poland also issued an air-raid alert for areas near the Ukrainian border, including Włodawa, Łęczyński and Świdnik counties and the cities of Chełm and Krasnystaw.
The attacks came alongside Russian strikes on railway infrastructure in several other parts of Ukraine.
Update: Diplomatic train may have been Russian drone’s target
Update 19:00: Ukrzaliznytsia later said a diplomatic train carrying security advisers from several EU member states and former European leaders, including former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson, had been at Yahodyn shortly before the strike. Another train at the station during the attack carried former CIA Director David Petraeus.
Ukrzaliznytsia said the Russian drone may have been targeting the diplomatic train, which departed earlier than scheduled as railway staff adjusted train movements in real time because of the ongoing threat of Russian strikes. The operator said it continues to change routes and schedules as tracks are damaged or blocked by attacks.
Russia targets railways across Ukraine
Ukrzaliznytsia said this was the second consecutive day of Russian attacks on the railway network.
On 12 September, Russian drones struck railway facilities in Lutsk, Volyn Oblast, including a passenger train, as well as Fastiv, Kyiv Oblast. Passengers were evacuated after the threat was detected.
Ukrzaliznytsia said its monitoring center and railway personnel remain on heightened alert as Russia continues targeting the network. Evacuations and diversions have caused delays on several routes, including services toward Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih.
Russia also attacked a railway infrastructure site in Vinnytsia Oblast on 13 September, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service.
Russia’s drone campaign is expanding
Russian attacks are increasingly reaching critical infrastructure and civilian areas across Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia struck energy facilities, railway sites, businesses and residential buildings during the latest wave of attacks, including missile and drone strikes on Odesa.
Zelenskyy said Russia had launched around 2,100 drones against Ukraine in the past week, alongside nearly 1,700 guided aerial bombs and 78 missiles.
He said Russia is using jet-powered Geran drones to “destroy the economy and destroy people’s lives.”
Russia has sharply increased its use of upgraded Geran attack drones in recent months, which are faster than earlier versions and can cover the long distances needed to strike targets deep inside Ukraine. Their growing speed and scale are putting additional pressure on Ukraine’s air-defense system, which has to detect and intercept large numbers of drones across the country.
“Russia’s terrorism is a common threat for many,” Zelenskyy said, arguing that the threat must be defeated in Ukraine rather than allowed to spread further into Europe.
Border crossings increasingly targeted
The strike near Yahodyn comes after Russia began targeting Ukrainian border crossings farther from the front line.
Since late August, Russian forces have struck at least five Ukrainian crossings with Moldova and NATO member Romania. The crossings handle civilian traffic, trade and logistics that are increasingly important to Ukraine as the war continues.
On 9 September, Russian drones struck the Starokozache crossing with Moldova, killing two civilians and injuring three others. One Russian drone entered Moldovan airspace and flew toward Romania, prompting NATO aircraft conducting air-policing duties to scramble.
Russia also struck the Orlivka ferry crossing on the Romanian border twice in early September.
The attacks prompted growing concern in Poland. On 10 September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Poland expected Russia could target Ukrainian border crossings with Poland as Moscow expands its strikes against transport and logistics routes.
Tusk said Poland had received intelligence indicating that similar attacks could occur against crossings involving other countries. He also warned that Poland and Europe needed to prepare for different scenarios along Europe’s eastern flank.
The strike near Yahodyn came only three days after that warning.
Poland expects Russia to target border crossings as attacks on Ukraine escalate – Russia has already hit crossings with Moldova and Romania
“Russia is trying to expand the geography of its terror”
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Russia was deliberately expanding the geography of its attacks.
“Moscow tries to expand the geography of its terror,” Sybiha said, arguing that Russia is trying to turn the entire territory of Ukraine into a battlefield as it fails to achieve its objectives on the front.
He said Moscow was targeting “civilians, trains, and the infrastructure that keeps the country moving.”
Sybiha called for stronger air defenses, interceptors and counter-drone capabilities, as well as measures targeting Russia’s drone production and supply chains.
In a separate statement after the Yahodyn attack, Sybiha said Russia’s strikes near the Polish border were “not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders.”
“This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” he said, urging European countries to respond with stronger sanctions.
Attacks moving closer to NATO
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said members of his ministry had been stuck at the same Ukrainian-Polish border crossing only hours before the latest images emerged because of the Russian drone threat.
“Russia’s attacks are becoming more intense and moving ever closer to NATO and the EU,” Tsahkna said.

How Israel’s destruction of south Lebanon is making displacement permanent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:09:22 UTC
22:09:22 KST

How Israel’s destruction of south Lebanon is making displacement permanent
With lost livelihoods, destroyed homes and little security, many displaced Lebanese are faced with an entrenched reality.
Beirut, Lebanon – More than six months after Israel intensified its war on Lebanon, a displacement crisis is slowly solidifying.
At its highest point in April, more than 1.2 million people were displaced by Israeli attacks on Lebanon.
Today, the figure stands at about 330,000, according to estimates by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) – but humanitarian workers say the drop should not be interpreted as permanent or even durable.
Nadine Mazloum, of the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR), said displacement patterns remain “highly fluid and often reversible” due to the possibility of renewed attacks.
While the “overall number of displaced people has fallen substantially from the peak of more than 1.2 million, that should not be mistaken for a resolution of the crisis”, she added.
‘This is our land’
Israel and the Lebanese group Hezbollah have been fighting since October 2023, with varying levels of intensity.
On March 2, 2026, Hezbollah responded to continued Israeli attacks on Lebanon for the first time in more than a year, saying it was in retaliation for more than 10,000 violations of a 2024 ceasefire and for the assassination two days earlier of Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on the first day of the United States-Israel war on Iran.
Israel then intensified its air attacks on Lebanon, while also reinvading southern Lebanon for the second time in less than two years. It currently occupies more than 50 villages.
The offensive has killed more than 4,380 people and drove hundreds of thousands from their homes – predominantly in southern Lebanon but also in the eastern Bekaa Valley and parts of the capital, Beirut, and its southern suburbs.
Displaced people took shelter wherever they could. In Beirut, some set up tents along the waterfront or corniche, or rented apartments in neighbourhoods deemed safer. But many of the displaced were also attacked, including in double-tap strikes.
A series of ceasefire announcements and a June framework agreement, which came after direct, US-sponsored talks between Israel and Lebanon, has not stopped the Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon.
However, bombardment on the rest of the country has eased, with more than 810,000 people either returning home or to places nearby – often to damaged houses with destroyed infrastructure.
One of them is Soujoud Ramadan, a woman from Froun, a town on a so-called “Yellow Line” – a military zone claimed by Israel that stretches roughly 10km (6 miles) north of the Lebanon-Israel border.
Froun was included in June’s framework deal under which Israeli forces were supposed to withdraw from “pilot zones” and the Lebanese army was intended to enter and disarm Hezbollah.
While much of Froun lies in rubble from Israeli air attacks, the Israeli military has not set foot in the town since 2024.
Ramadan has returned to her village, but with her home in ruins, she is staying at the local school, which is operating as a shelter for the displaced.
“We came back after the ceasefire,” she said, sitting in front of a small makeshift corner store she manages at the school’s entrance. “We came back because this land is our land and it is impossible for us to give it up.”
‘Ongoing cycle’
Despite their resilience and determination, UNHCR’s Mazloum said many returnees are still not living in complete stability.
“The reality is that many households continue to move between locations as conditions change, making displacement and return part of an ongoing cycle rather than a one-time event,” Mazloum said.
Over time, the impacts of prolonged displacement also compound, extending beyond the immediate needs for food and shelter.
“Many are facing a different set of challenges centred on exhaustion, instability and the gradual erosion of coping mechanisms,” Mazloum said. “Savings have been depleted, debts have accumulated and support networks are increasingly stretched. Families that have been paying rent for months often face mounting financial pressure at the same time that livelihoods remain disrupted.”
According to the latest IOM data, some 80 percent of displaced people are concentrated in five districts: Beirut hosts about 31 percent of the displaced, while Sidon, Tyre, Chouf and Aley host 15 percent, 14 percent, 11 percent and 9 percent, respectively.
The data also said 17,566 registered displaced people live in 184 collective sites, though that number has likely spiked in recent weeks, particularly with the intensification of Israeli attacks on southern areas, including in the city of Nabatieh. Of the displaced, some 75 percent are living in rented accommodation.
“This area has suffered greatly from the war,” Kamel Jaber, a journalist from Nabatieh, told Al Jazeera about the recent attacks on his city. “Hundreds of shops, warehouses and other [infrastructure] have been destroyed.”
He said that after the 2024 ceasefire, business returned to Nabatieh, but the resumption of the war has devastated the area’s infrastructure and economy. He also said locals began to feel “great anxiety and despair seep into their hearts” as the war has carried on without an end in sight.
‘Not one single standing wall’
Multiple videos have gone viral in recent weeks showing Israeli demolitions in southern villages, with dust shooting into the sky as explosions go off.
Al Jazeera visited the “Yellow Line” in early September and heard loud explosions every few minutes – what locals said were detonations of houses and other infrastructure on the other side of the zone.
Witnesses who have been able to go south of the “Yellow Line” say the closer to the border with Israel, the more widespread the damage is.
Maureen Philippon, the Norwegian Refugee Council’s country director in Lebanon, said that on a journey south, she passed through villages where there is “not one single standing wall”.
She said that after the 2024 ceasefire, many locals from southern villages close to the border returned home, but a “significant number had to flee again” after the resumption of attacks.
“Today they are not envisioning any returns,” said Philippon, warning that “these cycles of violence and damage” add a heavy “psychological weight” for many of the displaced.
With lost livelihoods, destroyed homes and little security or stability to have the confidence to rebuild, many Lebanese straddle displacement while others see theirs become entrenched.
Reports have recently circulated that Israel may pull back to a so-called “Grey Line” that extends up to 4km (2.5 miles) into Lebanese territory. That would mean the border villages would likely stay uninhabited and extend the displacement of the people from those areas. For those from further north, they may return to areas that have been completely demolished, leaving them without a home, electricity, or water infrastructure.
Experts are warning that the permanence of displacement in Lebanon, caused by Israel’s continued war, has far-reaching consequences.
“Humanitarian assistance remains essential, but so too are debris removal, rehabilitation of homes, restoration of public services, and support for livelihoods,” UNHCR’s Mazloum said. “Without those elements, many returns may remain fragile or unsustainable.”

Air defense, sanctions against russia, the path to peace, and EU accession - the foreign ministers of Ukraine and Estonia held a meeting
Ukraine

Air defense, sanctions against russia, the path to peace, and EU accession - the foreign ministers of Ukraine and Estonia held a meeting
Kyiv • UNN
The foreign ministers of Ukraine and Estonia discussed the front, diplomacy, air defense, and defense cooperation. Estonia reaffirmed its support for Ukraine and its accession to the EU.
Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine Andrii Sybiha held talks with his Estonian counterpart Margus Tsahkna, who arrived in Kyiv on a visit. Xinhua Headlines: Xi calls on BRICS to unite Global South, deepen cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13

* The international landscape is volatile and fraught with risks and challenges, Xi said, adding that to bring stability to the world and make it a better place, BRICS countries must seize the historical initiative, rally the Global South, and advance the well-being of all humanity.
* Xi proposed five initiatives on "greater BRICS" cooperation in areas of AI, trade and investment facilitation, digital industry, intelligent manufacturing, and science and technology talent development.
NEW DELHI, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sunday called on BRICS countries to strengthen unity among the Global South and play an active, stabilizing and positive role in global affairs.
In a speech when attending the second day of BRICS summit in New Delhi, Xi also outlined concrete proposals to further strengthen greater BRICS cooperation, with a focus on emerging areas including artificial intelligence, trade, digital industries and manufacturing.
KEY DRIVER OF MULTIPOLARITY
Xi pointed out that when changes unseen in a century are accelerating across the world, the Global South, with its collective rise, has become a key driver of world multipolarity.
At the same time, the international landscape is volatile and fraught with risks and challenges, Xi said, adding that to bring stability to the world and make it a better place, BRICS countries must seize the historical initiative, rally the Global South, and advance the well-being of all humanity.
Global South countries should jointly defend the rule of law in international affairs, safeguard the basic norms of international relations including sovereign equality, noninterference in internal affairs, and the peaceful settlement of disputes, Xi said. It should be ensured that international law and international rules are applied to all, and free from double standards, he added.
Global South countries should hold high the banner of multilateralism, uphold the authority and role of the United Nations, and support multilateral institutions in advancing reform and increasing efficiency, Xi said.
He also called for promoting the reform of the World Trade Organization in the right direction, as well as reforming and improving the international financial architecture to increase the representation and voice of developing countries.
Global South countries should stay committed to a people-centered development philosophy and strive to deliver on the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, Xi said.
Global South countries should also jointly advance security governance, tackle both traditional and nontraditional security threats, and improve global climate governance, Xi said, also calling for working faster to evolve a consensus-based global AI governance framework, so that new technologies can light the way toward shared prosperity.
"It is a solidarity that unlocks partnerships, unlocks democratization of the international system, unlocks an open international system, and unlocks an inclusive international system," said Charles Onunaiju, director of the Center for China Studies in Nigeria.
Rakhim Oshakbayev, director of the TALAP Center for Applied Research in Kazakhstan and former Kazakh vice minister for investment and development, said BRICS cooperation should "bring together developing countries' shared aspirations and promote coordination and cooperation."
BRICS countries should continue seeking common interests, he said, noting that the grouping's expansion had placed greater demands on internal coordination.
GREATER BRICS COOPERATION
During the speech, Xi proposed five initiatives on "greater BRICS" cooperation in areas of AI, trade and investment facilitation, digital industry, intelligent manufacturing, and science and technology talent development.
To accomplish great things and achieve major progress, the foundation of greater BRICS cooperation must be cemented, Xi said, calling for leveraging BRICS' close ties with fellow emerging markets and Global South countries, upholding open cooperation for mutual benefit, safeguarding stable and smooth industrial and supply chains, and fostering a large integrated market.
"We should build incubators for innovation, upgrade traditional industries, develop emerging industries, and deploy future industries," Xi said.
On the open source and inclusive AI initiative, Xi said that China will be a pioneer in establishing a BRICS AI open source community, support the cooperation in developing and applying large language models, hold specialized AI seminars and training courses, and build an open ecosystem for AI.
On the trade and investment facilitation initiative, China proposes to establish a BRICS special economic zone partnership, under which countries can set up an intelligent portal, coordinate policies, and build a new frontier for open development, Xi said, adding that in an effort to cultivate new drivers of economic and trade cooperation, China will hold the BRICS Forum on Trade in Services next year.
On the digital industry cooperation initiative, Xi said that China will push for establishing a BRICS digital ecosystem cloud platform, and conduct digital skills training, technological exchange and industrial alignment, so as to jointly enable the development of the digital economy.
On the intelligent manufacturing cooperation initiative, China stands ready to assist fellow BRICS countries in building smart factories and developing standards and norms, and jointly promote manufacturing transformation and upgrading, he said.
On the science and technology talent development initiative, China proposes to set up a BRICS engineer cultivation alliance for joint development of engineers and mutual recognition of competency standards, Xi said, adding that China will launch a BRICS youth exchange program for scientific and technological innovation, so as to cultivate more high-caliber talent.
The five initiatives proposed by Xi focus on key areas including technology, industry, trade and talent, providing concrete pathways to lay a solid foundation for practical cooperation among the broader BRICS community, said Serik Korzhumbayev, editor-in-chief of the Delovoy Kazakhstan newspaper.
It demonstrates China's firm resolve to share the opportunities of its modernization, a reflection of the spirit of openness, inclusiveness and mutual benefit that underpins BRICS cooperation, he said.■

====================================================================================================

Faster events, brighter stars, longer season - Coe outlines World Athletics' future
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
21:06:23 CST
22:06:23 KST

by sportswriters Zhou Xin and Chen Hao
BUDAPEST, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Faster competition, brighter stars and a longer global season -- World Athletics President Sebastian Coe says the inaugural Ultimate Championship offers a glimpse of where athletics could be heading.
"We are an innately conservative sport," Coe said at a media roundtable in Budapest on Sunday. "I just think we've moved slightly away from the risk-averse end of that spectrum. Not probably by much, but it's a start."
The inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship, held from September 11 to 13, was more than two and a half years in the making. Coe said many of its innovations grew out of spectator research conducted after the 2023 World Championships in Budapest.
Some of the findings, he admitted, were "counter-cultural."
Younger audiences did not want lengthy athlete introductions, long gaps between events or extended studio discussion while live competition was taking place.
"They just want the event," Coe said.
That thinking shaped a tighter competition schedule and broadcasts designed to give individual events and leading athletes more space. Coe said he had never understood why, for example, there could be seven minutes between heats of the women's 200 meters.
"It just drives me to distraction," he said.
Clearer graphics, rankings and predictions were also introduced to make athletics easier to follow, particularly for younger audiences.
Coe stressed, however, that the first edition was far from a finished product. Some disciplines could be added and others left out in future editions, but he said studying the popularity of different events was not about eliminating those ranked lowest.
Rather, the aim was to understand where resources and innovation could help raise a discipline's profile and make it more engaging.
Beyond the format, Coe added that athletics must make better use of its stars.
He described Swedish pole vault world record holder Mondo Duplantis as "the gift that keeps giving."
"He just wants to help," Coe said, adding that Duplantis understands that promotion has increasingly become part of the role of an athlete at his level.
Duplantis wrote the song "Gold" for the championship and is due to perform it at Sunday's closing ceremony. Athletes also took part in a pre-championship red carpet and other promotional activities designed to showcase personalities beyond competition.
Coe said the day-before activities generated well over one million hits and around 1,400 articles, underlining the appetite for seeing athletes away from the field of play.
Retired Jamaican sprint legend Usain Bolt represents another kind of star power.
"I sort of feel Usain is back in our sport again," Coe said.
He said he had met Bolt several times this year, including spending an afternoon with him at Wimbledon, where much of their conversation centered on the Ultimate Championship.
"He was very excited and just wants to do more in the sport," Coe said.
The challenge, he joked, was finding the right role.
"If I'd gone to Usain and said, 'Would you chair a committee or commission?' He's not going to want to do that."
Bolt has already been involved behind the scenes in junior athletics and promotional work, and Coe said World Athletics would continue looking for ways to keep him engaged.
For Coe, athletics is also fortunate to have an unusually deep generation of current competitors.
"We're really lucky," he said, describing them as "a group of people for the ages."
In previous periods, attention could be concentrated more heavily on either track or field, he said, but over the past two or three years athletics has developed "a far broader bandwidth of talent across all our disciplines."
Looking further ahead, Coe said the Ultimate Championship also addresses what he sees as one of athletics' structural weaknesses -- a season that remains too short.
"The sport comes together for the big magnesium moments between sort of June and September," he said. "That, across any metric, is a short season for a sport that's supposed to be professional."
World Athletics wants its World Championships and Ultimate Championship, where possible, to serve as the climax of the season.
Coe said athletics could not afford to have one year in every four when the sport "goes a bit dark out there," particularly compared with the vast global audiences generated by the Olympic Games and World Championships.
Different climates in southern California, South Africa and Australia could help extend the season while broadening athletics' global footprint.
"So this event could be in maybe late October in a few years' time," Coe said. "That would be my success."
Climate change could also force that shift, particularly for endurance events, as athlete welfare may make some traditional competition windows increasingly unsuitable.
But a longer season, Coe stressed, should mean more choice rather than more pressure.
"We don't put athletes under pressure to compete," he said. "I just want to give them more options and more opportunities for financial security."
He cited Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen, who had been weighing whether to continue competing after an injury-hit season.
"In reality, I care more about you than I do an event," Coe said he told him.
The same philosophy, he argued, lies behind higher prize money.
Athletes will not suddenly run faster because they are thinking about tens of thousands of dollars near the finish line, Coe said. The greater value lies in financial security -- helping them stay in the sport longer, afford better treatment when injured and prepare for life after competition.
He recalled British long jumper Jazmin Sawyers saying that 75,000 U.S. dollars would allow her to "stay on in the sport for another year and buy another sewing machine."
"When I was pushing prize money and raising the game generally, that's exactly what I had in mind," Coe said.
For a sport Coe describes as "innately conservative," the Ultimate Championship remains a work in progress.
"It's a start," Coe said. ■

Somali piracy resurgence threatens global shipping amid Red Sea crisis
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
21:06:00 CST
22:06:00 KST

MOGADISHU, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- A resurgence of Somali piracy off the northeastern coast and in the Gulf of Aden is growing amid Red Sea security risks, threatening global shipping costs and commodity prices to push up, analysts warned.
Following a string of vessel attacks and seizures since April, the International Maritime Organization (IMO), a specialized agency of the United Nations regulating maritime transport, issued a warning on Aug. 24 highlighting the rise in piracy and confirming that over 90 seafarers remain held hostage by pirate networks.
Experts emphasize that a persistent lack of economic opportunities, compounded by widespread illegal fishing by foreign vessels, is driving more Somalis toward piracy, viewed by many both as a form of socio-economic protest and a desperate survival strategy.
Mohamed Husein Gaas, director of the Raad Peace Research Institute, a think tank, noted that the security vacuum created as international naval forces shifted attention to the Red Sea crisis has given Somali pirate networks renewed operational freedom.
"Somali piracy is back not because the underlying problem disappeared, but because the security architecture that suppressed it has weakened," Gaas told Xinhua in a recent interview in Mogadishu, the capital of Somalia.
He noted that while international naval patrols and vessel defense measures previously suppressed piracy, root causes like weak coastal enforcement, poverty, and lack of governance remained unresolved.
"Piracy was suppressed, not solved," Gaas said.
Gaas said that the Houthi conflict has "changed the equation" by shifting shipping routes and diverting naval resources, creating ripple effects for maritime traffic near Somalia.
However, he cautioned against treating allegations of direct operational ties between Houthi networks and Somali pirate groups as established fact.
Meanwhile, commercial consequences are mounting in the region.
Abdirizak Sabriye, a member of the Somali Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the apex umbrella body for Somalia's private sector, noted that global ocean carrier Maersk has suspended new bookings to and from the Port of Berbera in northern Somalia citing operational scheduling conflicts and broader regional route realignments.
While Sabriye did not link the decision solely to piracy, he emphasized that it underscores the widespread logistics disruption hitting Horn of Africa trade.
For Somalia, an import-dependent economy, prolonged maritime disruptions threaten to drive up freight and insurance premiums, tighten domestic supply chains, and trigger consumer price inflation.
Yusuf Mohamed Mahadale, a prominent capital goods importer known locally as "Shakirow", said that these cost pressures are already spilling over into local markets.
"The prices of construction materials, fuel and even cooking gas have risen sharply in recent months," Shakirow said, linking the price hikes directly to growing risks along shipping routes and the broader regional maritime crisis.
Because much of Somalia's construction material is imported from China, Shakirow emphasized that the Indian Ocean-Gulf of Aden corridor serves as a vital economic lifeline for Somali businesses.
"When shipping companies avoid taking such risks, supply becomes tighter while market demand remains high," Shakirow told Xinhua.
Analysts have warned that the long-term economic fallout could escalate significantly if piracy evolves from isolated incidents into a sustained, systemic threat to Indian Ocean trade corridors.
"If piracy becomes sustained, shipping companies could again avoid the Gulf of Aden, raising insurance, freight and fuel costs and ultimately consumer prices," Gaas said.
"For Somalia, that would mean higher import costs and weaker maritime investment, while the wider region and global trade would absorb the larger shock," he cautioned.
Rising piracy highlights a shift in regional security dynamics as Western naval forces pivot toward broader Middle Eastern conflicts, opening space for Turkey, China, and Gulf nations to expand their influence around the Red Sea.
To address these vulnerabilities, a Somali government official stated that Mogadishu plans to join the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, the official noted Somalia will also consult with China to strengthen its naval capabilities and reduce reliance on Western defense coalitions.
Though Somalia's potential entry into the defense pact remains an unconfirmed diplomatic effort, Mogadishu is expanding domestic counter-piracy operations.
The foreign ministry reported ongoing land and sea interventions, highlighting the Aug. 29 liberation of the hijacked cargo ship MV Lutuf as a key success.
"Somalia will not permit its waters to become a haven for maritime crime," the ministry said.
The government is calling for international naval support to align with its national security framework and bringing the piracy issue before the UN Security Council, supported by Parliament's recent passage of updated anti-piracy legislation.
Gaas noted that naval patrols are insufficient on their own, arguing that lasting solutions depend on strong coastal governance, improved enforcement, and genuine economic opportunities for local communities. ■

Italian Ex-Foreign Minister Giulio Terzi: Italy Is Unequivocally on Ukraine’s Side
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:04:00 UTC
22:04:00 KST

Giulio Terzi di Sant’Agata, Italy’s former foreign minister who currently chairs the Senate’s Committee on European Union Policies, discussed with the Kyiv Post Italy’s support for Ukraine, Kyiv’s path towards EU membership, European defense, post-war recovery and accountability for Russian aggression. During his diplomatic career, he served as Italy’s ambassador to Israel and the United States, as well as Italy’s permanent representative to the United Nations in New York. He was appointed foreign minister in Mario Monti’s government in November 2011.
                                                                                                                                                                         
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ugo Poletti: Senator Terzi, drawing on your parliamentary and diplomatic experience, what specific role can Italy play in relations between Ukraine and the European Union today, distinguishing itself without weakening the unity of the member states?
Giulio Terzi di Sant’Agata: Since the beginning of Russia’s military aggression, Italy has distinguished itself as a strong and unequivocal voice in support of the Ukrainian people.
At the most recent summits – the G7 meeting in Evian, the European Council, the NATO summit in Ankara and, finally, the meetings of the Coalition of the Willing and the integrated ballistic-missile defense coalition – as on many previous international occasions, Italy has consistently upheld the inviolable principles of freedom and national sovereignty for which Ukraine has been fighting for more than four years.
Ukraine Is Better Prepared for Winter Strikes, Koretskyi Says
Italy has also worked to foster dialogue and cohesion among EU and NATO members in reaffirming their support for Kyiv. It has endorsed and voted for all 21 packages of sanctions against Russia, as well as the decision to end Russian gas supplies to Europe.
There can be no doubt that Feb. 24, 2022 was a watershed. Since then, security, deterrence and defense against the tangible threat of extremely serious military aggression have once again become central concerns. Italy wants to help develop a stronger culture of security and defense throughout European society.
This is connected with the need to build an increasingly cohesive Euro-Atlantic community, within which a genuine and credible European pillar of defense can be defined and established as quickly as possible. I believe that Ukraine is already an integral part of that pillar, even though the necessary legal, political and treaty conditions have yet to be fully established.
Does support for Ukraine, therefore, also provide a foundation for strengthening a common European security and defense policy? How can this be achieved without creating duplication or tension with NATO?
At the latest NATO summit, Italy reiterated a principle that has become more important than ever. “It is time for Europe to guarantee its own security,” Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said.
In addition to the US commitment to authorize the production of Patriot missiles in Ukraine, the summit consolidated one essential point: the Alliance must be judged by the concrete capabilities each country contributes to collective defense.
As the Meloni government has consistently argued, the European Union must therefore become an increasingly credible security actor within NATO – in terms of its technological and military capabilities, operational readiness and political determination.
Europe’s contribution to the Alliance must become strong enough for the European pillar to serve as the principal foundation of our continent’s security. This would consequently be of vital importance to our non-European allies as well.
Europe’s collective security rests on the indispensable value of Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, but also on Article 42.7 of the Treaty on European Union. The latter stipulates that, if a member state is the victim of armed aggression on its territory, the other member states are obliged to provide it with aid and assistance by all the means in their power.
                                                                                                                                                                         
These are rights, duties and responsibilities that European and Atlantic Alliance countries have signed and ratified over the years, without qualification or reservation. In principle, these provisions take precedence over national legislation. This is reflected in Articles 11 and 117 of the Italian Constitution and in comparable provisions in the constitutions of other member states.
Ukraine regards membership of the European Union as a strategic choice and a matter of national identity. Which reforms should it undertake most urgently, and what must the EU do to ensure that accession does not remain an indefinite promise?
Kyiv is demonstrating a firm determination to join the European family. That ambition has roots extending well beyond Putin’s aggression. It dates back to the time when the Ukrainian people and their government were alone among the former Soviet republics in refusing to join the Moscow-led Commonwealth of Independent States.
The European Council meeting of June 18-19 welcomed the intergovernmental conference on Ukraine’s accession to the European Union and the opening of the cluster covering fundamental issues on June 15, 2026. It also looked forward to the opening of the remaining clusters, in accordance with the merit-based approach. That said, let us be clear: Kyiv is already European. Ukraine is already a member of this family.
The progress it continues to make – in the rule of law, the judicial system and public administration – shows that Ukraine is genuinely mobilizing all the resources at its disposal in its struggle for freedom and independence, and to affirm itself as a sovereign nation in the face of Putin’s bloody designs. The progress already recognized by the EU in Ukraine’s alignment with European standards represents a series of fundamental steps.
I recently met Oleksandr Vasiuk, a member of the Verkhovna Rada’s Committee on Legal Policy, who explained in detail how the government in Kyiv is implementing the reforms required by the EU. He described the important results achieved in reforming the judiciary and the institutions of both constitutional and ordinary justice.
I was also pleased to learn of Kyiv’s strong drive to digitalize administrative documents and procedures. We should also consider the reforms of the anti-corruption system, which has now been strengthened through an independent National Anti-Corruption Bureau with procedural autonomy and a specialized anti-corruption prosecutor.
In my view, all these reforms represent important progress along the path towards Ukraine’s gradual integration into the European Union. We must hope that this process can be completed quickly.
European support for Ukraine now encompasses military, economic, humanitarian and diplomatic assistance. How can a partnership born during an emergency be transformed into a lasting, structural relationship?
This is already happening. A structural relationship is taking shape within the defense industry. Ukraine’s operational capabilities have been amply demonstrated – not only in defending its territory, but also in significantly slowing what, until a year ago, appeared to be an unstoppable Russian advance. Ukrainian forces have shown that they can operate at long range, making Russia’s frontline supply routes increasingly vulnerable.
Consider Ukraine’s drones and cutting-edge technologies, which are effectively unique in the world today. Europe is seeking to build a robust security architecture. This will involve not only institutions, but businesses above all. In countries such as Italy and Germany, a large proportion of small and medium-sized enterprises contribute to defense supply chains.
What will happen next? These companies will require further investment and expansion because defense manufacturing is extensive and highly interconnected. The F-35 production program, for example, relies on more than 2,100 suppliers worldwide, almost half of which are small businesses. There is therefore enormous potential for cooperation with Ukraine, which has acquired technological and operational expertise of unmatched value during these years of war.
That is not all. Cooperation with Ukraine is also extremely important in countering Russia’s hybrid warfare against the EU, including interference, disinformation, cognitive manipulation and cyberespionage.
There is now far greater awareness of the hybrid threats Moscow directs against Europe and the West as a whole. Russian aggression against our democracies does not consist solely of incursions into European airspace. It also takes the form of propaganda, political interference, cognitive manipulation and attempts to subvert our electoral processes.
Ukraine has experienced direct Russian military aggression since the conflict unleashed against Donbas and Crimea, culminating in the full-scale invasion of 2022. Even before then, however, Kyiv had faced an extraordinary wave of manipulation, violence and subversion, particularly from the time of the Euromaidan protests onwards.
Both hybrid warfare and the evolution of conventional warfare require sophisticated, technologically advanced instruments of deterrence. The EU and its member states are now working to develop those capabilities.
What practical contribution can Italy make to Ukraine’s reconstruction – not only through funding and business involvement, but also in such fields as public institutions, culture, education, healthcare and the protection of cultural heritage?
Ukraine’s reconstruction was a priority during Italy’s G7 presidency and has long occupied a central place on the European agenda.
In recent months, numerous meetings have been held in Kyiv between Italian ministers, ambassadors and business representatives and members of the Ukrainian government, confirming our country’s strong interest. The Ukraine Recovery Conference was held in Rome a year ago, where important commitments were made. One prominent example is Italy’s leading role in the reconstruction of Odesa Cathedral.
Rebuilding a country means bringing it back to life. It means reconstructing schools, hospitals and energy infrastructure, restoring livelihoods and creating the best possible conditions for Ukraine’s revival. In other words, it means providing Ukraine with genuine security. That security cannot be limited to empty promises and declarations such as those contained in the three great deceptions shamefully inflicted upon the Ukrainian people in the past.
The first was the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, under which the United States, the United Kingdom and Russia provided security assurances concerning Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity in exchange for Kyiv relinquishing its vast nuclear arsenal, which was subsequently transferred to Russia.
The second was the 1997 Russian-Ukrainian Friendship Treaty, a bilateral agreement in which Russia recognized Ukraine’s territorial integrity and the inviolability of its borders, including Crimea.
The third was the vague promise of Ukraine’s eventual NATO membership made by the Alliance at the 2008 Bucharest Summit. We cannot allow Ukraine to be deceived again. This time, reconstruction cannot begin without a full understanding of what genuine security for Ukraine entails in practice.
Important humanitarian questions must also be addressed. I recently met Yana Zinkevych at the Italian Senate. She is a member of the Ukrainian Verkhovna Rada and commander of the Hospitallers volunteer medical battalion. She recalled some tragic figures: more than 4,000 schools are unusable, 330,000 homes have been destroyed, and more than 1,000 kilometers of railway lines and bridges need to be rebuilt.
The EU – and Italy is once again at the forefront – wants to participate in this reconstruction. In a majority resolution approved by the Senate in preparation for the June European Council, the government was called upon to work to ensure that “the European institutions provide full political, economic and operational support to associations and organizations working to address the humanitarian consequences of the war of aggression.”
What minimum conditions must be met for a ceasefire to begin and open the way to a peace process?
First and foremost, the aggression must stop. Russia must cease bombing Ukraine – its homes and the facilities essential to civilian life, including hospitals, nurseries, schools and power stations. Russian raids are killing civilians. That is unacceptable.
Russia’s systematic attacks on Ukraine’s agricultural industry, ports, grain terminals and merchant vessels also demonstrate Moscow’s intention to spread chaos and continue the madness of these crimes. All of this must end before there can be a ceasefire and the beginning of serious peace negotiations.
When negotiations between the two sides eventually begin, there will clearly be certain points – or preconditions – that cannot be negotiated away. Russia must compensate Ukraine for the immense damage caused by the war. Ukraine’s full sovereignty, complete independence and national identity must also be definitively recognized and effectively guaranteed.
How can responsibility for crimes committed during the war be established, and how can the victims’ right to justice be upheld?
There is broad agreement that a special tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine is urgently needed, and its establishment is now taking shape. The Council of Europe and the European Union have signed an agreement concerning its financing.
I also want to emphasize the importance of initiatives such as the International Centre for the Prosecution of the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine at Eurojust.
Its work complements the arrest warrants issued by the International Criminal Court for Vladimir Putin and other Russian officials, including Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia’s Commissioner for Children’s Rights, in connection with the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia.
These issues cannot be relegated to the background. They concern human rights, the right to compensation for the damage caused by a war of aggression unleashed by President Putin, and the right of every family to be reunited with children deported to Russia.

Bangsamoro set for maiden elections in southern Philippines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:01:25 UTC
22:01:25 KST

Amir Latif 
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
The Philippines' Muslim-majority Bangsamoro autonomous region is set to hold its first parliamentary election on Monday, which is seen as a crucial step in the quest for self-governance and lasting peace after decades of resistance.
Nearly 2.4 million voters are set to make a choice, with 80 seats at stake in the elections that will determine members of parliament, the region’s legislative body, the state-run Philippine News Agency reported on Sunday.
These include 40 political party representatives, 32 district representatives, and eight sectoral representatives.
Voting will run from 7 am local time Monday (2300GMT Sunday) to 7 pm (1100GMT Monday).
The elections will use automated counting machines previously deployed during the May 2025 midterm elections.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao is home to around 5 million people, the majority of whom are Muslims.
It covers five provinces, three cities, and 63 villages across eight special geographic area clusters.
In January 2019, a referendum approved the "Bangsamoro Organic Law," officially establishing the "Bangsamoro Transition Authority" in the region, following decades of resistance by the Murad Ebrahim-led Moro Islamic Liberation Front.
Ebrahim was appointed as the first interim chief minister of the autonomous region the same year. He was succeeded by Abdulraof Macacua in March last year.
 
1st elections after several delays
Monday's elections will be held after being delayed four times.
The Philippine Supreme Court postponed the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro region for the third time last year.
The election, originally scheduled for 2022, was postponed to May 11 of last year, then rescheduled for October, before being postponed again.
For young voters and women, the historic polls are more than an exercise in choosing leaders.
"Among those preparing to take part are women and young Bangsamoro, whose voices are being given space in the new parliamentary system not only through their votes, but also through sectoral representation, voter education and participation in the electoral process," said a statement from the Bangsamoro government.
Under the Bangsamoro Autonomy Act, regional parliamentary political parties are required to ensure that at least 30% of their party nominees are women. As far as practicable, at least one in every three party nominees must be a woman.
The provision establishes a gender quota aimed at increasing women’s representation in the first regular Bangsamoro Parliament.
The election commission also reserves one seat each for women, youth, traditional leaders, and the ulama, and two reserved seats for settler communities and Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples in the Parliament.
 
Long struggle until 2019
The chair of the Commission on Elections, George Garcia, said the polls represent a continuation of the Bangsamoro struggle for self-government through the peace process.
The Moro Islamic Liberation Front led the region’s struggle for autonomy since the mid-20th century, ultimately resulting in peace talks and the transitional government’s formation after a referendum on Jan. 21, 2019.
Before the Bangsamoro Transition Authority was founded in 2019 following the referendum, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, led by Murad Ebrahim, had asked for a six-year transition period during peace negotiations with the Manila national government.
But negotiations resulted in a three-year transitional government under Ebrahim as chief minister until 2022.
The two sides agreed to allow the transitional government to take control of regional governance and run affairs until 2022, when elections were agreed to be held.

Philippines holding historic election in Muslim autonomous region
Unknown

Philippines holding historic election in Muslim autonomous region
Under a 2014 peace deal brokered by Malaysia, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front gave up its goal of a separate state in exchange for autonomy
Voters in an autonomous southern Philippine region will cast their ballots on Monday in the region’s first parliamentary elections, seen as a crucial step in the quest for self-determination and lasting peace after decades of insurgency and violence.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, or BARMM, covers five provinces, three cities and 63 villages across eight special geographic area clusters. It has nearly 2.4 million voters, with election officials aiming for an 80 per cent turnout after polling was postponed for several years.
There are 80 seats at stake in the elections that will determine members of parliament on September 14. These include 40 political party representatives, 32 district representatives and eight sectoral representatives.
Unlike the direct voting under the presidential system of the national government, the region’s chief minister, who heads the executive branch, is not elected by voters. Members of parliament will choose the chief minister from among themselves by a majority vote during their first parliamentary session.
Voters will choose one regional party, one district representative and six sectoral representatives. The 40 regional party-representative seats will be distributed to nominees based on a party’s vote share.
History of strife
Centuries of colonialism by Spain, the US and Filipino Christian settlers turned Muslims into a minority group in resource-rich Mindanao, the southern third of the Philippine archipelago from which the BARMM was carved out. The region has seen decades of intermittent but bloody conflicts over land, resources and political power.

Latvian Welfare Minister Reinis Uzulnieks (ZZS) may have been caught driving with a blood alcohol level of 3.09‰, LETA has learned.
The State Police confirmed to LETA that on Saturday, 12 September, municipal police officers stopped the driver of a Škoda in Stopiņi Parish, Ropaži Municipality, on suspicion of drink-driving.
The State Police were called to the scene. A breathalyser test showed an alcohol concentration of 3.09‰ in the Škoda driver’s breath.
The State Police have launched criminal proceedings over the incident.
According to Uzulnieks’ public official declaration, he owns a 2022 Škoda Kodiaq.
LETA previously reported that the board of the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) decided at an extraordinary meeting to recall Uzulnieks from the post of Welfare Minister. It was also decided to expel him from the party.
Viktors Valainis, chairman of the Latvian Farmers’ Union, which is part of ZZS, told LETA that the decision concerning Uzulnieks was unanimous, as the political force has zero tolerance for such incidents.
At the same time, he noted that Uzulnieks is still legally entitled to stand in the election and that the political party itself cannot prevent him from doing so.
ZZS has promised to provide further information on Monday, 14 September.
Uzulnieks is the lead candidate on the ZZS electoral list in Zemgale for the Saeima election scheduled for October this year.
In 2014, he became head of the office of Welfare Minister Uldis Augulis (ZZS) and later served as Parliamentary Secretary at the Ministry of Welfare.
Uzulnieks returned to the post of Parliamentary Secretary at the ministry in 2023. In 2025, during the government led by Evika Siliņa (JV), he became Welfare Minister, replacing Augulis after the latter was recalled from office.
In May 2026, Uzulnieks was confirmed as Welfare Minister in the government led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (AS).
According to information available in the LETA archives, Uzulnieks was born on 28 July 1986 in Talsi and studied at the Latvian Police Academy and Turība University.
Amendments to the Criminal Law that entered into force in November 2022 introduced criminal liability for driving or teaching someone to drive a vehicle if the alcohol concentration detected in a breath or blood test exceeds 1.5‰.
For such an offence, the Criminal Law provides for imprisonment of up to one year, probation supervision and a five-year driving ban.
Driving while heavily intoxicated is also subject to confiscation of property, namely the vehicle.

A spokesperson for the Barnet Group said she was the “strongest candidate” in a competitive field.

“She should not be in a position of power,” Daffarn said. “No one named in the Grenfell inquiry should be while we are still awaiting the outcome of the police investigation.”
The Metropolitan police said it was seeking charges against 57 individuals and 20 companies in relation to the fire, with the Crown Prosecution Service saying it expected to make decisions on charges by June 2027, the 10th anniversary of the disaster.

A spokesperson for the Barnet Group said: “Barnet Homes and Barnet council will not discuss matters relating to members of staff which took place during previous employment.
“Our thoughts remain with the survivors and family and friends of all those affected by the tragic Grenfell Tower fire. The safety and wellbeing of our residents is our top priority.”

The bird that changed Ecuador: how a chance discovery of a rare species helped to save many more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:00:05 UTC
22:00:05 KST

I have to confess that I rarely enjoy birding in montane cloud forests. The birds that live in these mountainous, cool and humid habitats are masters of disguise, usually passing themselves off as a leaf or other form of foliage. But if I want to see antpittas – elusive, ground-dwelling birds that rarely show themselves – then I have no choice.
So, on a cool, cloudy morning my guide, Juan Carlos Crespo, Fredy Ramón Castillo, a local ranger, and I are standing on a steep, muddy path close to Tapichalaca Lodge, 2,500 metres above sea level in the eastern Andes, waiting for the jocotoco antpitta to emerge from the undergrowth.
Fortunately, antpittas have a soft spot for food, especially the large, juicy earthworms Castillo has placed on a low branch nearby. He calls the bird, with increasingly loud and urgent shouts of “venga, venga!” (“come on, come on!”). The minutes tick by, until I begin to wonder if this is a lost cause.
Then, out of nowhere, a plump, thrush-sized bird with a chestnut back, grey front, black crown and white face-patch materialises just a few feet away. It proceeds to gulp down the earthworms as if it has not eaten for days.
I have seen a lot of different birds, but never one that so changed the course of bird conservation. In November 1997, a group led by the influential US ornithologist Robert Ridgely was exploring this area of southern Ecuador to see what they could find.
As they ascended a forest trail at dawn, they heard the sound of a bird in the far distance. As Ridgely recalled many years later, “It had this crazy call, sounding like an owl; but we had no idea what it was, and to be honest I never thought we would find out.”
Ridgely walked ahead of the group, and heard the sound much closer than before. He recorded the call and played it back to the mystery creature, which came crashing through the dense bamboo, right out into the open.
“I knew right away that this was something really special, which no one apart from the local people had ever seen – an entirely new species to science.” It was, in fact, one of the greatest ornithological breakthroughs of the late 20th century: while new species are sometimes discovered, they are rarely so large, noisy and so obviously different from other members of their family.
Talking to local farmers, Ridgely discovered that they were familiar with the bird, which they had named “jocotoco” to represent its loud, barking call. Two years later, the species was officially described, and named the jocotoco antpitta; the scientific name, Grallaria ridgelyi, commemorating its proud discoverer.
Ridgely soon realised that if the bird was to be saved from extinction its forest home needed to be urgently protected. He and a group of like-minded friends created an organisation dedicated to saving the bird and its habitat, raising funds from donors in the US and Europe to buy and restore the land. In 1998 the Jocotoco Foundation was born.
Today, the foundation protects and manages 19 reserves throughout Ecuador, covering about 50,000 hectares (193 sq miles), and manages a further 82,000 hectares of privately and communally owned land. Together, these sites are home to more than 1,350 species of birds – that’s 80% of all those found in Ecuador, and an astonishing one in eight of all bird species on the planet, as well as many other plant and animal species. The foundation also works closely with nearby communities, employing local people as park rangers – many of whom grew up on the land they now protect – and through jobs in wildlife tourism.
The model for the foundation’s reserves is simple and very effective. First, it restores habitat by planting a variety of native trees and other plants, or in some places simply allows the vegetation to regenerate on its own. Park guards, all of whom come from local communities, protect the reserves against illegal incursions such as cattle grazing, logging and poaching, aided by new technology including camera traps and audio recorders.
They also use these to monitor the fortunes of key species, while providing nest boxes to encourage them to breed, making up for the loss of natural tree cavities while the old-growth forests are being restored.
A recent study at Canandé, in the Chocó region of north-west Ecuador, revealed that even after deforestation, nature can recover very rapidly. The study showed that in just three decades – a single human generation – of being managed for biodiversity, formerly cleared lands have recovered 90% of the biomass – the weight of all animals – and 90% of the number of species found in nearby mature forests. While the new mix of species is not fully the same as in a mature forest, 75% of the original species present in an old-growth forest have returned.
Mike Parr, the president of the American Bird Conservancy, has no doubt about the importance of this work. “Beyond safeguarding Ecuador’s rarest birds, migrating species and incredible overall biodiversity, Jocotoco’s strategic integration of ecotourism, public awareness, community engagement and scientific research are world class. They have done an amazing job covering the previously unprotected endangered species of Ecuador.”
During recent visits to Ecuador I have visited 10 of the foundation’s reserves, including those in the Chocó region north-west of Quito and Copalinga in the Amazon foothills, along with the Los Petreles reserve on San Cristóbal Island in the Galápagos, a refuge for a critically endangered seabird, the Galápagos petrel.
On a visit to Buenaventura reserve, a restored cattle ranch in the western foothills of the Andes, we went in search of an even rarer bird: the El Oro parakeet. This charismatic parrot was only discovered as recently as 1980, and has a tiny home range, with fewer than 1,000 individuals.
Another early start took us to an open area of grassland and scattered trees where the birds are known to gather. Moments later, we heard a raucous call, and there they were: several flocks totalling about 20 of these emerald-green birds, the males with a distinctive red forehead.
But even this memorable moment was eclipsed by my visit to the Chakana nature reserve, more than 4,000 metres above sea level in the páramo grasslands of the high Andes – yet just an hour south-east of Quito. On an unexpectedly fine and sunny day, against a stunning backdrop of the snow-capped Cotopaxi volcano, we enjoyed closeup views of the Ecuadorian hillstar, a specialist high-altitude hummingbird, along with nine Andean condors soaring right around us, before they rose high into the clear blue sky.
Numbers of the Andean condor, the world’s largest flying bird by a combination of weight and wingspan, have fallen rapidly in recent years, due mainly to deliberate poisoning. But here, these mighty raptors are now returning to their ancestral home.
Dr Martin Schaefer, chief executive of Jocotoco, believes that even in these dark times there is room for optimism. “The power to restore what we have lost is in our hands.”
Ian J Davidson, Americas regional director for BirdLife International, agrees. “By creating a network of protected habitat ‘arks’, Jocotoco has given these remarkable species a genuine chance not only to endure, but to recover and expand beyond their remaining strongholds.
“Their work stands as a global conservation success story, an inspiring example of what determination, science and long-term stewardship can achieve for nature.”
At a time when President Trump has withdrawn US government funding for conservation projects around the world, the Jocotoco Foundation is a classic model of how scientists and local people can work together to save endangered birds and the precious places where they live.
