====================================================================================================

The end times fascists are plotting their escape from our world. Our mission is clear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:00:05 UTC
22:00:05 KST

When Jeff Bezos announced his plan for an opulent Venetian wedding in early 2025, many locals found the idea offensive, even obscene. A growing number of residents were struggling to find secure and affordable housing in a city overrun by tourists and Airbnb, and the billionaire was planning to, in effect, rent out the municipality for three days, forking over an estimated $50m for festivities that would clog central canals and block well-trafficked streets. Worse, Amazon’s carbon emissions were soaring, thanks to artificial intelligence and the datacentre build out – and that’s personal in Venice, where the streets already flood dozens of times a year.
Marta Sottoriva, a 35-year-old high school teacher, told us that she first heard about the wedding plans just when Bezos’s rocket company, Blue Origin, was grabbing headlines. Bezos had sent a “crew” of female influencers and celebrities, including his fiancee, Lauren Sánchez, and the pop singer Katy Perry, to the suborbital edge of space in a seemingly pointless publicity stunt. “The idea that you are so rich and powerful that you can use space as a 10-minute trip,” Sottoriva recalled, only intensified the “feeling that our city was being taken away from us in such an arrogant way”. Federica Toninello, another young activist, agreed, telling us that it felt as if both space and Venice were being “colonized”.
Colonizing space is exactly what Bezos hopes to do. Blue Origin, Bezos claims in his well-rehearsed sales pitch, will secure humanity’s survival by allowing a trillion people to one day spread across the solar system. The unbearable horror he imagines himself saving our species from? The threat of what he calls a “civilization of stasis”, otherwise known as having to contend with real ecological limits and devising a way to share the planet’s finite resources. To avoid this reckoning, Bezos imagines a future in which “Earth will be zoned residential and light industrial” and set aside as a sort of preserve out of reach for most of its native inhabitants. The vast majority of humans will pursue the nebulous benefit of “exponential growth” in the forbidding void of space, trapped on Blue Origin spacecrafts. It would seem that Bezos believes the prospect of humanity living sustainably and peaceably on our precious, singular home is a nightmarish possibility unworthy of his consideration.
Predictably, it turned out that most Venetians would rather continue living in magnificent Venice. Unlike Bezos, they don’t fret about hypothetical civilizational stagnation; they worry about economic stagnation as a result of government divestment, a lack of jobs and opportunity, and being forced out of the city and country they love. Young Italians often have little choice but to emigrate to find work; over the last decade, more than 1 million citizens have moved, a third of them between the ages of 25 and 34.
To date, the precarity and anger many Italians feel has mostly benefited the neofascist right. But those same forces also drew people to the anti-Bezos cause, helping to coalesce a budding, self-consciously antifascist movement.
The spirited, disruptive “No Space for Bezos” campaign tapped into wells of outrage against billionaires, climate breakdown and militarism – and it also gave the organizers a megaphone to broadcast ideas for different, less lethal ways we could choose to live together. Activists printed posters and stickers showing Bezos’s head on a rocket blasting into space. They made a dummy of Bezos clutching fistfuls of fake money while clinging to a giant buoyant Amazon package, then set it free to float down the canals. They unfurled banners from Venice’s iconic buildings and bridges and across its piazzas: “Tax the rich to give back to the planet.” And they chanted that the money for the wedding would be better spent rebuilding Gaza. For days, they caused gleeful chaos and relentlessly poked fun at the groom and his star-studded guest list, which included his billionaire bunker neighbors Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and a gaggle of Kardashians.
Not long before the wedding, officials announced that the event was being moved to a less central location due to the protests. Even Bezos’s two yachts, Koru and Abeona, were denied permission to dock locally. Organizers declared victory and celebrated. The international press devoured the visual-rich showdown. And the online right didn’t know who to root for: the Davos elites spraying one another with foam on a superyacht, or the leftist riffraff making agitprop?
Like Donald Trump’s enormous ballroom, Bezos’s extravagant wedding epitomized the obscenities of our networked gilded age. For the Amazon founder, it wasn’t enough to be part of one of Europe’s most beautiful cities – he needed to consume it and swallow it whole. A year later he would do the same with New York City’s Met Gala, sparking similar outrage and grassroots creativity.
The Venice protests, which dwelled on Bezos’s dreams of outer space at the expense of Earth, pointed to something fundamental about the age of end times fascism – a concept at the center of our new book, referring to an unholy alliance working toward an apocalyptic future from which only a chosen few will emerge unscathed. Today’s battle lines are not simply between people who struggle to survive under increasingly degraded and costly conditions and an oligarch class thinking of ever more ludicrous ways to waste their wealth. They are more cosmological than that.
On one side are those of us who have no escape plan, no bunker in the sky or underground, and who therefore are committed to staying right here, in the complexity of our earthbound reality, with one another. We know we need to do what is necessary to make “here” – this planet and all of its ecologies and communities – and safer for the multitude of beings who rely upon them, fully aware this is our one and only home.
On the other are those with rapturous plans to shield themselves and their families from the political and ecological fires burning our planet, whether those plans take the form of heavenly ascension, earthly bunkers and fortressed nations, or fantasies of colonizing space and merging with machines. Instead of improving conditions for actual people on Earth (or even pulling back from pouring fuel on the fires), end times fascists are plotting their escape, indifferent and oblivious to all that’s worth saving.
An absence of awe
Bezos’s fixation on space gets at something else that is key to understanding end times fascism and its fixation on bunkering and abandoning our shared world: the apparent inability of the people driving this project to marvel at, or even notice, the wonders that surround them.
That was glaringly apparent in 2021, when Bezos sent another crew to space. This time William Shatner, best known as Star Trek’s Captain Kirk, was on board (to fulfill one of Bezos’s boyhood fantasies, of course). “Space. The final frontier,” Shatner had said at the start of each episode. But as the now 90-year-old actor watched our blue-and-green planet recede from the window, he was suddenly flooded with terror. “The contrast between the vicious coldness of space and the warm nurturing of Earth below filled me with overwhelming sadness,” he later recalled, explaining that he had gained a much deeper appreciation for our planet’s sublime and fragile gifts.
“Every day, we are confronted with the knowledge of further destruction of Earth at our hands: the extinction of animal species, of flora and fauna … things that took five billion years to evolve, and suddenly we will never see them again because of the interference of mankind,” Shatner wrote. He took the trip expecting to be awestruck by the universe and instead he longed for home the minute he left: “I discovered that the beauty isn’t out there, it’s down here, with all of us.”
Perhaps Shatner’s insight about our precious imperiled planet resonates with the Amazon founder, but the billionaire’s plans for space colonization and his company’s large expansion of carbon-spewing data centers both suggest otherwise. And among tech oligarchs, Bezos is all too typical. Peter Thiel, for one, once revealed that his three best ideas for achieving true freedom are “cyberspace”, “outerspace” and “seasteading” (the idea of building new countries on floating oil rigs). In other words, this man, whose enormous wealth affords him access to the most spectacular settings our planet has to offer, actually believes these three cold, dead places are superior to the Earth we have, verdant and alive.
Something similar seems amiss with Elon Musk, a man who seems to look up at the wonders of the night sky and see only opportunities to fill that inky unknown with his own space junk. The venerable novelist Joyce Carol Oates highlighted these apparent limits in the fall of 2025 when she roasted him ruthlessly on his own platform, X. “So curious,” she wrote, “that such a wealthy man never posts anything that indicates that he enjoys or is even aware of what virtually everyone appreciates – scenes from nature, pet dog or cat, praise for a movie, music, a book (but doubt that he reads); pride in a friend’s or relative’s accomplishment; condolences for someone who has died; pleasure in sports, acclaim for a favorite team; references to history. In fact he seems totally uneducated, uncultured. The poorest persons on Twitter [X] may have access to more beauty & meaning in life than the ‘most wealthy person in the world.’”
The observation clearly got under the tech baron’s notoriously thin skin: he called her “a lazy liar” and began posting approvingly about various movies to prove Oates wrong. Yet in Musk’s euphoria on the day his aerospace company, SpaceX, went public, he made no attempt to hide his boredom with our blue planet and its challenges: “We want to solve [problems] here on Earth and we should solve them. But there also have to be things that get you excited about the future, that make you glad to wake up in the morning because you can’t wait to see what happens next.” It would seem that only abandoning Earth provides that thrill.
Most people have the capacity for awe, to gasp at the jeweled beauty of a songbird or the otherworldliness of a whale’s exhalation or the intricate latticework of an ancient holy site. Children have the capacity for pure awe; so do 90-year-old actors in suborbital space. To experience awe is to dissolve into the swirl of the universe, to feel small in the best way. This sense of interconnection is also why we grieve when we witness strangers suffering, and feel the great sorrow of extinction. The fact that this capacity seems to be missing from the men who hold our collective fate in their hands is a personal loss for them – and an existential crisis for the rest of us.
One dangerous part of the tech oligarchs’ world-abandoning project is that the tools they are building are designed to remake us in their own broken image. Popular platforms and apps train us to share Silicon Valley’s dream of discarnate freedom, perpetually nudging us to forsake real places and in-person connection in favor of simulations – and to view Earth, our bodies and our relationships as prisons to hack and flee. Altman, for one, has made it clear that he sees “certain advantages to being a machine”, and he has repeatedly insisted that his own children will never be smarter than AI, as though intelligence can be reduced to no more than computation. Like similar services, ChatGPT is trained to hijack our empathic response systems so we, too, will elevate machines and imbue them with more significance than they deserve.
The inability to appreciate this planet and its marvelous cast of characters helps explain why they are so prepared to sacrifice it. Indeed, the tech right’s willingness to eliminate our life-sustaining labor and replace human relationships with synthetic ones cannot be separated from their indifference to what little remains of the planet’s fast-vanishing wildlife and plant diversity. They don’t seem to know how to love this place, to savor the pleasure of other people’s company, or to marvel at the mysteries presented by other species.
In short, we are up against an ideology that has given up not only on the premise and promise of liberal democracy but on the livability of our shared world – on its beauty, on its people, on our children, on other species. There is something treasonous in this. Treasonous not to an abstraction like a flag or a nation, for we are not nationalists. But treasonous to the unspoken pact made with the web of life that sustains us.
They are traitors to creation, to the wonders of here.
The antithesis of fascism
There is no cut-and-paste formula for fighting end times fascism. Whether it’s Venetians taking on Jeff Bezos or Albanians telling Jared and Ivanka Trump that their country is not for sale or a small town in Kentucky organizing against a sprawling datacentre, every front in this fight takes on the character and texture of its place. There are, however, some guiding principles that are beginning to emerge across locations, and Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for mayor of New York City – and his approach to governance since his election – embody many of them. Start from love of place, then conjure a radically inclusive future where everyone can afford dignified lives, embrace common goals across difference, get outside and gather offline and in person, take on the powerful joyously, draw on history and don’t be afraid to stir the soul.
Mamdani has pounded away at his core policies to make the city more affordable, and has made good on many of those promises in his pursuit, for example, to lower rent and expand universal childcare. But he has also done something more sublime, dwelling on the boisterous, charming corners of the city that are the reason so many people choose to endure the pressures pushing them to leave.
As Mamdani’s star was rising, fascists and neofascists across the country and around the world did what they do. They sorted and separated, ranked and expelled. They sowed confusion and division by claiming Mamdani wasn’t a real American, and blamed the left for every social problem and grievance. They held up multicultural New York as a supposedly terrifying example of what happens when the “great replacement” succeeds. JD Vance spoke out in defense of people’s right to not want to live next to people from “a totally different culture”, and Stephen Miller railed on X: “NYC is the clearest warning yet of what happens to a society when it fails to control migration.”
As the fascists drew their rigid lines – in versus out, protected versus disposable, “heritage” versus. invader – the campaign to elect Mamdani threw a year-long party that celebrated one of the most racially and ethnically diverse places ever known, five boroughs shaped by wave after wave of new immigrants who have made their homes on Lenape lands. With its every action, the campaign asserted that shared identity can be forged not just by ancestry but by a commitment to a shared home, and to a shared set of values about how to live together in that home.
New York is a city of people carrying countless hyphenations and keeping myriad cultural practices alive. But as Mamdani put it: “No matter what you eat, what language you speak, how you pray, or where you come from, the words that most define us are the two we all share: New Yorkers.”
So Mamdani explained the complexities of ranked-choice voting in the Democratic primary using a line of mango lassis as props. He canvassed for votes at queer clubs, shouted out Haitian revolutionary history at the massive Bayo concert, shared his favorite bagel order, and broke fast during Ramadan over biryani in the Bronx. Once in office, he also turned the now legendary Knicks playoff run and the 2026 World Cup into a summer-long party few will forget. In these ways and others, Mamdani re-enchanted a city that had faced relentless vilification from Washington as dangerous, dirty and dysfunctional.
It was a perfect encapsulation of “hereness” – an idea developed by the Jewish Labour Bund, a Yiddish socialist group that was founded in the 19th century and grounded in fierce commitment to place and community not based on bloodlines. Molly Crabapple, a proud New Yorker and artist who recently published a bestselling history of the Bund, made the connection in a piece published in the Guardian. “Like New York itself, Mamdani’s campaign was multicultural, multiracial, polyglottal,” she wrote. “When Andrew Cuomo tried to bait him as un-American, he released ads in Spanish and Bangla, Hindi and Arabic. He ran a campaign devoted to class-first politics that sought to speak to everyone in their own idiom, while never once apologizing for who he was.
Amid all this celebration of difference, Mamdani’s campaign also emphasized the kinds of daily experiences and anxieties that are common and unifying for nearly all New Yorkers, lingering in the ordinary places that are too often overlooked or reviled. Mamdani rubbed shoulders with commuters on packed subway cars, paid homage to the glories of the Staten Island Ferry, and visited countless bodegas, approaching the strangers he met with nonjudgmental curiosity and a smile so wide it became a punchline on Saturday Night Live.
But the campaign was not only antifascist – in the myriad ways that it celebrated the unruliness that makes New York lovable, it was also the antithesis of fascism. More than a rejection of hate, it was an invitation to kindness, to a world in which we avert our eyes from no one. That meant lifting up and honoring the very people fascists are most eager to eject and discard: the working-class, immigrant workforce that keeps the city functioning. The campaign shined a spotlight on delivery workers getting ripped off by platforms such as DoorDash, on Amazon warehouse workers fighting to have their unions recognized, and on taxi drivers in line at LaGuardia, one part of a nocturnal workforce that makes it possible for New York to boast of being the city that never sleeps.
Faced with the prospect of a fairer city funded by marginally higher taxes, some prophesied a billionaire exodus. Hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman threatened to leave along with other high earners and Fox forecast a “Mamdani Migration”. Luxury real estate agents reported being bombarded with calls from clients wanting to sell their penthouses and move to Palm Beach.
The threats of defection only underscored the mutually reinforcing nature of the two core themes of Mamdani’s campaign – the joyous love of here, even if here is kind of a wreck, and the concrete plans for repair and improvement. Because the more devoted you are to a place, the easier it is to put in the resources and energy required to improve it. It’s a politics based not on wanting to escape this earthly realm, whether our cities or our animate bodies, but on a deep desire to stay, and to protect all that is irreplaceable, human and alive.
This is the very same spirit that we’ve seen motivating people to protect their air and water from sprawling datacenters and to defend their immigrant neighbors from ICE. While reporting on the weeks-long uprising in Minneapolis, the journalist Adam Serwer memorably described the guiding ideology of the resistance as “neighborism”, or the “commitment to protecting the people around you, no matter who they are or where they came from”. It was an openhearted, welcoming ethic that united huge numbers of ordinary people to do something deceptively simple: protect the most vulnerable members of their community from what looked very much like an invading army. That meant everything from braving bullets, to cooking dinner to opening up spare rooms to families who were no longer safe at home.
In these and countless other ways, Minnesotans rose up to insist that their neighbors were already where they belonged, whether they were, as Serwer put it, born in Minneapolis or Mogadishu.
The human networks that neighbors are building, block by block, group chat by group chat, are about more than refusal. In our time of serial shocks and intersecting crises, they are also the basis for a different kind of survivalism. But while the various strains of fascists build bunkers for the few, ours are survival networks grounded in the principle that every one of us, without exception, deserves to live and thrive. They are also bound by a belief that keeping one another safe when the inevitable shocks arrive is a sacred duty. Part of that involves telling new stories, stories that are truthful and inspiring enough to help our depleted fellow humans fall back in love with our one and only home and defiantly recommit to defending it with all they’ve got.
Some worlds must end
Those stories cannot be about returning to something called “normal”, to what passed for calm before Brexit and Trump and Silicon Valley’s authoritarian turn. Those were the years during which too many problems were allowed to compound and fester: fascism is always a warped response to real crises. And end times fascism is a response to real planetary-scale crises, including ever-concentrating levels of carbon in the atmosphere and wealth in the hands of the super-rich. The responses it proposes – mass sacrifices of humans and non-humans alike – are monstrous and must be purged from our midst.
To achieve this, we will have to figure out how to address the underlying crises contemporary fascism feeds off of. Because boundaries are being crossed. Limits are being exceeded. Walls are being hit. Fascists want us to believe that what is hitting the wall is the human story: it’s over, so make sure you are among the chosen who transcend to the next world. Pray to your God for salvation. Implant the chip, merge with the machines. Militarize and purify your bunkered nation. Arm yourself to the hilt and hide behind your fortune. Don’t worry about the humans, the animals, the trees, the rivers and reefs that won’t make it.
But they are wrong. It’s not the human story that is hitting the wall. Rather, it is the story we have been trapped inside of. The one about how greed must be the engine of civilization. About how growth can go on for ever. About how there are always more efficiencies to be found, more workers to be rationalized, more resources to be sacrificed, more people, places and planets to colonize. These myths are hitting the wall of reality and much will have to change as a result.
The logics that must be abandoned should be clear by now. Unlimited violence. Unconstrained exploitation. Insatiable wealth. Unchecked dominance. Those are the drives that make coexistence impossible. Looking forward, two paths beckon. We can abandon and betray this world, or we can break with capitalism and build new economic and political systems that honor life and prioritize care and repair.
Thankfully we are not starting from scratch. Our movement ancestors have left us maps to earthly Zions where everyone is welcome, to inclusive futures where peace and safety are core principles. Not the post-human future desired by end times fascists, but a post-capitalist and pro- (all of) life one. Deeply democratic, socialist, feminist, multiracial, multispecies, internationalist, generous, courageous and animate. Embodied and sensory, proudly earthbound.
And that, fundamentally, is the prospect that terrifies end times fascists more than anything else. It’s why Thiel denounces anyone attempting to regulate fossil fuels and AI as the antichrist; and why Trump and Vance smear nonviolent Minnesotans defending their neighbors as “domestic terrorists”. What keeps these men up at night is … us. It’s the possibility that a popular and vigorous movement will rise up and defend this planet and the many life-forms who call it home.
We didn’t choose to be born into a fight quite so fateful, but we have reached a choice point. We can either follow end times fascists into oblivion, or we can commit to building the unruly, boundary-crossing movement they so deeply fear. One that wrests away their weapons, holds them accountable for their crimes, and defends the paradise of here.

Plugging gap: Why 67,000 EV charging points aren't enough for India’s electric dreams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:59:54 UTC
21:59:54 KST

According to a landmark study by Rubix Data Sciences released in September 2026, citing baseline projections from the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), India will need 13.2 lakh EV charging points by 2030 to support the growing number of electric vehicles.
When Siddharth Das, a Delhi-NCR based working professional and long-time motor enthusiast, traded in his petrol sedan for a brand-new electric SUV, he wasn’t just buying a new car. He was also trying to make his daily commute what he describes as "future-ready".But switching to an electric vehicle brought a different kind of calculation."My previous petrol car cost me 10 to 12 rupees a kilometre. With an EV, even if I use commercial chargers at 15 to 21 rupees per unit, my running cost is just 3 to 3.50 rupees a kilometre. If I could charge at domestic home rates of 8 rupees a unit, it would drop to 1 rupee per kilometre."However, Das faces a problem even before he leaves his residential building."I live in an apartment complex where parking is in the basement, and the society isn’t allowing home chargers due to safety protocol concerns," he explains.His experience shows one of the bigger challenges in India's shift to electric vehicles. The cars are improving quickly, but the charging system around them is still developing and can be difficult to access.
67,000 plugs down, 13 lakhs to go
According to a landmark study by Rubix Data Sciences released in September 2026, citing baseline projections from the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), India will need 13.2 lakh EV charging points by 2030 to support the growing number of electric vehicles.But how far is India from that target?Data from the Ministry of Heavy Industries shows that, as of August 2026, India had 67,657 public charging points across the country including 1,139 battery-swapping station interfaces. This is in comparison to only 5,000 public chargers in early 2022 and 29,151 in December 2025.But even after this growth, the current network is only about 5 percent of the 13.2 lakh charging points expected to be needed by 2030.In simple terms, India still needs to add more than 1.25 million to reach the projected requirement. This gap matters because the number of EVs on the road is also increasing, meaning charging infrastructure has to grow fast enough to keep up with vehicle sales.There is also a major geographical imbalance. The Rubix analysis says the top 10 states, led by Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh, account for 78 per cent of all public chargers in India.
As of August 2026, India had 67,657 public charging points across the country including 1,139 battery-swapping station interfaces. This is in comparison to only 5,000 public chargers in early 2022 and 29,151 in December 2025.
That means nearly four out of every five public chargers are concentrated in just 10 states. For EV users in other parts of the country, especially smaller towns and less-developed regions, finding a public charger can therefore be much harder.
Power disconnect: Built for scooters, not long-haul trips
The problem is not only the number of chargers. It is also how much power those chargers can provide.Out of the 66,518 non-swapping fixed chargers installed across the country as of August 2026, most are on the slower side:
48,709 chargers, or about 73 percent, are rated below 30 kW.
15,753 chargers are in the 30–60 kW range.
1,513 chargers offer 61–120 kW fast charging.
Only 534 chargers provide 121–240 kW, while just nine chargers offer more than 240 kW nationwide.
These figures are important because a charger’s power rating affects how quickly an EV can be charged. A large network may therefore look impressive on paper, but if most chargers are low-power units, drivers travelling long distances may still have to spend considerable time charging.The current charging mix also reflects the kinds of electric vehicles being sold in India. Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA) figures cited in the study show that the switch to electric vehicles is currently strongest among three-wheelers, where EVs have a 60.77 per cent market penetration, and two-wheelers, at 8.88 per cent.Electric four-wheeler passenger cars have a much lower penetration of 5.70 percent.This helps explain why India has a large number of lower-powered chargers.Low-power AC chargers can work well for e-rickshaws, electric two-wheelers and vehicles used mainly for short city trips. But the same infrastructure is less suitable for electric cars travelling long distances or for heavy commercial vehicles that need to cover hundreds of kilometres.
Divide in driver experience: Home charging vs range anxiety
For EV owners who have private parking and can install a home charger, everyday use can be relatively simple. Bishwajeet Kumar Seth, who bought his electric SUV in April 2026, relies entirely on home charging."I have a 7.2 kW charger installed at home," Seth says. "My car has a real-world range of around 550 km with the AC on. When I drove from Delhi to Mathura, I didn't even need to plug in on the road. At home, it costs me 7 to 8 rupees a unit. At a highway fast charger, they were charging 19 rupees per unit. I thought, why bear double the cost when I don't need to?"But the experience can be very different for people who do not own an EV or who rent one occasionally. For them, "range anxiety" remains a major concern.Mohammad Sarim, who rented an EV during a trip to Kerala, came away hesitant."I had the car for 12 hours to cover 150 km, but the display showed a total range of 200 km," he shares. "Being in the outskirts, I didn't spot a single charger. The anxiety of the battery running down made it feel less convenient than a petrol car"Saad Abbasi, a commuter in the NCR region, also says the lack of infrastructure affects buying decisions. "Unless you live in Central or South Delhi, NCR has limited infrastructure. It's fine for home-to-office daily commuting if you can charge at home, but the moment you travel away from major cities, it becomes an issue."
Operator crisis: Empty stations in tier-2, tier-3 towns
While EV buyers worry about finding a charger, charging operators face almost the opposite problem: their chargers often do not get enough customers.Data from the Rubix Data Sciences report shows that public chargers across India currently have a utilisation rate of only 1 to 5 per cent.This means that, for much of the time, many public chargers are sitting unused. That creates a difficult business case, particularly for operators in smaller cities and towns. They have to spend a large amount of money upfront, but may not have enough vehicles using the chargers to recover that investment quickly.Amit Kumar Sahu, a fuel station owner who operates a public EV charging setup in Giridih, Jharkhand, explains the financial challenge faced by local businesses."In private dealer-owned fuel stations, the entire investment falls on the dealer," Sahu says. "Setting up a 60 kW DC charger costs around 8.5 to 9 lakh rupees for the machine alone. On top of that, buying a dedicated 63 kVA transformer takes another 5.5 to 6 lakh rupees in deposits and grid connection expenses. You end up spending 15 to 16 lakh rupees.""In small towns like Giridih, if only 2 to 4 vehicles show up a day, you can't recover your costs," Sahu adds. "That is why private pump dealers in Jharkhand and Bihar avoid installing them. The vehicles aren't there yet, and without footfall, nobody wants to lock in Rs 15 lakhs."This creates a cycle that is difficult to break. EV owners need chargers before they feel confident buying electric cars, but operators are reluctant to invest in chargers until there are enough EVs using them.To deal with low utilisation, operators are now looking at other business models.According to the Rubix report, charge point operators (CPOs) are moving towards fleet leasing contracts, revenue-sharing arrangements with site owners and open-roaming networks. These models can help operators get more regular usage and reduce the risk of investing in chargers that remain empty.
Technical frameworks & heavy freight road ahead
India is also trying to reduce fragmentation in its charging system. Standard-setting bodies such as the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) and the Department of Science & Technology (DST) are working on charging standards and technologies that can make charging more uniform and suitable for different types of EVs.
LECCS (light electric vehicle combined charging system): Under standards such as IS 17017 Part-2 Sec-7 and IS 17017 Part-31, LECCS combines AC charging of up to 7 kW and low-voltage DC charging of up to 12 kW into one standard plug for two and three-wheelers. The aim is to make charging more consistent instead of having different systems for different vehicles.
Universal Sockets: These are intended for destination charging at places such as urban parking complexes. They can support charging from 2 kW to 22 kW using a standard Type-2 socket with detachable smart cables. This can reduce dependence on different proprietary charging systems.
The bigger challenge will come with heavy commercial vehicles and long-distance transport. Chargers below 60 kW are generally not enough for trucks and other heavy vehicles that need to recharge quickly and get back on the road.DST frameworks therefore include much higher-powered charging systems. These include Split-Type DC chargers, which can dynamically distribute 40 kW to 240+ kW across several charging posts; Dual-Gun 500 kW systems; Overhead Pantographs offering up to 600 kW; and Megawatt Charging Systems (MCS), which can provide up to 3.75 MW of peak power for heavy logistics fleets.The difference in power is significant.A system designed for a scooter or a car used for city commuting cannot simply be used as the main charging solution for a fully loaded electric truck travelling long distances. As India's electric vehicle market moves towards larger commercial vehicles, the charging network will therefore need to become not only bigger, but much more powerful.
India’s transition to electric vehicles has moved beyond its early stage. As driver Siddharth Das prepares for his upcoming long-distance EV trip to Nepal, he is already planning his route around fast chargers, with charging stops mapped roughly every 150 km using route planners.Reaching the projected target of 13.2 lakhs by Rubix study by 2030 will require much more than simply adding chargers in existing EV hubs.The network will need to expand beyond major cities and states that already have a large share of the country's chargers. At the same time, operators will need easier transformer and grid connections, charging standards will need to become more consistent, and fast chargers will need to become more widely available on national highways.For consumers, the difference could determine whether an EV remains mainly a city vehicle or becomes a practical option for longer journeys across India.
Vijaya Srivastava is a journalist and feature writer whose expertise lies in covering human-centred developments. Her stories explore how policy, technology, economic shifts and social change influence people's everyday lives. Her work also focuses on bringing depth, context and a human perspective to complex issues.
Her reports primarily cover society, healthcare, safety, public policy and emerging trends, alongside other political developments.

Japanese ambassador pledges support for Asian Para Games

Allameh Tabataba'i University Opens International Admissions for English-Taught Master’s Programs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:57:28 UTC
21:57:28 KST

Allameh Tabataba'i University Opens International Admissions for English-Taught Master’s Programs
Allameh Tabataba'i University (ATU), Iran’s leading specialized public university in the humanities and social sciences, has launched international admissions for its English-taught Master of Arts and Master of Science programs for the first semester of the 2026–2027 academic year.
Renowned for its rigorous academic traditions, influential faculty, and vibrant campus life in Tehran, ATU invites qualified international graduates and scholars from across the globe to apply for Master’s degree programs delivered entirely in the English language.
Available Master’s Degree Programs
Eligible international candidates may apply for admission in one of the following six disciplines (applicants must select a field corresponding to their Bachelor’s specialisation):
- Actuarial Science
- Cultural Studies
- English Language and Literature
- International Relations
- Regional Studies (Specialisations: Central Asia & the Caucasus / Middle East & North Africa / Southeast Asia)
- Teaching English as a Foreign Language (TEFL)
Key Eligibility Criteria and Academic Regulations
To qualify for admission, candidates must meet the following official requirements:
- Non-Iranian Citizenship: Applicants must hold a valid foreign passport. In accordance with national regulations, dual nationals holding Iranian citizenship are not eligible to apply through the international student track.
- National Academic Clearance (ADAB Platform): Prior to registering in the university’s application portal, all applicants must register on the national ADAB system (https://adab.saorg.ir/PortalADAB/fa) and obtain an official tracking/clearance code designated specifically for Allameh Tabataba'i University. Note: Securing simultaneous clearance codes for multiple Iranian universities will result in automatic disqualification.
- Undergraduate Qualifications: Applicants must possess a recognised Bachelor’s degree in a discipline related to the intended Master’s program.
- Full-Time Commitment & Legal Status: All programs are strictly full-time. Distance, short-term, or part-time study tracks are not available.
- Language Training: Although academic instruction is conducted in English, enrolled international students are required under Ministry of Science, Research and Technology regulations to attend concurrent Persian language courses starting from their first semester, submitting a Persian language proficiency certificate prior to graduation.
Application Procedure and Timeline
The admissions procedure is fully digitised, centralised, and transparent:
Application Deadline: 15 September 2026
Application Platform: Submissions must be made exclusively through the official ATU International Student Admission Portal: https://apply.atu.ac.ir/. Applications submitted via email, postal mail, or in person will not be accepted. The portal is accessible in English, Persian, and Arabic.
Direct Registration / Agency Notice: Applications may be completed by the prospective student or an authorised, licensed international recruitment agency. Sponsoring agencies must register using the applicant’s verified personal email address. Submissions managed by unauthorized third parties or intermediaries will be rejected.
Required Application Documents
Applicants must upload clear, flatbed-scanned copies of the following documents to the admission portal (smartphone photos or blurred scans will be automatically disqualified):
Passport-Sized Photograph: Color photo with dimensions of 600 (H) × 400 (W) pixels (File size: 50 KB – 100 KB).

Ukraine, Poland say Russia hit Warsaw-bound passenger train

Ukraine, Poland say Russia hit Warsaw-bound passenger train
September 13, 2026
Russia launched two drone strikes on western Ukraine, close to its border with NATO member Poland, Ukrainian and Polish authorities said on Sunday.
One of the drones hit a locomotive of a passenger train at the Yahodyn railway station in the Volyn region., some two kilometers (1.24 miles) from the border crossing.
"The monitoring team gave the train crew advanced warning, and thanks to that, no one was injured," Ukrainian railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said in online post.
Separately, Poland's PKP Intercity confirmed that they have taken control of the affected train following the attack in the Ukrainian territory.
"The train is carrying 206 people. There are no Polish citizens among the passengers," the operator said online. "After completing customs clearance, it will continue its journey towards Warsaw."
Senior Western figures said to be at station before train strike
Ukrzaliznytsia later said that senior Western figures, including Boris Johnson and former CIA Director David Petraeus, were at the station shortly before the Warsaw-bound train was struck.
"Shortly before the locomotive was hit at the Ukrainian-Polish border, a diplomatic train was at Yagodyn station," Ukrzaliznytsia said in a statement.
"There were, among others, security advisers from several EU member states and former European leaders on board, including former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson. In another train that was at Yagodyn station at the very moment of the attack was former CIA Director David Petraeus."
Johnson didn't specifically mention that he had been near the vicinity of the attack, but called for more action to be taken against Russian President Vladimir Putin, once reports of the attack emerged.
"I don’t know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning," Johnson said.
"When are we going to give them the air defences they need? Why won’t we unfreeze Putin’s cash and give it to Ukraine? There is more than €140 billion ($163 billion) in a Belgian bank account — and about £10 billion (€11.7 billion or 13.5 billion) in London," Johnson said, adding that Britain could lead the way in this regard.
"This wasn’t our train, but the one just minutes after us by the border crossing. It was evacuated as the drone approached and no one was hurt," Carl Bildt, Sweden's former Prime Minister said on X.
Poland says attacks on its territory cannot be ruled out
Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski urged for increased support for Ukraine, calling the incident an "escalation."
"This is an escalation, this is another great challenge for Ukraine and for the hypothetical future victims of Russian aggression and this means that we should double our efforts to support victims of aggression," Sikorski told a press briefing.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk chaired an emergency meeting on Sunday to address Russian drone attacks near the border and warned the country must be prepared for the possibility that drones could target Polish territory.
"The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side," Tusk said, adding Poland "cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory."
Zelenskyy: Locomotive 'deliberately burned'
On Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the locomotive was "deliberately burned" and a gas station damaged in Volyn.
"It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand," he said.
Moscow did not immediately comment on the reports.
Ukrainian officials also reported another drone strike on Yahodyn overnight, some half a mile (800 meters) from the Polish border.
The border with Poland serves as essential transit point for military and humanitarian aid.
'Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors' — Ukrainian foreign minister
Commenting on the Yahodyn incident, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric" attacks were more than "just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders."
"This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he said in an English-language post on X.
He urged Ukraine's Western allies to make Russia "feel the consequences of its terror. Not just half-decisions, but uncompromising, powerful steps. Full trade embargo. Full entry bans. Full sanctions on the military-industrial complex."
"Putin needs to understand that his barbarism will be met with decisive action that increases the cost of war for him to an unacceptable level," he added.

Moscow reveals potential timeline for trilateral Ukraine talks
Trilateral talks between Russian, Ukrainian, and US representatives could begin in October, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, the official stated that Moscow “does not rule out such a possibility.”
“We’re specifically talking about the foreseeable future. That is, presumably of course, October,” Peskov clarified.
Earlier this week, the Kremlin spokesman stated that Moscow hopes “for a restart of negotiations between three parties – Russia, Ukraine, and America.”
The trilateral format was last used in Geneva in February, following two earlier rounds in Abu Dhabi. However, the talks later stalled without any significant breakthroughs, as the US shifted its focus to its war against Iran.
Peskov’s recent comments have followed a fresh round of shuttle diplomacy by US President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who held a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow last week before visiting Kiev for talks with Vladimir Zelensky.
The Kremlin described the discussions with the US negotiators as constructive and “extremely candid,” while Witkoff said that progress had been made toward scheduling a three-way meeting. The potential resumption of talks in this format was also among the topics Putin and Trump discussed by phone on Tuesday, according to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov.
At around the same time, Zelensky suggested that the next round of trilateral negotiations could take place in the UAE, Türkiye, Switzerland, or another country as early as September or October.
Moscow has repeatedly said it remains open to diplomacy, as long as the root causes of the conflict are addressed and the new realities on the ground are respected. Ukraine has in turn ruled out making territorial concessions to Russia.

Estonian PM: Herem knows where he has more work to do as defense minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:53:00 UTC
21:53:00 KST

Estonian PM: Herem knows where he has more work to do as defense minister
Amid critics' concerns about the appointment, Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) says Herem knows where he still has work to do as Estonia's next defense minister.
Quite a few former generals have said Martin Herem becoming defense minister concerns them, citing for one thing that he's coming from the defense industry and still has continued close ties to it, creating a clear risk of conflict of roles. How much of a risk do you see here, and how do you plan to prevent it?
Avoiding a potential conflict of interests or roles here is quite simple: all financial interests must be left at the Defense Ministry door when you walk in. In a small country, I think it's reasonable to work closely with defense industry companies at this level, as long as all those interactions are properly documented and added to the lobbying register.
The government has also sought to maintain close ties with the Estonian Defense and Aerospace Industry Association (EKTL) to help the defense industry grow. There can be both advantages and disadvantages to that, but when it comes to a minister, of course I expect their financial interests to stay at the door. Martin Herem has also said they will.
How can you ensure that?
We have several mechanisms for that. There are formal procedures for checking how those interests have been relinquished, and we also have law enforcement agencies that have been very thorough in handling these matters.
With the Estonian Defense Forces' (EDF) stockpile problems being one issue raised in the National Audit Office's report, another criticism is that the new defense minister was himself involved in those problems and is now expected to fix them. How do you envision someone who was part of that situation now being able to fix it?
I think it's important for people to distinguish between two problems identified in the NAO report.
One concerns the five percent GDP we spend on defense — specifically, how the EDF's assets and stockpiles have been managed. Martin Herem has said both on Estonian Public Broadcasting and elsewhere that he tried to put things in order, and he succeeded in some areas, but not in all. That needs to be fixed, and Martin Herem, [EDF Commander Lt. Gen.] Andrus Merilo and everyone else all agree on that.
The second issue concerns procurements at the Estonian Center for Defense Investments, or ECDI. These are the ammunition procurements made for Ukraine with European funding, and [ECDI director general] Elmar Vaher is currently working to put that area in order.
Both areas need to be put in order. Herem knows where he succeeded and where he still has more work to do. An outside partner should definitely be brought in too.
The government's decisions made two things clear: first, those in charge must clearly be held accountable, and second, an outside partner needs to be brought in to restore public trust in the sector.
Another point of criticism is that things are being done too hastily. In other words, we've ended up with these current procurement issues because things have been rushed. Meanwhile, Martin Herem has once again been talking about the need to "hurry, hurry, hurry," and there has also been talk of intelligence being politicized somehow. How can that be avoided?
No one can change the fact that things are urgent, of course. Even our opponents all say that when it comes to defense procurements and operations, what Ukraine has needed has had to be procured in a race against time and Russia.
The same older ammunition was procured that Ukraine has been using to defend itself against Russia. It hasn't been easy, and as we've seen, there have also been fraudsters or at least substandard goods involved.
Of course the background checks need to be better, and that's ultimately still the job of the people involved in procurement or working at the procurement agency. That is not the role of the minister as a politician.
And yet, a minister resigned over this.
As I've said, [outgoing Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform)] certainly wasn't personally at fault, but he took political responsibility for it. The permanent secretary was responsible for the management, which is pretty logical.
One condition Martin Herem has allegedly asked for is that he be able to make decisions as quickly as possible. There has been talk of laws and various mechanisms. How could that work when it's largely the Riigikogu, not a single minister, that handles legislation?
I think you've clearly understood the current legal framework correctly, and as an MP, I can confirm that is indeed how it works.
What Herem asked for — and what we are definitely aligned on — is that defense spending stay at 5 percent and not be allowed to fall below that. That's been my initiative as well. It's an initiative of the government coalition, and given the threat posed by Russia, I think it's only right. That's the first thing.
The second thing he asked for was political support for reforms, so that things could be put right exactly as the NAO has called for. He also asked that any changes needed to improve the effectiveness of national defense be made. I think that is perfectly natural.
But legislation is a public process: if the government submits something, it then goes to parliament, where it is debated before parliament makes a decision about it.
He isn't joining the Reform Party, though. You're implementing the government's policy and he'll be a member of the government, yet in a sense, he won't be, because he isn't a party member.
His message was that in becoming defense minister, he didn't want joining a political party to be a requirement, and I accepted that. Where he chooses to join in the future is up to him. He's very clearly stated that he hasn't ruled out joining a party or running in elections. That is his decision, and I respect it.
Whose policy will he be pursuing, then? Martin Herem's policy, Reform Party policy or the government's policy?
The government is a collegial body and pursues a single policy — the policy of the Government of the Republic. Any proposals submitted to parliament are decided collectively by the government.
There has also been speculation about whether people like Veiko-Vello Palm and Kusti Salm will take up posts at the Defense Ministry. Has Martin Herem given you any indication of what his team will look like and who will be on it?
He has said he doesn't think it's likely either of the two aforementioned people will be joining the Defense Ministry — or, to put it more directly, that they won't.
As for the rest, he'll certainly need to find himself a good permanent secretary and a solid team. I'll definitely help as much as I can, but that team will ultimately have to come to the Defense Ministry.
What do you make of the Social Democrats (SDE) and other parties saying the way Kaimo Kuusk was dismissed was unlawful?
There is no other way to remove a permanent secretary from office. The same legal basis has been used for the secretaries general of the Ministry of Agriculture and Ministry of Justice. It is the only legal basis for the government to dismiss a permanent secretary: a failure of cooperation.
That was the basis for his dismissal, and it wouldn't have made much difference who the next defense minister would be. Both government coalition parties had already included accountability for those in charge among the relevant points of their decisions last week.
We discussed it within the cabinet and said we wanted to see what accountability there would be for those in charge. The outcome would have been the same regardless of who became minister.
--

Lukashenko is preparing to wage war against his own people - intelligence

Details
The regime of Alexander Lukashenko, which for years has justified its obedience to the Kremlin by citing an external threat, has finally admitted whom it fears most. This is evidenced by the surprise combat-readiness inspection Lukashenko ordered for the interior troops, ostensibly to determine how thoroughly the security forces had absorbed the lessons of the war in Ukraine

Belarusian Security Council Secretary Volfovich explained the aim without unnecessary hints: ensuring public order amid destabilization of the situation in the country. Behind this wording lies the dictatorship’s familiar fear of its own population. The regime is analyzing how to apply unconventional methods to counter hybrid threats and what measures to take to maintain order, but there is not and will not be a single word about arming civilians or territorial defense. Belarusians will not be allowed access to weapons, because for the regime the main threat is not external but internal

Saudi pipeline outage threatens loss of 4% of global oil supply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:49:12 UTC
21:49:12 KST

Breadcrumb
Saudi pipeline outage threatens loss of 4% of global oil supply
Saudi Arabia will run out of oil stocks for exports if it doesn't restart its major pipeline to the Red Sea within days, leading to a loss of up to 4% of global supply, Saudi oil buyers and traders said.
A further decline in Saudi flows will worsen the global supply crunch, which has already pushed global fuel prices to record highs, spurred inflation around the world and sent U.S. bond yields to the highest levels since the 2008 financial crisis.
Since drone attacks forced Saudi Arabia to shut its huge east-west oil pipeline on Friday, Riyadh has not given full details about the extent of the damage or how long the route will stay off-line.
Sources that spoke to Reuters gave varying estimates, with one saying the damage could take as long as five to six weeks to repair, while another said it could be fixed sooner and could resume pumping partially while repairs are ongoing.
Saudi Arabia's government media office and energy ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
For the past six months, the pipeline running through the desert across the Arabian Peninsula has spared Saudi Arabia from the brunt of the impact of the wartime shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz that has crippled exports from its neighbours.
The world's biggest exporter has used the pipeline to reroute around 4 million barrels per day — around 4% of global supply — to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea.
But with the pipeline out of service, Yanbu now has stocks to maintain exports for just five to seven days, according to three industry sources familiar with Saudi exports.
Saudi Arabia also has stocks to supply customers for several days from Egypt's ports of Ain Sukhna on the Red Sea and Sidi Kerir on the Mediterranean, a fourth source said.
Yanbu storage capacity stands at around 35 million barrels, according to industry estimates, with Ain Sukhna and Sidi Kerir able to store 18 million and 20 million barrels respectively.
Stocks are not full and will ultimately run out without the east-west pipeline resuming operations, the four sources said.
Saudi oil supply has already fallen to a more than three-decade low in August on reduced flows via Hormuz and the Red Sea, the International Energy Agency said on Friday.
World oil supply will decline this year by 5.7 million bpd, or about 6%, the IEA, which coordinates Western energy policies, said.
In addition to the attack on the pipeline, Houthi fighters in Yemen who have threatened Saudi oil shipments seized an island on Friday in the mouth of the Red Sea.
The Middle East supplied around 22 million barrels per day of oil before the war. Flows through the Strait of Hormuz have slowed to just 6 million to 9 million bpd, industry sources say.
Saudi Arabia told OPEC last week that its oil production had dropped to just 6.2 million bpd in August from 10.9 million bpd in February before the start of the war.
(Reuters)

The Iran war reveals the limits of BRICS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:46:58 UTC
21:46:58 KST

The Iran war reveals the limits of BRICS
The bloc struggles to translate its economic weight into geopolitical sway. But there may be a silver lining to it.
This year’s BRICS summit has wrapped up in New Delhi with the usual promises of deepened cooperation and expanding economic ties. But there was an important absence.
Although the US-Israel war on Iran has affected most of BRICS’ 11 members and 10 partner countries, the declaration issued by the bloc did not address it directly. Nor did it condemn the United States, which – objectively speaking – is the aggressor state in the conflict.
The wording allowed all members to remain inside the same diplomatic tent. It also revealed just how difficult it is for BRICS to turn shared dissatisfaction with the Western-led order into coordinated geopolitical action.
The Iran test
The problem was already visible months before the summit. In May, the BRICS foreign ministers’ meeting in New Delhi failed to produce a common position on the war on Iran. The outcome document acknowledged differences among members and avoided naming either the US or Israel.
Iran wanted the group to condemn the US and Israeli military campaign, while the UAE opposed language that ignored Iranian attacks and its own security concerns. That failure was more than a diplomatic embarrassment. It was a clear sign of the political cost of BRICS expansion.
The group’s enlargement has increased its global reach, but it has also imported regional rivalries into the organisation itself. Iran and the UAE are a particularly clear example. Both belong to BRICS, yet their strategic calculations in the Middle East collide. Their participation in the same organisation therefore creates a built-in ceiling on how far the group can go in confronting a conflict that directly affects both.
The September summit produced a declaration, but the compromise was telling. Rather than taking a clear, strong position, BRICS became a platform for managing disagreement.
The episode therefore suggests that the central problem facing the bloc is not a lack of economic or diplomatic weight. It is the difficulty of converting that weight into a single geopolitical instrument.
Standing up to the US
While BRICS has emerged out of a desire to challenge the US-dominated world order, it has failed to reach a common position on Washington. That is because its members have divergent interests when it comes to dealing with the US.
India illustrates the dilemma most clearly. New Delhi sees BRICS as a vehicle for strategic autonomy, not as an alliance against the US. It is deepening its relationship with Washington, participating in the Quad and maintaining extensive defence and economic ties with Western partners. At the same time, it remains deeply engaged with Russia and China.
For India, the value of BRICS lies partly in preserving room for manoeuvre between competing centres of power. Turning BRICS into an anti-American bloc would undermine precisely that strategic flexibility.
China and Russia also have reasons to avoid transforming BRICS into a mechanism for direct confrontation with the US. For Russia, BRICS is unquestionably an important platform for reducing the political and economic impact of Western economic pressure.
Yet, pursuing more aggressive policies through military alliances could push Moscow into a conflict with the US and NATO – something it wants to avoid at all costs.
For China, the calculation is even more complex. Beijing wants a stronger multipolar order and greater influence for the Global South. It also wants to reduce the structural advantages enjoyed by the US in global finance, trade and international institutions.
But China has little reason to turn every BRICS dispute into a binary confrontation with Washington. The US remains an important market for its exports and an important factor in global trade.
Brazil and Indonesia add another layer of complexity. Brasilia wants a more representative international system, greater development finance and stronger bargaining power for developing countries, but has little incentive to turn BRICS into an instrument of Chinese or Russian geopolitical strategy. Similarly, Jakarta sees BRICS as a way to widen its strategic and economic options rather than as a vehicle for choosing sides.
The polycentric trap
BRICS is caught in what appears to be a polycentric trap. Its greatest strength is its diversity. That diversity gives the group legitimacy across regions that have historically had little influence over the architecture of global governance.
But the same diversity makes collective geopolitical action difficult. Every new member adds economic resources, diplomatic reach and political legitimacy. It also adds another set of national interests that must be accommodated. This explains why BRICS is more likely to become a powerful bargaining coalition than a coherent geopolitical bloc.
Its members can agree on reforming international institutions, increasing representation for developing countries, strengthening South-South trade, expanding development finance and reducing excessive dependence on Western financial infrastructure. They can also cooperate on local-currency payments, development lending, energy and food security.
But agreement becomes harder when cooperation requires members to choose sides in an actual geopolitical confrontation. The war on Iran makes that contradiction unusually visible.
That does not mean BRICS is irrelevant. Quite the opposite. Its influence may ultimately come from doing something less dramatic but more sustainable: changing the bargaining environment in which the existing international order operates.
BRICS does not need to destroy the current global system to challenge the US. It can push for greater representation in the IMF and the World Bank, strengthen alternative development institutions, expand non-dollar payment mechanisms and give developing countries more diplomatic options. That may prove to be its most consequential role.
Therefore, the limits of its geopolitical action could also be a blessing. Avoiding hard confrontation could allow for more space for gradual change and a shift in the balance of power.

How Gujarat's villagers turned mangroves into a natural coastal shield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:45:48 UTC
21:45:48 KST

In the 1980s, when much of Gujarat’s coastline was losing its mangrove cover, some coastal communities began protecting the few patches that remained. What looked like a small act of conservation would eventually become part of one of India’s most striking mangrove recoveries.Government data shows just how dramatic that transformation has been.According to the Forest Survey of India (FSI), Gujarat had around 427 sq km of mangrove cover in 1987. By 1999, that figure had more than doubled to 1,031 sq km. It reached 1,164.06 sq km in 2023, making Gujarat home to nearly one-quarter of India's mangrove cover. In 2026, the cover has grown to 1177.27 sq km.It attributes the growth to a combination of large-scale plantation programmes, public-private partnerships, community participation and better protection of existing forests.Mangroves are much more than trees growing in salty mud.Their dense network of roots holds sediment together, reduces coastal erosion and slows waves and storm surges before they can reach settlements further inland. The forests also provide breeding and nursery grounds for fish, crabs and other marine species, making them important to both coastal ecosystems and livelihoods.The numbers also reveal how significant Gujarat's recovery has become.
The state's 1,164 sq km of mangroves in 2023 accounted for 23.66% of India's entire mangrove cover, second only to West Bengal.But the recovery has not been a simple story of trees being planted by the government. In several parts of Gujarat, conservation efforts have involved coastal communities in protecting and regenerating mangrove areas. That local involvement matters because mangroves occupy a difficult landscape — one constantly shaped by tides, salinity, grazing, cutting and human activity.The government has now taken the approach nationwide through MISHTI, launched in 2023 to restore and promote mangrove ecosystems along India's coast. Under the programme, mangroves are increasingly being treated as natural infrastructure — ecosystems that can perform some of the protective functions that would otherwise require expensive coastal engineering.
Gujarat's story therefore offers an unusual lesson in climate protection: sometimes the most effective coastal defence is not something built against the sea.It is something that grows between the land and the sea.And in Gujarat, decades after villagers began protecting those seemingly insignificant patches of mangrove, they have grown into forests spanning more than 1,100 sq km — forming a vast, living barrier along one of India's most exposed coastlines.

Radio France staff strike over appointment of far-right weekly editor
Staff at public broadcaster Radio France began a two-day strike on Sunday over the appointment of Charles Sapin, deputy editor-in-chief at far-right weekly Valeurs Actuelles. Unions accuse Sapin of promoting far-right ideas ahead of next spring's presidential election, while management has defended the appointment in the name of pluralism.
Staff at France's public radio broadcaster began a two-day strike on Sunday over the appointment of a commentator whom unions accuse of promoting far-right ideas ahead of next spring's presidential election.
Charles Sapin, deputy editor-in-chief at far-right weekly Valeurs Actuelles, has since late August been presenting a weekly political commentary segment on France Inter, the country's most-listened-to radio station.
Management has defended the appointment in the name of pluralism ahead of the April-May election to choose a successor to President Emmanuel Macron.
Polls suggest far-right leader Marine Le Pen has her strongest chance yet of winning the Élysée Palace.
Staff have expressed their opposition to the appointment, arguing that Valeurs Actuelles' editorial values are at odds with Radio France's public service mandate.
Read moreOnly the beginning? German far right's breakthrough shakes Europe to its core
Due to the strike, Sapin's weekly column, scheduled to air early on Sunday, was not broadcast.
Other segments of France Inter's morning programme were also taken off the air and replaced with music.
Morning programmes on franceinfo and France Culture, the public group's other radio stations, were broadcast as normal.
The magazine, which describes itself as conservative, has faced numerous legal controversies, including convictions for racial public insults.
In an opinion piece published in daily Le Parisien on Saturday, around 300 public figures including filmmakers, writers and lawyers described France Inter's recruitment of Sapin as "outrageous" and called for him to be stripped of his political commentary slot.

A delegation from the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) visited imprisoned PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan on Sept. 13 on İmralı island, marking the first such meeting since parliament approved a landmark legislative framework governing the disarmament and dissolution of the terrorist organization.
DEM Party lawmakers Pervin Buldan and Mithat Sancar, accompanied by lawyer Faik Özgür Erol, traveled to the high-security prison island off Istanbul for the meeting. The delegation last met with Öcalan on Aug. 2.
The Sept. 13 meeting was the first between the delegation and Öcalan since the Turkish parliament passed the legislation, which is seen as a key step in the implementation of the government’s “terror-free Türkiye” initiative.
The parliament on Aug. 10 approved the 12-article framework law aimed at facilitating the disarmament and dissolution of the PKK, with more than two-thirds of lawmakers voting in favor. A total of 468 lawmakers backed the law, while 88 voted against it, following nearly 10 hours of debate.
All political parties except the İYİ (Good) Party supported the bill, although there were a small number of defections.
The legislation lays out judicial and administrative procedures concerning the PKK’s disarmament and dissolution.
The measures can be applied only after security agencies verify that the PKK/KCK and affiliated formations no longer maintain an operational presence and have surrendered all weapons and ammunition.
The National Security Council must endorse that finding in a decision published in the Official Gazette.
Last week, Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş said that the PKK would begin disarming and handing over its weapons to Iraq’s central government in October as part of the implementation of the “terror-free Türkiye” process.
Meanwhile, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zeidi said PKK-affiliated elements in the Sinjar region would begin handing over their weapons to the state, adding that Mount Sinjar would come under the full control of the federal government.

Ukraine May Have Hit Russia’s Caspian Flotilla Flagship Tatarstan
Ukraine may have struck the Russian Navy’s Caspian Flotilla flagship Tatarstan during an overnight attack on the city of Kaspiysk in Russia’s Dagestan region, according to the Ukrainian OSINT project Exilenova+ on September 11.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The analysts published a satellite image that they said may show damage to the vessel following the attack. Tatarstan is a Project 11661K Gepard-class patrol ship that entered service in 2003 and serves as the flagship of Russia’s Caspian Flotilla.
The vessel was designed for patrol and maritime security missions, as well as operations against surface ships, submarines, and aerial targets. Its armament includes the Uran anti-ship missile system, the Osa-MA short-range surface-to-air missile system, artillery, and anti-submarine weapons.
Project 11661 vessels were also designed with measures intended to reduce their radar signature. The reported strike has not been independently confirmed, and Russian authorities have not publicly confirmed damage to the Tatarstan.
The possible attack came during a broader series of Ukrainian strikes against targets inside Russia on September 11. Explosions and fires were also reported in Saratov and Volgograd, including at an oil refinery, an Ozon logistics facility, and an industrial site.
In May, Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces struck a Russian Project 10410 Svetlyak-class patrol ship in Kaspiisk, Dagestan, nearly 1,000 kilometers from the front line. Footage released by SBS showed an FP-1 strike drone hitting the vessel near its stern.
Kaspiisk hosts the headquarters of Russia’s Caspian Flotilla and has increasingly come under Ukrainian long-range drone attacks targeting Russian naval assets in the region.

Poland responds to Russian attacks on western Ukraine
Poland’s Deputy Minister of National Defence Cezary Tomczyk made the statement on X, according to Ukrinform.
“Anyone wondering whether Ukraine should be supported militarily should draw conclusions from this night,” Tomczyk wrote.
He said that for many people, the war “may still seem like something distant and almost surreal, but in reality, it is happening very close to the Polish border.”
“Today’s attacks show this very clearly,” the Deputy Defense Minister stressed.
According to Tomczyk, in a single night, Russia launches hundreds and sometimes nearly a thousand aerial attack weapons at Ukraine – ballistic and cruise missiles, guided aerial bombs and drones. Some of them head westward.
“Every missile destroyed and every drone shot down is a threat that does not fly any farther,” Tomczyk stressed.
He noted that the Polish Air Force operates almost every night in the airspace over the Lublin and Podkarpackie voivodeships.
Tomczyk stressed that Ukraine’s victory in the war is in the interests of Poland and all of Europe.
“Russia is waging a terrorist war, and Putin bears responsibility for it. The sooner this war ends, the better it will be for the security of our region,” he said.
At the same time, Poland’s Deputy Defense Minister emphasized that “there will be no lasting peace without a strong Ukraine and without the unity of states that understand what the Russian threat means today.”
Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz also commented on Russia’s overnight attack on Ukraine.
“Before dawn, our systems detected an attack by several Geran-5 jet-powered drones in western Ukraine. One of them struck one kilometer from the Polish border, another five kilometers away,” Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote.
According to him, during the attack, Polish airspace was monitored by F-16 fighter jets, helicopters and a Saab airborne reconnaissance aircraft. No violation of Polish airspace was recorded.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said Russian forces are “changing their attack tactics, increasingly using jet-powered drones, launching several at a time and thereby exhausting Ukrainian air defenses.”
The official stressed that Poland’s air defense remains on constant alert.
As reported by Ukrinform, overnight on September 13, a gas station near the Yahodyn border crossing on the Polish border was damaged in a Russian attack on Ukraine’s Volyn region.
In addition, Russian forces attacked the locomotive of a passenger train two kilometers from the Polish border.
In Poland, an air raid alert was issued in the Lublin and Podkarpackie voivodeships in response to the Russian attack on Ukraine, and Polish fighter jets were scrambled. Processing of documents at Polish-Ukrainian border crossings was also temporarily suspended.
