The Houthis’ escalation in Yemen could flop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:39:50 UTC
21:39:50 KST

The Houthis’ escalation in Yemen could flop
The Houthis and Iran are seeking to gain leverage, but they may instead get a unified front in the Red Sea.
The speed of the Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast has changed the strategic landscape. After capturing Mocha, Houthi forces moved into Dhubab and reached Mayyun, or Perim Island, at the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandeb strait. These are not peripheral gains. They give the movement unprecedented leverage over one of the world’s most important maritime corridors.
This latest escalation in Yemen is not simply another episode in its long civil war. It is also not simply an escalatory move by Iran against Gulf states, particularly Saudi Arabia.
It is at once a struggle for the control of Yemen, a renewed confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, and another front in the wider war involving Iran, Israel and the United States.
Several factors contributed to it, including the false sense of balance of power in Yemen, the Houthi desire to secure a stronger negotiating position, and the spillover of the Iran war.
Flawed peace
The latest offensive cannot be understood without considering the false sense of peace that preceded it.
A United Nations-mediated truce took effect in April 2022. Although it formally expired six months later, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis largely maintained a de facto ceasefire. Saudi and Omani delegations travelled to Sanaa a year later. In June 2023, direct flights resumed between Sanaa and Saudi Arabia to carry Yemeni pilgrims to Hajj, the first such flights since 2016. In September 2023, a senior Houthi delegation visited Riyadh for talks on ending the war.
These were important confidence-building measures. But they also encouraged the dangerous assumption that Yemen’s conflict was gradually resolving itself.
The internationally recognised government appears to have mistaken the absence of major fighting for a durable balance of power. Despite repeated talk since April 2025 of an offensive along the western coast, its leaders remained divided, and its armed formations answered to competing commands. Rather than using the pause to rebuild legitimacy, improve governance and establish a coherent military structure, the government and its supporters became complacent.
The Houthis used the same period very differently. The reduction in fighting gave them time and strategic space to consolidate their administration, reorganise their forces, expand their missile and drone capabilities, and recruit on a vast scale.
A 2024 report by United Nations experts estimated that the Houthis’ fighting strength had risen from approximately 220,000 in 2022 to 350,000, compared with just 30,000 in 2015. Such figures must be treated cautiously, but they indicate how extensively the movement expanded during what others regarded as a period of peace. It should be noted that this process also involved documented coercion and child recruitment.
The genocide in Gaza also gave the Houthis a powerful mobilising cause. Palestine is close to the heart of almost every Yemeni, cutting across many of the country’s political, regional and sectarian divisions. By presenting their attacks on Israel and their Red Sea operations as direct action in defence of Gaza, the Houthis portrayed themselves not merely as one party in Yemen’s civil war, but as perhaps the only Arab force willing and able to impose a cost on Israel.
Iranian deterrence strategy v Houthi priorities
For the first six months of the war, Iran appears to have tried to keep the Red Sea from becoming another major front. It had a clear interest in keeping Saudi Arabia and Egypt (the two pivotal Arab powers bordering the Red Sea) outside a US-led military alignment. Renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia or commercial shipping risked pushing Riyadh and Cairo closer to Washington.
It is reasonable to assume that Tehran initially pressed the Houthis not to provoke Saudi Arabia. But the Saudi strike on Sanaa International Airport in July changed the calculation. Reportedly intended to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing, it gave the Houthis a reason to retaliate and evidence that restraint would not protect them.
Iran may not have wanted a Saudi-Houthi confrontation, but once the Houthis decided to respond, Tehran could hardly demand that they remain passive without undermining the credibility of an alliance it had spent years cultivating.
The escalation also serves Iran’s interests. Its disruption of Gulf supplies was losing some of its force as Washington and its partners helped the international market adjust through alternative suppliers and routes bypassing Hormuz.
Oil prices are high, but the shortage Iran may have hoped to create has not fully materialised, while additional sanctions and the blockade are beginning to bite.
Bab al-Mandeb offers another pressure point: Disrupting international trade and driving up oil and transport costs ahead of the US midterms could make the war politically and economically more costly for the Trump administration, possibly forcing it to reconsider its terms for ending it.
This does not mean that Iran ordered the Houthi offensive. Iranian weapons, training and technical assistance have been central to the movement’s transformation, but support should not be confused with authorship. Iran and the Houthis are allies, not identical actors.
The Houthis have their own interests. They are seeking an independent bargaining position before any regional settlement can be negotiated over their heads. Their blockade of Saudi vessels, attacks on Saudi infrastructure and advance towards Bab al-Mandeb were not simply undertaken on Iran’s behalf; they were also intended to make the Houthis indispensable to any future negotiations. Control of territory overlooking the strait gives them leverage over Saudi exports, Egyptian interests and, most importantly, navigation between Asia and Europe.
A silver lining for the US
While the Trump administration is likely following this escalation in Yemen with concern, given the skyrocketing fuel prices and inflation woes at home, there may be a silver lining for it.
Until now, the US has struggled to persuade its regional and international allies to join its confrontation with Iran. Saudi Arabia and Egypt have had every reason to keep their distance. A direct threat to the Red Sea changes that calculation.
Disruption at Bab al-Mandeb would endanger Saudi oil exports, further reduce Egypt’s Suez Canal revenues and threaten Europe’s principal maritime connection with Asia. NATO members and other European states may consequently be more willing to support a US-led operation presented not as a war against Iran, but as the defence of international navigation.
Israel, too, will find the opportunity difficult to resist. Even without formal cooperation, US coordination could place Israeli, Saudi, Egyptian and European forces on the same side of a maritime confrontation. This could revive the security logic behind Saudi-Israeli normalisation just when Gaza had made political rapprochement appear impossible.
The Houthis may therefore achieve the opposite of what Iran originally intended. By threatening Bab al-Mandeb, they could draw Saudi Arabia and Egypt closer to Washington while creating new, largely unacknowledged forms of coordination with Israel.
That may look like a silver lining for the US, but it is a dangerous one for Yemen. Experience shows that a naval coalition may protect shipping, but it will neither resolve the conflict on land nor reduce civilian suffering. It could instead widen Israeli military operations, pull Saudi Arabia back into a war it had tried to leave, and further internationalise a conflict that can ultimately be settled only through an inclusive Yemeni political process.
The 2022 ceasefire was not a mistake; it saved lives. The mistake was to confuse a pause in the fighting with progress towards peace. Saudi Arabia used the pause to reduce its exposure and help it focus on its economic development plans. The Houthis used it to recruit, rearm and prepare. The Yemeni government used it poorly.
The danger now is that a coalition assembled to defend the Red Sea will make Yemen’s next peace even harder to reach.

Hong Kong teen battling rare disease creates AI avatar to ensure his story lives on
Chen Tsz-kin, 17, who suffers from muscular dystrophy, says that while life may come to an end, AI can allow his message of perseverance to continue
A Hong Kong teenager with a rare muscle-wasting disease has created an AI version of himself, hoping the digital twin can continue sharing his life story and message of perseverance even after he is gone.
Chen Tsz-kin, 17, unveiled “AI Tsz-kin” at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) on Sunday, weeks before his 18th birthday – an age the student said he had long feared reaching because he was once told it was the average life expectancy for people with his disease, Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
“Life may come to an end, but through different means, AI can allow [my message] to continue,” he said. “Even if one day I am no longer here, I just hope people remember the spirit behind it.”
Tsz-kin was diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy when he was just 1½ years old.
The progressive rare and deadly condition causes muscles to weaken over time, and he now uses a wheelchair, wears a back brace and relies on a breathing machine at night.
Even so, he has spent much of his childhood pursuing experiences that might have seemed impossible, including travelling to the Kyrgyz highlands, completing a 100km desert expedition with support from volunteers, paragliding and diving.

AA Photo
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has pledged to safeguard every inch of Türkiye’s territory “whatever the cost” and to work with full determination to achieve the country’s goals.
In a message posted on social media on Sept. 13 to commemorate the 105th anniversary of the historic battle, Erdoğan said the Turkish nation demonstrated through the Sakarya campaign the scale of the struggle it was prepared to wage for its freedom and independence.
“One of the greatest victories in the Turkish nation’s centuries-old struggle for independence, the Battle of Sakarya demonstrated just how great a struggle this nation would undertake for its freedom and independence,” Erdoğan said.
The Battle of Sakarya, fought between Turkish and Greek forces from Aug. 23 to Sept. 13, 1921, was a decisive engagement in the Turkish War of Independence. The battle took place along the Sakarya River, roughly 80 kilometers west of Ankara, and ended in a Turkish victory.
The battle is regarded as a decisive turning point in the Turkish War of Independence and is widely seen as the battle that halted the Turkish army’s long retreat, which had continued for 238 years following the Ottoman defeat at Vienna in 1683.
Erdoğan said Türkiye will draw strength and determination from its history of military victories and the rich civilization inherited from previous generations.
“Drawing strength and determination from the glorious victories of our past and the rich civilization bequeathed to us by our ancestors, we will ensure that our state endures forever and protect every inch of our homeland, whatever the cost,” he said.
He also pledged to safeguard the Turkish nation’s rights and work with all its strength to accomplish the country’s objectives.
Erdoğan highlighted the unity the Turkish people demonstrated during the battle despite severe hardship and deprivation, saying the victory had earned a place in the history of warfare.
“Even under the most difficult circumstances and amid profound deprivation, the Turkish nation demonstrated to the entire world that it could stand united and together. Through the struggle it waged at
Sakarya, our nation achieved a victory that would go down in the annals of world military history,” Erdoğan said.
His remarks came after Erdoğan also marked the anniversary of the 1980 military coup, saying that Türkiye’s path of development and political stability will not be derailed again.
Erdoğan characterized the coup as a deliberate attempt to undermine Türkiye’s future, stressing that the hardships and injustices suffered by the Turkish people during the period must remain a lasting reminder.
Erdoğan said the country would not allow its progress to be disrupted by military intervention again, underscoring his government’s commitment to preserving Türkiye’s political stability and pursuing its development goals.

What does American football look like in a country most Americans couldn’t find on a map?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:39:00 UTC
21:39:00 KST

Bison and Hurricanes are normal names for American football teams. How about the Litwins, though? Well, it’s normal if you happen to be in Belarus and in love with the real form of football. This July, the Litwins were crowned league champions after slaughtering the Bison 42-0 in the American Football League 9 Final. But just how is such a foreign sport surviving in a country that most Americans couldn’t find on a map?
The country’s leading club, the Minsk Zubrs (Bison), were formed in 1991 and initially had to rely on competition outside the country. They became three-time champions of the CIS nations, champions of Ukraine, Baltic champions, and, finally, properly Belarusian champs having faced Belarusian opposition. The founders, who all came from other sports, formed a vibrant community in the Belarusian capital, proselytizing to show the newly independent nation that there was, according to an early recruiting slogan, a “better form of football.”
However, attempts to expand and grow new clubs have proved difficult, as despite assistance from the Ministry of Sport and local governments, preference in Belarus goes to Olympic sports, with other pursuits seen as hobbies. The similarities between rugby and American football helped. Many players switched back and forth between the two, getting their fix for hitting people or being hit. Nevertheless, difficulties remain.
“It is hard for clubs,” Yevhen told me over a coffee in downtown Minsk. “The costs to play are a lot and we don’t [have] reserves of players.”
Yevhen has played for the Zubrs, having previously had a decent career at the national level in track and field.
“I got to play because, you know, you finish one sport, then just the gym is left, but still want to compete and one [colleague] invited me. It was difficult because it was expensive and not so many games.”
Lack of game time was mentioned by everyone that I spoke with in Belarus. As one player joked, “It’s like preparing for your wedding every day, but never getting married.”
Making a ‘wedding’ more difficult is the divorce of Belarusian football from international competition. The Baltic states, especially Lithuania, vehemently refuse to even contemplate interaction with local teams, while playing with Ukrainian clubs is not on the horizon for now.
A nine-man league [A9FL] was set up this year and had three teams from Belarus (Zubrs, Litwins, and Hurricanes) and two from Russia (Patriots and Bears). Set up to succeed, it streamed online and got decent coverage in the national media, but an incident from the Hurricanes-Litwins playoff semifinal game precipitated a very public falling out amongst the Belarusian clubs.
The Litwins won the game and proceed to face the Zubrs in the final, but two Hurricanes had been ejected in the game. The A9FL management called for a meeting of team heads to decide if those ejections were legitimate, to the ire of the finalists, who decided to unilaterally play the final. The Moscow Bears, upon hearing the news, promptly withdrew from the league, leaving the competition with an uncertain future.
Rumors that the St. Petersburg Griffins and Moscow Dragons might join in 2027 persist, with a fourth club in Belarus also getting a chance to play. The resilient aficionados of American football are determined to not only keep the game alive, but to have it thrive, especially given the obstacles they’ve overcome. But they are less than a minority sport, they are a sport unknown by followers of the game in their own country.
On Christmas Day 2024, while down in Minsk for a shoot, I found myself at a loose end and ended up, surprisingly, in an Irish pub. Having a burger and beer, I found myself watching the Chiefs punish the Steelers, with a dozen American football fans, all locals. None ever played the game, but all had recently become Chiefs fans. One, happily inebriated 30-something ex-army officer named Sergey, told me, “I love Mahomes.” I kind of got that, as he was wearing a Chiefs shirt with Mahomes across the shoulders. “We come here and everything stops,” he grinned.
Another of the Chiefs cheerleaders, a stocky policeman whose name I never got, was totally unaware that there were teams playing in Belarus. “They’re probably sh*t!” he said with great gusto. There are lots of locals who love American football; they just don’t engage with the local version.
That’s what Pasha, an IT specialist who moved back from Germany in 2018 to found a start-up company, told me.
“In Germany, where I lived [Frankfurt], there was an active [football] community and leagues. Europe has a lot of Americans who join in and coach. But here, we have to do our best. For those of us who lived outside and felt it, it gives us something to believe in and that we’re part of a big world. And those who love the game but don’t involve with us, it’s their loss.”
Since becoming a father, Pasha has become a spectator but is hopeful for the game’s future in his homeland. “I want my boys to play the game, but we have to have kids sections first.”
That is a major failing in the local game. They have relied on luring in enthusiasts from other sports, or international students, or the occasional American, to fill out their ranks.
Tatyana, a 26-year-old beautician whose husband has played for three different clubs in Belarus, told me that it’s not easy for them [clubs], but that they are what sport is about.
“It’s very difficult for coaching kids, so many regulations, costs, my husband wants, but work, money, time, no opportunity,” she said, adding that many of those playing are more concerned with getting games and “having the TV for themselves on Sundays for NFL.”
This May, on a warm Sunday afternoon, I was passing through Minsk and decided to take in the Hurricanes-Patriots game. The visitors from Moscow had a couple of familiar faces, ones I knew from playing rugby in Russia. On the go since 1999, they have been champions of Russia on at least 15 occasions and comport themselves like professionals.
There wasn’t the pageantry or excitement I saw, for example, in regional league football in Germany. Back in 1999, I went to see my home team the Marburg Mercenaries host the Straubing Spiders on a similar May day and there were cheerleaders, hotdogs, cold beer, and even fan engagement activities being run to recruit kids to the academy. The game in Minsk was more barebones, with the action on the field more important than the fan experience.
Despite being formed just last year, the Hurricanes put on a show to thrill a decent home crowd, blowing away the Russians in 66-36. I asked some of the spectators what they thought.
“It’s my first game live and I loved it. It makes [association] football look like little girls playing,” said Galina, a language student who was going to the US on an exchange program this past summer.
“My boyfriend is playing and I didn’t want to come to watch, I’m glad I did,” beamed Maria, whose beau caught a TD pass.
Speaking with some of the visiting players afterwards, I asked how difficult it’s been for them since 2022. Yuri, a versatility player who can play both ways, laughed and said that the game is what keeps him going some days.
“I played rugby and loved it. Then I moved [to Moscow from Siberia] and I joined the Patriots. That’s what, since 2018. It’s become like life. We meet on weekends to watch college ball or NFL, and we all like different teams and it’s very [democratic].”
I asked about the set-up in Minsk. “Hey, for the first time and a new club, they did a great job. It just needs time.”
Remember in the first Mighty Ducks movie, where Gordon Bombay’s players were all wearing cast-off gear or worn out kit, basically ‘Ragball Rovers’, as we’d say back in Ireland? I had a little feeling of that watching some of the games this season.
Not as bad as ‘The Waterboy’, where jockstraps were passed between players coming off and on the field – almost everyone had their own helmet, or an individual one – but there was a definite lack of some equipment, which hasn’t been helped by Belarus’ recent isolation.
“It’s a costly pastime,” Grigory laughed as we took a stroll in Gorky Park, the Minsk version. He was pushing a stroller with his nine-month old draining a bottle of formula and oblivious to our sports talk. “My wife said me, you have now a baby [their third], you can’t miss work with injury and then pay for all things.”
The graphic designer, who played two seasons, broke his right wrist, toes on both feet, dislocated his shoulder, and suffered two concussions. I should add he was a cornerback and safety.
“I miss it and the team, but not being injured,” he smiled and reminded me that he’d also broken “many” fingers. In his earlier sports life, he had played professional basketball.
One of the minds behind the new A9FL league said that with the increased discourse between Belarus and the US, there might be a chance of links with “even high schools.” He said that in the past kit had been donated via Christian charities to teams in Belarus, and hoped that John Coale will work some magic there. Coale is the US special envoy to Belarus who has been instrumental in re-opening channels between Washington and Minsk.
But even if the thaw continues between Belarus and the US, can an amalgamated team from the nation return to European competition, now that there is a boom time for top level leagues on the continent?
The game in Europe has never been more popular, or fractured, than right now. The European League of Football (ELF), which began play in 2021, was gathering momentum until it wasn't, and infighting saw teams breakaway after the 2025 season and form not one, but two new leagues. Both began play in 2026.
The American Football League Europe (AFLE) and the European Football Alliance (EFA) went head-to-head this year, producing mixed results.
On September 6, the AFLE’s ‘Gold Bowl’ was ‘contested’ by the Vienna Vikings of Austria and Panthers Wroclaw of Poland. I say ‘contested’ as the Vikings, who finished the regular season 11-1 and averaging a respectable 5,278 fans, skewered the Poles 68-5. It was a fitting end to a confusing first season. As good as Vienna were, at the opposite end of the eight-team scale, Italy’s hapless Firenze Lions went winless through 12 games, drawing an average of…67 fans. Yes, you read that right. Numbers that even the original version of Vince McMahon’s XFL would be unable to put a positive spin on.
Rival league, the EFA, wrapped their season up with Denmark’s Nordic Storm overpowering Germany’s Munich Ravens 48-28 in the EFA Championship Game. A little more polished, also with local TV deals, broadcasts on YouTube, bigger sponsors, and just six teams, the EFA leaned into legacy by bringing in recognized names from the US. Former NFL Coach of the Year Jack Del Rio and ex-Carolina Panthers and Oakland Raiders coach John Shoop, both laid down markers in leading the Paris Musketeers and Nordic Storm to the playoffs. And investment in coaches and players showed in ticket sales with the Frankfurt Galaxy (4-6) averaging 5,197 fans and bottom feeders Prague Lions (2-8) still drawing 1,185.
Attempts to harmonize the two top leagues in Europe, and even re-unite the EFA with the ELF, have so far failed with both active leagues planning solo expansion in 2027. Neither outfit is interested in taking teams from Russia or Belarus.
Former ELF chief Ingo Schiller told Capital Sports, in 2021, that having teams from the former Soviet Union, meaning the Baltic States, Ukraine, Belarus, and Russia, would only be a “positive” for American football in Europe. However, both the AFLE and EFA categorically ruled out accepting any teams from the five nations, with an AFLE executive, who didn’t wish to be named, telling the writer that “the league’s American owners would be happy enough, but could you just imagine the idiots protesting if Minsk or Moscow came to play in Poland or Germany?”
When I joked that Belarusian newcomers the Hurricanes were drawing more than 67 fans to games, the executive laughed and said “Europe is not in a good place right now.”
The A9FL offers much needed hope. If they continue play in 2027, holding onto the four existing teams and adding one or two new ones, sponsors and media attention will continue.
Ex-Zubrs player Yevhen is confident that the league will continue, “It got the attention of the media, even the national sports channel [Belarus 5] and the club will have more players because of it. You can’t just train and train without a chance of playing.”
A sports journalist with Belarus 5 was keen to point out that not being just a local league means something. “In the KHL [Kontinental Hockey League], the interest is high because Dinamo Minsk play Russia, Kazakhstan, it’s national pride. And American football is too. If they are beating Russian clubs, then we Belarusians are proud.”
Keeping the sport alive is enough to be proud of. However, if they manage to keep the current A9FL going for another couple of seasons and start to set up youth structures, it will revive the game in the Belarusian provinces and create a sustainable ecosystem.
So who knows, maybe an NCAA college team or two will find a nugget in Belarus, or one of the top European leagues will invite a franchise from the country to take part. No matter what, the games in Minsk will definitely, beyond the shadow of a doubt, average more than 67 fans per game.

Part of workshop destroyed: OSINT analysts reveal damage to Russian chemical plant from Flamingo missile strike
OSINT analysts from the Exilenova+ community have released satellite imagery showing the consequences of a strike on a Russian speciality chemicals plant in Volgograd. A Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile destroyed part of a workshop at the facility.
Source: Exilenova+; Fire Point, Flamingo's manufacturer
Details: Exilenova+ explained that Ukraine's defence forces struck the Volgogradpromproekt plant on the night of 10-11 September. A missile hit the plant's main workshop.
"One of the FP-5 missiles completely destroyed a 20x15-m section of the main workshop," Exilenova+ stated.
The use of the Flamingo missile was confirmed by its manufacturer Fire Point. According to the company, the FP-5 completely destroyed an annex building.
"As a result of the strike, a building covering approximately 380 sq m completely collapsed and was destroyed," the company said.
Meanwhile, the OSINT analysts reported that one of the missiles did not reach the plant. A crater from a Flamingo strike was recorded near the facility in Volgograd.
The Volgogradpromproekt plant specialises in speciality chemicals, producing organophosphorus compounds, flame retardants, resins and other chemical components for industry. Its products are used in Russia's aviation and shipbuilding industries and the defence industrial base.
The plant produces ferrocene-containing combustion catalysts and develops chemical production technologies.
Background: On the night of 11-12 September, Ukraine's defence forces attacked the Tolyattikauchuk plant in Russia's Samara Oblast. The plant supplies Russia's military-industrial complex.

Israel steps up strikes on Gaza as elections approach

2026-09-13

Breadcrumb
Israel steps up strikes on Gaza as elections approach
Palestinians in the Gaza Strip continue to face deadly attacks by Israeli forces on an almost daily basis despite a theoretical "ceasefire", amid upcoming elections in Israel due to be held in October.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the ICC for war crime, faces an increasingly competitive electoral battle in Israel and seeks to maintain a tough image on "security".
On Sunday, an Israeli drone strike hit a civilian vehicle in the Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood, west of Gaza City, killing two Palestinians and injuring 13 others, according to local sources and eyewitnesses.
The strike set the vehicle ablaze as it travelled through the area. The Palestinian Red Crescent confirmed that two people were killed and 13 wounded, some critically, and said its teams transported the injured to hospital.
The Israeli army had not immediately commented on the attack.
The strike came as Israeli authorities also closed the Rafah and Kerem Shalom crossings to the movement of people and the entry of goods, tightening a de facto siege of the territory.
According to the Gaza Ministry of Health, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the ceasefire took effect in October, 2025.
The figures bring the overall Palestinian death toll since the start of Israel's war on Gaza on 7 October 2023 to 73,783, with 174,783 people wounded.
Netanyahu turns to 'security' as election race tightens
The continued Israeli attacks come as Israel moves towards elections for the 26th Knesset, with Netanyahu's Likud party facing growing competition from opposition parties.
Recent opinion polls suggest that Likud is losing ground to Yashar, a party led by former Israeli army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot. Out of five recent polls, four show Eisenkot's party ahead, while Likud came first in an i24NEWS poll.
An average of the five surveys puts Yashar on 23.6 projected seats in the Knesset, compared with 21.4 for Likud. Naftali Bennett's Bennett 2026 party follows with an average of 12.4 seats.
The wider political picture remains divided. Netanyahu's bloc, including Ofer Winter's party, averages 53.4 seats, compared with 53.6 for the opposition, while Arab parties are projected to win around 12.2 seats, according to i24NEWS poll.
If Yoaz Hendel and Ron Zilcha join the opposition after it passes the electoral threshold, the opposition could reach approximately 54.4 seats.
The narrow margins have made security a central issue in the emerging campaign, with Netanyahu seeking to reinforce his credentials among right-wing voters by presenting himself as the leader best positioned to confront what he claims are threats facing Israel.
Gaza-based Palestinian political analyst Hossam Al-Dajani told The New Arab that Netanyahu understands the importance of security issues in shaping Israeli voters' choices and is therefore seeking to keep the war and Gaza high on the political agenda.
"Netanyahu is attempting to present himself to the Israeli public as the man most capable of managing the war and protecting Israel," he said.
He argued that continued military operations reinforce Netanyahu's political narrative and allow him to portray himself as a leader capable of confronting security threats.
"The close polling makes it particularly difficult for Netanyahu to make major concessions over Gaza or significantly reduce military operations," he continued.
"Any significant scaling back of operations or concessions regarding the Gaza issue could be exploited by his opponents to accuse him of weakness," he explained.
Gaza remains central to Netanyahu's political calculations
Ramallah-based political analyst Esmat Mansour similarly linked the continuation of Israeli attacks during the ceasefire to Netanyahu's domestic political calculations.
He told TNA that Netanyahu was seeking to keep Gaza at the centre of Israeli political debate and prevent the war from being overshadowed by questions about domestic accountability and the failures surrounding the 7 October attacks.
"Netanyahu is facing a crisis linked to the failures of October 7," Mansour said, arguing that the prime minister is attempting to recast himself as a leader engaged in an "ongoing war" rather than one facing scrutiny over the political and security failures that preceded it.
With elections approaching, Mansour said, security is likely to remain one of the most important issues for Israeli voters.
"The electoral battle will not merely be about who ends the war, but about who can present themselves to Israelis as the most capable of ensuring security," he added.
For Netanyahu, maintaining pressure on Gaza could therefore serve a dual purpose: keeping the security issue at the heart of the campaign while strengthening his position among right-wing voters.
But Mansour cautioned that the strategy also carries political risks.
An escalation that results in further Israeli military casualties or generates stronger international criticism could ultimately damage Netanyahu rather than strengthen him, he said.
For Palestinians in Gaza, however, the political calculations in Israel continue to have deadly consequences.

South Africa's president calls for independent AI oversight mechanism under BRICS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:35:02 UTC
21:35:02 KST

Busra Nur Cakmak
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa on Sunday called for BRICS to establish an international mechanism for the independent scientific evaluation of artificial intelligence, warning that technological capabilities must not advance beyond humanity's ability to understand and control them.
Speaking at the BRICS summit in New Delhi, Ramaphosa said AI could usher in a new era of productivity and human progress, but warned of risks associated with increasingly powerful systems.
"The capabilities of artificial intelligence models are becoming increasingly more powerful and are rapidly reshaping almost every area of economic and social life," he said.
If used "effectively and responsibly," AI could help reduce inequality, poverty, and underdevelopment, and transform medicine, education, scientific discovery, and agricultural productivity, he added.
Ramaphosa, however, said governments should pay close attention to warnings coming from those developing the world's most powerful AI systems.
He cited risks, including advanced cyber operations, assistance in biological weapons development, autonomous action, manipulation, mass surveillance, and disruption of employment, as well as the possibility of systems whose capabilities become difficult for humans to control.
"We should therefore neither fear AI nor approach it recklessly," Ramaphosa said. "Our responsibility is to ensure that human governance advances as rapidly as artificial intelligence itself."
The South African president specifically backed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's calls for greater external oversight of AI developers.
"We agree with those in the industry, in the AI industry, that is, such as Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, who are arguing that AI companies should be subject to formal external checks, to audits and to government authority," he said.
Ramaphosa said such oversight is already standard practice in industries whose activities have significant implications for human safety and well-being, citing aviation, pharmaceuticals, nuclear power, and financial institutions.
"We must never reach a situation where technological capability has moved beyond our capacity to understand it, supervise it and control it," he said.
Ramaphosa proposed that BRICS establish an international mechanism for the independent scientific evaluation of AI, backed by "meaningful human control principles" and mandatory reporting of serious incidents.
He also called for progressively stronger safeguards as AI capabilities increase, alongside investment in sovereign AI capacity for developing economies.
Ramaphosa welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping's proposal to establish an AI ecosystem for BRICS, saying South Africa supports the initiative.

Surging inflation puts interest rates back in focus as policymakers meet in Japan, US and UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:33:16 UTC
21:33:16 KST

Central bankers in economies including the US, Japan and the UK will face a moment of truth this week, as surging inflation raises the prospect of higher interest rates.
Policymakers in all three countries will set rates in the next seven days against the backdrop of turbulent global bond markets.
In particular, investors will be watching closely to see if Kevin Warsh, the new chair of the US Federal Reserve, can face down Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts and instead persuade Fed governors to raise them on Wednesday.
Warsh was handpicked by the US president, who has repeatedly demanded lower interest rates. In a Truth Social post this month, Trump claimed the US should have the “LOWEST RATE of any country in the World”.
He added: “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change.”
However, the central bank’s board of governors is having to contend with a renewed rise in oil prices after the US-Iran conflict intensified again.
The cost of a barrel of crude surged past $100 last week for the first time since July, as the strait of Hormuz remained all but closed to tanker traffic and Houthi rebels advanced along the Red Sea coast, threatening to choke off Saudi oil supplies.
Oil prices eased slightly on Friday amid hopes of fresh talks to reopen the waterway but remained well above levels in the summer, when Middle East hostilities temporarily abated.
Higher energy costs are expected to feed a fresh rise in US inflation, which has been above the Fed’s 2% target for more than five years. In a speech this month, Warsh said without continued progress towards the target, Fed policymakers would have “work to do”. Data published on Friday showed annual US inflation unchanged at 3.4%.
Andrew Bailey, the Bank of England governor, has struck a calm note about above-target inflation in the UK, saying rising mortgage rates have done some of the work of a rate rise without the Bank taking action. Markets and economists are predicting the Bank will hold rates at 3.75% on Thursday.
However, three of the nine members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted for a rate rise in July, and data published on Friday showing stronger-than-expected economic growth could amplify fears about inflation.
Thomas Pugh, the chief economist at RSM, a consultancy firm, said the latest rise in energy prices had “materially increased the chance that the MPC will eventually follow other major central banks and raise rates”.
But he predicted a “hawkish hold” from the Bank when the MPC convenes on Thursday: a decision to leave rates unchanged, but with the published minutes pointing to potential future rises.
Financial markets are betting on four UK rate rises over the next 12 months – up from the three they were expecting before the latest surge in oil prices.
In Tokyo, Bank of Japan (BoJ) policymakers will announce their decision on Friday and are widely expected to raise interest rates, validating the recent recovery of the yen on foreign exchanges.
A quarter-point increase in the BoJ’s policy rate, to 1.25%, would take it to levels not seen for more than 30 years, since Japan first began fighting an extended battle against deflation, or falling prices.
The US Treasury joined Japanese authorities in intervening in foreign exchange markets to support the yen in July and Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, has made it clear that he expects rates to rise.
At an event at Southern Methodist University in Texas on Tuesday, Bessent said: “When we intervene with the Japanese yen, I have pretty good insight into what the Bank of Japan is going to do, what Japanese policymakers are going to do. I have asymmetric information. I am the house now. You can bet against me if you want.”
The European Central Bank raised interest rates on Thursday. Christine Lagarde, its president, said: “The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period.”

US-Israeli failure to bomb Iran into submission was preordained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:30:04 UTC
21:30:04 KST

US-Israeli failure to bomb Iran into submission was preordained
From Nazi Germany to Vietnam, history is rich with examples of countries that simply refuse to surrender to bombing
Winston Churchill famously praised the resilience of the British people during the Blitz, describing the nightly bombings of London as a “cruel, wanton, indiscriminate” attempt by Adolf Hitler to break the spirit of a tough “island race”.
He was not wrong about the toughness and courage of his fellow citizens. But as one of the United Kingdom’s greatest leaders and historical writers, he created a false impression of the uniqueness of the British wartime experience.
Strategic bombing alone, without the reinforcement of ground troops, almost never achieves its purpose. British resistance was not the exception but the rule.
Just by surviving, Tehran is winning. He said that “the Iranians have really survived an attack that almost no other country in the region would be able to survive”. He added: “They have been attacked by two nuclear-weapon states and they have essentially come out on top… As a result, their deterrence [against] the other states has increased, and their leverage has increased internally.”
That seems obvious. Yet leaders such as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump have boasted that they could bomb their adversary into submission and that its people would rise up to overthrow their government. In his latest escalation, Trump called on the Iranian people to rise up: “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?” Aside from the criminality, that way of thinking seems absurd.

Union Home Minister Amit Shah stated India has entered a new era of performance politics. He said corruption, casteism, and dynastic politics have ended since 2014.
Union home minister Amit Shah on Sunday said the Narendra Modi government had moved India away from corruption, casteism and dynastic politics and ushered in an era of “politics of performance”.Addressing a press conference to announce the ‘Seva Sankalp Abhiyan’, Shah said the month-long campaign would run from September 17 to October 17 to mark Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday and “25 years of Modi rule in Gujarat and Centre”.Taking a direct jab at the Congress, Shah claimed that Indian politics had moved away from what he described as the three major scourges of the pre-2014 era — corruption, casteism and dynastic politics — towards a “politics of performance”.“Before 2014, Indian politics was suffering from three scourges -- corruption, casteism and dynastic politics. The Union Home Minister also highlighted the government’s foreign and defence policies, saying India’s interests had been placed at the centre of decision-making.
“For the first time in 12 years, the people have witnessed a foreign policy with a strong backbone. Whether it is our defence policy or our foreign policy, the guiding principle is ‘India First.’ India’s interests are paramount to us,” he said.
Shah also cited India’s economic performance, saying the country had moved from the “Fragile Five” to the top five economies. “Recent first-quarter data shows India leading the major economies with a GDP growth rate of 7.8%,” he said.He further referred to the government’s policies on Indian languages, counter-terrorism and internal security.“We have demonstrated this to the entire world while addressing three long-standing issues—Article 370, Naxalism, and the situation in the Northeast—that had threatened the nation’s internal security for nearly five decades,” Shah said.The ‘Seva Sankalp Abhiyan’, whose slogan is “Jan Seva Hi Prabhu Seva” (public service is service to God), will seek to promote public participation in the goal of making India a developed country by 2047, Shah said.

Modi-Xi's Ukraine offer to Putin, strong message to West &amp; new Brics playbook: Key outcomes of summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:22:19 UTC
21:22:19 KST

Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivers opening remarks at the Brics Summit Session on 'Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth' at Bharat Mandapam, on Day 2 of the 18th BRICS Summit, at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on Sunday. (@MEAIndia X/ANI Photo)
NEW DELHI: The 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi brought together leaders of the expanded 11-member grouping for two days of high-level diplomacy, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi holding key bilateral meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.The summit saw a renewed push to stabilise India-China ties, a reaffirmation of the India-Russia strategic partnership and discussions on the West Asia crisis, Ukraine, maritime security, trade and energy. Alongside formal negotiations, images of PM Modi with Xi, Putin and Pezeshkian projected a strong message of engagement and unity within the expanded grouping.The summit also featured informal diplomatic moments, including PM Modi and Putin travelling together by car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex, leaders attending a gala dinner featuring a specially curated Indian menu, and a symbolic Banyan tree plantation highlighting India's emphasis on sustainability and interconnectedness.The two-day summit also produced a series of initiatives covering agriculture, health, technology, startups, energy, urban mobility, supply chains, skilling and global governance. The New Delhi Declaration, adopted after intensive negotiations, provided the summit's principal political outcome, covering terrorism, conflicts, trade, sanctions, energy, finance and development.
PM Modi-Xi meeting signals push to stabilise ties
PM Modi and Xi Jinping held a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Brics Summit, with both leaders stressing the need to view India-China relations from a strategic and long-term perspective.
The two sides expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question. PM Modi stressed that differences should not become disputes and said the relationship should be guided by mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest.The leaders also discussed maintaining peace and tranquillity along the border, economic and trade relations, trade imbalances, supply chains and people-to-people exchanges. Both sides underlined the need to address each other's concerns and facilitate meaningful and predictable market access.Also read: 'Have opportunity to discuss cooperation': PM Modi welcomes Xi; bilateral talks beginPM Modi also thanked China for its support and cooperation during India's Brics chairship and conveyed best wishes to China as it prepares to assume the Brics chairship next year.Xi said China and India should continue to approach their relationship from a strategic perspective and keep long-term bilateral development in mind. He also stressed the importance of cooperation between the two major Global South countries.
Modi-Putin talks focus on Ukraine, West Asia
PM Modi and Putin held an over 45-minute bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the summit, reviewing the India-Russia strategic partnership and discussing major regional and global developments.The two leaders discussed the impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the West Asia crisis on maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers. PM Modi reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy remained the way forward in resolving conflicts and said India was ready to assist peace efforts.Also read: Modi-Xi-Putin bonhomie, car diplomacy, gala dinner, Pahalgam condemnation and New Delhi Declaration: Brics Summit key takeawaysThe discussions covered defence, energy, critical minerals, civil nuclear cooperation, fertilisers, infrastructure, technology and industrial cooperation. India and Russia also agreed to work towards increasing bilateral trade to $100 billion by 2030 and discussed implementation of the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030.Putin invited PM Modi to Russia for the 24th India-Russia Annual Summit, with dates to be finalised through diplomatic channels.
Putin car ride becomes summit highlight
One of the most closely watched visual moments came after the Modi-Putin meeting, when the two leaders travelled together in the same car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex before attending the Brics Business Forum.The image underlined the longstanding India-Russia relationship at a time of continuing geopolitical tensions surrounding Moscow and highlighted India's effort to maintain strategic autonomy.Also read: PM Modi, Putin share car ride again in Delhi, weeks after traveling together in Bishkek - watchPM Modi also presented Putin with a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, the classical Tamil work attributed to poet-saint Thiruvalluvar."Two thousand years ago, Thiruvalluvar wrote the Thirukkural. It includes the entire gamut of human life. It has been translated into the Russian language. I am confident that the people-to-people contact will increase with the translation of the Thirukkural into Russian, which will play a big role in strengthening our relations," Modi told Putin.
Kremlin says PM Modi, Xi offered help on Ukraine
Russia said PM Modi and Xi offered their "good offices" to help find a solution to the Ukraine conflict during their separate interactions with Putin on the sidelines of the summit.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Putin welcomed their readiness, saying: “During their bilateral meetings, Modi and Xi took a keen interest in the Ukraine settlement and actively offered their good offices to help find a solution,”.The development came amid continuing international efforts to find a settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war.
PM Modi-Pezeshkian talks centre on West Asia
PM Modi also met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, with the discussions focusing on India-Iran ties, Brics cooperation and the escalating conflict in West Asia.PM Modi reiterated India's consistent position that disputes should be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy and stressed the need for lasting peace and stability in the region. The two leaders also discussed freedom of navigation and commerce and the safety and well-being of seafarers amid disruptions to shipping routes.The meeting followed their earlier interaction on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek. India has also stressed the need to expand and diversify bilateral trade channels with Iran.
Iran-UAE engagement amid regional tensions
Pezeshkian also held talks with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the sidelines of the summit.The meeting was significant as Iran and the UAE have had differences over regional security, while Gulf states maintain varying degrees of security cooperation with Western powers.Their interaction highlighted the diplomatic space created by Brics, which brings together countries with competing interests and positions on major geopolitical issues.
Modi-Xi-Putin-Pezeshkian project Brics unity
The summit was accompanied by a series of high-profile visuals involving PM Modi, Xi, Putin and Pezeshkian.PM Modi was seen greeting Putin and Xi together, holding their hands and sharing smiles. In another visual, PM Modi walked alongside Putin, Xi and Pezeshkian.PM Modi was also seen holding hands and walking alongside Pezeshkian and other leaders during the Brics Business Forum. The visuals projected unity among members despite differences over conflicts and other major geopolitical issues.The interactions were particularly significant for India as it sought to use its Brics chairship to build consensus among countries with sharply different political and strategic priorities.Also read: PM doubles down on friendship with Iran, seeks win-win strategy; hope mounts for BRICS declaration
Gala dinner adds cultural dimension
Brics leaders also attended a gala dinner during the summit, providing an informal setting for interaction among heads of state and government.The specially curated Indian menu showcased regional flavours, traditional recipes and contemporary interpretations of Indian cuisine. The menu included Khandvi Mille-Feuille, Khumb Galouti, Paneer Lababdar, Gucchi Marmik, Carrot Bean Poriyal, Thakkali Belle Saaru, Millet Pulao, Beetroot Raita and assorted Indian breads.Desserts included Old Delhi Fruit Cream with Jalebi and Shahtoot Phirni.The cultural evening added a softer dimension to a summit otherwise dominated by negotiations over conflicts, terrorism, trade, energy and global governance.
Banyan tree plantation highlights sustainability
A symbolic Banyan tree plantation ceremony was also held during the summit, with Brics leaders participating in the initiative.The Banyan tree, with its extensive roots and interconnected branches, was presented as a symbol of continuity, resilience and interconnectedness. The gesture complemented India's 2026 Brics theme of "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability".The plantation also reflected India's effort to connect the diplomatic agenda with sustainability and environmental cooperation.
Brics Business Forum pushes trade, investment
The Brics Business Forum brought together heads of state, ministers and business leaders for discussions on trade, investment, finance, technology and development.PM Modi highlighted the economic weight of the expanded grouping, saying Brics countries account for 50 per cent of the world's population, 40 per cent of global GDP and more than 25 per cent of global trade."The growing scale, speed, and optimism of BRICS are clearly evident among us. This forum, hosted in India, is the largest BRICS Business Forum to date,” the Prime Minister said.Pezeshkian called for Brics to convert its economic potential into practical cooperation through trade, investment and joint financing. Putin stressed that business-to-business ties and economic partnerships could help build more resilient international economic relations.
PM Modi pushes people-centric Brics
India's chairship sought to connect Brics cooperation more directly with ordinary citizens while focusing on resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability.Addressing the summit, PM Modi said, "It gives me immense pleasure to welcome and greet you all to India. India’s BRICS chairmanship is based on a people-centric and humanity-first approach."He said resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability had remained India's priorities, with special emphasis on connecting Brics cooperation with common people."Alongside these priorities, we have placed special emphasis on connecting BRICS cooperation with the common people. With this vision in mind, more than 350 meetings were organised. We had the opportunity to welcome your teams to approximately 30 cities..."India organised more than 350 meetings and high-level engagements across around 30 cities during its 2026 chairship. The programme covered political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.
Agriculture and healthcare get major push
Brics countries advanced cooperation in sustainable agriculture through Centres of Excellence on agro-ecology, a Digital Agriculture Network and the Brics AGRIN framework covering agricultural inputs, genetic resources and information.The Digital Agriculture Network is intended to expand the use of AI, geospatial technology, Internet of Things-enabled monitoring and advanced data analytics to support farmers.In healthcare, the Brics Mission for Healthy Lifestyle and a roadmap for joint cooperation on healthy lifestyles were launched. Members also agreed to strengthen cooperation in traditional, complementary and integrative medicine.A greater focus was placed on mental health through the Brics Training Hub Network and Network of Centres of Excellence, with NIMHANS India serving as the coordinating centre.
Energy, climate and urban cooperation expanded
Brics adopted guiding principles on energy storage and smart grids and launched a Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage.The grouping also established a Brics Urban Mobility Hub to promote knowledge sharing and technical cooperation on sustainable urban transport. Members adopted voluntary principles on climate-resilient urban infrastructure and established an Urban Research and Knowledge Network.PM Modi also emphasised the importance of balancing development with environmental protection and said technology and critical minerals should not become instruments that hinder shared progress.
Startups, MSMEs and skilling receive boost
India advanced cooperation among small businesses and startups through a Brics MSME Cooperation Portal designed to connect MSMEs, financial institutions, technology centres, trade associations and policymakers.The Brics Incubator Network will connect startups and incubators across member countries, while the Brics Startup Innovation Fund is intended to support early and growth-stage startups.The Brics Science and Research Repository was also welcomed as a platform for scientific knowledge sharing.Through Brics CONNECT, members also advanced cooperation on skills, employability, women's workforce participation, social security and digital public infrastructure.The Brics Youth Cooperation Framework 2026 was adopted to provide greater continuity and structure to youth cooperation, while sports technology cooperation was institutionalised through a dedicated working group.
Supply chains and global value chains strengthened
Brics members agreed on a Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework aimed at improving resilience, sustainability and connectivity.The grouping also advanced cooperation on global value chains through the GVC Action Plan 2026-2030, including a Technical Council and joint study.Members also gave in-principle approval to an agreement on cooperation and mutual administrative assistance in customs matters, aimed at facilitating trade, reducing transaction costs and improving border security and trade facilitation.
Global South gets stronger voice
PM Modi used the summit to push for greater representation of developing countries in global decision-making institutions.He argued that the Global South should move from being a rule-taker to a rule-shaper and called for reforms in global governance, including greater representation in the UN Security Council.Brics also reaffirmed support for comprehensive UN reform and a more democratic, representative and inclusive international system.China and Russia reiterated support for the aspirations of India and Brazil to play a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.
New Delhi Declaration: 140 points, 45 pages
The Brics countries adopted the New Delhi Declaration 2026, a 45-page document containing 140 points, after intensive negotiations that continued into the early hours of Saturday.The declaration brings together the grouping's positions on terrorism, unilateral military action, West Asia, global governance, trade, sanctions, energy, finance, development and the interests of the Global South.Its adoption was particularly significant because the expanded Brics includes countries with differing positions on major geopolitical conflicts, including Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. India worked to bridge differences and secure consensus among members.
Pahalgam attack explicitly condemned
The declaration strongly condemned terrorism in all its forms and manifestations and called for "zero tolerance for terrorism".It specifically condemned the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terrorist attack, in which 26 people were killed. The declaration also condemned the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens.Brics reaffirmed that terrorism cannot be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group and called for those involved in terrorist activities and their support to be held accountable.The grouping also called for progress towards adopting the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism under the UN framework.
West Asia: Restraint, ceasefire and diplomacy
The declaration expressed deep concern over the continuing escalation in West Asia and called on all parties to exercise maximum restraint.It stressed dialogue, consultation and diplomacy as the means to address conflicts and called for the protection of civilians and humanitarian assistance.On Gaza, Brics called for upholding a ceasefire, ensuring unhindered humanitarian assistance and ending the forced displacement of Palestinians. It reaffirmed support for a two-state solution based on the internationally recognised 1967 borders.
Unilateral military action condemned
The declaration condemned unilateral military action without naming any country.The language assumes significance against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts in West Asia and the wider divisions within the expanded grouping.The consensus was reached after negotiations continued into the early hours of Saturday, with India working to reconcile competing positions and produce a common statement.
Trade, tariffs and sanctions
Brics expressed concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures that distort international trade and create uncertainty for businesses and supply chains.The grouping reaffirmed support for a rules-based multilateral trading system centred on the World Trade Organization and called for restoration of a fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism.Brics also voiced opposition to unilateral coercive measures that it considers inconsistent with international law and the principles of the UN Charter, calling for such measures to be eliminated.
Local currencies and financial resilience
The declaration backed efforts to promote cross-border payments and trade settlements using Brics members' local currencies while respecting national priorities.Members acknowledged work on the interoperability of payment and messaging systems and discussions on facilitating trade settlements and investment using local currencies.The push forms part of a broader effort to strengthen financial resilience and reduce vulnerabilities in international economic relations.
Critical minerals and energy security
The declaration stressed the importance of reliable, diversified, resilient and sustainable supply chains for critical minerals.It called for benefit sharing, value addition and economic diversification in resource-rich countries while recognising their sovereign rights over mineral resources.Brics also stressed the importance of critical minerals for zero and low-emission technologies, energy security and resilient energy supply chains.On energy, the declaration called for diversified sources, resilient infrastructure and stable markets. It recognised that fossil fuels would continue to play an important role, particularly for emerging and developing economies, while backing equitable and inclusive energy transitions.
Health and universal health coverage
The declaration reaffirmed Brics' commitment to universal health coverage and resilient, inclusive and people-centred health systems.Members emphasised the coordinating role of the World Health Organisation and backed continued multilateral cooperation on global health.The declaration also covered the Pandemic Agreement's Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing negotiations, efforts to end tuberculosis, strengthening the health workforce, digital health and integration of traditional medicine.
Women, development and global governance
Brics recognised women as leaders, decision-makers and drivers of economic growth and social transformation.The declaration stressed women's participation in governance and economic life, financial and digital inclusion, skill development, entrepreneurship and climate action.The grouping also reaffirmed the importance of reforming global institutions to reflect contemporary economic and political realities and strengthen the voice of developing countries.
The New Delhi Summit came as Brics entered its third decade with 11 full members: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE.India's 2026 chairship was its fourth after previous presidencies in 2012, 2016 and 2021. The latest chairship sought to build on those earlier efforts while adapting the grouping's agenda to its expanded membership.In his concluding remarks, PM Modi said the discussions had strengthened the view that Brics had evolved beyond a traditional grouping and could function as an ecosystem for practical solutions."Our discussions over the past two days have further strengthened our conviction that BRICS is not merely a grouping of nations, but an ecosystem of solutions. We hope that the New Delhi Declaration adopted at this summit will provide a clear direction for our shared vision and future cooperation. We must translate all outcomes into time-bound actions that deliver last-mile impact. We will work together to ensure that our framework moves beyond mere documentation and creates a tangible impact in real life," he said.PM Modi also said the world now expected concrete results from Brics rather than only ideas and commitments, as the grouping prepares to enter its third decade.

BEIJING, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS), held in the Chinese capital of Beijing from Sept. 9 to 13, has deepened consensus on strengthening cooperation in the services sector and injected strong momentum into the world economy.
Fruitful outcomes were achieved during the five-day fair, which saw the holding of nearly 100 conferences and forums as well as over 100 matchmaking and promotion events, said Zhu Guangyao, an official with China's commerce ministry, at a press conference on the conclusion of the fair.
Zhu said the successful event sent a clear signal to the world that China will unswervingly expand high-standard opening up and promote high-quality development.
According to Lu Huiling, deputy head and spokesperson of the Beijing municipal commerce bureau, the 2026 CIFTIS has achieved more than 1,200 outcomes in seven categories, effectively promoting resource matching, exchanges and cooperation. As the guest country of honor, Norway signed six cooperation agreements with Chinese enterprises and institutions, she said.
This year's fair gained rising popularity, drawing an increasing number of visitors to Shougang Park, the event's venue. As of Sunday noon, the core areas of CIFTIS had received nearly 420,000 visits, up 36.6 percent year on year, Lu said.
Themed "Global Services, Shared Prosperity," the event saw more than 1,800 enterprises exhibit on site, including over 470 Fortune Global 500 companies and industry-leading enterprises. Exhibitions showcased new technologies, solutions, and achievements in services trade, including information and communication, fintech, digital and intelligent healthcare, smart education, energy conservation and environmental protection.
According to Zhu, China will continue to deepen international cooperation in services trade, innovate cooperation models, expand cooperation areas, tap cooperation potential, align with the development strategies and cooperation initiatives of various countries, and use major exhibition platforms such as CIFTIS as a bridge to promote mutually beneficial cooperation among countries.
"We welcome service enterprises from around the world to explore the Chinese market and share in the opportunities of China's super-large market," Zhu said.
Trade in services, a key component of international trade, is playing an increasingly important role in driving global economic growth and industrial upgrading. According to guest speakers at the fair, services are becoming an increasingly integral part of global supply chains, supporting not only production but also design, management, logistics, and distribution.
The CIFTIS, as one of the world's largest platforms for trade in services, embodies a vision of openness, cooperation and shared development, according to Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, who also serves as the current chairperson of the African Union. By bringing together governments, international organizations and investors, this fair provides a unique opportunity for exchange, sharing of experiences, and the creation of opportunities, he said. ■

Yemeni gov't forces say over 500 soldiers killed during Houthi west coast offensive

ADEN, Yemen, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's government forces said Sunday that more than 500 soldiers were killed and about 1,500 wounded in month-long battles with the Houthis along the western coast, as the group mounted a sweeping advance toward the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.
In a statement carried by Al-Joumhouriya TV, the government's National Resistance Forces said the casualties were recorded between Aug. 9 and Sept. 10, while claiming that more than 1,000 Houthi members were killed and thousands wounded. The figures could not be independently verified.
The statement said the fighting began with Houthi missile, drone and explosive-boat attacks before expanding from Hays in the southern part of the Red Sea province of Hodeidah to several fronts in neighboring southwestern Taiz province.
The casualties came amid a sweeping Houthi offensive launched on Sept. 3 that rapidly redrew front lines along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with the group capturing several government-held areas in Hodeidah province and neighboring Taiz province.
The Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mocha on Thursday before pushing south on Friday into the Bab al-Mandab area and seizing Mayun Island at the heart of the strait, tightening their grip on the vital shipping chokepoint connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
Houthi forces subsequently advanced farther south toward neighboring Lahj province, where retreating government forces had regrouped, bringing the fighting closer to Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government.
Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014 when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government. ■

Feature: Rooftop terraces lift Beijing urban renewal to new heights
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
20:19:22 CST
21:19:22 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- "If you think you've seen Beijing, you haven't been here yet," Elizaveta, a Russian woman who has lived in China for seven years, wrote on her social media account.
The "here" she refers to is a rooftop terrace atop a commercial building on the site of the original Longfu Temple, a 15th-century Buddhist landmark. Now part of a vibrant cultural hub, the terrace offers one of Beijing's most compelling vantage points, where history and modernity meet beneath the skyline.
To the east, Beijing's glass-and-steel skyline rises against the horizon. To the west lies the older city, with the glazed roofs of the Palace Museum glistening, the forested slopes of Jingshan Hill stretching and the white pagoda of Beihai Park standing gracefully in the distance.
"For a moment," Elizaveta wrote, "I really feel like I'm standing at the edge of two eras."
The terrace reflects a broader citywide shift. Earlier this year, Beijing issued a plan for high-quality urban development, vowing to make better use of historic streets and industrial heritage, upgrade key commercial districts, and create new consumption scenarios. The initiative is part of a national drive to turn 1,500 old neighborhoods and industrial districts into new engines of consumption and culture by 2030.
Subject to building height limits, Beijing's central areas preserve a low skyline defined by iconic imperial red walls, yellow-tiled roofs and traditional alleys, where residents still live amid dense greenery. These open vistas offer visitors ample opportunities to appreciate the city's distinctive architectural heritage.
Amid urban renewal efforts, Beijing's Dongcheng district, home to many of the capital's most treasured historic sites and blocks of siheyuan, or quadrangle courtyards, launched in 2025 a "Breeze Terrace" initiative to turn idle rooftops into public gathering spaces.
Government, residents and merchants have worked together to bring in viewing decks, reading corners, dining spaces and craft workshops. According to planners, the idea is to let people see the city from a different angle without major demolition or construction.
Since its launch, the initiative has drawn more than 1 million visits. This summer, it added about 300 terraces across the district, linked by four themed routes covering Central Axis vistas, hutong discoveries, literary corners and night tours.
Chen Shiqi, an influencer who scouts shops and restaurants for his followers, called terraces "one of the surest ways to go viral" on Chinese social media. Comparing his own posts on Xiaohongshu, a popular Chinese lifestyle-sharing app, he found that using terrace photos as cover images consistently draws more readers.
Over the past year, about 30 to 40 percent of the spots Chen has reviewed have been rooftop venues. Sometimes when he doesn't name the location, followers message him privately to ask where it is.
Chen's observation points to a broader trend of the social media era. Visitors no longer simply experience a view. They photograph and share it, and rooftop terraces, with their sweeping backdrops and curated aesthetics, serve that purpose perfectly.
Yet all of this would be unthinkable without the blue skies above. Beijing's anti-pollution campaign, launched in 2013, has cut the annual average of PM2.5, the fine particles linked to respiratory disease, from 89.5 micrograms per cubic meter to 27 last year, a sharp drop of nearly 70 percent. "Beijing blue," once a novelty worth a social media post, has become the background of daily life.
In addition, Beijing's temperate climate and relatively low rainfall provide more clear-sky days for rooftop outings than many other major Chinese cities -- Shanghai included -- giving the city a natural edge for its growing terrace economy.
On a rooftop garden of the Jinbao Place shopping mall, visitors can join sunset yoga, pick herbs, attend moonlit cocktail parties, try on Hanfu, or even hold a wedding. The once-forgotten space has become a vibrant consumer destination.
"Rooftop terraces, as a key setting for urban renewal, hold great potential to nurture new consumption, improve public spaces and revitalize the old city's cultural heritage," said Xing Yan, deputy chief planner at the Beijing Tsinghua Tongheng urban planning and design institute.
The next step, Xing added, is to extend Beijing's urban renewal efforts across the ground level, building facades, and rooftops, unlocking greater value from the city's existing space.
The growing appeal of these rooftop spaces makes them a must-visit for Chen and his photography-obsessed friends.
"The only problem," Chen said with a laugh, "is that my friends are so obsessed with getting the perfect shot that they can easily spend an hour taking photos."
"Sometimes the food gets cold, and we have to ask the waiter to reheat it!" ■

Jilin University team develops deep Earth exploration system
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
20:19:19 CST
21:19:19 KST

Professor Wang Yanzhang (C) discusses with doctoral students at a laboratory of Jilin University in Changchun, northeast China's Jilin Province, Sept. 8, 2026. Professor Wang Yanzhang, the executive deputy director of the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Exploration and Imaging at Jilin University, and his team have been deeply engaged in the field of deep Earth exploration for over a decade.
The team has developed an integrated exploration system combining airborne electromagnetic surveying with SERF magnetometry. Their self-developed helicopter-borne electromagnetic equipment acts like a "CT scanner for the Earth," revealing underground geological structures, while SERF magnetometers detect minute variations in the Earth's magnetic field. Together, the technologies make underground rock formations, mineral resources and geological hazards measurable and visible.
Since 2021, the team has conducted airborne exploration in various areas of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region and Qinghai Province, acquiring subsurface geological information by penetrating ground surface to depths of over one kilometer. The technological advances have significantly enhanced the efficiency, depth and precision of deep resource exploration in China. (Xinhua/Zhang Nan)

Protests reported in Syria amid fuel price hikes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
20:19:12 CST
21:19:12 KST

DAMASCUS, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Protests and transport disruptions were reported in parts of Syria on Sunday following sharp increases in fuel prices, which authorities attributed to rising international costs, heavy dependence on imports and the shutdown of a major refinery for maintenance.
The Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported protests, road blockages and a strike by some public transport drivers in several areas, particularly in the northeastern provinces of Hasakah and Deir al-Zour. Demonstrations and road disruptions were also reported in parts of Raqqa province.
The protests came hours after new temporary prices took effect at midnight, with diesel recording the steepest increase.
Under the new pricing bulletin, diesel rose 40 percent from 125 new Syrian pounds (about 1.03 U.S. dollars) to 175 pounds per liter. The price of 95-octane gasoline increased 28.3 percent to 195 pounds per liter, while 90-octane gasoline climbed 25.9 percent to 185 pounds.
Abdul Hamid Sallat, a media official with Syria's energy authorities, told the state-run Syrian Arab News Agency on Sunday that the authorities recognized that the increases would place an additional burden on Syrians already struggling with difficult living conditions and low incomes.
However, he said Syria's heavy reliance on imported energy products meant domestic prices could not be insulated from international market fluctuations. He said Syria currently produces around 100,000 barrels of crude oil per day, covering only about one-third of domestic demand. ■
