NASA-backed scientists turn plastic waste into edible cookies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:54:36 UTC
20:54:36 KST

NASA-backed scientists turn plastic waste into edible cookies
Scientists are engineering yeast to turn plastic waste into protein-rich cookies that could someday feed people on Earth, the Moon, or Mars.
- Date:
- September 13, 2026
- Source:
- American Chemical Society
- Summary:
- Scientists have engineered yeast to turn PET plastic and agricultural waste into ingredients for protein-rich, 3D-printed cookies called µBites. Developed partly for NASA’s Deep Space Food Challenge, the system can produce proteins, fats, vitamins, and even vanilla flavoring from waste materials. Researchers hope the unusual technology could eventually help address both plastic pollution and food insecurity, while also supplying food in extreme environments such as deep-space missions.
- Share:
Plastic bottles and cookies may seem to have nothing in common, but researchers are finding a way to connect the two. By engineering yeast, scientists have developed a system that can transform compounds from plastic and agricultural waste into edible proteins, vitamins, flavorings, and other food ingredients.
The approach could provide a new way to reuse difficult waste while also helping produce food in places where conventional supplies are limited. Potential applications range from disaster zones on Earth to human missions deep into space.
The researchers presented their results at the fall meeting of the American Chemical Society (ACS) during the "Undergraduate and Graduate Research in Biochemistry and Chemical Biology" symposium at McCormick Place.
"Microbes are very clever. So, we are using their traits to solve the problems we created." — Lahiru Jayakody
Turning Plastic Waste Into Food
Plastic pollution and food insecurity are two major global challenges, and researchers at Southern Illinois University (SIU) Carbondale are exploring whether one problem could help address the other. Their goal is to use microorganisms to convert waste materials into food that people can safely eat.
The research grew out of a NASA-led project focused on producing food in the resource-limited conditions of deep space exploration, where astronauts cannot depend on regular shipments from Earth.
"We were trying to develop technologies for plastic upcycling to make more valuable products. We thought, why not focus on making food? Because plastic is carbon and food is carbon," explains Associate Professor Lahiru Jayakody.
A major target is polyethylene terephthalate (PET), a widely used plastic found in products such as soda and water bottles. PET contains carbon-rich molecules that can potentially be broken apart and rebuilt into useful compounds, including components that can ultimately become proteins.
Scientists could perform some of those transformations using chemical reactions and laboratory solvents. The SIU Carbondale team instead turned to microbes, which can carry out complex biochemical processes naturally.
Jayakody adds, "Microbes are very clever. So, we are using their traits to solve the problems we created."
Engineering Yeast as Tiny Food Factories
Using microorganisms to manufacture useful substances is already well established. Yeast, for example, can be genetically programmed to produce valuable molecules. Insulin, which was once obtained from animal pancreases, can now be made using engineered microbes.
Jayakody and graduate student Sandhya Jayasekara applied a similar idea to waste. They programmed several types of yeast, including baker's yeast, to take molecules derived from plastic and agricultural leftovers and convert them into proteins, vitamins, and flavoring compounds.
Before the yeast can use those materials, however, the waste has to be broken into more manageable pieces.
The researchers process PET plastic, discarded corn stalks and leaves, and other biomass using a proprietary technique known as oxidative hydrothermal dissolution. Developed by SIU Carbondale Geology Professor Ken Anderson, the process combines water and oxygen under high temperature and pressure to break resistant materials into compounds microbes can access.
Those smaller molecules are then fed to the engineered yeast. The microorganisms transform them into new food components, including proteins, fats, and acids.
From Waste Materials to 3D Printed Cookies
Once the yeast-derived ingredients have been produced, researchers combine them with fiber, starch, and sweetener. The mixture is then pushed through a 3D printer to create protein-rich cookies called µBites (pronounced "microbites").
The available data indicate that µBites are safe to eat, although the researchers are still waiting for institutional approval before conducting formal taste tests.
For now, participants have evaluated the cookies based on their aroma. Most said they would be willing to eat µBites in situations where food resources were scarce.
The researchers are also working to make the cookies more appealing to people who have other food choices.
Jayasekara engineered yeast strains capable of producing additional food ingredients. Baker's yeast can now generate vanilla flavoring from plant biomass. Another yeast strain can use ethylene glycol derived from PET to produce beta carotene, which the human body can convert into vitamin A.
"We're using microbes to develop the cookie into a more attractive, consumer-friendly product," says Jayasekara.
Making More of the Cookie From Microbes
The team ultimately wants microbes to produce even more of the ingredients needed for µBites. That includes the starch, fiber, and sweetener that currently have to be added separately.
Jayakody hopes the cookies could be ready for public consumption within the next few years. Beyond everyday use on Earth, the technology could be especially valuable in environments where carrying or delivering large quantities of food is difficult.
Possible settings include submarines, disaster areas, and eventually human settlements on the moon or Mars.
The researchers also see the technology as one possible response to growing pressure on the global food supply.
"Global food demand is expected to rise 35-56% by the year 2050, and about 30% of the world population will be at risk of hunger in the future. The way to address that, I believe, is by using microbes," he concludes.
The research was funded by the NASA Deep Space Food Challenge and a National Science Foundation Faculty Early Career Development Program (CAREER) grant.
Story Source:
Materials provided by American Chemical Society. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Scholar says Abe reshaped Japan’s Taiwan policy

Unknown Publisher

11:51:31 UTC

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former Japanese Prime Minister Abe Shinzo left one of the most important strategic legacies in Taiwan-Japan relations, Lai I-chung (賴怡忠), president of the Prospect Foundation, said Sunday.
Abe’s statement that a contingency for Taiwan is a contingency for Japan and for the US-Japan alliance changed the way Japan views Taiwan, Lai said, per CNA. This shift in thinking has gradually become a key foundation for Japan’s political discussions on the Taiwan Strait, he added.
Lai said that in the past, Japan often viewed Taiwan “through the lens of China.” Japanese government officials handling Taiwan affairs were mostly from the so-called “China School,” with expertise in China.
Taiwan also tended to position itself within the Japan-China-Taiwan framework, seeking to compete with China for Japan’s support, according to Lai. He said that after the DPP first came to power in 2000, Taiwan elevated its framework to “US-Japan-Taiwan.”
Lai also cited TSMC’s investment in Kumamoto as an example of structural changes in Taiwan-Japan economic ties. “It is no longer just Japan supporting us; we are also able to help Japan,” he said.
While the two peoples share goodwill and maintain close exchanges in disaster relief, tourism, and culture, security and strategic cooperation between their governments remain limited, Lai said.
He suggested that Taiwan and Japan should set clear, measurable shared goals. For example, the two countries could set targets for bilateral investment and define the level of cooperation in scientific research and advanced technology following TSMC’s investment in Japan.

"All employees must cease their work in Russia as of September 13, 2026," Goethe-Institut Secretary General Gitte Zschoch said in a statement on Tuesday. "No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany."
DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities have labeled DW an "undesirable organization," making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense.
'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams
Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates.
Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard.
"I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said.
DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany.
"My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said.
It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online.
Goethe-Institut closures hit teachers hard
The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years.
"This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote.
"I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW.
"It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote.
Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services have remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025.
'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions'
Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany.
"We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians."
Some DW readers from Russia specifically drew attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions.
"Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries.
Part of the audience considered Moscow's decision expected.
"The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote.
Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship
Some Russians, however, believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia.
"German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants.
A 2011 bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so.
Gesche Joost, president of the Goethe-Institut, called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations."
According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed.

Russia Weaponized Claude AI to Spy on Ukraine and Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:49:26 UTC
20:49:26 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Weaponized Claude AI to Spy on Ukraine and Europe
A Russian-linked hacking operation used Anthropic’s Claude artificial intelligence models to automate cyberespionage targeting Ukrainian government officials, military personnel, diplomats, defense companies, and drone technology suppliers, with more than 20 organizations identified as targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a threat intelligence report published by Anthropic on September 10, the company tracked the group as GTG-20006 and said its attribution was consistent with public reporting linking the activity to Midnight Blizzard, a Russian state-linked hacking group.
Anthropic said the hackers used customized AI-driven workflows to automate much of the attack process, including reconnaissance, acquiring infrastructure, phishing, maintaining access to compromised systems, and extracting stolen information.
The company identified more than 20 organizations targeted during planning, reconnaissance, or active operations. They included government ministries, intelligence and defense agencies, diplomatic missions, think tanks, and defense companies, primarily in Ukraine and Europe.
Ukrainian government, military, and diplomatic personnel were among the most frequent targets. The group scanned email and remote-access systems belonging to more than two dozen Ukrainian government organizations, according to Anthropic.
Drone technology was another major focus. The hackers exported mailboxes belonging to at least two drone component manufacturers, targeted a military drone producer, and stole a proprietary software development kit used for a drone vision system.
Anthropic said the attackers spent several days reverse-engineering the stolen software, reconstructing the system’s architecture, hardware components, supplier dependencies, and details of an unreleased product. Firmware related to military drone control and AI-based vision systems appeared to be of particular interest.
Claude was also incorporated into malware development and evasion. Anthropic found that AI agents monitored whether security software detected the group’s malicious programs. When a tool was flagged, the system could identify the affected component, modify it, rebuild the malware, and repeat the process until existing security products no longer detected it.
The hackers also used AI to research and register domains, configure phishing infrastructure, send malicious emails, monitor successful compromises, harvest credentials, and move through victims’ networks.
According to Anthropic, Claude assisted with processing and organizing hundreds of gigabytes of stolen information, including bulk exports from compromised email accounts. The AI was also used to help preserve access to infiltrated systems and automatically register attacker-controlled devices inside compromised organizations.
The operation sometimes targeted organizations connected to intended victims rather than attacking them directly. Anthropic said the hackers compromised at least three companies providing hotel guest Wi-Fi services and changed DNS records to redirect connected devices toward infrastructure controlled by the attackers.
The technique allowed the group to collect information about hotel guests and deliver malware to Windows, Android, and iOS devices. Individuals connected to Ukraine, including government officials and drone manufacturers, were among the targets.
The hackers also targeted WhatsApp accounts by linking attacker-controlled devices to victims’ profiles. Using automation tools, they suppressed read receipts while exporting conversations in Ukrainian and Russian. Anthropic said at least two former senior Ukrainian officials were targeted through the method.
In another part of the operation, the group exploited authorization weaknesses in video surveillance services to obtain tokens providing access to victims’ live camera feeds.
The same actor was linked by Anthropic to an intrusion into a North African government technology agency, where hackers stole a database containing more than 300,000 national identity records and commercial registry information covering more than half a million companies.
Russian-linked hackers have also been tied to major cyberattacks against Western companies. In June, The New York Times reported that Russian hackers were behind the 2025 attack on Jaguar Land Rover, which halted production for five weeks and caused an estimated $2.5 billion in damage to the UK economy.

AI giants call for slowdown over ‘serious’ risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:47:31 UTC
20:47:31 KST

AI giants call for slowdown over ‘serious’ risks
OpenAI chief Sam Altman and xAI owner Elon Musk have backed calls to immediately slow the development of increasingly powerful AI models. Their statements came after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that AI could outpace human control and cause catastrophic damage within months.
Four days ago, researcher Jacob Coxon publicly resigned from Anthropic, accusing both the company and his previous employer, OpenAI, of racing towards self-improving super-intelligence without “acting responsibly.” He also claimed that the technology could “kill us all” by the end of the decade.
In a 3,800-word essay published on his personal website on Saturday, Amodei, who co-founded Anthropic with his sister Daniela in 2021, outlined “serious” dangers, including loss of control over AI systems, their misuse for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and major economic disruption. He said commercial competition could fuel a “race to the bottom” and exacerbate the threats.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote.
Altman agreed that the industry needed to “pace the frontier,” describing Anthropic’s proposal to give independent evaluators employee-like access to its systems as “a great idea.”
Musk, whose xAI is among the companies competing to develop increasingly advanced models, endorsed the call on X. “Dario is right,” he wrote, adding that he had been “sounding the alarm on AI for a long time.”
Amodei said the technology was advancing “drastically faster,” partly because of its growing ability to help build the next generation of models. Citing an incident in which OpenAI agents reportedly escaped a confined testing environment, he said that within six to 12 months a more capable swarm could “take over the entire internet” and cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage.
He proposed a three-step plan that he said could temper development without “sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States’ lead in AI.” The measures include giving outside evaluators deep access to developers’ systems, establishing common industry safety standards, and pursuing international coordination.
Anthropic was the first frontier AI company to deploy its technology on classified US government networks. Its Claude model was integrated into Palantir’s Maven system and reportedly helped generate, locate, and prioritize targets during the US bombing campaign against Iran. It was also reportedly used in the raid that captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
Anthropic later refused to lift safeguards against mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons, arguing that current models remained too unreliable to make life-or-death decisions without human involvement.
The Pentagon insisted that providers must allow their technology to be used for “all lawful purposes” and subsequently designated Anthropic a national security supply chain risk. The company challenged the decision, with a California judge ruling in August that the department’s measures were “illegal and baseless,” although separate proceedings in Washington remain unresolved.
Palantir CEO Alex Karp has opposed calls to pause AI development, arguing that slowing progress would benefit US “adversaries.”

A dignified life is a ‘distant dream’ for many Iranian families amid US war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:45:24 UTC
20:45:24 KST

A dignified life is a ‘distant dream’ for many Iranian families amid US war
With constant degradation and no real prospects of improvement in the foreseeable future, people in Iran are losing hope.
Tehran, Iran – Iranians born in the 1980s have often considered themselves to be the “burned generation”, living in a period marked by the political and economic turbulence that followed Iran’s 1979 Islamic revolution.
The United States embassy hostage crisis, when Iranian activists in 1979 detained American diplomats and others for 444 days, set the tone for a decade ahead.
What followed in the 1980s was eight years of gruelling war with neighbouring Iraq, a cultural revolution undertaken by the nascent Islamic Republic, the executions of political prisoners, sanctions and economic uncertainty.
Bardia, a 23-year-old living with his parents in eastern Tehran, said many people his age feel they have it even worse than the 1980s generation, due to worsening sanctions creating an even more volatile job market and inflation.
“Becoming independent or forming a family, emigrating away, buying a home, a shop, a car or even a new phone is becoming more of a distant dream every day,” he told Al Jazeera, asking to remain anonymous due to security concerns.
Decades of woes
Decades of domestic mismanagement and corruption paired with external intervention have made life difficult for most of the about 90 million Iranians, even before the US and Israeli war on the country began on February 28.
Months of US bombing, intensified sanctions, and naval blockades have significantly worsened the situation this year, in addition to the January antigovernment protests and state-sanctioned restrictions on internet use by the population.
Last week, the government hiked petrol prices, which will likely have an inflationary effect, with a feeling that the situation will get worse before it gets better.
For people like Bardia, who works at a cafe in downtown Tehran while studying for a business administration degree, it is difficult just to get by.
Bardia’s pensioner father is working with online ride-hailing apps and using a 15-year-old low-quality Iranian car to make some money. His mother is a retired garment worker who makes intermittent earnings from sewing at home.
After accounting for government cash subsidies and food assistance, the family have about 800 million rials (about $350 at the current exchange rate) per month, while expenses are surging by the day.
“We buy meat maybe once every six to eight weeks,” Bardia said. They can no longer afford to eat out or get takeaway, buy new clothes or household appliances, and are hoping that their medical bill does not upend their household budget.
By late August, year-on-year inflation was at 89 percent, while food inflation stood at more than 127 percent compared with the same month last year, according to the latest figures released by the Statistical Center of Iran.
Iran’s national currency has also continued on a downward spiral, hitting a new all-time low of more than 1.37 million rials per US dollar in Tehran’s open market last week.
The rate slightly improved to about 1.31 million on Sunday, after Iranian media said an understanding with Oman over facilitating limited transit through the Strait of Hormuz might materialise before planned talks with regional states in Oman on Monday.
But Iran still insists that negotiations with the US will not happen until Tehran’s conditions for Hormuz, lifting the blockade, the sanctions and other demands are met. In the meantime, a maritime blockade has halted most Iranian oil exports, while US sanctions and regional tensions have blocked or hampered air, overland and rail routes, making life difficult for Iranians.
“I remember the day my dad bought a car with 10 million tomans [100 million rials – currently worth just $43]. I also remember the day my dad bought a piece of land with 10 million tomans. Today he came home with a little bit of meat and said it was 10 million tomans. I’m in shock; I’m just 24 and I’ve seen all of this!” one Iranian user wrote on X.
The number of Iranians posting videos online about the exorbitant amounts they paid for small quantities of food and other essentials has gone viral in recent weeks. But instead of complaining, they, likely ironically, claimed they were happy, because authorities might imprison or execute them if they protested.
Last week, a state television report said such videos were “a new project” of dissent by those wishing to overthrow the Islamic Republic by instigating “riots”.
‘Erosion of resilience’
After decades of pressure, the economy has shown immense resilience in the face of political upheaval, sanctions, currency fluctuations, and the deadliest COVID-19 pandemic of the Middle East. In less than a year, Iranians have lived through energy crises and two wars started by the US and Israel.
But Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian and several other Iranian leaders have repeatedly expressed a desire to end the current “no war, no peace” status quo as it begets uncertainty for all Iranians and derails the economy.
Economist and market analyst Behnam Samadi said that status quo has come at a cost, with political and economic uncertainty making it difficult for decision-makers – whether the government or families – to act decisively to make the situation better.
“Households focus on preserving their purchasing power rather than planning for the long term; businesses set aside more resources to manage risk and maintain existing operations rather than undertake new investment; and the government is compelled to devote more resources to social support, securing foreign currency and crisis management,” he told Al Jazeera.
Many are not asking whether Iran’s economy is about to collapse, but how long the current state of degradation can last and at what cost.
Households are gradually changing lifestyles and consumption patterns, limiting expenditure on leisure, education and even healthcare, while credit purchases or instalment plans are rapidly on the rise. Iranians are essentially transferring some of the present financial pressures to the future.
“Perhaps the most accurate description is that Iranian households are adapting, but this adaptation does not mean their standard of living is staying the same. A substantial part of Iran’s economic resilience is sustained through reduced consumption, lower savings and a decline in household welfare,” Samadi said.
“And this is precisely the point that requires attention: If this situation persists, what we call ‘resilience’ today may gradually turn into an ‘erosion of resilience’.”

How our sense of beauty takes shape in the brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:44:24 UTC
20:44:24 KST

Stand in front of Turner’s Sun Rising Over Water (1825-30) and something odd tends to happen. The painting holds you, even though observers might struggle to say why. Maybe it is the colour, the balance, the composition, or the strange stillness the artwork seems to carry.
Whatever it is, you feel it long before you can explain why. And the stranger next to you, looking at the same canvas with the same awe in their eyes, very likely feels it too.
We often say that beauty is in the eye of the beholder. Yet show almost anyone a misty Chinese Song-dynasty mountain landscape, or the softly brushed figure of the Mona Lisa, and nearly everyone agrees that something striking is unfolding before them.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Beauty feels intensely private, and, at the same time, we keep discovering that we collectively share it. That contradiction is one of the longstanding puzzles in “neuroaesthetics”—the science of how the brain responds to art and beauty. How does our sense of beauty actually take shape in the brain?
In our latest study, published in Nature Communications, we tried to map that shared experience. We found that instead of representing it as a single entity, the brain instead splits aesthetic experience into two major strands. One strand handles what an image shows, whether a landscape, an object or a figure.
The other tracks how much pleasure it gives us, drawing on the same circuits that respond to food or money. These two separate neural systems combine to shape every judgment of beauty we make when viewing visual artworks.
Neuroscientists have long argued about this question, from positions that compete as often as they overlap. One camp focuses largely on perception, on how the brain takes in composition, contrast and form.
Another emphasizes evaluation and reward, placing beauty in the brain’s value circuitry. A third looks to the brain systems behind imagination and self-reflection. Each account captures something real, but they had rarely been tested together in a single study.
Algorithms for art
We asked 34 volunteers to look at 96 traditional Chinese watercolor paintings inside a 7T MRI scanner, powerful enough to pick up the small shifts in blood flow that track the brain’s activity. Once they were out of the scanner, each participant rated how the paintings made them feel.
Instead of working straight from those raw ratings, however, we borrowed a tool from somewhere less obvious: the recommendation engines that power services such as Netflix and Spotify.
Known as collaborative filtering algorithms, these tools excel at detecting patterns of agreement buried in people’s preferences. When applied to our aesthetic ratings, they pulled out two dimensions running underneath everyone’s responses.
The first sorted the paintings from most figure-like to most landscape-like, a measure of what each picture conceptually depicts. The second sorted them from most disliked to most liked across all participants, a measure of emotional value, or hedonic value (the sensory enjoyment someone gets from an experience).
Despite their complementary contribution to the overall aesthetic experience, the brain kept these two dimensions remarkably separate. Visual content was read out along the visual pathways, the familiar circuits that let us tell a face from a scene.
Hedonic value, on the other hand, was decoded somewhere else, within deeper regions that handle reward and pleasure. Put simply, the brain seems to judge a visual painting with much the same machinery it uses to judge the rest of the world around us.
Changing the brain
We also found that how strongly the brain encoded this two-dimensional aesthetic landscape depended on a person’s expertise in visual arts. In particular, the difference showed up in the default mode network, a system of connections in the brain tied to imagination, consciousness, self-reflection and meaning-making that several leading theories place at the heart of aesthetic experience.
These results suggest that, beyond mere exposure, training in visual arts appears to change how the brain represents beauty in the first place.
This last point carries significant weight. If aesthetic experience has a measurable structure in the brain, and if making and viewing art can reshape it, then arts education starts to look less like enrichment and more like a kind of training that alters how perception, emotion and meaning are wired together. The clinical implications run along the same line.
Art-based therapies for depression, trauma and dementia have long been valued on instinct and anecdote. A clearer neural account gives us a way to test and sharpen them. Finally, as more of the images around us, in advertising, in design and on our screens, are generated by machines, knowing what beauty looks like inside the human brain matters more than ever.
Most often, we tend to treat beauty as something purely personal and assume that asking scientific questions about it misses the point. Building on pioneering work in the field of neuroaesthetics, our results suggest otherwise.
Beauty has a structure, and that structure says something about the kind of creature we have become over countless years of evolution. We do not simply look at the world, instead we cannot seem to stop judging it for its beauty.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

Turkish authorities have detained at least 47 people following a series of raids on the offices of LGBTQ+ associations in a probe into prostitution and obscenity, prosecutors said.

Turkey targeting LGBTQ+ community under guise of promoting family safety
Dubbed "My Family is Safe," the government's crackdown comes as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan promotes a "Decade of Family and Population," an initiative designed to tackle falling birth rates and an aging demographic.
Rights groups have accused the Turkish government of increasingly targeting the LGBTQ+ community in recent years through a hardening of rhetoric and restrictions.
"The real name of this operation is not 'My Family is Safe'; it is state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society," the Turkish Human Rights Association said on X.

Netanyahu may seek broad national government after election, sources in Ben-Gvir's camp believe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:43:09 UTC
20:43:09 KST

Sources close to Otzma Yehudit chairman Itamar Ben-Gvir believe Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has already made a preliminary decision to try to form a broad national government after the election, even at the cost of leaving Ben-Gvir outside the coalition.
According to sources familiar with discussions in Ben-Gvir’s circle, Netanyahu’s change in messaging, from the “full, full right-wing government” slogan used in previous elections to the current emphasis on a “broad national government,” is seen as a sign that he is seeking to move in a more statesmanlike and centrist direction this time.
The sources claim that Ben-Gvir believes Netanyahu does not want to repeat a term in which he himself is positioned as the coalition’s leftmost member, with all his partners to his right. In their assessment, if election results allow it, Netanyahu would prefer to bring in a figure from the opposing camp, and in one possible scenario even former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, while leaving Ben-Gvir outside the government.
Ben-Gvir’s associates point to several signs that they say indicate this direction. One is Netanyahu’s use of the phrase “broad national government.” According to them, the choice of this wording, instead of the previous emphasis on a right-wing government, reflects a strategic shift.
They also point to Netanyahu’s political relationship with Ben-Gvir during the election campaign. Among other things, they cite the fact that Netanyahu did not appear with him at the Altalena event, as well as moves regarding surplus-vote agreements with right-wing parties, which they interpret as an attempt to create greater separation between the Likud and Otzma Yehudit.
From their perspective, these are not isolated incidents but part of a broader trend: an effort by Netanyahu to create greater room for maneuver ahead of the day after the election.
The assessment: Netanyahu will want to return to the center
The main argument among Ben-Gvir’s associates is also based on how they analyze Netanyahu’s political conduct over the years. They claim that the current coalition, in which all the partners are positioned to the right of Likud, was an exception and not necessarily Netanyahu’s natural preference.
They point to 2009, when Netanyahu brought Ehud Barak and the Labor Party into his government, while the National Union remained outside the coalition. According to them, National Union figures expected for an extended period to join the government but ultimately remained in the opposition.
They also note that in 2013, one of the first partners with whom Netanyahu reached agreements was Tzipi Livni. A government was later formed with Yesh Atid and the Jewish Home, while the haredi parties remained outside.
According to Ben-Gvir’s associates, beginning in 2015, Netanyahu’s room for maneuver gradually narrowed, partly because of political boycotts against him. That year, he was initially forced to establish a narrow government with 61 Knesset seats, and only later was Yisrael Beytenu added.
They claim that the peak of this pattern came after the 2019-2020 election cycles, when Netanyahu formed a parity government with Benny Gantz. Ben-Gvir’s associates note that in that government Netanyahu effectively abandoned advancing a broad judicial reform and agreed that the Justice Ministry would be placed under Avi Nissenkorn of Blue and White.
Judicial reform could also be abandoned
Ben-Gvir’s associates estimate that a move by Netanyahu toward a broader government would require him to give up some of the issues identified with the current right-wing government, foremost among them the continuation of the judicial overhaul.
According to their assessment, bringing a centrist party or a party from the opposing camp into the coalition would require significant compromises on issues related to the judicial system and would allow Netanyahu to present a more statesmanlike term in office.
The sources also link this to the assessment that this could be one of Netanyahu’s final terms as prime minister and that he may place greater weight on the legacy he leaves behind.
At the same time, Ben-Gvir’s associates acknowledge the argument working in the opposite direction. Netanyahu knows that Otzma Yehudit, if it joins a right-wing coalition, could provide him with a stable partner for a full term. By contrast, a government with Eisenkot could be more complicated and include significant ideological gaps.
Therefore, if the right-wing bloc wins 61 seats or more, leaving Ben-Gvir outside in favor of a government with Eisenkot could represent a gamble for Netanyahu: choosing a broader government that may nevertheless be less stable.
One scenario raised by Ben-Gvir’s associates is that Netanyahu may assume that even if a centrist partner later leaves the coalition, Otzma Yehudit could join at that stage and extend the government’s lifespan.
Their assessment is even more decisive in a scenario where the right-wing bloc fails to reach 61 seats even with Otzma Yehudit. In that case, Ben-Gvir’s associates are convinced that Netanyahu would prefer to bring in a party from the opposing camp rather than be dragged into another election campaign.
From their perspective, the central question ahead of the day after the election is therefore not only how many seats the right-wing bloc will win, but how much freedom of choice Netanyahu will have.
The more options available to him for forming a government, they believe, the greater the chance that he will return to the pattern that characterized him in the past: a broader coalition with a balancing force to the left of Likud, rather than a right-wing government in which he himself is the most moderate figure.

Putin’s Economic Growth Claims Diverge From IMF Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:43:00 UTC
20:43:00 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed during the BRICS summit in New Delhi that Russia’s economy had outpaced global growth rates over the previous three years, assertions that diverge from official International Monetary Fund (IMF) and European statistical data, The Moscow Times reported.
Addressing leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday, Sept. 11, Putin contended that Russia’s gross domestic product expanded by 10.3% between 2023 and 2025.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He attributed the performance to domestic structural realignment that he argued made Russia more resilient despite facing more than 30,000 international sanctions.
Putin further asserted that Western economies had suffered severe self-inflicted blowback, including mounting sovereign debt, widening budget shortfalls, and an 8% contraction in EU industrial production.
However, official data contradicts the Russian leader’s figures. According to Eurostat statistics, EU industrial output contracted in 2023 and 2024 before rebounding sharply in 2025, leaving a net three-year decline of approximately 0.6% rather than the 8% claimed by Putin.
Similarly, IMF figures show that the global economy grew by 10.7% from 2023 to 2025, marginally outpacing Russia’s 10.3% rate.
While the Russian economy expanded faster than the global benchmark in 2023 and 2024 on the back of historic wartime state spending, domestic growth decelerated to roughly 1% in 2025 as the global economy expanded by 3.5%.
Hard Times Ahead: Russian Attacks put Ukraine’s Finances Under Pressure
Stagnating momentum and widening fiscal deficits
Russia’s own official economic forecasts indicate that the growth divergence is set to widen further. The Russian Ministry of Economic Development projects GDP growth of just 0.4% in 2026, compared to the IMF’s global growth forecast of 3%.
Under those projections, Russia would substantially lag behind major economies such as the US at 2.3%, China at 5%, and India at 6.4%.
Moscow projects only modest acceleration in subsequent years, estimating growth of 1.4% in 2027, 1.9% in 2028, and 2.4% in 2029, representing cumulative growth of 5.8% over the three-year period.
The upbeat rhetoric at the summit also sits uncomfortably against recent domestic economic indicators. The Russian economy grew by 1.3% in the second quarter of 2026, while first-half growth reached just 0.6% – roughly half the pace recorded during the same period in 2025 and nearly seven times slower than the initial 2023–2024 wartime mobilization boom.
Fiscal pressures are simultaneously accumulating. On Sept. 3, Putin acknowledged that the federal budget deficit was expanding, with the January-July shortfall reaching 2.8% of GDP against a full-year government target of 1.6%.
Domestic supply constraints
Speaking at the BRICS Business Forum, Putin acknowledged that Russia has become the world’s most heavily sanctioned state, while claiming that the restrictions had ultimately strengthened national economic sovereignty and prompted a successful pivot toward non-Western trading partners.
Yet despite the official optimism, Western restrictions and persistent Ukrainian drone strikes against domestic energy infrastructure have exerted visible operational strains on the Russian economy.
Ukrainian strikes on refineries throughout 2026 have disrupted domestic processing capacity, prompting Moscow to enforce fuel export bans and compelling at least 26 major Russian airports – including St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo hub – to introduce severe refueling restrictions for commercial airlines.
Wartime labor shortages, persistent inflation, high central bank interest rates, and mounting fiscal deficits continue to weigh heavily on Russia’s economic outlook, even as the Kremlin continues to portray its economy as an insulated model for the Global South.

The first ministers of Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland are set to meet in Cardiff on Monday to discuss the possibility of leaving the United Kingdom through constitutional change and cooperation between the three UK nations, according to The Telegraph.
Scotland's First Minister John Swinney, Wales' First Minister Rhun ap Iowerth, and Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill are expected to sign a memorandum of understanding calling for greater cooperation on economic, energy, European and constitutional issues.
Sinn Fein President Mary Lou McDonald is also due to attend the summit in Cardiff.
The agreement is expected to state that Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland have the right to determine their own constitutional futures through democratic means.
The meeting comes amid renewed debate over Scottish independence and Irish reunification.
US President Donald Trump said he would "love" to see a united Ireland and suggested that unification "may as well happen now" during a joint news conference with Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin on Saturday.
"I don't want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified," Trump said.
"I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now."
Under the Good Friday Agreement, a referendum on Northern Ireland's constitutional status can be called if it appears likely that a majority would vote for the territory to leave the UK and become part of a united Ireland.
Swinney said Sunday that Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland being led by pro-independence parties represented a significant development in the debate over the future of the UK.
“For the first time ever, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are led by pro-independence first ministers,” Swinney said, arguing that the development demonstrated growing support for constitutional change.
The Scottish leader said he expected discussions in Cardiff to focus on cooperation between the nations and their respective approaches to independence.
Meanwhile, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that another Scottish independence referendum could take place if there were a "clear consensus" in Scotland in favor of holding one.
However, Burnham later wrote to Swinney to reiterate the government's position that another independence referendum would not be supported before the next general election.
He added that there was currently no consensus for another independence referendum in Scotland and no clear evidence that a majority in Northern Ireland wanted to leave the UK.

Pope Leo XIV marks 25 years since 9/11 attacks, calls for renewed commitment to peace
Pope Leo XIV, the first American pope, called for a renewed commitment to peace on Sunday as he marked 25 years since the Sept. 11 attacks on his home country.
The Chicago-born pope made his first public comments to commemorate 25 years since the attacks, speaking in English at the end of his traditional Sunday noon blessing from his studio window overlooking St. Peter's Square.
"Two days ago marked the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in the United States of America," Leo said. "I renew my prayers for those who lost their lives and for those who continue to bear the wounds of that tragic day."
He added that "at a time when conflict and violence afflict so many of our brothers and sisters, I invite everyone to pray that the Lord will bestow his gift of peace upon the world."
Speaking in Italian, he added: "The memory of the tragic events of 25 years ago pushes us to renew our commitment to peace, above all with prayer."
On Sept. 11, 2001, the former Robert Prevost was in Rome attending a big assembly of his Augustinian religious order. At the time, he was the Chicago provincial leader of the Augustinians. Prevost was elected superior of the entire order on Sept. 14, his birthday, a position he held for two consecutive terms until 2012.
Vatican News on Sunday republished excerpts of his first homily as superior, delivered on Sept. 21, 2001. In it, the future American pope reflected on the attacks.
"We cannot fail to remember the tragic events that shook the United States on Sept. 11," he said in his homily. "The violence that the world witnessed last week in the United States is a tragic expression of a series of problems that are becoming increasingly acute everywhere.
"Hatred and violence will continue to grow as long as so many people are forced to live in extreme poverty and are oppressed by so many forms of injustice."
Two popes have visited Ground Zero: Pope Benedict in 2008 and Pope Francis in 2015.

Americans have worse view of Muslims 25 years after 9/11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:33:09 UTC
20:33:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Americans have worse view of Muslims 25 years after 9/11
A study released earlier this month found that Americans' view of Muslims is today twice as negative as it was in the wake of the 9/11 attacks 25 years ago.
Multiple US-led wars fought in the name of countering terrorism, namely in Afghanistan and Iraq; prominent politicians building their brands on demonising Muslims and other marginalised communities; and the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel, have all contributed to a negative image of Muslims among Americans.
A Pew research survey found that 43 percent of US adults believed that Muslims were less patriotic than other Americans and 42 percent said Muslims were having a negative impact on the country.
“9/11 gave a pass to further demonise Muslims and invade Muslim countries,” Mirvette Judeh, president of the Arab American Caucus of California, told The New Arab.
“9/11 gave governments a pass to surveille everyone. It destroyed our countries and destroyed our communities here. Whole communities were demonised and terrorized. I feel like the hate and fear have gotten worse,” she said.
In March 2002, six months after 9/11, 25 percent of adults surveyed by Pew said Islam was more likely than other faiths to encourage violence. In another survey this year, 51 percent gave the same response to the question.
Despite these highly negative views of Muslims 25 years after 9/11, a growing number of Muslim Americans are becoming more civically engaged, with many running for elected office and taking on other public roles.
“There’s optimism in the fact that our community is getting more comfortable being visible,” Amr Shabaik, legal director of the Los Angeles chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, told TNA. “Other communities have gone though this and have seen increased participation.”
Arguably the most prominent example of a successful Muslim American politician is New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who gave one of the main speeches at the 9/11 memorial on Friday.
Though there was a petition to prevent him from speaking at the event, the mayor was warmly received and stood out as the only senior elected official to stay at the ceremony after all of the names were read.
Among family members of the victims at the ceremony was Michael Massaroli Jr., who lost his father in the September 11 attacks. As the last one of the victims’ relatives to speak, he urged people not to spread hate in response to 9/11.
"I think the one parting thing I want to leave everyone with is that you do to my dad’s legacy and the legacy of all these victims no honour by using this tragedy to spread hate," he said. "I've had to grow up and spend the past 25 years seeing people use it to hate on our Muslim brothers and sisters, do hate on people who don't look like them, and that's wrong and that does no honour to the victims here."

Oktoberfest 2026: All the rules visitors need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:31:29 UTC
20:31:29 KST

Visitors are reminded to follow the rules while enjoying the event as it is meant to be, with a hearty "Ein Prosit der Gemütlichkeit!"
Next Saturday, when Munich Mayor Dominik Krause taps the first beer barrel on the city's Theresienwiese, the famous cry of "O'zapft is" will ring out once again as Oktoberfest 2026 kicks off.
From Saturday, 19 September to Sunday, 4 October, more than six million visitors are expected at Oktoberfest, Germany's world-renowned folk and beer festival.
But attendees will have to keep some important rules in mind.
Cannabis
Munich’s Oktoberfest is a cannabis-free zone.
Back in July 2024, the Bavarian state parliament passed the "Bayerische Cannabisfolgenbegrenzungsgesetz," banning the consumption of cannabis in certain places.
Anyone caught smoking cannabis on the festival grounds faces a fine of €1,500, while repeat offenders could have to shell out more than €5,000.
In the official final report for last year, Munich police recorded a total of 27 breaches of the cannabis ban at Oktoberfest. Simply possessing cannabis is allowed, as long as adults stay within the nationwide legal limit of up to 25 grams.
Smoking tobacco is permitted on festival grounds and in beer gardens, although a strict smoking ban has been in place inside beer tents since 2010. Most tents offer designated smoking areas or balconies, however.
There are potential fines of up to €1,000 for anyone who does not follow the rules.
Rules for children
As lively as the atmosphere may be between beer steins, music and candy floss, the law does not make exceptions for the youngest visitors.
Anyone strolling across the fairground with a pram or buggy should keep an eye on the clock. From Sunday to Friday, children in prams are welcome until 6 pm. After that it gets too crowded – and therefore too dangerous. The rules are even stricter on Saturdays and on 3 October, when prams and buggies are completely prohibited for safety reasons.
When it comes to youth protection, organisers have clear boundaries.
For the very youngest, the evening in the beer tent ends at 8 pm. Children under six, even when accompanied by their parents, must leave the tents at that time. For children and teenagers under 16, the rule from 8 pm is that they are no longer allowed on the fairground without a legal guardian. Those aged 16 or 17 may stay on the site until closing time without their parents – although in certain tents such as Käfer or the Weinzelt the night ends at midnight.
Anyone coming to the Wiesn by bicycle, e-scooter, scooter, skateboard or inline skates must leave them outside the entrance to the festival grounds. They are not permitted on the site itself.
Anyone who gets on an e-scooter or a bicycle afterwards should remember that the same alcohol limits apply as for motor vehicles. Starting at a blood alcohol concentration of 0.5%, you risk a €500 fine, two penalty points on your license, and a potential one-month driving ban.
Cocaine
Cocaine is among the most commonly detected illegal drugs at Oktoberfest. In 2025 alone, around 100 people were caught using it.
The Bavarian State Office of Criminal Investigation (BLKA) reported in April 2025 that the number of cocaine offences in Bavaria had risen from 2,148 in 2020 to 3,972 in 2024 – an increase of almost 85% within four years. The agency said a "cocaine surge" across Germany was also being felt in Bavaria.
The figures are also rising in Munich. In 2025, 1,396 drug offences involving cocaine or crack were recorded, up from 1,227 in 2024 – an increase of 13.8%.
Drinking contests banned
Despite all the rules, people are of course allowed to enjoy themselves at Oktoberfest – but organisers draw a clear line between a lively atmosphere and a loss of control.
Drinking contests in which guests down their Maß as quickly as possible or encourage each other on to drink to excess are not welcome. Anyone who also starts clambering around on tables or benches and puts other guests at risk may find themselves being thrown out.
Oktoberfest visitors will also have to dig deep into their wallets in 2026, as beer is becoming increasingly more expensive.
A Maß now costs between €14.80 and €15.90. This puts the average price 2.38% above last year.
Visitors are also reminded to keep their hands to themselves and follow the rules while enjoying the event as it is meant to be, with a hearty "Ein Prosit der Gemütlichkeit!"

Carney pushes idea of making Canada 'associate member' of EU, WSJ reports

Carney pushes idea of making Canada ‘associate member’ of EU: Report
BRUSSELS – Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney wants closer links with the European Union and is exploring whether his country could become an “associate member” of the bloc, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sept 13.
The EU, which has not been flexible about membership rules in the past, is open to the idea of granting Canada a yet to be created status of associate membership, the newspaper reported, citing unnamed officials both from the EU and Canada.
The Canadian embassy in Brussels and spokespeople at the European Commission did not respond to separate requests for comment.
Canada’s escalating trade war with the United States has added urgency to its strategic pivot towards other trading partners.
Canada’s relations with Washington have deteriorated sharply since US President Donald Trump returned to the White House in early 2025, with disagreements on trade and other issues.
The trade spat has led to tariffs on tens of billions of dollars in cross-border trade.
Canada and the EU are discussing ways to let Canada’s goods, services and workers involved in strategic supply chains such as energy, AI, defence and critical minerals move freely, thus effectively shifting the EU border, The Wall Street Journal said.
Canada and the EU are also talking about laying underwater cables, jointly constructing data centres, cloud storage and new satellite networks and infrastructure to ship Canadian energy to the EU, the newspaper said.
Carney has spoken regularly with several EU leaders, most notably French President Emmanuel Macron, about the possibility of letting Canadians live and work visa-free in the EU, WSJ said, citing two unnamed officials familiar with the matter.
Both leaders are set to meet later in September.
Macron’s press office did not respond to a request for comment.
Macron’s office separately confirmed that he will meet Carney on Sept 20 in the French territory of Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a group of islands off Canada’s Atlantic coast.
The meeting marks the first official visit by a Canadian prime minister to the archipelago and “symbolises the strength of the relationship that unites our two countries,” the Elysee said.
Any project to forge closer ties between Canada and the EU likely faces challenges, however, based on past efforts to implement a more modest trade deal, which has faced fierce opposition within Europe.
More than a decade after the deal was struck and nine years since it provisionally entered into force, several EU countries still have not ratified it. REUTERS

77 pilgrims, 3 volunteers of Isha Foundation remain unaccounted for

The death toll from flash floods in Nepal rose to 1,386 on Saturday as rescuers recovered more bodies from eight affected districts, authorities said.The floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages across northern and central Nepal.The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 5,130 people remain missing, while 13,728 have been rescued so far.
Only 104 bodies have been identified and handed over to families. Meanwhile, 339 people are receiving treatment in 19 hospitals and 3,761 displaced people are staying in 37 holding centres.The foundation said identification details, photographs and other relevant material had been shared with authorities and search-and-rescue teams where required. The team has been coordinating with hospitals, mortuaries, police and government offices and has shared information on missing individuals with the Nepal Police and Nepal Tourist Police.The foundation said contact had also been established with the Nepali Army and that details of those missing had been passed to personnel involved in search-and-rescue efforts.Following the floods, volunteers visited hospitals and mortuaries to gather information and understand identification procedures, the statement said. The team also visited a DNA centre to understand the requirements for identification, with the process being coordinated through the respective countries' consular services.
Isha said information received from embassies and authorities was being passed to the affected families, particularly emergency contacts, along with details of the next steps.The foundation said international media were granted access on the 12th day after the disaster, but that subsequent reports had not yielded new facts.It added that a volunteer team was responding to calls and emails through a dedicated hotline operating across eight countries. Families are also being assisted with practical arrangements, including the shipment of belongings left behind in Kathmandu.The foundation said it would continue coordinating with authorities and emergency services and share verified information with families as it becomes available.

The talks mark the countries’ highest-level meeting since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, as the UAE has been making it clear through presidential diplomatic adviser Anwar Gargash that "trust is the mountain we will have to climb," as "geography leaves us no alternative to engagement," but that those relations will need to be judged by actions and not words to rebuild the shattered trust.

On 19 August, the UAE’s foreign ministry announced that it had halted all trade and financial transactions with Iran until further notice, citing regional escalation.
The same statement reaffirmed the UAE’s commitment to dialogue and regional cooperation. Saturday’s account of the meeting did not announce a change to the trade restrictions or a specific agreement between the two countries.
Former head of Israel’s military intelligence research department Danny Citrinowicz explained in a post on X that "despite all the bad blood between Abu Dhabi and Tehran, the emerging Gulf approach, and particularly the UAE’s, is increasingly clear: manage the Iranian risk rather than push Tehran into a corner."
"This does not mean trust. Rebuilding even a basic level of confidence between the two sides will take years. But from Abu Dhabi’s perspective, maintaining channels with Tehran is itself a form of strategic hedging. The UAE has little interest in becoming a frontline state in another regional war," the Israeli security analyst said.
Calls to protect trade and energy
Both countries are members of BRICS, the group of emerging economies that includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.
They backed the summit’s New Delhi Declaration, adopted on Saturday, which expressed concern over escalating tensions in the Middle East and called for “maximum restraint”.
The declaration urged the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, respect for national sovereignty and a lasting settlement through diplomacy. Leaders also called for cooperation to keep global trade, supply chains and energy moving, in line with international law.
Chinese President Xi Jinping urged BRICS to help bring peace to the region, saying China would work with other members towards that goal.
The declaration also criticised unilateral tariffs and sanctions and supported further work on international payments and trade using members’ own currencies.
Speaking on Sunday at the BRICS Plus outreach session, which brings members together with other invited countries, Pezeshkian said attacks on a country’s economic and energy infrastructure had consequences beyond its borders.
He said unilateral sanctions affected food security and people’s welfare, and called for greater use of national currencies and a stronger role for the New Development Bank, the lender established by BRICS countries.
Hormuz talks planned in Oman
Separately, Pezeshkian said Arab foreign ministers were due to meet in Muscat on Monday to sign an agreement establishing a joint Iran-Oman shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, disregarding the Gulf countries' united position that the strait must be open to free international navigation.
The UAE president's diplomatic advisor Anwar Gargash underlined days ago the country's firm position that it would not accept a single state's control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz and that it was unacceptable for oil tankers to be threatened and attacked while attempting to transit the key waterway.
“Our energy exports will not be held hostage, nor will our trade and economic activity,” Gargash said.
In an interview published on Saturday, Pezeshkian said the International Maritime Organisation would then be informed of the agreement.
Iran had already announced on 5 August that it had agreed the location of a proposed shipping route with Oman.
At the time, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the arrangement alone could not guarantee safe navigation while the US naval blockade and other actions against Iran continued.
Pezeshkian also said in Saturday’s interview that Iran would reopen the strait when the United States ended its blockade and attacks. His remarks did not set a date for reopening the waterway.
On Sunday, Qeshm governor Amir Teymouri said one person had been killed after a merchant vessel was struck near Iran's Hengam and Qeshm islands. He did not identify the source of the strike.

Advertisement

The government is unlikely to meet its target of building 1.5m homes in England, Angela Rayner has acknowledged, saying there was only a “slim chance” enough houses would be built before the next election.
The manifesto pledge to build 1.5m houses by the next election was a “stretch target”, the communities secretary added, but said it was not being ditched and she was “definitely not giving up”.
The government’s target has been significantly hampered by inflation owing to the US war with Iran. Housebuilders have cut back the number of developments despite Labour’s planning reforms which were hoped to increase the numbers of new homes.
Rayner, who returned to the role after Andy Burnham became prime minister, acknowledged for the first time on Sunday that she could miss the target.
She told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: “It’s a slim chance, but I’m definitely not giving it up. I think it’s really important that we keep a target that it was always a stretch target.”
Rayner said Burnham’s main focus was now on building council houses, suggesting that was taking priority over efforts to increase the overall target.
“The prime minister wants us to make sure we’re building council houses. He’s made that absolutely, fundamentally clear,” she said. “We’ve just announced £10bn into a social and affordable homes programme. We’re seeing home starts up by 15% last year, so we are making a difference.
“But the headwinds that are coming our way internationally and through those construction costs are having a negative effect on that target.”
Burnham recently backtracked on plans for cash from the 10-year affordable homes programme to be spent entirely on social homes, which he had suggested he was minded to do. Instead the £10bn will be spent on the mix of subsidised housing types in England, in line with the Starmer government’s policy.
The funds will build 70,000 homes outside London, about 60% of which will be social rented houses. The rest will be other types of accommodation such as shared ownership schemes and sheltered housing. London will get another £6bn, which will be allocated at a later date.
Ministers are keen to find other ways to relax regulations for private sector builders, including instructing councils to give a “default yes” approach to housing developments that are within a reasonable walking distance of well-connected train and tram stations.

Physicists discover a hidden “curveball” in quantum light
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:22:01 UTC
20:22:01 KST

Physicists discover a hidden “curveball” in quantum light
- Date:
- September 13, 2026
- Source:
- Paul Scherrer Institute
- Summary:
- Researchers have experimentally demonstrated the optical Magnus effect for the first time, revealing that a tightly focused laser interacts most strongly with an atom slightly away from the beam’s center. The unexpected shift is similar to the physics that makes a spinning table tennis ball curve through the air. Because lasers are used to control qubits, the effect could create errors in quantum computers, but it might also provide a new way to couple qubits together.
- Share:
Table tennis players can make a ball suddenly curve by giving it just the right spin. That motion is caused by the Magnus effect, a familiar piece of physics that also influences the flight of larger balls in sports such as soccer.
Now, an international team working at the Paul Scherrer Institute PSI has observed a related effect at the atomic scale. For the first time, researchers have experimentally demonstrated the optical Magnus effect by focusing laser light on a single ion and measuring how the light interacts with it.
Instead of causing an atom to follow a curved path, the effect shifts the location where the laser interacts most strongly with the ion. That interaction point moves slightly sideways, a finding that could matter for quantum computers that use laser light to control qubits with extreme precision. The results were published in Physical Review Letters.
A Laser's Strongest Interaction Is Slightly Off Center
At first glance, it seems reasonable to expect that an ion would interact most strongly with a laser exactly at the beam's brightest point. But when laser light is focused very tightly, the structure of its electromagnetic field becomes more complicated.
Because of that altered field structure, the strongest interaction does not occur exactly at the center of the beam. Instead, it appears slightly to one side. This small sideways displacement is the optical equivalent of the Magnus effect that makes a spinning table tennis ball curve through the air.
That tiny shift could become important in quantum computing. Lasers are often used to change the states of qubits with very high precision. If the optical Magnus effect is ignored, it could interfere with that control and contribute to errors.
The same effect may also be useful. "The forces it generates could be used to couple qubits to one another, enabling more complex computations," explains first author Philip Leindecker from the PSI Center for Photon Science and the Department of Physics at ETH Zurich.
Using a Single Ion to Map Laser Light
To detect the effect, the researchers used a single calcium ion as an extremely sensitive probe. The electrically charged atom was held nearly motionless in an ion trap, which uses electromagnetic fields to keep the ion fixed in place.
Trapped ions are also widely used in quantum computing. They can function as qubits, with their quantum states manipulated using carefully controlled laser pulses.
In the experiment, the team moved the calcium ion through different parts of a tightly focused laser beam and measured how strongly it interacted with the light at each position.
"Our ion acts like a tiny sensor that we can use to feel out the structure of the laser light," Leindecker explains. "This makes it possible to measure a shift of just a few hundred nanometers."
The measurements uncovered another surprising feature. The size of the sideways shift depends only on the wavelength of the light and not on how tightly the laser beam is focused.
Researchers at the University of Amsterdam had predicted the optical Magnus effect theoretically several years ago. By using a trapped calcium ion as a microscopic probe, the team has now observed the effect experimentally for the first time and measured its behavior in greater detail.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Paul Scherrer Institute. Original written by Benjamin A. Senn. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Philip Leindecker, Louis P. H. Gallagher, Edgar Brucke, Dominique Zehnder, Luka Milanovic, Matteo Marinelli, Rene Gerritsma, Robert J. C. Spreeuw, Jonathan Home, Cornelius Hempel. Direct Observation of the Optical Magnus Effect with a Trapped Ion. Physical Review Letters, 2026; 137 (6) DOI: 10.1103/kj5p-qqs5

Voting under way in Sweden with far right eyeing first role in government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:17:15 UTC
20:17:15 KST

Sweden’s centre-left bloc looks set to take power after a high-stakes election, according to exit polls.
If the results hold, it is likely to lead to a brand new left-leaning Swedish government led by the Social Democrats, supported by the Left party (Vänsterpartiet), the Centre party and the Green party.
It would also mark a strong rejection of the current centre-right coalition government and the far-right policies of the Sweden Democrats (SD). If the exit polls are correct, SD has slipped from being Sweden’s second biggest party to third.
According to the broadcaster SVT’s Valu exit poll, the left-leaning parties, led by Social Democrats leader, Magdalena Andersson, are predicted to get 51.3% of the vote. The rightwing parties, led by the Moderates prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, are predicted to get 46.8% of the vote.
It comes after an unusually heated and polarised campaign punctuated by personal attacks between leaders, accusations of misinformation and Maga-inspired ads. Polls suggested an extremely tight race, with one showing just 0.3 percentage points between the left and right blocs.
Polling stations across the country opened at 8am local time (7am UK time). Enthusiasm among voters appeared to be high. A record 3.6 million voters took part in early voting and there were reports of long queues at some polling stations.
Early indications of results came at 8pm local time when the first exit polls were released. They were due to be followed by a forecast from the broadcaster SVT an hour later. The first preliminary vote count is expected between 10.30pm and 11pm. Whatever the result, coalition talks are expected to take weeks if not months.
The right-leaning bloc, made up of what are known as the Tidö parties, has been in power for four years. It is formed of the Moderates, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals with a supporting role for SD, Sweden’s second biggest party.
The opposition left-leaning bloc is formed of Sweden’s biggest party, the Social Democrats, the Centre party, the Green party and the Left party.
The rightwing coalition broke a longstanding taboo in 2022 by going into partnership with SD, which has neo-Nazi roots.
SD has attempted to make itself more palatable to the mainstream by toning down its overtly racist rhetoric, while arguing that immigration is responsible for Sweden’s crime problems.
After four years in a supporting role for the Moderates-run coalition government, however, during which it has shifted much of the Swedish establishment to the right and had a strong influence on policies, SD’s approach to the election has been more brazen. If the right-leaning coalition wins, the party has been promised a prominent role in the government, including key ministerial positions.
SD’s campaign slogan of “make Sweden Sweden again” was reminiscent of Donald Trump’s “make America great again”. Its controversial ads on buses – with messages including: “Do you miss Mogadishu? The repatriation grant will help you get home” – were taken down after drivers refused to work in vehicles displaying them.
The party leader, Jimmie Åkesson, was accused of sexism after asking the Social Democrats’ leader, Magdalena Andersson, why she was so angry during a TV debate.
Another leading SD figure, Gustav Gellerbrant, came under national scrutiny after an investigation by the publication Expo connected his partner to Russian state actors and the spread of Russian propaganda. His partner, who is Russian, works as a civil servant for SD in parliament. Gellerbrant said in response that it was “isolated information” intended to raise suspicion about her Russian origins and has since gone on leave.
Andersson, who voted on Sunday morning in the Stockholm suburb of Nacka, said the campaign had been “a tale of two sides”.
“There have been a lot of lies and bickering, but at the same time there are so many sensible people out there across the country,” she told SVT. “The focus is on winning and setting a new direction for Sweden.”
Abba’s Benny Andersson showed his support for the Social Democrats’ leader by performing a reworked version of Mamma Mia to supporters at the party’s headquarters, replacing the words “Mamma Mia” with “Magdalena”.
The prime minister and leader of the Moderates, Ulf Kristersson, has put considerable focus in the final days of campaigning on the penalty discount applied to criminals convicted of various offences. He accused Magdalena Andersson of not standing up for female rape victims. In response, she accused him of weaponising men’s violence against women.
After voting in the town of Strängnäs, west of the capital, Kristersson said “momentum is on our side”. Despite dropping in the latest polls, he said the role of his party was to be “team leaders … uniting for the best of the country”.
Voters say the most important election issues are healthcare, law and order, immigration and the economy. But much of the election debate has been focused on personal finance, said Radio Sweden’s senior political correspondent, Fredrik Furtenbach. “The parties have tried to outdo each other with promises of more money. It has been a sort of auction.”

"We are continuing to monitor aerial threats, ensure the smooth running of trains and take every possible measure to ensure the safety of passengers and railway staff," it added.

Poland scrambled military aircraft
