Over the past two decades, far-right leader Jimmie Akesson has steered the party with neo-Nazi roots into the mainstream.
It is now hoping to enter government. Kristersson has promised the far right key cabinet posts if the right-wing wins the election.
“I think it’s a very important election this year, and hopefully a lot of people will realise that we have to change course... so that everyone will feel included in society,” store manager Linda Eriksson, 48, told AFP as she voted at a polling station.
Ingrid Rudien, a 64-year-old assistant secretary, said she hoped the country “can unite together as a nation even though we may have a close result”.
‘We’ve already won!’
Akesson was confident of victory at a final election rally on Saturday in the Swedish capital.
“We’ve already won!” the 47-year-old said to thunderous applause in Stockholm’s Kungstradgarden Park.
“Sweden is becoming safer, better, and more Swedish,” he said, surrounded by blue and yellow campaign posters blaring “Make Sweden Sweden Again”.
Agneta Andersson, a 78-year-old pensioner attending the rally, told AFP she was voting for the far right.
“Like Jimmie, I want it to be like it was when I was young, in the old Sweden. I can’t cope with all this violence in society.”
Voting stations close at 8:00 p.m. when exit polls were to be published, with the first reliable results expected several hours later.
Some eight million people are eligible to vote in the election, in a country of 10.6 million where voter turnout regularly tops 80 percent.
Around half of voters have cast their ballots in advance.
If the right wing were to win the election, the formation of a new government would be fairly straightforward.
But as the four left-wing parties are splintered ideologically, tough negotiations would be needed to form a government even if they hold a majority.

Russia hits Ukraine’s military logistics – MOD (VIDEO)

In Ivano-Frankivsk Region, western Ukraine, Governor Svetlana Onischuk said that a drone attack damaged an industrial facility and an apartment building. Separately, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service reported that a logistics warehouse in the Borispol district not far from Kiev also came under attack.
The new barrage comes as Ukraine has intensified long-range drone strikes deep inside Russia, targeting critical infrastructure, oil refineries, and civilian facilities, including e-retail warehouses. Moscow has retaliated by attacking Ukraine’s defense industry and military-related facilities, and maintains that it never targets civilians.

Rosh Hashanah 2026: Israel’s 78-year miracle was never supposed to happen - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:07:19 UTC
20:07:19 KST

As we start 5787, let’s take stock of the incredible times we live in.
In May 1948, a battered remnant of a people declared a state on a sliver of land no one else wanted. Five regular armies crossed its borders within hours. Twenty more governments wished it were gone.
The Jews inside had no oil, no great-power patron willing to fight for them, almost no heavy weapons, and a fifth column already shooting from behind. The smart money said the experiment would last weeks.
Seventy-eight years later, that experiment is a regional power, a technological engine, and the most successful national revival in modern history. The odds were not merely long. They were absurd. That is precisely why the story matters.
The first war was supposed to finish what the Holocaust began. Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, and Iraq sent trained armies against a militia that had spent the previous decade smuggling rifles in crates of oranges.
Inside the new borders, thousands of Arabs took up arms against the government that had just offered them citizenship. The Jews absorbed 6,000 dead, 1% of the entire population, and still held the line. They have not lost a war since.
In 1967, they were outnumbered on three fronts and finished the fighting in six days. In 1973, they were surprised, bled, and then drove the attackers back across the canal and the Golan.
Every subsequent campaign has followed the same pattern: Israel is smaller, Israel is condemned, Israel survives and wins.
Survival was only the first miracle. The second was the ingathering. Nearly a million Jews fled or were expelled from Iraq, Yemen, Egypt, Libya, Syria, and Morocco. They arrived with suitcases and trauma.
Then came the remnant of European Jewry, the Soviet aliyah of the 1990s, the Ethiopians, the Indians. Israel did not merely house them. It turned refugees into citizens, conscripts, engineers, and rabbis.
No other country in the 20th century absorbed so many people, from so many civilizations, in such a short time, while fighting for its life.
The economic story is almost as improbable. For decades, the Arab League enforced a boycott designed to strangle the Jewish state in its crib.
Later came the BDS campaign, campus resolutions, and the ritual 69-plus-1 votes at the United Nations, the 22 members of the Arab League plus a rotating bloc of 48 African and Asian states that treat isolation of Israel as a standing agenda item.
Accusations escalated from “occupation” to “apartheid” to “genocide,” language borrowed from the worst crimes of the century and applied to a country that withdraws from territory, accepts cease-fires, and vaccinates its enemies. The intended result was pariah status.
Instead, Israel became the Start-Up Nation. A country with no natural resources except human capital now punches far above its weight in cybersecurity, medical devices, drip irrigation, desalination, and semiconductors.
Israeli firms list on Nasdaq in numbers that embarrass far larger economies. The same people who once rationed margarine now export intelligence software to governments that once would not stamp an Israeli passport.
Poverty has not disappeared, inequality is real, and the cost of living is high. None of that cancels the larger fact: a poor, blockaded state became rich by selling brains.
Wishes for the new year
Diplomacy followed the same improbable arc: the US, after early hesitation, became Israel’s indispensable ally. That relationship is now so deep that it survives administrations and wars.
Meanwhile, Israel quietly signed defense and commercial agreements from Colombia to Finland, India to Japan, and, most strikingly, with several Arab states that once led the effort to erase it.
The Abraham Accords did not end the conflict. They proved that the old consensus, no recognition until every Palestinian demand is met, was never as solid as its advocates claimed.
The least-noticed success may be the most Jewish. The study halls of Europe were ash. The great yeshivas of Lithuania and Poland existed only in memory and a handful of surviving rabbis.
Today, Israel houses the largest concentration of full-time Torah scholars in history.
The numbers dwarf anything that existed in Vilna or Pressburg. Kolels, women’s seminaries, and community kolels have multiplied. Hesed (kindness) networks, food, medical care, burial, and mental-health support operate at a scale the shtetl never imagined.
Observance is not uniform; Israel is argumentative by nature.
Yet the sheer volume of learning, the density of mitzvah performance, and the public presence of Jewish life exceed anything seen since Sinai, and, in raw numbers of people sitting before open volumes, arguably surpass it.
A people that was supposed to vanish rebuilt the very institutions the murderers tried to erase.
None of this was inevitable. It was the product of divine providence, Jewish resilience, improvisation, and a refusal to accept the verdict of demographics, geography, or the General Assembly.
Critics will always list the failures, the uncertainty in Gaza and Judea and Samaria that has lasted too long, political divisions, high costs of war, and the unfinished conflict with the Palestinians.
Those criticisms are not imaginary. They simply do not outweigh the central fact.
A state that should have died in 1948, or 1967, or 1973, or under the weight of boycotts and resolutions, is still here, still growing, still inventing, and still arguing about the meaning of its own existence.
The next 78 years are not guaranteed. Iran’s nuclear program, demographic trends, internal cohesion, mitzvah neglect, and the endurance of Western support all remain open questions. But the record already compiled is not a fluke. It is evidence.
Small peoples with a long memory and a short list of alternatives can rewrite the odds.
Israel did not merely survive. It turned the most lopsided bet of the 20th century into a massive success, and, for millions of Jews who had nowhere else to go, into a home.
That is not a miracle in the sense that it required no human effort. It is a miracle in the only sense that matters: it happened when every reasonable calculation said it would not.
As we start year 5787, let’s be grateful to God for the providential success we’ve enjoyed, the dedication and efforts of our leaders, soldiers, and civil servants who have made this country a success, and commit ourselves to greater Torah observance, dedication to helping our neighbors, and the growth of the Jewish nation.
The writer is a Zionist educator at institutions around the world and recently published a new book, Zionism Today.

Rosh Hashanah 2026: What does ‘shana tova’ mean in an Israel divided by politics? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:07:17 UTC
20:07:17 KST

What do we mean when we wish our friends, acquaintances, and passersby a shana tova (good year)?
If we are speaking on the personal level, the answer is simple: we are speaking of good health, happiness, prosperity, a good education for their children, satisfaction in everything they do, etc.
I suppose this also expresses the hope that we shall have a government that will enable us all to realize all these wishes, such as properly functioning health and education systems, and a solid economy. But all this is innocent and more or less politically neutral.
The moment we come to political issues, both short-term and long-term, we find ourselves in trouble, for here we are deeply divided in our beliefs and aspirations. Nothing exemplifies this division more clearly than the approaching general elections and the current election campaign.
For half of the Jewish population in Israel, the wishes for a good year are for the continued rule of the existing Right/religious coalition, at least for the time being, under its current leader – Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
This half of the population is inclined to reject a negotiated settlement of the issues that are the cause of the war on seven fronts of the last three years, supports a major, revolutionary legal reform, and the weakening of the vestiges of Israel’s liberal democracy.
Much of this bloc also wishes Israel to become more religious, and large parts of it do not seek coexistence with Israel’s Arab population – whether citizens or only inhabitants – but rather its “voluntary” emigration.
For the other half of the Jewish population, getting rid of the current government and its head are considered primary goals – not only for ideological reasons, but also because it believes that this government is a badly functioning government in almost all spheres, but most notably health, education, economics, foreign affairs, justice, transportation, and environment.
This part of the population is inclined to believe that the use of military force must be accompanied by diplomacy and clear political goals based on non-religious realpolitik. It believes that the prime minister must be motivated exclusively by national interests rather than by an ambition to remain in power at any price.
Belief that government is tainted by corruption
It is also inclined to believe that the current government is more tainted by corruption and illegality than any previous Israeli government.
There is no doubt that each of the blocs believes that the victory of the other bloc in the election will be a catastrophe, so the “good year” of each side clashes with that of the other. If we wish a good year to whoever we happen to come across, we place ourselves in a stormy medley of irreconcilable contradictions.
Today’s government bloc believes that a government formed after the elections by the current opposition and supported by even a single Arab party – whether or not it includes Jews among its members – will be dangerous to Israel’s security and existence as a Jewish state in the religious sense.
Supporters of this bloc also believe that the return of today’s opposition to power will also cut short the current government’s efforts to do away with an alleged “deep-state” within Israel’s administration, its universities, its legal system, and even its military establishment – a deep-state which prevents the Israeli Right, and the various Jewish religious groups in the state, from effectively manifesting their numerical strength in the Israeli power structure and society.
Parts of the government supporting bloc even believe that certain elements in the opposition – primarily the Democrats and their leader, former IDF deputy chief of staff Yair Golan – are no less than traitors who collaborated with Hamas and other enemies of Israel.
On the other hand, the opposite bloc believes that a victory of the existing government bloc will bring about the end of Israel’s liberal democratic system and turn Israel into an authoritarian state, which disregards the international law on which the State of Israel was established 78 years ago, and is treated as a pariah state by its former friends in the enlightened world.
Furthermore, this bloc believes that Israel has been led for much too long by a man who started as a breath of fresh air, but today is not only flimsy with facts but whose cognitive and decision-making faculties are no longer as sharp as they were in the past, and is no longer surrounded by an entourage that elicits confidence and respect.
Netanyahu’s failure to appoint to the Likud list for the elections respected and inspiring personalities such as former chief of staff Gabi Ashkenazi, former Likud minister and confident Ron Dermer, and former Likud minister Yuval Steinitz (all of whom declined the offer), and the persons who were finally appointed (such as Yaakov Bardugo, a former TV presenter and commentator on channel 14), points to his declining power of persuasion.
The real danger, of course, is that even though there is still a small chance that one of the blocs will win a decisive victory, if neither side manages to form a government after the election – especially if the Arab parties win (as predicted) 13-15 Knesset seats – neither side will actually enjoy much of a good year.
Unless, under such circumstances, the two sides opt for a grand coalition (an unlikely occurrence) and the current government will turn into a transition government, with new elections for the 27th Knesset being called within several months, the situation will only get worse.
Such a development will be more favorably received by the current coalition than by the opposition, but it is still nobody’s vision of a good year.
Why is the vision of a grand Zionist coalition unlikely? First, because the current opposition bloc simply does not trust Netanyahu. Secondly, because a grand coalition would require rotation in the premiership, and as long as Netanyahu is on trial, he can serve as prime minister but not as a minister.
Thirdly, because neither of the two parties running in the elections that advocate such a government – Benny Gantz’s Blue and White, and the new union between Yoaz Hendel’s Reservists Party and Yaron Zelekha’s New Economic Party – are likely to pass the qualifying threshold.
So at the moment, let us stick to personal wishes of a shana tova to everyone, but especially to those wounded physically and/or mentally in the course of fighting during the last three years, and who are far from recovery, and to those who have lost loved ones on October 7, as hostages in the Gaza Strip, or in the fighting on seven fronts in the last three years and are still mourning.
In the final reckoning, we could all do with a better year.
The writer has written journalistic and academic articles, as well as several books, on international relations, Zionism, Israeli politics, and parliamentarism. From 1994 to 2010, she worked at the Knesset Library and the Knesset Research and Information Center.

Five sea turtles return to nature after rehabilitation, Israel Nature and Parks Authority announces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:06:51 UTC
20:06:51 KST

Five sea turtles were released back into the sea on Friday at the Beit Yanai National Park beach after completing their rehabilitation process at the Israel Nature and Parks Authority’s National Sea Turtle Rescue Center.
About 250 people, mostly families and children, arrived at Beit Yanai National Park beach to watch the release of Miriam, Chapa, Matzav, Ran and Nidal, the five sea turtles that made their way back to the sea.
The turtles spent recent months at the National Sea Turtle Rescue Center receiving veterinary care after arriving with limb injuries caused by entanglement in plastic bags. Their rehabilitation has now been completed, and the turtles were released near the shoreline to help them reach the water quickly.
The Israel Nature and Parks Authority emphasized that anyone who finds an injured or dead sea turtle must report it to the authority’s hotline (*3639). The authority instructed the public not to remove strings or plastic waste from sea turtles, but instead to bring the turtle, along with the plastic bag or waste entangling it, to the rescue center for appropriate treatment.
The authority has received reports of numerous sea turtles washing ashore entangled in plastic bags. However, contrary to the authority’s instructions, some people who found the turtles removed the material themselves and returned them to the sea.
Around 50,000 visit nature parks during Rosh Hashanah holiday
The release took place as around 50,000 visitors toured nature reserves and national parks during the Rosh Hashanah holiday, with some visitors witnessing the return of the turtles to their natural habitat.
Among the most visited sites were Habonim Nature Reserve, Ashkelon National Park, Ein Hemed National Park and Yarkon Tel Afek National Park.
Around 2,600 people also chose to spend Rosh Hashanah Eve at the Israel Nature and Parks Authority’s overnight campgrounds, with the most popular locations being Tel Dan and Achziv.

Territory Remains Main Obstacle to Ukraine-Russia Deal, Kushner Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:05:00 UTC
20:05:00 KST

Territorial disputes remain the central obstacle preventing Ukraine and Russia from reaching an agreement to end the war, US presidential special envoy Jared Kushner said on Sunday during the Yalta European Strategy (YES 2026) forum in Kyiv.
Addressing conference participants, Kushner explained that while mediators have assembled frameworks covering nearly all other facets of a prospective settlement, the division over front lines and sovereign borders has stalled diplomatic efforts.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He stated that Russian President Vladimir Putin had detailed Moscow’s specific territorial objectives during recent Kremlin consultations, but Ukraine firmly refuses to make concessions or pull back its military forces.
“The main issue will be territories, and that is precisely where the sides have not yet reached an agreement,” Kushner said, as reported by Ukrinform.
“President Putin laid out his position regarding what he wants to achieve. If Ukraine wanted to retreat to that line, we would have already prepared and agreed on the remaining terms of the deal. Currently, Ukraine does not want to do this.
And our task as mediators is to figure out how we can find a creative solution that does not contradict their desires, helps them achieve their goals, and compels Russia to end the conflict so both sides can move forward within a framework that prevents a recurrence.”
Russia Fired 2,100 Drones and 78 Missiles This Week, Zelensky Says
Kushner did not address the widespread war crimes committed by Russian occupation forces or the legal question of Russian accountability for launching the full-scale invasion. Instead, he characterized both nations as enduring “a lot of pain” and asserted that both Kyiv and Moscow harbor a determination to bring fighting to an end.
“[US] President [Donald] Trump is very, very committed to this cause. Steve [Witkoff] and I are very committed. President Zelensky is very committed. From what we have seen and heard, President Putin is also very committed to this cause,” Kushner claimed. “It is simply a matter of finding the right formula that will hopefully satisfy everyone to move forward.”
Pre-winter ceasefire uncertainty and security guarantees
Asked whether a cessation of hostilities could be achieved before the onset of winter, Kushner gave a cautious response, acknowledging that diverse ideas have been floated by multiple actors without achieving a diplomatic breakthrough.
Kushner detailed that diplomatic discussions over recent months have concentrated extensively on future security architecture and security guarantees designed to assure Ukraine that any cessation of combat represents an enduring peace rather than an operational pause for Moscow to regroup.
He stressed that sovereignty, security, and economic prosperity form the three non-negotiable pillars of any just outcome for Ukraine.
Kushner revealed that during previous trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi, delegations from Ukraine, the US, and Russia finalized practical mechanisms for conflict prevention and ceasefire verification involving military personnel. He stated that this monitoring structure is engineered to take effect the moment political leadership resolves the territorial dispute.
“We have developed a monitoring mechanism that involves the military, and everyone agrees that once there is a definitive resolution regarding frontlines or territorial issues, a mechanism will exist that everyone can hopefully abide by,” Kushner explained.
“I think this is something that satisfies both sides, representing genuine progress in that regard.”
Post-war prosperity as an incentive for lasting peace
Outlining subsequent stages of the US diplomatic initiative, Kushner argued that long-term stability must be anchored in economic prosperity and mutual financial incentives.
He contended that both Ukraine and Russia should leverage a post-war settlement to attract international capital, create jobs, and raise living standards, suggesting that societal economic interest in stability serves as the most effective defense against renewed conflict.
“When you end a war, people must have something to look forward to,” Kushner said, asserting that President Trump shares this philosophy.
“Both countries need to consider how they can seize this opportunity after the war to attract investments, create employment, provide greater prosperity, and increase incomes. That is what motivates societies to invest in and feel enthusiastic about peace. In many ways, it becomes your greatest security guarantee. If everyone lives well and maintains a personal stake in security, it will hopefully produce something durable and sustainable.”
Kushner’s remarks arrive following multi-stage consultations held in Kyiv on Sept. 6 alongside fellow envoy Witkoff and European national security advisers, which succeeded a three-hour meeting with Putin in Moscow. During those talks, Putin insisted on achieving his stated war aims, with Kremlin insiders reiterating that Moscow will refuse any frontline ceasefire until Russian forces capture the entire Donbas.
President Volodymyr Zelensky and senior Ukrainian officials have categorically dismissed territorial concessions as unacceptable capitulation, maintaining that restoring territorial integrity and securing legally binding Western defense guarantees remain indispensable to any durable settlement.

Ukrainian Drone Evades Russian Helicopter Fire and Strikes Sanctioned Oil Tanker Near Sochi
Unknown

- Category

Ukrainian Drone Evades Russian Helicopter Fire and Strikes Sanctioned Oil Tanker Near Sochi
A Ukrainian drone struck the sanctioned Russian oil tanker Armada Leader near Sochi after maneuvering under fire from a Russian helicopter attempting to intercept it, as Ukraine continues a broader campaign targeting Russia-linked maritime traffic in the Black and Azov seas.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Footage released by Commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces Robert Brovdi showed a Russian helicopter pursuing the drone and opening fire as it approached the vessel. The drone maneuvered to evade the fire before continuing toward the tanker and striking its target.
The strike was carried out as part of the Unmanned Systems Forces’ “MoLoChKa” operation, a campaign targeting vessels involved in Russian maritime transportation across the Black and Azov seas.
Brovdi said Ukrainian forces had struck 285 vessels during the first 10 weeks of the operation. The figure includes 215 vessels in July, 54 in August, and another 16 between September 1 and September 11.
The operation is aimed in part at disrupting maritime routes used for Russian oil exports and supplies to temporarily occupied Crimea, according to Brovdi.
He said Russian shadow-fleet tankers transporting oil toward the Bosphorus provide revenue that can be used to finance Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Earlier, on September 6, the Russian-flagged cargo ship Lady Mariia was reportedly struck 12 times by drones in the Mediterranean Sea while allegedly transporting Iranian weapons and armored vehicles to Russia. The sanctioned vessel had departed Algeria, though Ukraine’s involvement and details of the cargo were not independently confirmed.

Dover unrest exposes serious flaws in Britain’s handling of far-right extremism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:00:06 UTC
20:00:06 KST

To anybody watching the videos of a group of masked men, all wearing black, descending on the port of Dover last weekend, it was immediately obvious that something novel and disturbing was happening: a mass intimidation in uniform not seen in Britain since the 1930s.
Yet to the police and the rest of the UK’s intelligence apparatus, the arrival of the men chanting “stop the boats” was a surprise, despite the fact that residents of a village 18 miles away tried to report that dozens of men were congregating there on the Friday, threatening to go to Dover and “attack Muslims”.
Intelligence specialists describe the events in Dover and the day after in Portsmouth as protests, as if they are on a par with cardboard-carrying campaigners marching on an approved route. The same definition was used by Kent police and Sarah Jones, the policing minister, on Monday. “Protest activity,” she told MPs.
Such semantics are important to the state, though they appear to misunderstand the recent events. In a democracy, it is argued it is not the job of MI5 and police to spy on campaign groups, as undercover police did so zealously on leftwing groups from the 1960s to the 1990s, sending reports to the Security Service.
Nigel Brookes, an assistant chief constable at Kent police, said this week: “The right to peaceful protest is an important part of our democracy and applies irrespective of the political views being expressed.” No arrests were made in Dover, though traffic was halted for several hours before the masked men dispersed.
The contrast with Palestine Action is sharp. The group was designated and banned as a terror organisation after some members broke into RAF Brize Norton and sprayed two military planes with red paint.
Terror arrests in Great Britain were at record levels for the year to March as thousands of mostly elderly supporters were arrested, many holding placards reading: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”
Monitoring every protest group would be too intrusive, it is argued. Yet Patriot Platform, created in June by the far-right agitator Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, is clearly somewhat different, with its emphasis on recruitment of “English men”, vetting, uniforms and hostility to migrants arriving in the UK by small boats.
“In the next three or four weeks, we are going to ask you to be part of one of the biggest pushbacks this country has seen from its men since world war two. Are you up for it or what?” Thomas was reported by Searchlight as having said at a “national recruitment day” event at Burton Dassett, south of Coventry, last month.
The language is calibrated, not explicitly racially charged or inciteful. Those dressed in balaclavas and black were careful to avoid violence in Dover, though there were clashes the night after in Portsmouth. Police used batons and synthetic pepper spray to control people blocking the road away from the port, down which 120 disembarked migrants were expected to be taken for processing.
It appears that the aspiration is to agitate or provoke at a level just below the criminal threshold: grey zone tactics. In Dover, protesters were handing out a “legal reference sheet” justifying their right to obstruct the highway outside the port where migrants on boats are taken to and processed, citing the rights to freedom of expression and freedom of assembly under the Human Rights Act.
The question is, where is this heading? That is difficult to predict, but it is the job of intelligence to discover and assess genuine risks to the public and the country. Perhaps it is reasonable for masked gangs to block roads and turn up outside newspaper offices, but there is the possibility that intimidatory actions could escalate. The situation at Portsmouth, a day after Dover, was notably more tense, and the RNLI, the lifeboat charity, has stepped up security at south coast sites.
Nick Lowles, from the campaign group Hope Not Hate, said: “One of the ways in which the police were able to swiftly shut down far-right activity during the riots in 2024 [after the Southport attack] was making arrests.
“This time, the police response exposes serious failings in the authorities’ approach” to intimidatory far-right activity, he added. Being caught by surprise in Dover was flat-footed at best.

Oliver, 22, London
Occupation Journalist for ConservativeHome
Voting record Conservative
Amuse bouche Oliver goes to a different park every Sunday to feed the ducks, and he posts where he’s going on Instagram. Others, usually his friends, join him, then they go for a pint
Adrian, 63, West Wycombe
Occupation Retired. Used to work in PR
Voting record Labour or Green. In any general election under first-past-the-post, would vote Labour
Amuse bouche Adrian went coffee-picking in Nicaragua when he was 25 to show solidarity with the Sandinistas. He came away with an understanding of what was going on, and full of hope, which has since been cruelly quashed
For starters
Adrian He was really a nice young guy, a lot younger than I expected.
Oliver He came in wearing shorts. I felt overdressed in chinos. But he was a really friendly guy. We shared a burrata watermelon chaat. Some coconut tofu. Hoisin duck pancakes.
Adrian It was all vegetarian, so it was mock duck. But I don’t know if he knew that.
The big beef
Adrian As far as Oliver is concerned, it’s too easy and too attractive to claim benefits. I think the welfare budget has to be determined by the need that’s there. We shouldn’t do anything that stigmatises or penalises people who need support.
Oliver If the welfare bill keeps going up, no amount of tax is going to be enough. He said, obviously there’s people that need it. And I said, yeah of course, but particularly with young people, it’s been open to exploitation. The number of graduate claimants has gone up massively since Covid. We need to make it easier for businesses to employ people. Current legislation, employer national insurance rises, are making it harder.
Adrian You have all this idealism when you’re young, and I couldn’t quite work out what that was for Oliver. He seemed very politically minded, but in a very strategic, pragmatic way. Everything was determined by what might get the Conservative party elected. Without really any ideas or even an ideology, to be honest.
Oliver I’m a Tory. I believe in fiscal conservatism. The culture war, I don’t really care about that. I think people should be able to live freely.
Sharing plate
Adrian We agreed we needed more housing stock. He thought we needed less regulation, whereas I thought there was a sticking point in terms of developers land-banking and choosing not to build houses, and wanting to build them in inappropriate areas, so you get out-of-town developments where people have to drive everywhere.
Oliver I said we needed to relax the planning system. I mentioned a specific niche recommendation: every window needs to be cleanable by 95% of elderly ladies. He said we need more regulation, the free market has failed. He thinks all new housing developments should have an inbuilt windfarm or energy source. I said that’s going to make it even harder to build houses. He thinks we need to be thinking of the future. I said we’ve got a shortage now – we should worry about the rest later.
For afters
Adrian There’s a clear case for accelerating change, cleaner energy, more electric vehicles, more heat pumps, a working home insulation programme. He challenged that in terms of who would pay for it, whether that would be passed on to consumers and whether people could afford that. My point was that you make polluters pay, to disincentivise pollution.
Oliver We’re both in favour of moving towards an economy that’s more supportive of net zero. We agree that there are job opportunities there. At the end of the day, net zero is an arbitrary target. There’s no real meaning in it. Kemi Badenoch doesn’t deny that climate change exists. She just wants to rethink how to tackle it in a practical way, rather than pursuing a policy blindly, without thinking about the possible consequences on jobs and the economy.
Takeaways
Adrian He’s clearly got the ambition, but maybe he will find a different way to channel it. I don’t know. It was a really nice evening and he’s a nice young man.
Oliver He was this really nice guy. By the end of the meal we agreed on quite a lot – we just want politics to be better and the country to be less divided. It was really wholesome.

‘The show choir definitely helped me’: the dos and don’ts of joining student societies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:00:02 UTC
20:00:02 KST

Clubs and societies are a huge part of student life, though many miss out on them. According to a recent survey by Savanta, 67% of students, particularly those who live at home while studying at university, did not take part in societies, clubs or social activities at least once during term.
But if you ask the students and graduates who did benefit from extracurricular activities, they’ll tell you they are well worth the trip. Here are their dos and don’ts.
What to do
Sign up to more than just one. “You’ll probably end up joining more societies than you might be able to keep up throughout your time at university and that’s totally normal,” says Dell*, 25, a graduate of Japanese from Oxford University. “I definitely recommend joining at least two, because it is such a great way to meet people. It can be quite a great escape from when you’re feeling stressed about university work or other situations.”
Izzy Clark, 20, an anthropology student at the University of Aberdeen, agrees. “Join maybe three or four and then decide whether or not you like them, because it’s harder to join the societies midway through the semester after they’ve settled into a routine,” she says. “I had no idea whether or not I would enjoy joining the show choir, as I wasn’t a particularly confident person, but I found that it definitely helped me.”
Remember, everyone is in the same boat, says Isabella*, 26, a film-making graduate from the University of Sussex. “I think just realising that can help when you’re going around the freshers’ fair,” she says. “The people running the socs want people to join, so I think it’s good to just go up to their desk and say you’ll join.”
Put societies on your CV. Even activities that aren’t directly related to your chosen field can end up making the difference in a future job search, says Alex Frost, 24, a history graduate from the University of Edinburgh. Frost says his experience on the committee of his orchestra was more useful in his current career working at a prison than anything he learned on his degree course. He learned “a lot of skills in how to interact with people and leading projects,” he says. “For example we had someone who needed financial support to buy an instrument and we dealt with that. We also organised a tour to the Lake District. And that’s the sort of stuff that you have to do in a real job. You have to get out of your comfort zone.”
Isabella’s time as social secretary of her cheerleading squad gave her leadership and organisation skills, she adds. “I became social sec around the time when people realised you could make a career out of social media – and it was really helpful for me to put on my CV.”
Ask for taster sessions first to cut costs. Radhika*, 22, a medicine student at Queen’s University Belfast, advises freshers to first ask for taster sessions before joining any clubs. “Asking if they’ve got any free taster events allows you to see if you’d like to join that one and potentially commit to membership. It just means you’re saving money, especially considering how expensive everything is nowadays.”
And try meeting other members online first, says Martha Page, 23, who graduated from the Lancaster University: “My main advice is to join WhatsApp group chats and connect with people online first.” Page, who is blind and suffers from anxiety, says this helped “take the pressure out” for her when joining a new group felt daunting. “Before the session, that can open some doors so I would advise anyone to do that first.”
What not to do
Don’t ignore sport just because you’re not an athlete, Isabella advises. “As a thoroughly unsporty 18-year-old, I somehow settled on one of the two cheerleading groups at my university,” she says. “I was as coordinated as a newborn foal. We were not a competitive cheer club, and we didn’t have a coach, but we had big sparkly bows and each other.”
Don’t feel like you have to drink the whole time. “I definitely think a lot of student culture revolves around drinking,” says Dell, looking back on her slightly underwhelming time at a Marxist society. “Regardless of whether it’s a structured society or not. But I think the less structured societies are more susceptible to just becoming excuses to get really drunk together.”
But whatever you do, don’t go without trying any societies at all. As Isabella says: “My only bad experience is I wish I had done even more.”
*Surnames withheld on request

‘Spraying should be the last option’: how farmers are exploring alternatives to pesticides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

For two decades, Phyllis Nduva, 72, has grown mangoes and citrus in Wote, a town in Kenya’s eastern Makueni County. In the beginning, she only had to worry about ordinary fruit flies. She handled them simply, buying chemical pesticides and spraying her trees whenever they appeared.
But then, in 2014, the false codling moth turned up on her farm. The small brown creature had been causing havoc in South Africa for years, and in 2007 it was spotted in Kenya.
Research into how to deal with the moth was continuing, but no one Nduva knew had information about how to stop it from spreading across her 8-hectare (20-acre) orchard.
“We tried looking for answers, but we couldn’t get [any],” she said. “So we continued using readily available pesticides, but they were not effective.”
Driven by desperation, she sprayed her trees frequently but in 2016 lost more than 60% of her harvest to the pest. That was when she began to investigate the alternatives and became interested in integrated pest management (IPM), where farmers reduce their pesticide use and instead combine approaches including traps, natural predators, field sanitation and selective pesticide use.
IPM was developed in response to steadily increasing pesticide use and became internationally recognised in the 1960s and 1970s after concerns grew about pesticide resistance, environmental pollution, health risks to farmers and consumers and destruction of beneficial insects such as bees and natural predators.
A review by the British government in 2020 found that IPM could be effective at reducing pesticide use while controlling pests and diseases. It was complex, but it reduced costs for farmers and was beneficial for biodiversity.
Willing to try anything, Nduva started small by placing fruit fly traps around her farm. It helped, but her orchard was already heavily infested. To fight back properly, she deployed a full arsenal of IPM techniques, including nocturnal solar traps and augmentorium bags, used to break pest breeding cycles by collecting the infected fruits and sealing them away so the pests die off, reducing future infestation.
“The shift from chemical pesticides to IPM was not just an agricultural decision; it was a moral one,” Nduva said. “I realised that what I was doing was harming the environment, exposing my family and consumers to chemicals and contributing to climate change.
“Before, we would just leave the damaged fruits on the farm. This caused the pests to continue multiplying. Now we are controlling pests in a way that protects both the crop and the environment.”
Pesticide use in Kenya has risen steadily over the past few decades: pesticide imports surged from 6,400 tonnes in 2015 to more than 15,600 tonnes in 2019, with farmers now spending an estimated $70m (£52m) annually.
A 2026 study in the Journal of Environmental Management found that climate breakdown was increasing pest pressure on crops, driving up pesticide use among smallholders.
Roughly 63% of these are classified as highly hazardous and 44% contain active ingredients banned in the EU. The ecological toll is severe: a 2025 study detected 56 different pesticides in water systems around Kenya’s Lake Naivasha, while a Nature Sustainability study in 2024 linked rising pyrethroid and neonicotinoid use to widespread declines in the wild bee population.
The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization said it reflected a global trend. In an analytical brief on pesticide use and trade, it said: “Total pesticides use in agriculture in 2024 was 3.92m tonnes of active ingredients, a 5% increase from 2023, an 18% increase in a decade and more than a doubling since 1990.”
But Nduva and other IPM adopters have experienced ecological and economic recovery. Nduva’s harvest losses have dropped to under 20% and pollinators have returned to her farm, boosting fruit quality. Without the mandatory chemical withdrawal periods, she can harvest and sell her fruit the moment a buyer is ready.
Her organic approach commands a premium. A kilogram of her fruit fetches 400 shillings (£2.30) in the market, while pesticide-treated fruits sell for 50 shillings. Today most of her harvest is bought by off-takers for export.
“This gives us more flexibility, improves marketability and ensures that our fruits are safe and healthy for consumers,” she said.
Other horticulture farmers in east African countries, particularly in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania, have been turning to IPM as export markets tighten their rules on pesticide residues. The method is supported by the government in China and is being adopted by farmers in Brazil and India.
In Kenya, Nduva trains other farmers: 600 in Makueni County alone have adopted IPM, although according to Josephine Makumbi, the Wote/Nziu ward agricultural officer, its use across the area remains uneven. About three in every 10 farmers in her ward have adopted IPM practices.
Cost remains a barrier. An augmentorium bag, for instance, costs about 6,000 shillings, while fruit fly traps are approximately 350 shillings, and IPM requires at least four an acre. For many smallholders such upfront investments are difficult to afford, but the county is now giving out some of the tools for free.
Kelvin Musyoki, 29, a plant doctor trained by the Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International, the shift towards low-chemical farming is not only helping to fight pests naturally but is also addressing a growing concern: food safety.
“It’s not every time you see a pest that you spray,” Musyoki said. “There are biological ways, there are cultural practices. Spraying should be the last option.”

Three-way negotiations between Russia, Ukraine and the United States aimed at ending the war in Ukraine could take place as early as October, the Kremlin said on Sunday, according to Russian state media.

The comments come as Washington seeks to revive stalled diplomatic efforts to end the more than four-year conflict, with US negotiators travelling to Kiev and Moscow and President Donald Trump holding phone talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Zelenskyy offers December meeting with Putin
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that he would be willing to meet Putin at the G20 summit in Miami in December to discuss ending the war.
Peskov rejected the proposal, calling such a meeting “impossible” and reiterating Moscow’s position that any direct meeting between the two leaders should take place in the Russian capital.
Putin has repeatedly rejected calls for a face-to-face meeting with Zelenskyy as part of efforts to end the conflict.
Meanwhile, Moscow and Kiev have intensified long-range strikes against each other in recent months, contributing to the highest civilian death toll since the early stages of the war.
The conflict has killed thousands of people and severely damaged both countries’ economies, while diplomatic efforts have so far failed to bridge major differences over territory and the terms of a potential peace agreement.

Some Dutch people are about to be more equal than others
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:56:53 UTC
19:56:53 KST

Some Dutch people are about to be more equal than others
Robin Pascoe
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Earlier this month the SNBN, a foundation which lobbies for better rights for Dutch nationals who live abroad, held its annual campaign day in The Hague. The event included a panel discussion about legislation which would allow Dutch expats to retain their Dutch nationality if they adopted a second one – and which would also clear the way for more foreigners who become Dutch to keep their original passports as well.
The legislation, drawn up by D66 and the former Labour party, PvdA, has been around for almost 10 years but was dusted off again last year. It should have been debated in parliament in June but that was postponed to October. Now the debate has again been delayed – this time to December 7.
Should all the foreign nationals in the Netherlands who pay tax, contribute to society and would like to become Dutch but can’t because of practical considerations be cheering? Is the country really about to align with most of the rest of Europe and allow dual citizenship? Not at all. If the SNBN panel discussion made anything clear, it is that the VVD – part of the current coalition administration – is not in favour of allowing foreigners dual nationality at all.
Security risk
After all, as MP Bente Becker told the panel, they could be foreign agents, using their diaspora to do the work of foreign governments and posing a security risk. “If you come to the Netherlands, you have to really opt for the Netherlands,” she said. “Being a Dutch citizen,” she added, “is something very special.”
Becker made it clear that without change, her party will not support the legislation – which means, once again, it will either go on the back burner, or the part about extending dual nationality rights to foreigners will be cut out. The CDA, she said, thinks the same way.
D66 MP Jan Schoonis was extremely coy when pressed several times about whether he would be prepared to butcher his party’s bill. “We are here to talk about Dutch people abroad and that is what we are going to organise,” he told the audience. “Everything else we will talk about later.” Not exactly a promising answer.
Exceptions to the rule
I was able to get a Dutch passport while keeping my British one in the wake of Brexit because I am married to a Dutchman and have lived here for over 15 years. I am one of the lucky ones, along with the over-65s who have lived here for a long period, and children who were born here and stayed until the age of 18.
In fact, around 50% of the people becoming Dutch do so by using one of these escape clauses – known as the optieregeling. You opt in to become Dutch. The rest, however, have no choice but to go for naturalisatie and give up their original nationality – with all the problems that can entail.
Discrimination
Legal experts argue that it would be discriminatory to allow people who are originally Dutch to have more than one passport but not new Dutch nationals, and the Council of State, the government’s highest legal authority, has also said that treating people differently would conflict with the constitution.
But the debate about dual citizenship in the Netherlands is not about the legal situation. It is about the loyalty of immigrant groups. Research from 2017 by Maastricht University indicates that the Dutch themselves are more tolerant of Dutch emigrants taking on a second nationality than of immigrants to the Netherlands becoming Dutch and retaining their original one.
The situation is unlikely to have improved since then, given the further rise of the far right.
Anti-foreigner feelings
What the VVD are saying is that Dutch people who are born in the Netherlands and have Dutch parents can have two nationalities without any problem if they move abroad, but those people wishing to become Dutch need to be regarded with suspicion – they must have an ulterior, and possibly sinister, motive if they want to keep their original passports as well.
It’s indicative of the current anti-foreigner sentiment running through large chunks of Dutch society. And it’s a sad reflection on the Netherlands and its “very special” passports.
Do you want to become Dutch and are you faced with giving up your original nationality, or have you already done so? Or have you decided against such a step? Croatia: 'Monster' fire triggers evacuation on Brac island
September 13, 2026
Nearly 700 people were evacuated amid a wildfire on the Adriatic island of Brac, Croatian media outlets reported on Sunday, following a tense night which saw hundreds of firefighters defending homes and tourist accommodations from the approaching blaze.
The situation was especially dramatic near the small town of Milna on the island's western coast.
"Last night was a disaster. It was simply impossible," Milna Mayor Frane Lozic told Net.hr news outlet. "I would have not believed that [the fire] can wipe out everything in its path so quickly."
The fire was first reported on Thursday, but firefighting efforts were complicated by inaccessible terrain.
Even so, Lozic said that the authorities believed they had the situation in hand by Saturday.
"We thought we got it reined in yesterday, that it is all over, and then it happened: Sea wind starts blowing at 9 p.m. and out of nowhere, there is a monster," he said.
No deaths reported in blaze
Tourist ships joined the rescue efforts overnight, with many tourists spending the night at the beach, waiting to be evacuated.
No deaths were reported due to the blaze. However, one 76-year-old Croatian woman was hospitalized in critical condition, according to Index.hr news portal. The woman is believed to have fallen off a ship during the evacuation process. A 27-year-old man required medical aid for smoke inhalation and was then released.
Authorities estimated some 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) were affected by the fire, according to a report by the AFP news agency.
Officials confirmed some buildings were damaged, but said it was too early for a full damage assessment.
Firefighting planes active on the scene
As of Sunday morning, Croatian authorities said there were no more "open fires" but added teams were still in the field to prevent reignition. Four specialized firefighting planes are also operating in the area.
Two government ministers and the head of Croatia's national firefighting service are set to attend a high-level meeting on Brac this afternoon with local officials and leaders of the local firefighting teams, after which they are expected to provide more information about the blaze.

Cycling in Switzerland twice as dangerous as in Netherlands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:54:00 UTC
19:54:00 KST

Cycling in Switzerland twice as dangerous as in Netherlands
The accident rate in Switzerland is twice as high as in the Netherlands when measured in terms of kilometres cycled, according to a new study.
Between 2019 and 2022, an average of 0.19 cycling accidents were recorded per 100,000 kilometres cycled in Switzerland – compared with 0.09 in the Netherlands, as shown by the analysis published in the specialist journal Journal of Safety Research.
For the study, researchers from the University of Twente in the Netherlands and the federal technology institute ETH Zurich analysed more than 86,000 police-recorded cycling accidents from 2019 to 2022 in Switzerland and the Netherlands.
The findings revealed that locations in Switzerland where cyclists encounter other road users are particularly problematic. For instance, the risk of accidents for cyclists at public transport stops in Switzerland is significantly higher than in the Netherlands, and tram tracks also prove to be accident blackspots. The risk is also significantly higher at junctions in Switzerland.
More
Cycling accidents in Switzerland rise by 50% in ten years
More cycling infrastructure, less risk
The researchers cite differences in infrastructure as a possible explanation for the higher risk of accidents in Switzerland.
According to lead author Georgios Kapousizis, bus and tram stops are a clear example of this. While in Swiss cities bicycles often ride directly past waiting buses or pedestrians, in the Netherlands cycle paths usually run behind the stops, Kapousizis explained to the Swiss News Agency Keystone-SDA. This means they do not get in the way of cars on the road or passengers getting on and off, and vice versa.
To improve road safety for cyclists, Kapousizis suggests that Switzerland could focus on the three problem areas identified in the study: public transport stops, tram tracks and junctions.
“Switzerland and many other countries do not need to reinvent the wheel,” he said. At stops, it could adopt the Dutch model; at junctions, protected cycle lanes and dedicated cycle traffic lights could help. Where tram tracks are concerned, structural solutions are needed to prevent bicycle wheels from getting caught in the rails.
Where physical separation is not possible, Kapousizis recommends lower speed limits. The study shows that on roads with a 50km/h speed limit, the probability of an accident was almost three times higher than on those with a 30km/h limit.

Chinese researchers extend future memory endurance 100-fold in semiconductor advance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:52:17 UTC
19:52:17 KST

Chinese researchers extend future memory endurance 100-fold in semiconductor advance
Restricting nitrogen-vacancy movement in wurtzite ferroelectrics looks to improve the reliability of next-generation storage, scientists find
Chinese researchers have developed a way to make an emerging type of memory chip much more durable, potentially overcoming a critical reliability barrier to its use in high-performance computing and future artificial intelligence systems as the AI boom drives demand for more advanced semiconductors.
The team demonstrated more than 10 billion writing cycles in wurtzite ferroelectrics, a class of materials that can switch between two electric states to store data. The result was roughly 100 times the endurance previously achieved with the same material and could help advance a potential next-generation memory technology, according to an online report published on Saturday by local media outlet Xian Daily.
The breakthrough looks to bring ferroelectric memory closer to practical use in future computing hardware.
The research, led by scientists at Xian-based Xidian University in collaboration with City University of Hong Kong and Fudan University, was published on Thursday in the journal Science.
In recent years, wurtzite ferroelectrics such as aluminium scandium nitride, or AlScN, have gained attention as promising next-generation memory materials because they offer rapid switching speeds and potentially low energy consumption.
Crucially, AlScN is also compatible with existing semiconductor manufacturing processes, potentially streamlining its integration into future memory devices.
However, the material has faced a significant hurdle: deterioration after repeated electrical switching. Existing AlScN devices have typically failed after roughly 100 million writing cycles – far shy of the billions required for commercial application.

The governing right-wing bloc led by Ulf Kristersson is competing against Magdalena Andersson’s center-left opposition, while a victory for the right could bring the far-right "Sweden Democrats" into government for the first time. Reported by Reuters, as UNN reports.
Details
On Sunday, Swedes voted in a tense election that could either bring a far-right party into government for the first time or return the country to the liberalism for which it has long been known. Several opinion polls published this week showed Sweden’s center-left opposition with a slight lead over the governing right-wing bloc ahead of the September 13 parliamentary election. But Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, who had trailed in opinion polls throughout his four years in office, has been catching up in the final weeks of the campaign, while his rival Magdalena Andersson and her Social Democrats have been losing ground
Kristersson said that, if the right-wing bloc wins, he is ready to include the "Sweden Democrats" in the government.
We can unite parties, voters and issues for joint action. That is why we are succeeding
At the same time, government critics believe that its policies restrict civil liberties and increase demands on immigrants to comply with Swedish cultural norms. This also includes incentives and punishments aimed at changing migrants’ behavior.
We have become a harsher society, a quieter society, but also a poorer society, because our growth is well below our potential, and households are seeing their wages buy less and less

Rajasthan SET 2026: Students boycott exam in Jaipur over delayed papers, alleged irregularities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:51:35 UTC
19:51:35 KST

(Representative image): The candidates also alleged that they were asked to either enter the examination hall and remain quiet or leave when they questioned officials about the delay.
Students walked out of a Rajasthan State Eligibility Test (SET-2026) centre in Jaipur on Sunday after alleging that question papers were distributed nearly 30 minutes after the scheduled start, triggering protests and a boycott over what they described as serious exam irregularities.The disruption took place at Pink City Senior Secondary School on Bainar Road, where candidates said the exam was due to begin at 11am. They alleged that the question papers did not reach the centre until around 11.30am. Several candidates then left the centre and protested outside.The candidates also alleged that they were asked to either enter the examination hall and remain quiet or leave when they questioned officials about the delay.Anita Lamba, one of the candidates, questioned whether the same leniency would be extended to students who reached an examination centre even a minute after the gate-closing time."When we questioned the institution, they threatened us, saying that if we wanted to give the exam, we should go inside and sit quietly, or we could leave...This has been happening with children in the past, continues to happen, and will happen in the future," she told reporters.
Candidates claim exam was cancelled
The situation escalated after candidates approached the police and raised their concerns with authorities present at the centre.Lamba said that after discussions with the police, the principal showed the candidates a notice stating that "the exam is being cancelled"."We have accepted the fact that the exam is cancelled," she said.However, there was no official notification confirming cancellation of the examination at the time of reporting.Another candidate, Sania Kaval, alleged that students were repeatedly asked to wait for five or 10 minutes as they waited for the question papers to arrive. When the papers eventually came, candidates were reportedly told that they would be given additional time to compensate for the delay."The invigilator at my centre was an 11th-grade student; she was signing papers as clumsily as a toddler might scribble. We asked why the paper hadn't arrived by 11:00 AM, and they told us it was on the way, asking us to wait for five minutes, then another ten minutes. The paper still didn't arrive, and when it came ten minutes late, they said we would get extra time...we want the cancelled exam to be held again, and second, we want this centre to be cancelled," she told ANI.Candidates said they ultimately agreed to appear for the examination after raising their concerns with the authorities. However, the delay and the manner in which the situation was handled led to a boycott by students at the centre.
Exam irregularities have repeatedly triggered protests
The Jaipur episode comes against a wider backdrop of repeated complaints over the conduct of competitive and government recruitment examinations in India. Delayed papers, question-paper leaks, impersonation, technical failures and allegations of administrative lapses have repeatedly led to cancellations, re-examinations and protests by aspirants.
The Rajasthan Eligibility Examination for Teachers (REET) has previously been hit by question-paper leak allegations and other irregularities, while the state has also seen recruitment examinations disrupted by paper leaks and cheating allegations. The Rajasthan Police constable recruitment examination, for instance, had a paper leak controversy in 2022, leading authorities to cancel the affected paper and order a re-examination.For the SET candidates in Jaipur, the immediate demand is for clarity on whether Sunday's examination will stand or be cancelled. They have also demanded that the Bainar Road centre be removed from future examinations and that the test be conducted again if it is formally cancelled.

China Threatens to Cancel US Summit Over Taiwan Arms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:49:00 UTC
19:49:00 KST

China has warned the US that it will cancel a planned leaders’ summit later this month if Washington approves fresh arms transfers to Taiwan before the meeting takes place, Japanese news agency Kyodo reported.
According to diplomatic sources, Beijing reiterated that Taiwan remains the foremost “red line” in Sino-American relations as preparations continue for Chinese President Xi Jinping to meet US President Donald Trump.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Beijing views the self-governed democratic island of Taiwan as an integral part of its sovereign territory, asserting it is prepared to achieve reunification by military force if necessary.
Friction surrounding the status of Taiwan escalated during a bilateral leaders’ meeting in Beijing in May, when Xi designated Taiwan as the most critical issue in bilateral ties and warned of direct conflict if the matter was mismanaged.
In a subsequent television interview, Trump remarked that arms sales to Taiwan could serve as a “very good bargaining chip” in broader negotiations with China – comments that intensified scrutiny among Asian allies over the durability of Washington’s regional security guarantees.
According to Kyodo, Trump places an emphasis on staging a high-profile summit with Xi ahead of November’s midterm congressional elections, viewing the prospective meeting as an opportunity to project foreign policy successes to domestic voters.
9/11: Geopolitical Legacy 25 Years On
Taiwan Relations Act
US defense transfers to Taipei are governed by the Taiwan Relations Act, enacted by the US Congress in 1979 after Washington severed formal diplomatic recognition of Taipei in favor of Beijing. The statute authorizes the US to supply defense articles and services necessary to enable Taiwan to maintain a sufficient self-defense capacity.
In December, the Trump administration announced an $11 billion arms package for Taiwan – the largest in US history – drawing sharp condemnation from Beijing.
The deal coincided with heightened military exercises by the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) across the Taiwan Strait, stoking international apprehension over a potential cross-strait blockade or invasion that could draw the United States and regional allies into a direct military confrontation.
The dispute over weaponry also intersects with regional maritime maneuvers.
In early June, Beijing launched a targeted maritime law enforcement and traffic control operation in Pacific waters directly east of Taiwan, aiming to project administrative jurisdiction and display an operational capacity to monitor transit routes along the island’s eastern flank.
Concurrently, Taiwan’s legislature advanced a $25 billion defense appropriation bill dedicated to procuring advanced US-made deep-strike systems and loitering munitions, while Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te reiterated that foreign powers cannot determine the island’s democratic future.
Beyond cross-strait security, bilateral negotiations between Washington and Beijing are being directed by the US Department of the Treasury and the Department of Commerce to assemble a broader diplomatic package.
The two leaders are expected to review a range of economic arrangements, including a proposed agreement to lower reciprocal tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods, as well as a preliminary framework agreement governing artificial intelligence safety standards.
The summit agenda may also address Beijing’s posture regarding Tehran. China remains one of Iran’s vital economic and commercial partners amid broader hostilities in the Middle East.
According to a source cited by Kyodo, Beijing has maintained a constructive posture on the matter and has not sought to disrupt dialogue with Washington.

British fintech company Revolut confirmed that sensitive customer information was disclosed to an unauthorized third party after it received fraudulent requests sent from a legitimate government agency email domain, a spokesperson for the company told Reuters.
The company is in the final stages of talks with the Bank of Israel to obtain a license to operate in the country.
"Upon detection, we immediately blocked the address and alerted the relevant government agency as well as enforcement agencies, data protection, and financial regulators," Revolut's spokesperson said without disclosing the exact number of individuals affected by the breach, adding that "Revolut systems and customer funds are unaffected."
The compromised data included customers' birth dates, postal and email addresses, and phone numbers, as well as copies of their identity documents, including passports and driver's licenses, according to a TechCrunch report.
After a lengthy period of negotiations and delays stemming from the war and other regulatory hurdles, Revolut is about to obtain a license to operate in Israel as a "light" bank and offer Israeli customers a broader range of financial services, including accepting deposits and providing credit.
About a year and a half ago, Revolut reached an agreement with Uri Natan, the former CEO of Leumi's digital banking arm, Pepper, to appoint him CEO of its Israeli operations.
Revolut is planning for a potential public listing and aiming for a valuation of up to $200 billion. It is one of the most successful European fintech companies, with no physical bank branches.
This is not the first time Revolut has been breached. Three years ago, criminal organizations exploited a flaw in the fintech giant's payment systems to steal more than $20 million from the company.
In that case, the thieves exploited discrepancies between Revolut's U.S. and European systems, causing some transactions to be declined and then mistakenly refunded.

Interview: BRICS cooperation creates new opportunities for Global South, says South African scholar
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:47:39 CST
19:47:39 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Deepening practical cooperation within BRICS is creating new opportunities for the Global South to strengthen economic resilience and advance sustainable development, a South African scholar has said.
"BRICS has become an important source of global economic dynamism, particularly driven by the scale and growth of its emerging-market economies," Mogomme Alpheus Masoga, deputy vice-chancellor for teaching and learning at the Central University of Technology, Free State, told Xinhua in a recent interview.
Masoga said the significance of BRICS expansion goes beyond its growing membership, with cooperation increasingly extending from traditional trade to infrastructure, digitalization, green energy and technological innovation.
"Deeper intra-BRICS trade, investment, infrastructure financing and payment-system cooperation could diversify markets, strengthen supply-chain resilience and expand development-finance options," he said.
Such cooperation has become increasingly important amid rising protectionism, geopolitical tensions and supply-chain restructuring, Masoga added.
On China's role in the group, Masoga described the country as "an important driver of practical economic cooperation," particularly in emerging fields such as the digital economy and artificial intelligence (AI), saying that China's technological capabilities and experience could support joint research, skills development, digital infrastructure and technological solutions across BRICS countries.
He also noted the launch of the BRICS AI Industry Cooperation Network at the 2025 World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai, saying that China's proposed open-source AI initiative and action plan could help Global South countries develop technologies suited to their own development needs.
For South Africa, Masoga said BRICS cooperation provides opportunities to address infrastructure constraints, expand trade and investment, advance the energy transition and strengthen industrial capacity, as well as support the broader African development agenda.
The group's greatest value to the Global South is "its potential to turn collective economic weight into practical development cooperation," Masoga said. ■

SANAA, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group freed 210 of its members held by government forces after seizing a prison during its rapid advance along the country's Red Sea coast, a Houthi military official told Xinhua on Sunday.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Houthi forces stormed a government-run prison after capturing the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha in southwestern Taiz province on Thursday.
"Before retreating, the mercenary forces gathered all 210 prisoners in a large hall and locked them inside," the Houthi official said, referring to government forces. "Our fighters broke into the facility and freed them."
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV confirmed the arrival of the 210 prisoners in Sanaa on Saturday.
The Yemeni government had not immediately commented on the release. In May, the two sides agreed in UN-sponsored talks in Jordan to exchange about 1,750 detainees -- the largest such deal since the conflict began -- but the agreement has not yet been implemented.
The release came amid a sweeping Houthi offensive launched on Sept. 3 along Yemen's Red Sea coast. The Houthis have captured Mocha and Mayun Island and pushed south toward Lahj province, bringing the fighting closer to Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government.
Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014 when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year in support of the internationally recognized government. ■
