Warning: our democracy won’t survive the death of reading. Read on if you still can | John Harris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:00:05 UTC
18:00:05 KST

Imagine this. Quite by chance, your TikTok feed presents you with footage of the fascists who recently took part in highly organised shows of strength in Dover and Portsmouth (and, on Wednesday, outside the London offices of the Daily Mail, demanding a new house for the mother of their leader, Daniel “Tommo” Thomas). For as long as the images hold your attention, you see and hear flashes of explanation, but then, as usual, you scroll away to someone leaping off a tall building, a fight on the London Underground, or a trick-performing dog.
Hypothetically, TikTok users are able to skip through 260 videos in under 35 minutes. And it’s this distracted, quick-fire way that so many people receive information that may be responsible for a worrying statistic from YouGov last week. Its poll on the Dover and Portsmouth events showed that 53% of people aged 18-24 years old simply didn’t have a point of view on whether the masked demonstrations were “a legitimate way of protesting”. Further, 43% of those of all ages were either unaware of the story, or not following it at all.
Those figures probably highlight one of the most worrying aspects of the times we live in: the decline of reading. Millions of us know what that phenomenon feels like: trying desperately to keep your attention glued to a book or news article with the nagging certainty that you will be tempted back to the more ephemeral attractions offered by your phone. But a background in the pre-digital world helps people not just follow national and global events, but clarify and contextualise them. In this case, at the risk of sounding hopelessly pompous, the fear many of us felt as we watched what happened in both ports was surely full of the perspectives gleaned from years of soaking up books and newspapers – and the sense that history often either repeats itself, or rhymes.
Black-clad – let’s be honest: uniformed – men who want to “reclaim our borders, restore order and send a clear message: Britain belongs to the British”, while claiming to be protecting women and girls: the whole spectacle was pitched halfway between Oswald Mosley’s blackshirts – and, therefore, Hitler and the Nazis – and the Ku Klux Klan, with the seemingly ubiquitous balaclavas lacing everything with a flavour of the Troubles. But if you receive most of your information in the form of a distracting and seemingly infinite jumble of random moving images, what would you know about most of that?
All this crossed my mind thanks to an excellent new book marking what may well be a transformative moment for societies all over the world. The New Dark Ages is the work of the Times columnist James Marriott, and subtitled The End of Reading and the Dawn of a Post-Literate Society. Presumably to accommodate itself to the changes it describes, it is short: 208 pages. But it is also full of insight and urgency.
In the 20 years since the UK’s National Literacy Trust began looking at children’s and young people’s reading, there has been a 36% fall in the number who say they enjoy reading in their spare time, to its lowest level on record. In 2024, the Guardian reported a survey by the Reading Agency charity, which found that 35% of adults said they were now “lapsed readers”, meaning that they used to regularly read for pleasure, but “rarely or never” did any more.
The Atlantic magazine recently ran an article baldly headlined The End of Reading Is Here, whose author, Rose Horowitch, made plenty of sobering claims. “The literate era will prove to be a brief interlude between the oral and digital ages,” she wrote – and drew on no end of evidence and anecdotes. A program director at the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, for instance, ran focus groups asking high-school students about recreational reading. The conclusion: “most thought of it as an alien practice”. When Marriott first wrote about this, he says, “some professors reported that it was not that the young men and women in their classes were unwilling to read, but that they seemed almost unable to”.
In Britain, more than 320 newspapers closed down between 2009 and 2019, a statistic the book follows with a stark suggestion: “It is increasingly possible to get through life without any exposure to the news at all.” In the wake of the 2016 Brexit referendum, I met people who said they had simply stopped paying attention to current affairs because they were so maddening: now, I wonder if what was really powering this switch-off was technology. The resulting ignorance – a strong word, but it feels justified – is firewalled by phone screens: it feels as if the only stuff that can break through has to be angry, paranoid and visually shocking.
And because of the decline of reading, the people who purvey all the nonsense and poison can be increasingly confident that fewer and fewer people will come across anything halfway critical or analytical. In that sense, the screen age is exemplified by – oh yes – Donald Trump, who, according to an economic adviser in his first term, “won’t read anything – not one-page memos, not the brief policy papers, nothing”. His style of speechmaking is equally non-literate: as Marriott writes, “he doesn’t supply evidence for his ideas. Rather than organising his information analytically via clauses and subclauses in the manner of literate communication, he merely piles up assertions”.
His proposed election bribe of $5,000 is one surreal example, but there are plenty of others. I recently watched an online video of Sean Duffy, the former Fox Business host who is now Trump’s secretary of transportation. He was rejoicing in the administration’s quest to do away with start-stop ignition buttons in cars – mainly, I sensed, because of some weird quasi-Freudian attachment to the phallic(ish) shape of traditional keys. Written down in an attempt at coherent argument, his case would have looked ridiculous. But folksily barked out as Duffy’s “pet peeve”, I could imagine it being warmly greeted by exactly the people it was aimed at. The same, of course, applies to any number of much more malignant Trumpian positions and passions: climate denial, brazen racism towards Somali-Americans, unapologetic Islamophobia and the idea that the US is about to be overrun by criminals and the occupants of other countries’ prisons and mental institutions.
“Mass literacy is a recent phenomenon,” Marriott writes. “So is mass democracy. We simply don’t know whether one can survive without the other.” Meanwhile, on millions of screens, fascist faux-militias, populists funded by crypto tycoons, and other merchants of loathing and absurdity blur into acrobatic skateboarders, arguments on the tube and dogs that do tricks. That strips them of context and thereby normalises their rise – and inch by inch, we move towards a future with echoes of the past that too many people will have failed to understand. And this time, there will be no books to burn, because we will have stopped reading them.
John Harris is a Guardian columnist

====================================================================================================

‘Really helpful’: the AI bootcamps aimed at addressing UK youth unemployment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:00:04 UTC
18:00:04 KST

In a youth centre opposite Preston bus station, the UK government is trying to address two of the greatest challenges facing the national economy: AI and youth unemployment.
The hope is that one will solve – rather than cause – the other. In a room at the recently opened Vault, a community hub in the Lancashire city, an “AI bootcamp” is under way – part of a trial in the north-west to give 16- to 24-year-olds AI training.
The bootcamp tutor is standing in front of a video screen and guiding the five attenders sitting around a long table on laptops through a task designed to emphasise the importance of glitch-free data in AI models.
“Does that make sense?” he asks. The room nods.
Everyone attending these sessions is either a 16- to 24-year-old not in education, employment or training – Neet, for short – or likely to join that bracket.
Youth unemployment is a problem in the UK. Nearly a million young people are Neet – just over one in 10 people in that age group. The advent of AI, either a threat or boon to the job market depending on your perspective, is now another factor to take into consideration when tackling the youth joblessness crisis.
Khudeija Rafique, who is attending the course, sees potential in the new tech. “It would be really helpful with whatever job I would like to go into,” the 18-year-old from Burnley says.
These taxpayer-funded bootcamps are a pilot scheme, open to 70 people who will undergo a three-week programme specially designed for Neets to learn how to build AI tools, understand how businesses use AI, and learn to use the technology responsibly. The retailer JD Sports, food company Heinz and IT firm Agilysys are among the partners offering AI apprenticeships specifically designed for the attenders to join at the end of the course.
There are two types of apprenticeship available: one for aspiring content creators to become AI marketing specialists, another to join IT helpdesks that need AI expertise. If a boot-camp trainee gets an apprenticeship, they will be going to an organisation that wants these skills and has an AI-focused role to fill.
“This is an opportunity to bridge a gap, to improve productivity and bring AI into organisations,” says Lauren Monks, an executive at IN4 Group, the company contracted to run the programme.
Amid general concerns about the availability of entry-level jobs and whether AI is stifling that market, being on top of the technology can be an advantage if you’re seeking your first job.
This is common advice from graduate recruiters, but experts say it can apply to Neets as well, depending on what sector of the economy they are joining.
Remy Simms, 17, is interested in applying for the content creator apprenticeship and says the Preston course has “changed my opinion” on AI. “It shows that you can work with AI and you don’t have to work against it,” he says. “I’ve got a better understanding of it and I know more about how it works.”
Alan Milburn, a former Labour cabinet minister, warned in a recent report that the country was “at risk of a lost generation” without government action on the Neet crisis. Milburn’s prescription goes a lot further than AI bootcamps – he calls for reform of the welfare system, for instance – and his report points out that work programmes by successive governments have failed to answer the problem.
Concerns about AI’s impact on employment have focused on the graduate job market so far, not on school leavers and non-graduates, amid expectations that it will be able to do the “grunt work” associated with junior employees in areas such as banking, consulting and law.
The impact on non-graduate work was unclear, according to Dr Bouke Klein Teeselink, who is researching AI and the future of work at King’s College London.
“We don’t have really good insights into how AI affects the non-graduate market compared to the graduate market,” he says, but suggests this scheme could help answer the puzzle of getting more young people into the labour market.
The key test of the bootcamps and ensuing apprenticeships, Teeselink says, would be the thoroughness of the AI training and whether these newcomers made a real difference to their employers’ productivity. “I hope the policy will be rolled out in a way that allows the government to answer both those questions,” he says.
So will the bootcamps make a difference to Neet numbers? Experts say there is no single cause of the crisis and any comprehensive solution must be multi-faceted.
Chris Goulden, the deputy chief executive of the Youth Futures Organisation, a non-profit that researches how to help young people find employment, says he does not believe AI is a driver of Neet numbers. The country still needs to increase the amount of apprenticeships it offers, and guide children who are not on a pathway to university into vocations, he says.
“Our sense is that AI is not driving the increase in Neets since the [Covid] pandemic,” he says. “It’s more to do with mental health issues and a general slowdown in the economy. But that’s not to be complacent, because AI is doing new things every day and it’s going to affect lots of jobs.”
Goulden says if the “first rung of the ladder” is being taken away by AI, it is logical to give young people a foothold in the technology. “Teaching young people to use AI is part of how we prepare them for the future,” he says.
In Preston, the bootcamp attenders are keen to take the next step.
Asked whether he wants the content creator or the IT helpdesk apprenticeship, 16-year-old Hamid Muhammad-Asif, from Blackburn, says: “I’m happy with both.”

====================================================================================================

Religious Vance seeks to avoid Maga schism as he keeps the faith for 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:00:03 UTC
18:00:03 KST

US vice-president JD Vance has worn his religion on his sleeve since converting to the Catholicism in 2019. He recently published a book, Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith, and memorably met the late Pope Francis at the Vatican on Easter Sunday in 2025, a day before the pontiff died.
But his religious identity could take on new weight as he positions himself for a presidential run in 2028, in which a successful campaign would make him only the third Catholic president in US history. Vance’s winding spiritual path – combined with his avowed evangelical roots – have the potential to stymie him, as he seeks to retain the Christian nationalist voters that have sustained Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement while wooing fellow Catholics.
His presidential ambitions and religious convictions were both on show in a keynote speech to the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday evening, where he invoked scripture and the Apostle Paul in paying homage to the rightwing activist Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated last year.
“We live in the city of man, not the city of God,” Vance said. “But I believe that our founders built this nation on a promise that echoes our creator.”
The address amounted to “the beginning of 2028 Republican primary competition”, according to Larry Jacobs, a political scientist at the University of Minnesota.
“Vance has thrown his hat in the ring,” he said. “One of the dimensions that JD Vance is bringing to the Republican ticket is the white Christian nationalism. He is trying to put together a coalition that will support him, and he wants the white Christian nationalists to be a key part of that.”
One impediment to that, some religious analysts say, is his conversion to Catholicism – something they believe could leave him with an identity crisis that alienates both evangelicals and Catholic voters.
Both ways
Vance expounded on his beliefs and the evangelical influences that shaped his upbringing in a recent interview with Bryce Crawford, a 22-year-old Christian podcaster with 929,000 subscribers on YouTube.
Commentators say his dilemma was crystallized when Crawford asked for his views on “end times”, an event signifying the second coming of Christ that is much discussed in evangelicalism, but much less so in Catholicism.
Vance expressed a long-held fascination with “end times” beliefs – saying that he had owned a John Hagee bible, which emphasizes end times teachings – before subtly trying to sidestep the issue.
He said: “What I’m trying to focus on is doing as much of God’s work as possible right now, and if that leads to the end times, OK. And if that leads to, you know, us building a better world that thrives and survives for a very long time after I’m gone, that’s great too.
“I just think you’ve got to kind of try to have an attitude of the end times may be coming. In fact, they are coming. It’s just a question of whether they’re coming thousands of years down the road, or a few months down the road, and we’ve got a lot of work to do right now. I‘ve got to try to do the work I can right now.”
The response showed Vance trying to “have things both ways”, suggested Robert Jones, president and founder of the Public Religion Research Institute.
“It reminded me of the kind of conversation that young evangelical men would have sitting around in their dorm room at university,” argued Jones, who comes from an evangelical Christian background. “He’s basically saying, ‘I have no stake in the debate.’
“Anyone schooled inside that evangelical debate would find that position either dismissive of theological of deep theological concerns, or deeply uninformed about them.”
After Pope Leo XIV criticized the Trump administration over the Iran war this year, Vance risked upsetting Catholic voters by telling the pontiff to be “careful” if he was “going to opine on matters of theology”.
The exchange followed an earlier difference of opinion with Pope Francis, in February 2025, when Vance invoked the medieval Christian concept of “ordo amoris” – which translates from Latin as order of love – to justify the Trump administration’s hardline policy of detaining and expelling undocumented people.
“You love your family, and then you love your neighbor, and then you love your community, and then you love your fellow citizens in your own country,” he wrote on social media. “And then after that, you can focus and prioritize the rest of the world.”
The late pope wrote an open letter rejecting the idea and citing the parable of the Good Samaritan.
‘A huge threat’
Daniel Hummel, director of the Lumen Center, a Christian research group in Madison, Wisconsin, said Vance’s public statements highlighted potential pitfalls as he tries to win over both evangelicals and Catholics.
“Vance is a recent Catholic convert, and he still talks a lot like an evangelical,” he said.
That, in itself, could be sufficient to antagonize even conservative Catholics, warned Hummel. “There’s a certain way that Catholics, even conservative Catholics, who might actually disagree with the pope – his view on the Iran war, or something – but respect the pope and would never speak ill of whatever he says, versus an evangelical tradition, where … it’s fine to tell Christian leaders to stay in their lane.”
Vance, who has said he drifted from his evangelical upbringing into atheism by the time he joined the US Marines Corps, may face a further barrier to his political ambitions through a lack of clarity around his religious views.
“It’s pretty clear to me that he understands himself to be a Christian, who is being driven into politics in part because of his Christian faith,” said Hummel. “But it’s unclear to me – even as someone who observes him regularly – what exactly is the content of that Christianity.
“It’s unclear sort of where he’s actually drawing his ideas from when it comes to political theology or how he understands the relationship between religion and politics.
“I think that’s a huge threat to him, because he’s with communities that have strong opinions on these things, and talk about them in very certain ways. So there’s a danger he’ll either commit too much to one side, or the other, and then alienate the other side.”
Authenticity
Jacobs, the University of Minnesota political scientist, said Vance – once a fierce critic of Trump, and warned that he could be “America’s Hitler” – could be derailed by less abstract factors than theological differences.
“The challenge with Vance is authenticity,” he said. “The thing with Trump is the guy resonated authenticity with a variety of Americans, even if the reality behind the scenes would suggest otherwise. He came off as someone who meant what he said.
“But JD Vance too often comes off as someone who is playing the political game.”
Jones said Vance’s appeal to Christian values was underpinned by demographic factors that showed self-identified Republicans to be “more than two-thirds white and Christian”. “A majority of them explicitly support this Christian nationalist movement,” he said.
Vance’s interview with Crawford revealed a further “deeply troubling” trait in his religious beliefs, according to Jones, when the vice-president professed to seeing God’s actions in small coincidences.
The vice-president cited the failed assassination attempt against Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. Shots fired by a lone gunman left Trump with a grazed ear, but killed one rallygoer and critically injured two others.
Vance appeared to attribute that to divine providence, noting that Trump had bowed his head slightly to look at a chart on immigration at the instant the bullet passed. If Trump had been killed, he argued, millions of Americans would not have accepted the election result, and the US would have been irreparably split.
Jones said: “A view like that, un-interrogated – especially from a leader as high up as he is – is quite dangerous, because it is always interpreted as the hand of providence when it is something that favors you.
“If Trump had been killed that day, he even says he would not have taken that as the hand of God. He would have taken that as a grand conspiracy. So that tells you right there that the hand of God will only be seen in things that benefit you.”
The Guardian contacted Vance’s office for comment.

A Lithuanian hotelier bringing cold pink soup to Cambodia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Silvija Andruškevič, a graduate of Simono Konarskio Gymnasium, now runs a hotel on Cambodia's Koh Rong island where Lithuania's cold pink soup, šaltibarščiai, is also part of the menu. "Now I can confidently say that this is my place," she says.
Silvija Andruškevič began her travelling adventures while she was still at school. At first, she travelled to neighbouring countries, but later ventured further afield. Eventually, tourism became her profession.
"Later, I became increasingly interested in more distant countries. I also worked in tourism – I was a guide and a resident representative for a tourism company in Poland.
"I had the opportunity to work in Kenya, Bulgaria, the Philippines and Croatia, so these were my longest and most significant trips away from home, as I lived in each of those places for six months," Silvija recalls.
It was during these trips that she developed an increasing affection for Asia. Later, drawing on her experience in information technology and the opportunity to work remotely, she began considering living outside Europe.
"I really enjoyed it and also fell in love with Asia and its culture. I wanted to go and live there for a while one day. Later, I found a job I could do remotely, as I was also working in information technology, so it wasn't difficult for me.
"I travelled to Thailand with some friends. After the trip, they had to return to Lithuania while I was going to stay. But things worked out differently: I was offered a job in Cambodia managing a hotel owned by Polish people. I accepted the offer and left," she says.
The difficult start
Silvija's first few months in Cambodia were nothing like the dream of a tropical holiday. She took on the role of hotel manager and was effectively responsible for everything. The owners lived in Poland, so most of the responsibilities fell to her.
"The beginning in Cambodia was very difficult. I wasn't happy because there was so much work – I sometimes had to work 16 hours a day. The climate was difficult; it was hot. The first six months were very hard. There were many days and nights when I cried.
"I would ask myself: why did I come here? But it was also because the hotel was fairly new and everything had to be put in order and organised, as I was the main manager. I managed the hotel from A to Z," she says.
Over time, however, the situation began to change. Once the hotel had been put in order and the most difficult period was over, Silvija began to see her surroundings in a completely different way. What had initially seemed like a difficult place to live gradually started to look more like a paradise island where she could build her future.
"It's paradise on Earth. It's a beautiful place, there are wonderful people here, and there is also a very large Polish community. I also started looking at it from an investment perspective and realised that it was a good place to build a life of my own," the Vilnius native says.
Her own hotel and a new chapter in life
After a year and a half working at the Polish-owned hotel, Silvija began looking for her own place in business. Initially, she planned to build a hotel of her own. But life offered her another opportunity – to buy an existing hotel run by a well-known figure in the restaurant business.
"I found someone who could replace me because I already knew that I wanted to leave and hand over the management of the hotel to someone else. I started looking around the island and thinking about the opportunities it offered for further personal growth," she says.
At that point, an opportunity arose to buy another property. The hotel belonged to someone involved in the restaurant business. After several years of doing business on the island, he decided to sell the property. Silvija knew the hotel and thought very highly of it, so she decided to buy it.
"I was here and I really love this hotel because it's wonderful, and it also has very good food. I realised that it was a very good opportunity, because the price also seemed much more attractive than in Europe," she says.
Lithuanian šaltibarščiai on the hotel menu
Despite being thousands of kilometres from her native Vilnius, Silvija says she wants to preserve elements of Lithuanian and European traditions. One of these will be the food. At her new hotel, she definitely plans to serve Lithuanian šaltibarščiai, a cold beetroot soup particularly well suited to Cambodia's hot climate.
"I'm changing the menu at my hotel now, and I definitely want to include šaltibarščiai because some dishes are difficult to make here. For example, I could eat cepelinai every day, but I doubt the local cooks would be able to make them. Šaltibarščiai, on the other hand, are perfect for this kind of weather because it's constantly hot here and they are refreshing, so they will definitely be on the menu," she says with a smile.
Business is not the only area in which Silvija has become involved in life on the island. Local people live much more modestly than residents of European cities. Together with others living and working on the island, she helps children and the local school while also trying to create jobs for local people.
"Local people on the island mostly live modestly. There is also a big difference between life in the city and in the provinces. On the other hand, these people don't need much. We try to help local people by providing them with jobs, organising various initiatives and charity drives, and helping the school. Recently, drinking water was brought to the school, and repair work will also be carried out there now," she says.
Other Europeans living on the island are also involved in helping the community. One of Silvija's friends, who is from Poland, set up a Lions International club there and started a project to build a kindergarten.
"It's an international charity organisation, and it has now started a project to build a kindergarten on the island. So we try to help local people in whatever ways we can," Silvija says.
Helping does not always mean large, organised initiatives. Sometimes it starts with a very simple gesture. Silvija recalls an incident she noticed while riding a scooter. She saw children walking along the tarmac without shoes. She knew that their flip-flops often wore out, so she simply went to a shop.
"I know more or less all the children in my small village. Quite often, their flip-flops wear out. Once, while riding my scooter, I noticed that the children were simply walking barefoot on the tarmac, so I quickly went to buy them some flip-flops. But things like that actually happen quite often in everyday life. We buy them a drink or even a chocolate bar, because, like all children, they enjoy those things," she says.
Over the past year, Silvija's business activities in Cambodia have expanded significantly. Alongside running the hotel, she has also become involved in tourism. She was invited to help set up a travel agency and became its director. As she explains, the new business also complements her main venture.
"We now organise trips to Cambodia, mainly from Europe, but we also arrange excursions for local residents. We organise transport to the island as well as stays on the island itself. This is one of the new areas of my business, and it greatly helps my main venture – the hotel – because I can promote my hotel through the agency," Silvija says.
The agency operates through an officially registered company and is overseen by the Ministry of Tourism. Appropriate licences are required to operate such a business. Silvija says her business partner has many years of experience in Cambodia's tourism sector and good contacts within the ministry.
"My business partner has very good contacts at the Ministry of Tourism. He is an adviser to the ministry and ran this company in Cambodia for more than 20 years. During the Covid-19 pandemic, the business slowed down somewhat, so he was looking for partners to revive it," she adds.
As Silvija explains, Cambodia does not have the four seasons familiar to Europeans. The year is broadly divided into the dry and rainy seasons. However, the latter does not necessarily mean endless downpours. Silvija points out that temperatures remain around 30C even during the rainy season, while rainfall is often short-lived.
The term "green season" is increasingly being used instead of "rainy season" to encourage tourists to visit Cambodia at this time of year.
"You don't see the sun, but you can still get a tan through the clouds, so quite a lot of people actually prefer this so-called 'rainy season'. We now call it the 'green season' to change the perception somewhat and make people less afraid of the rain. 'Green season' sounds friendlier," Silvija says.
Attracting more Lithuanians and Poles to Cambodia
Silvija, who is from Vilnius, says she would like to use her connections in Central and Eastern Europe to promote Cambodia in Lithuania and Poland. In her view, both markets still have considerable potential because Cambodia is not as popular a destination there as, for example, Thailand.
At present, the largest groups of foreign tourists are French, British and American. According to Silvija, particularly large numbers of French visitors come to Cambodia, partly because of the country's history.
"There is now a direct flight from Prague to Cambodia, which is also a big development for us. From December to April, during the peak tourist season, there will be flights from Prague, which will also help promote this market. In general, we get a lot of French, British and American visitors. Cambodia was once a French colony, so the French have developed a particular fondness for the country," she explains.
Although travelling from Europe to Cambodia can be expensive, particularly because of the cost of flights, expenses once in the country can be considerably lower. Silvija says the country remains affordable for the average tourist.
"Cambodia is still very attractive in terms of prices; it is quite cheap. For €5-7, you can have a very good meal. You can find a hotel for around €40 a night, depending on the location and region. It is slightly more expensive on the islands, but on the mainland it is genuinely quite cheap, and you can find practically everything at an affordable price," she says.
Although tourism is one of the country's most important economic sectors, it is not the only area in which Cambodia is developing rapidly. Increasing amounts of investment are coming from other Asian countries.
"Tourism is the main sector, but other sectors are also developing very quickly in Cambodia. Japan is now building a seaport – the largest in Cambodia. The Chinese are building roads, while South Koreans are also investing heavily in the beauty industry because Korean aesthetic medicine is quite popular. So all these countries are also actively investing in Cambodia. Various factories and companies are being opened – the country really is developing rapidly," she says.
In her view, the changes taking place in the country will mean Cambodia increasingly comes onto the radar of Europeans.
'This is my place'
For Silvija, promoting Cambodia is not simply a business task. As she admits, after spending many years in the country, she increasingly feels that she has chosen to build her life there. Whenever she returns to Europe, she finds herself comparing life there with her everyday life in Cambodia.
"It's not even a task, but probably my destiny – to show people this country, because it really is wonderful, very friendly and safe," she says.
Although the beginning was full of doubts, Silvija no longer hesitates when asked whether Cambodia has become her home. She has a business there, plans new investments and helps the local community. She has also brought her brother Jokūbas to live with her.
"Now I can confidently say that this is my place. Considering all the plans for the hotels, I will probably have to spend the next 15 years in Cambodia," Silvija says.

Trump envoy names key obstacle to Ukraine peace

Trump envoy names key obstacle to Ukraine peace
The territorial dispute between Moscow and Kiev remains the main obstacle to ending the Ukraine conflict, Jared Kushner, US special envoy and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, has said. His comments came after he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Moscow and Kiev for high-level talks on ending hostilities.
Speaking via video link at the annual YES 2026 conference in Kiev on Friday, Kushner said that Moscow “wants to discuss a way to resolve” the conflict, but “the hardest issue is still territory,” partly because the question is to a degree dictated by a battlefield situation that remains highly dynamic.
“Seeing the advancement in the technology and the way that the battlefield has happened is, I think, beyond the expectation of both sides. And I think one thing I’ve learned in politics is [that] any expert you talk to will give you a ton of ideas, but nobody has any idea what’s actually going to happen,” Kushner said.
Despite this hurdle, Kushner still sounded optimistic about the overall progress. During earlier trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, he said, US, Russian and Ukrainian representatives “completed a deconfliction mechanism and a monitoring mechanism,” with the US military involved in the discussions.
Once the territorial question is resolved, Kushner said, that framework could provide “a real mechanism both to enforce it, protect it and oversee it.”
He stressed that much of the rest of a potential deal could fall into place if Moscow and Kiev overcome the territorial dispute. “I think the sides feel good about” the arrangement, he added. “And that’s actually real progress in that regard.”
Kushner and Witkoff travelled to Moscow earlier this month, where they held more than three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin before heading to Kiev.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov described the Moscow meeting as “substantive, constructive and extremely candid,” saying Putin stressed Russia’s battlefield gains and the need to address the conflict’s root causes.
Following the talks, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow hopes trilateral negotiations with Washington and Kiev can resume in the “foreseeable future,” with Ushakov naming Abu Dhabi as Russia’s preferred venue.
Moscow has long insisted that a sustainable settlement is possible only if Kiev recognizes the “new territorial realities,” as well as commits to neutrality, demilitarization and denazification. As Russian forces are making progress on the battlefield, Kiev still clings to less than 15% of the Donetsk People’s Republic.

Nepal flood survivor says rescue efforts must continue
Nepali hydropower worker Sanjay Sah survived in darkness inside a flooded tunnel, drinking muddy water for 10 days while praying for rescue
For 10 days, Nepali hydropower worker Sanjay Sah survived in darkness inside a flooded tunnel, drinking muddy water and losing all sense of time as he desperately prayed for rescue.
When a disaster response team finally pulled him to safety on September 4, Sah’s first question showed how deeply the ordeal had disoriented him.
“When I was rescued I first asked, how many days has it been?” Sah, aged 30, said in an interview, while on his way back home in Saptari district on Sunday.
“He said that it has been 10 days. I thought it had been just a few days.”
Sah’s extraordinary survival was a rare ray of hope after a disaster that killed at least 1,429 people and left more than 5,640 missing, the majority in Nepal.
Family, friends and neighbours celebrated Sah’s return with garlands and a cake, and his home was adorned with balloons and colours.

Niger military government reshuffles army command weeks after deadly mutiny
New chief of staff appointed after failed mutiny tested military rulers’ grip on power.
Niger’s military government has named a new chief of the armed forces as it reshuffled its top military command following a failed mutiny late last month.
A decree read on state television on Friday announced that General Mamane Sani Kiaou, previously the army’s chief of staff, would take over as head of the armed forces, replacing General Moussa Salaou Barmou.

Both men had held senior posts since a July 2023 coup brought a group of army officers – led by General Abdourahamane Tchiani – to power.
No reason was given for Barmou’s removal.
General Abdourahmane Abou Zataka has been promoted to succeed Kiaou as army chief of staff, according to the same decree.
Regional broadcaster RFI reported that General Ismael K Sidi Omar has also been named the new second-in-command of the general staff. Sidi Omar previously commanded Base 101, RFI reported, the airport base at the centre of the mutiny, and remained loyal to Tchiani throughout the crisis.
The mutiny that began on August 28 lasted almost 24 hours, drawing in fighting at the presidential palace, Niamey’s international airport and a nearby military base.
Mostly young soldiers took fellow servicemen hostage and opened fire on several sensitive sites, according to Niger’s Ministry of Defence.
Military government forces needed support from Russia’s Africa Corps, a state-backed force that has replaced the mercenary group Wagner in several African countries, which stepped in with ground and air support.
Dozens of mutineers were killed or arrested, along with three members of the presidential guard, though the government has not disclosed an overall death toll or said what charges detained soldiers might face.
Analysts and diplomats told The Associated Press news agency that the mutineers appeared driven by anger over worsening attacks by armed groups and poor conditions within the military.
Kiaou is a field commander who has led operations against armed groups in Niger’s western Tillaberi region and the southeastern Diffa region, and helped negotiate the withdrawal of French and United States troops after the coup.
State media reported he recently completed a tour of the country’s main garrisons intended to restore unity among the ranks.
Tchiani’s government seized power in July 2023 from elected President Mohamed Bazoum, who remains in detention, arguing the civilian government had failed to contain armed groups and violence.
Since then, Niger has cut military ties with France and the US and drawn closer to Russia, even as the security situation has continued to deteriorate.
Niger has accused France of being behind last month’s mutiny, an allegation the French government dismissed as “pure fantasy”.

Swedes vote in tight election that could bring far-right into government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
08:41:21 UTC
17:41:21 KST

Swedes began voting on Sunday in a closely contested general election that could see the far-right Sweden Democrats enter government for the first time or the left-wing opposition return to power.
Opposition leader Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats was among the first to cast her ballot after polling stations opened at 8 a.m. local time.
The 59-year-old former prime minister voted with her husband at a school in her home municipality of Nacka, south of Stockholm.
Polls had long given the four-party left-wing bloc a comfortable lead over conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s four-party alliance, which includes the Sweden Democrats. But the gap narrowed to a virtual dead heat in the final days of the campaign.
“It is now up to the Swedish people to decide which direction our country should take,” Andersson told reporters after voting, warning that the election could produce a government dominated by the Sweden Democrats.
Far-right seeks historic government role
Kristersson’s government has relied on Sweden Democrats support since 2022, giving the far-right party significant influence over immigration and crime policy.
The party, led by Jimmie Akesson, has roots in the neo-Nazi movement but has moved into the political mainstream over the past two decades. Kristersson has pledged to offer the party cabinet posts if the right-wing alliance wins.
Kristersson has highlighted falling levels of deadly shootings and bombings linked to organized crime, as well as record-low asylum applications, while promising to improve everyday life for Swedes.
“We want to use our new and far better preconditions to improve the lives of ordinary people ... to make Sweden great again,” he said before the vote.
Welfare, crime and the cost of living
Andersson’s Social Democrats, Sweden’s largest party, have campaigned on strengthening the welfare state and helping households cope with rising living costs.
Akesson, meanwhile, expressed confidence in victory at the party’s final rally in Stockholm on Saturday, telling supporters: “We’ve already won!”
Around 8 million people are eligible to vote in the election, with turnout in Sweden regularly exceeding 80 percent. About half of voters have already cast ballots in advance.
Polling stations close at 8 p.m. local time, with exit polls expected shortly afterward and reliable results several hours later.
A right-wing victory could make government formation relatively straightforward. If the left wins a majority, however, negotiations could prove more difficult because of ideological divisions among the four parties.

====================================================================================================

World faces information warfare without rules — GFCN chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
08:40:37 UTC
17:40:37 KST

MOSCOW, September 13. /TASS/. Information warfare is being waged without rules, making basic fact-checking skills essential to personal safety, Vladimir Tabak, president of the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN), told TASS ahead of the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum.
Conventional warfare is governed by established rules, he noted, and violations are referred to "a regulatory body that considers sanctions or other consequences." Information warfare has no comparable framework, he said. "Is inducing a teenager to commit murder or arson as part of information warfare equivalent to using cluster munitions in an armed conflict?" Tabak asked. "I believe it is. That goes beyond information confrontation as I understand it."
"Even when we are talking about ourselves and our opponents in this information war, there must be certain rules. Unfortunately, those rules have yet to be defined," he said. "Every adult should have at least basic fact-checking skills to protect themselves in everyday life."
Global rules: difficult but necessary
Tabak described agreement on global rules for information warfare as a difficult but necessary step.
"We understand the geopolitical situation, particularly if we were to propose them ourselves. Nevertheless, I believe these rules must be established. That is the next step," he said.
Fact-checking is no longer "a purely journalistic discipline," he added. Professional skills are also needed by "ordinary people working for private companies or the state, or independently as investigators or in related fields."
Journalism’s changing role
Despite its growing popularity, fact-checking has yet to become firmly embedded in journalism, Tabak said.
"For all the interest and hype surrounding fact-checking, it has not yet become a fundamental part of journalism," he said.
"We must also recognize how much journalism has changed. As a graduate of Moscow State University’s journalism faculty, I can say that the profession today is entirely different from what it was even 15 years ago. Many major publications are now wondering how to survive: today’s media consumption habits and the revenue models they generate seem to leave little room for news outlets of their scale," Tabak said. "The question, then, is not simply how fact-checking will fit into journalism, but what will become of journalism itself in the coming years."
GFCN
The Global Fact-Checking Network brings together experts and fact-checking organizations worldwide. Founded by the TASS news agency, the nonprofit organization Dialogue Regions and the New Media Workshop, the association works to combat disinformation. More than 125 journalists from 55 countries already collaborate with GFCN on fact-checking.
The international Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum will take place on September 22 at the Russia National Center in Moscow. TASS is the event’s strategic partner.

Voting under way in Sweden election that could see far right in government
The far-right Sweden Democrats party could enter government for the first time if right-wing bloc wins.
Voters in Sweden are heading to the polls in an extremely close general election that will see either the far right enter government for the first time or the centre-left opposition reclaim power.
Opposition leader Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats was among the first to cast her ballot after polling stations opened at 8:00am (06:00 GMT) on Sunday.

The 59-year-old, who in 2021 became the first woman to serve as Sweden’s prime minister, voted with her husband at a school in her home municipality of Nacka, south of Stockholm.
Pre-election opinion polls have long credited the four parties in her left-wing bloc with a comfortable lead over conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s four-party alliance, which includes the far-right Sweden Democrats.
But the gap narrowed significantly in the final days of the campaign.
“It is now up to the Swedish people to decide which direction our country should take. Should we have a government entirely dominated by the Sweden Democrats? Something that has never happened in Sweden before? Or should we have a government led by me, which will steer Sweden in a new spirit of cooperation?” Andersson told reporters after voting.
Her party has pledged to boost the welfare state and help struggling households cope with the rising cost of living.
Kristersson aims for second term
Outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson is seeking a second four-year term at the helm of the European Union nation.
He has led Sweden since 2022 with a three-party centre-right coalition. It relies on outside support from the Sweden Democrats, an anti-immigration, far-right party that has moved towards the political mainstream, for a parliamentary majority.

Kristersson has promised to focus on improving Swedes’ everyday lives, following his government’s clampdown on organised crime and immigration.
“We want to use our new and far better preconditions to improve the lives of ordinary people … to make Sweden great again,” Kristersson told news agency AFP before the vote.
The Sweden Democrats, a party with neo-Nazi roots, took 20.5 percent of the vote in the 2022 election to become the biggest party on the right.
Kristersson announced in April that his conservative Moderates would allow the party into government if the right has a majority – though he would remain prime minister even if the Sweden Democrats are the stronger party.
Voting stations close at 8:00pm (18:00 GMT) when exit polls are expected to be published, with the first reliable results expected several hours later.
Some eight million people are eligible to vote in the election, in a country of 10.6 million where voter turnout regularly tops 80 percent.

The complex includes Tatneft’s TANECO facility, ranked among Russia’s five largest oil refineries with an annual crude processing capacity exceeding 16 million metric tons, alongside the adjacent TAIF-NK refinery, which processes more than 7 million tons of crude petroleum and gas condensate annually.
The industrial hub also hosts Nizhnekamskneftekhim, a Sibur subsidiary and one of Europe’s largest synthetic rubber and polymer producers, which holds a dominant domestic market share in synthetic rubber and industrial plastics utilized across civilian and defense manufacturing sectors.
Ukraine Tests Automated Drone Warning System for Gas Stations
Fire ignites at Slavyansk-on-Kuban refinery
Concurrently, overnight drone attacks struck the Slavyansk-on-Kuban oil refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar Krai, triggering a blaze at the facility, Astra reported.
Geolocated video footage published by local residents on social media showed a large fire and an orange glow illuminating the night sky above the plant. Regional authorities have not released an official assessment of the structural damage or casualties.
The Slavyansk refinery, operated by Slavyansk ECO, has an annual processing capacity of approximately 4 million tons of crude oil. The facility had previously halted processing operations following Ukrainian drone strikes in late April and June that caused fires in the plant’s atmospheric distillation units.
Subsequently, the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine (HUR) confirmed that operators from the Department of Active Operations and the Department of Unmanned Systems of the Main Intelligence Directorate, as part of a joint deep-strike operation with the Ukrainian Defense Forces, struck the “Slavyansk-ECO” oil refinery in the city of Slov ’yansk-on-Kuban in the Krasnodar Krai.
“As a result of the operation, a key oil refining facility and the company’s tank farm – which fuel the criminal war against Ukraine – were struck,” HUR stated.
Thick smoke and the glow from the major fire at the Russian oil refinery are visible from dozens of kilometers away.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine also reported that units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the “Slavyansky” oil refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban, Krasnodar Krai, and the “Taneco” oil refinery in Nizhnekamsk, Republic of Tatarstan, as well as command posts and storage facilities for the Russian invaders’ attack drones.
Expanding campaign against Russian energy and chemical sectors
The overnight strikes in Tatarstan and Krasnodar Krai follow an intensified campaign by Ukrainian forces against Russian defense manufacturing, fuel distribution networks, and chemical plants over the weekend.
On Saturday, Sept. 12, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Ukrainian forces struck two major chemical industry enterprises in Russia’s Samara and Perm regions, alongside targets in the Black Sea and occupied territories.
In the Samara region, overnight drone strikes on Saturday ignited a blaze at the KuibyshevAzot chemical facility in Tolyatti, which produces roughly 50% of Russia’s caprolactam and 75% of its industrial tire cord.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine subsequently confirmed a direct strike on the nearby Tolyattikauchuk plant, which produces synthetic rubbers, monomers, and high-octane gasoline additives essential for manufacturing solid rocket fuel used in tactical and ballistic missiles.
In the Perm region, long-range drones targeted the Azot plant in Berezniki on Friday, Sept. 11, which manufactures nitric acid and ammonium nitrate – critical industrial precursors for military-grade explosives.
Simultaneously, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) conducted an operation against five military and logistics installations in Taganrog, Rostov region, striking a first-person-view (FPV) drone production workshop, two UAV warehouses, an oil storage tank, a P-18 radar station, and a Pantsir-S2 air defense system.
Ukrainian long-range drones have targeted Russian oil refineries over 70 times since early 2026, significantly reducing domestic fuel output and compelling at least 17 Russian regions to introduce fuel sales rationing.

Mild-mannered Canada shows the world how to take the fight to Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
08:30:08 UTC
17:30:08 KST

Zhou Xiaoming is a senior fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation in Beijing and a former deputy representative of China’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office in Geneva.
For anyone who has spent time living in Canada, the country’s default posture towards its southern neighbour has long felt almost hard-coded: polite, deferential, almost allergic to confrontation.
I saw this first-hand as a visiting scholar in the country in the early 1980s, when I met locals who embodied the national stereotype of moderation in all things. Canadians preferred compromise even when they had a right to push back, treating their far larger ally as a partner to be accommodated, not challenged.
This was not weakness but a deliberate choice rooted in geography, history and a belief that good relations with the United States were essential to Canadian prosperity. This is why Canada’s recent decision to walk away from talks and impose counter-tariffs on American goods landed like a thunderclap.
On August 22, after the US applied 50 per cent tariffs on US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that Canada would impose matching tariffs on American exports of the same scale.
Canada sends nearly three-quarters of its merchandise exports to the United States, it shares a border of nearly 9,000 kilometres with it and it is deeply integrated with its military and security apparatus through the North American Aerospace Defence Command. Its choice to stand up to the US is more than a news story – it is a turning point.
This rebellion of the reasonable carries three profound implications for the global order. For one, Canada’s stance should shatter any lingering illusions among US allies. The Trump administration’s treatment of Canada – including openly suggesting Canada should become the 51st state and reportedly demanding rollbacks of French-language and Quebec cultural protections – shows its nationalist world view respects no friendship, however old or intimate.

'This is the test': All eyes on US Fed to tackle high inflation

AFP Photo
The U.S. Federal Reserve goes into a key rate-setting meeting this week with markets expecting policymakers to pull the trigger on a rate hike to tackle persistently high inflation — and analysts say central bank chief Kevin Warsh's credibility is on the line.
The world's largest economy has been dealing with years of higher-than-target inflation, and prices have surged in the wake of US President Donald Trump's war on Iran, his signature tariff policies and the ongoing AI boom.
The Fed has held rates steady since January, choosing to wait to gauge the effects of energy price shocks and to let the tariffs' effects on prices ripple through the economy.
In recent weeks, however, several Fed policymakers — including Warsh himself — have hinted that if inflation does not show clear signs of slowing, the central bank will have to act by raising interest rates.
On Sept. 11, new data on consumer inflation for August showed it remaining steady at 3.4 percent — no change from the month before, but still well above the Fed's long-term 2 percent target.
Market expectations of a 25-basis-point rate hike on Sept. 16 surged in the wake of the data, with the probability at more than 85 percent according to CME's FedWatch tool.
The Fed last raised rates three years ago, when it was fighting surging inflation in the wake of the pandemic. They currently stand at between 3.5 and 3.75 percent.
Trump has railed against the Fed over interest rates since taking office for his second term, launching unprecedented attacks on the central bank's independence as he demands lower rates to spur economic activity.Warsh was appointed by Trump and analysts say this is his first real test since taking office: Will the Fed raise rates to combat inflation, or hold steady in line with what the White House prefers?
"This is the test. This is what comes with that job, and now he has to decide how to handle it," said David Wessel, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.
"He's either going to completely disappoint the markets, or he runs the risk that he's going to start to anger Donald Trump."
"It's quite likely that the Fed will raise interest rates next week," said Claudia Sahm, chief economist at investment firm New Century Advisors who previously worked at the Fed.
But "it's not a done deal," she cautioned in comments to AFP. "This is a difficult decision for them to make."
Sahm warned such a move was "not a magic wand and it is a costly medicine."
She said the Fed could still hold rates steady rather than administer that medicine, but it would have to explain its decision clearly to markets.
"If they surprise markets and they can't explain why they're surprising markets, then Wednesday afternoon will be pretty messy," she said.
Since taking office, Warsh has changed the way the Fed communicates about its decisions, advocating for less transparency into the process as he thinks it locks policymakers into courses of action that may need to be adjusted.
Investors have had mixed reactions to the cut in what is known as "forward guidance," with analysts saying it has introduced more uncertainty into how financial markets price in inflation and interest rate expectations.
Warsh has advocated in the past for lower interest rates due to expected productivity gains from AI technology, but in recent weeks he has doubled down on the Fed's mandate to bring inflation down.
"There's always been this doubt about whether Kevin Warsh is going to be like his predecessors and do what's right for the economy, even if it's politically inconvenient," said Wessel of Brookings.
"If he raises rates now and Trump goes ballistic, he will have established his credibility as an independent Fed chair for the rest of his term.

The 2026/27 heating season: when Ukrainians can expect heat in their homes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:26:26 EEST
17:26:26 KST

The 2026/27 heating season: when Ukrainians can expect heat in their homes
Kyiv • UNN
Heating will start after three days with an average temperature of up to +8 °C, by decision of the local authorities. Communities are 79.2% ready.
With the first nighttime cold spells and frosts, despite the fact that it is still only the beginning of September on the calendar, Ukrainians have many questions about the new heating season. People want to know when to expect heat in a particular city, who decides when heat supply to buildings begins, and whether the condition of the networks will allow hot water to be supplied to radiators.
When Ukrainian homes will be warm and what needs to be known about the new heating season was выяснено by UNN.
What determines the start of heat supply to buildings
It is worth recalling that in Ukraine there is no single day when heating is switched on simultaneously in all cities. The start of the heating season is tied primarily to the temperature, while the final decision is made by local authorities.
Under the current rules approved by Resolution No. 830 of the Cabinet of Ministers, the decision to begin the heating period is made by local self-government bodies, taking into account the weather and the requirements of technical and sanitary standards. Under these standards, the heating period must begin no later than when the average daily temperature does not exceed +8 °C for three consecutive days. It is important to emphasize that this refers specifically to the average daily temperature, not the thermometer reading in the morning or at night.
The +8 °C standard for three consecutive days also does not mean that heating will automatically be switched on in all regions of Ukraine on the fourth day. In different regions, temperatures fall to this level at different times, and heating networks are in different condition. Some social infrastructure facilities, including hospitals, kindergartens, and schools, may be connected separately based on decisions by communities and requests from institution heads.
How decisions on the start of the heating season are made in cities
The mechanism is decentralized: the city, town, or village authorities determine when the heating period begins in their community, after which heat-supply companies start the equipment and connect consumers. After that, heat does not necessarily appear simultaneously in all buildings in the city. The heat-transfer medium is supplied in stages, while the actual time when heat reaches a particular apartment depends on the operation of the boiler house, the condition of the networks, and the building’s internal system.
Communities began preparing for the 2026/27 heating season in advance. According to Cabinet of Ministers data, as of September 7, the readiness of Ukraine’s housing stock to receive the heat-transfer medium stood at 79.2%. This means that more than 114,000 of the nearly 144,000 planned buildings had already been prepared for winter.
Damage to energy infrastructure caused by Russian attacks remains a separate factor. Thus, Naftogaz has already reported that since the beginning of 2026, Russian forces have carried out 287 attacks on facilities belonging to its group. Therefore, this season, the start of heating depends primarily on a particular community’s ability to maintain heat supply in the event of accidents or power outages.
What to do if your home is cold after heat is supplied
If the heating season has already been declared in the community, but the radiators in an apartment remain cold, the first step is to contact the service provider or building manager and document the problem. The address, the time during which heat was absent, and the temperature in the room should be reported. For residential premises in buildings whose design documentation was approved before October 1, 2005, the standard temperature is +18 °C. For newer housing stock, the relevant state building standards apply.
If the heat-supply service is provided improperly or heat is not supplied to the building at all, the law gives consumers the right to demand an inspection and the preparation of a statement of claim. The State Service of Ukraine on Food Safety and Consumer Protection explains to Ukrainians that a representative of the service provider or building manager must arrive within the period specified in the contract, but no later than one day after the request. Following the inspection, the representative draws up a statement. If the preparation of the statement is refused, or if a representative of the management company fails to arrive at all, residents may prepare the document themselves, with the signatures of the consumer and other residents.
If a confirmed violation is established, the consumer may demand a recalculation of the service charge. At the same time, it is worth remembering that the cause of the low temperature may lie not only in the work of the heat supplier. The thermometer reading in a room is affected by the condition of the building’s internal system, windows, building insulation, and so on.
When to expect heat in apartments in 2026
As of September 11, it is impossible to name an exact nationwide start date for the 2026/27 season. The decisive factors remain the actual temperature conditions in autumn and the security situation in the country, which affects the technical ability to supply heat to apartments.
The Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center forecast an average monthly temperature of 11–18 °C for September, which is close to the climatic norm. Therefore, there are currently no grounds to expect the mass start of heating in September. Consequently, October traditionally remains the reference point for consumers.
However, heating may be needed earlier in the northern, western, and mountainous areas of the country, while in the southern regions the season may shift to a later date. Therefore, Ukrainians should focus more on the actual temperature and announcements by local authorities than on October 15, a date that people have traditionally regarded as the unconditional start of the heating season.
Reminder
At the end of August 2026, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy put into effect a decision of the National Security and Defense Council on the status of implementation of the Comprehensive Plans for Regional Resilience and preparations for the 2026/2027 heating season. The National Security and Defense Council obliged the regions to strengthen infrastructure protection, increase backup power supplies by 20%, and create a two-week fuel reserve.

A new Arab cold war is breaking out in North Africa. Who’s involved – and what are they fighting over?
This week, Algeria made an unexpected announcement that it was severing diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE ambassador was summoned to the Foreign Ministry and given 48 hours to leave. In an official statement, Algerian authorities accused Abu Dhabi of increasingly frequent “provocative and hostile actions,” noting that all “efforts to preserve bilateral ties had been exhausted.” However, no specific incident that could have triggered this decision was cited.
The first practical consequence of the break in diplomatic ties was the closure of Algerian airspace. Starting September 11, the country’s airspace is closed to UAE civil and military aircraft. A temporary exception remains for commercial flights headed to and from Algiers’ Houari Boumediene Airport; they may continue to operate until the end of 2026, when the air services agreement signed in 2013 expires.
For its part, the UAE expressed hope that the rupture of relations will be temporary. Anwar Gargash, an advisor to the president of the UAE, noted (without, however, directly mentioning Algeria) that diplomacy should be based on clear interests rather than “riddles and signals requiring decoding.”
In fact, there is no mystery here. The decision had been in the making for months, and the reasons for the diplomatic rupture are scattered all over the map of North Africa – from Western Sahara to Libya’s Fezzan province and Mali. In these regions, Algeria has increasingly encountered the presence of the UAE, which usually sided with Algeria’s rivals.
From partnership to suspicions
Diplomatic relations between the two Arab nations were established in 1974 and developed for decades without any major crises. In 2015, UAE Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed described Algeria as one of the UAE’s most important partners. A joint commission was active, and dozens of agreements were signed.
In February 2023, the two sides intended to elevate their relationship to the level of a strategic partnership. Non-oil trade turnover stood at approximately $800 million, while UAE investments in Algeria were valued at $600 million. Among the Gulf monarchies, the UAE was Algeria’s largest trading partner. However, economic and political interests increasingly diverged.
Algeria traditionally prioritizes non-interference and the preservation of existing borders. The UAE, meanwhile, combines investments in ports and infrastructure with military cooperation and the support of certain forces. For Abu Dhabi, this is a standard method of converting capital into influence. From Algeria’s perspective, such activity becomes alarming when directed at countries vital for its own security.
The Moroccan issue
Morocco lies at the heart of the conflict. Algeria and Morocco have been at odds for decades over the territory of Western Sahara. Rabat claims the territory as its own, whereas Algiers supports the Polisario Front and the Sahrawi people’s right to self-determination. The land border between the two countries has been closed since 1994, and in 2021, they severed diplomatic relations entirely.
The UAE made a clear choice in this dispute. In November 2020, it became the first Arab state to open a consulate general in Laayoune, a city in the Moroccan-controlled part of Western Sahara. For Rabat, this was a diplomatic victory; for Algiers, it was a clear demonstration of support for its primary regional rival.
That same year, both the UAE and Morocco normalized relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords. Subsequently, cooperation between Morocco and Israel expanded to the military sphere and collaboration between intelligence agencies. From Algeria’s perspective, Morocco, Israel, and the UAE formed a sort of alliance. As their ties deepened, Algeria increasingly spoke of external pressure exerted by the UAE. These suspicions were further fueled by UAE investments in Moroccan infrastructure, including Dakhla port in Western Sahara and Nador port. Local media estimate that UAE investments in Morocco have reached €15 billion. Given the closed border and the conflict in Western Sahara, Algeria viewed these new ports primarily through a geopolitical lens.
A troubling ‘belt’ in the south
A second issue lies to the south of Algeria. For years, Algeria acted as a mediator between the Malian government and the Tuareg movements. However, following a series of coups, its influence waned and relations with Bamako deteriorated. Russia, Türkiye, Morocco, and the UAE have increased their presence in the Sahel. Abu Dhabi cultivated ties with the region’s new authorities, extended loans to Chad, and expanded its presence in Sudan. Algeria views this as the strengthening of Morocco’s closest partner at a time when Algeria’s own relations with its southern neighbors are in crisis.
Libya is a particularly sensitive issue. The UAE has long been a key external backer of Khalifa Haftar, whose forces control the country’s east and much of southern Fezzan. For Algeria, this is not a distant civil war: Fezzan province borders its territory, and the movement of armed groups in the area is perceived as a direct threat. Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune warned that his country would take action should Haftar’s forces approach its borders.
This creates the impression of a troubling ‘belt’ encircling Algeria: Morocco to the west, the unstable Sahel to the south, and UAE-aligned forces in Libya to the east. There may not be a unified plan to “encircle Algeria,” but in foreign policy, a perceived threat is often just as significant as an actual threat.
A red line within the country
Algeria’s most serious grievances against the UAE concern alleged interference in its internal affairs. Media outlets affiliated with the Algerian government have accused the UAE of ties to the Movement for the Self-Determination of Kabylia. This organization, which has been designated a terrorist group by the Algerian authorities, advocates for the independence of the predominantly Berber region.
Operating primarily from abroad, the movement maintains relations with Morocco and Israel and advocates for Kabylia’s independence.
No public evidence of UAE funding of the organization has been presented. However, for the Algerian leadership, any foreign involvement in the Kabylia issue constitutes a red line. In this regard, Western Sahara and Kabylia mirror one another: Algeria supports self-determination for the Sahrawis, while Morocco supports the Kabylia movement; in Algeria’s view, the UAE aligns itself with Morocco on this issue.
Until recently, both sides avoided direct accusations. In 2024, Algeria’s High Security Council referred to “hostile acts by a certain Arab state” without naming the UAE directly. Later, Tebboune stated that Algeria enjoyed good relations with all Gulf monarchies “except one,” which he accused of interference and fueling conflicts in Libya and Mali. Everyone understood which country was implied, yet diplomatic missions continued to operate.
In February 2026, hints gave way to action: Algeria initiated the process of cancelling an air services agreement with the UAE. Already then, a complete rupture in relations seemed inevitable. The latest decision to recall the ambassador merely made the longstanding conflict official.
Algeria no longer confines itself to its customary defensive posture. Following a severe crisis, relations with Mali began to improve; in the summer of 2026, the two nations reinstated their ambassadors and reopened their airspace. Simultaneously, Algeria stepped up activities in Niger, effectively signaling a readiness to deploy the armed forces beyond its borders to safeguard its interests. Consequently, the rift with the UAE can be viewed not only as a reaction to external pressure but also as part of Algeria’s bid to reclaim its role as a leading power in the Sahel.
An air border
The economic impact of the severed ties will be significant but not critical. While the partners are important to one another, they are not indispensable. The political message carries far more weight. Algeria is prepared to pay the price for a decision it deems a matter of national security, whereas the UAE is unlikely to reconsider its partnership with Morocco simply to reconcile with Algeria.
The rivalry between Algeria and Morocco has long ceased to be a dispute between two neighbors; the Gulf monarchies, Israel, and the Sahel states have all been drawn into it. Now, any port, consulate, or loan is evaluated through the prism of influence and the concern of who will benefit from it in North Africa.
Therefore, the closure of airspace is more than just a technical extension of the diplomatic rift. Since it shares no land border with the UAE, Algeria is drawing a political border. A narrow air corridor will remain open between the two countries until the end of the year, but the era when trade could be developed independently of the struggle for influence is already over.

1,200 designers submitted visuals for new euro banknotes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
08:24:00 UTC
17:24:00 KST

1,200 designers submitted visuals for new euro banknotes
With new security features now available, the European Central Bank wanted to redesign euro banknotes, says designer Anne Pikkov. She represented Estonia on the jury that carried out the pre‑selection for the new euro banknote designs.
"Euro banknotes have been in our wallets for more than 20 years. During that time, new security measures have been invented, paper and inks have improved, and values have changed. When the first series was created, Europe was united through architectural styles and heritage. The ECB wanted to review whether these visuals still speak to Europeans today, or whether new unifying elements are needed," Pikkov said.
The ECB set certain criteria. "Two themes were selected: 'European Culture' and 'Birds and Rivers'. Otherwise, designers had free hands. A total of 1,200 designers across Europe submitted proposals."
The jury included not only designers but also psychologists and neuroscientists. "We discussed the size of numerals, color intensity, and how the people depicted should represent specific fields," Pikkov said. "If the previous banknotes showed objects, the new ones will show the European person — their skills and achievements."
The public will also have a say. "Right now the vote is in people's hands. Anyone interested can indicate which directions they prefer. Based on this, the ECB will shape its final decision," she noted.
Five Estonian designers took part in the competition, though none reached the final selection.
For birds, the criterion was that they must be European species that migrate between European countries. "For rivers, designers could depict rapids, puddles, rain — even water crystals."
Although cash use may seem rare in Estonia, half of all transactions in Europe are still made with banknotes. "Digital payments didn't replace anything — they simply added another option," Pikkov said.
Existing banknotes will remain in circulation; the new designs will be added alongside them.
The new visuals can be viewed on European Central Bank 's website.

Alexander De Croo, head of the UN development agency, said this in an interview with the BBC, Ukrinform reports.
According to him, Ukraine is entering the winter period "from a very weak base" due to Russia's "very systematic" targeting of civilian and energy infrastructure.
"This is petrol stations, it's shopping malls, it's business centers, but it's especially energy infrastructure, energy transmission lines, and so on. There is absolutely no justification for that," the UN official said.

"With the temperatures that you would get here [winter temperatures in Ukraine can drop to -20C] that would lead to circumstances which would be really close to humanitarian catastrophe. […] This winter is going to be the toughest one since the war," the UN official said.
He said there was now a "race against the clock" to repair the power network before winter sets in and temperatures plummet. UNDP is helping Ukraine restore damaged infrastructure and develop more resilient and decentralized energy facilities that are less vulnerable to Russian attacks.
De Croo described restoring the energy system amid constant attacks as "almost an impossible task." He stressed that workers are forced to repair facilities during air raid alerts, and they know they are working at a site that is a target, while the threat of strikes means some work has to be suspended.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said earlier that Ukraine was significantly better prepared for Russian attacks this winter than it was a year ago.
