Swedes vote in close general election that could usher far right into government
Swedes are heading to the polls Sunday for a general election that will either bring a far right party into government for the first time or shift the country back towards the liberalism it has long been known for. The centre-left opposition holds a narrow lead over the ruling right-wing bloc but Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's four-party alliance – which includes the far right Sweden Democrats – has been catching up in the final weeks of campaigning.

Polling stations opened across Sweden on Sunday in a close general election that will see either the far right enter government for the first time or the left-wing opposition reclaim power.
Opinion polls have long credited the four parties in the left-wing bloc with a comfortable lead over conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's four-party alliance, which includes the far right Sweden Democrats.
Read more'Swedish society has changed': The rise of the far-right Sweden Democrats
But the gap narrowed to a dead heat in the final days of the campaign.
"We all knew it was going to be a very close election, I've said that all along," Magdalena Andersson, the 59-year-old opposition leader and head of the centre-left Social Democrats, said at a campaign rally in Stockholm on the eve of the vote.
"Now it's up to voters: do they want a government that will be totally dominated by the Sweden Democrats, or do they want a government led by me?" said Andersson, the first woman to serve as prime minister in 2021-2022.
Her party, which governed the Scandinavian country for the better part of the 20th century and remains the biggest party, has pledged to bolster the welfare state and help struggling households cope with rising costs.
Outgoing Prime Minister Kristersson has meanwhile vowed to focus on improving Swedes' everyday lives now that his government's clampdown on organised crime and immigration had achieved its intended results.
An otherwise tranquil country, Sweden has endured over a decade of deadly shootings and bombings by organised crime networks.
The violence has decreased significantly in recent years, and asylum applications are at a record low.
Read moreThousands rally for climate action in Sweden ahead of general election
"We want to use our new and far better preconditions to improve the lives of ordinary people ... to make Sweden great again," Kristersson told AFP, borrowing US President Donald Trump's famous catchphrase.
His three-party minority coalition cut a deal in 2022 with the Sweden Democrats giving them influence over government policy, in particular on immigration and crime, in exchange for their support in parliament.
Far-right leader Jimmie Akesson, who has headed the party for over two decades, is now hoping to enter government, culminating the party's meteoric rise since entering parliament in 2010.
Kristersson has promised the far-right key cabinet posts if the right-wing wins the election, with Akesson widely expected to be given the migration portfolio.
'We've already won!'
Akesson was confident of victory at a final election rally on Saturday in the Swedish capital.
"We've already won!" the 47-year-old said to thunderous applause in the Kungstradgarden Park.
"Sweden is becoming safer, better, and more Swedish," he said, surrounded by blue and yellow campaign posters blaring "Make Sweden Sweden Again".
Agneta Andersson, a 78-year-old pensioner, told AFP she was voting for the far-right.

Forget low-calorie food, Chinese youth turn to tasteless, chewy snacks to lose weight
One individual even admits to chewing on dog chew sticks to help alleviate severe exam anxiety
Young dieters in China are increasingly turning away from low-calorie foods in favour of a new trend: chewy snacks.
On social media, they are sharing their new-found favourites, including beef jerky, frozen buns, and even baby teething biscuits – each characterised by their toughness and chewiness.
Many prefer chewy foods as a way to keep their mouths busy and trick their brains into feeling satisfied, reducing the urge to eat more.
For these dieters, taste is not the top priority; instead, the focus is on the toughness of the snacks. The harder to chew, the more effective they believe it is.
One 37-year-old netizen from Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, using the handle @yigexiangmujingli, has taken to munching on dangshena root thought to bolster the spleen and lung in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) – as her chewy snack of choice.
She shared with the SCMP that while she maintains a workout routine, she struggles with self-control around food. Hence, she seeks chewy snacks that keep her focused at work without adding weight to her body.

'Woman Unknown' wins Golden Lion award at the 83rd Venice Film Festival while 'Naza' wins special jury prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:04:20 UTC
15:04:20 KST

El-Toukhy's drama depicts the life of a young nanny and housekeeper who marries her wealthy and older widower employer, but harbours a shameful secret that threatens to unravel her new life and status in the post-World War II anarchy.
“Woman Unknown,” a drama about Denmark in the aftermath of the Nazi occupation directed by May el-Toukhy, won the prestigious Golden Lion at the 83rd Venice Film Festival on Saturday.
El-Toukhy was the only woman to have solely directed a film in the main competition this year.
Her film centres on a young Marie, played by Mathilde Arcel, whose Best Actress win makes it a rare double victory. Marie is a nanny and housemaid who is about to marry her wealthy employer in the immediate aftermath of the war. But she harbours a secret past intimate relationship with a German soldier that threatens to upend her reputation.
South Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong’s poetic portrait of class and labour, “Possible Love,” won the Silver Lion grand jury prize, the runner-up award. “Possible Love” is Lee’s first film in eight years, following his acclaimed 2018 title “Burning.”
“NAZA,” a harrowing documentary about military strategies employed in the war in Gaza from Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was awarded a special jury prize.
“It is really, really especially important to us that Israelis watch this film,” Abraham said.
The film was added to the main competition late — at the request of the filmmakers — and debuted late in the schedule as well, but its impact was felt: It received a record-breaking standing ovation, lasting some 25 minutes, after its premiere.
Shot on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night in extreme secrecy over three years, “NAZA” features testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders including intelligence officers and soldiers give who insight into the war in Gaza and what they say is the systemic killing of Palestinian civilians.
The jury gave the Silver Lion for directing to Ilya Krzhanovsky for his film “Dau,” a project about the Soviet physicists who built the atomic bomb that has taken over 20 years to make.
Krzhanovsky, who renounced his Russian citizenship in protest of the war in Ukraine, dedicated the prize to Ukrainians, including his mother who was born there.
The Maggie Gyllenhaal-led jury announced the winners in a ceremony on Saturday night, which included a best actor prize for John Malkovich for his performance in the dark CIA comedy “Wild Horse Nine”.
Malkovich was not in attendance at the ceremony, but he sent a video message, explaining that he is shooting in Montreal.
“I am humbled to be chosen for this award which has been given to so many wonderful actors,” Malkovich said.
Martin McDonagh's Wild Horse Nine was also met with a standing ovation, lasting well past 10 minutes. The dark comedy follows two CIA agents travelling to Easter Island shortly before Chile's 1973 military coup.
The film's stars John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell's performances were among the elements that drew attention at the premiere.
McDonagh has previously premiered two films at the festival, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri and The Banshees of Inisherin.
He has previously won screenplay prizes for both films, while Colin Farrell received an acting award for the latter.
“Unknown Woman” star Mathilde Arcel was visibly emotional accepting the best actress award, which she said was very heavy and decided to place on the floor while she spoke.
“This is my first lead role in a movie and my first time at a film festival,” she said. “I’m extremely honoured.”
French director Stéphane Brizé’s won the screenplay prize for his corporate drama “A Good Little Soldier.”
Malou Khebizi was given the Marcello Mastroianni award for emerging actor for her role in Cédric Kahn’s “15/18 (A Place to Heal)” which is set in an adolescent psychiatric ward in a public hospital.

The dinner was accompanied by a performance by an ensemble of more than 100 artistes drawn largely from India and other Brics member countries.India is hosting the Brics Summit on September 12-13, with leaders of the 11 member countries and 10 partner countries, besides representatives of international organisations, attending the event.

Musk, Altman, Hassabis back Amodei’s call to slow pace of AI development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:00:36 UTC
15:00:36 KST

Busra Nur Cakmak
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Some of the most prominent figures in artificial intelligence have backed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call for the industry to slow the pace of frontier AI development and introduce stronger safeguards.
Elon Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis voiced support for Amodei after he published an essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” in which he argued that the AI industry should slow down and outlined a three-part plan for doing so.
“Dario is right,” Musk said in a brief response to Amodei’s post on US social media company X.
Altman also agreed with the proposal, saying pacing the frontier had been a major subject of recent discussions at OpenAI.
“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks,” he said.
Altman particularly endorsed Amodei’s proposal to give independent evaluators extensive access to advanced AI systems.
“Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We’ll have more to share soon,” he added.
Hassabis said Amodei’s essay pointed “towards the right path forward,” while acknowledging that details of the approach still needed to be worked out.
“The direction is correct for meeting this critical moment,” he said.
Hassabis linked Amodei’s proposal to Google DeepMind’s recent call for an industry-wide standards body for frontier AI.
In an essay released Saturday, Amodei expressed concern about whether humans will be able to maintain control over AI models capable of improving themselves. He also pointed to a recent incident involving AI agents that independently carried out cybersecurity attacks as another reason for concern.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”
“AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious. … They include the risk of losing control of AI systems, misuse of AI for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption. A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute,” he added.
Earlier this week, an Anthropic researcher announced that he was leaving the company because of concerns that Anthropic and rival firms were not developing AI systems responsibly.
Jacob Coxon, who had also worked at Anthropic competitor OpenAI, said the companies appeared to be prioritizing competition with one another over ensuring the safety of their AI products.

Beijing pushes AI-assisted chip design as part of self-sufficiency drive

Beijing pushes AI-assisted chip design as part of self-sufficiency drive
Agentic AI is creating a ‘paradigm shift’ in semiconductor design, chairman of domestic EDA leader Empyrean Technology says
Artificial intelligence agents are increasingly taking the wheel in designing China’s next-generation semiconductors, as Beijing and domestic technology firms accelerate efforts to integrate AI into chip design software to bolster national self-sufficiency.
Empyrean Technology, China’s top maker of electronic design automation (EDA) tools, has been accelerating the chip design process by using AI-optimised algorithms and agentic tools, according to company chairman Liu Weiping.
By applying an AI agent to its simulation and layout tools, the company slashed the time needed for a circuit layout task from four weeks to just one week, Liu said.
Agentic AI has brought a “paradigm shift” to chip design, moving away from “humans operating tools” to “humans commanding agents”, Liu said at the 2026 International Integrated Circuit Innovation Expo in Shenzhen on Wednesday.
This shift would also apply to the business model of the industry, which was changing from the traditional software licence model towards a new model based on token consumption with agentic EDA, Liu said.
Empyrean was developing an agentic EDA platform, which the company considered core to its future strategy, that would allow its own agentic tools to work with its partners’ agents, according to Liu.

A taste of home: discovering Sweden’s local food heroes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:00:01 UTC
15:00:01 KST

‘It’s a magical place, and not just because of the hotel.” Standing outside the greenhouses at Högbo Brukshotell, two hours north of Stockholm, Stefan Johansson is talking about far more than hospitality. The former head chef, now responsible for sustainability at Högbo, has spent much of the past decade helping reshape the way this corner of Sweden grows, cooks and thinks about food.
The catalyst was disarmingly simple. Years ago, a journalist asked Johansson why he was cooking the food he was cooking. Like many ambitious Swedish chefs, Stefan trained in Stockholm’s top restaurants, where ingredients from around the world were only a phone call away. The question lingered long after the interview ended.
“Before, I wanted food to be spectacular; I didn’t really care where it came from,” he says. “Then I closed the window of where we source from down to the region. It was the best thing I’ve ever done.” Instead of looking farther afield for inspiration, he began looking closer to home.
Högbo Brukshotell sits in the former Högbo ironworks, a quiet pocket of forest, waterways and historic buildings north of Sandviken. The area’s industrial past is still visible in its old manor houses, smithies and mill buildings, but since the factories fell silent in the mid-19th century, the woods have reclaimed their place. Walking, cycling and cross-country ski trails now lead into the forest, while the old bruk buildings house cafes, workshops and small businesses.
Ingredients that once arrived at Högbo from far away are now grown here. The Made in Högbo project began with lamb, with animal rearing and butchery brought in-house. Vegetable production followed. Now greenhouses sit alongside kitchen gardens, producing ingredients for the restaurant and creating opportunities for people who might otherwise struggle to find work.
Refugees from Myanmar helped establish some of the early growing projects. New arrivals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo have joined the initiative, splitting their time between Swedish language classes and work placements, their influence visible in the rows of papaya, bananas and other plants rarely associated with Sweden. There are plans for an aquaponics system that will combine greenhouse cultivation with tilapia fish farming. In farm buildings there are now also a bakery making sourdough and cakes, a microbrewery run by one of the chefs, a dairy making fresh cheeses, and an excellent deli.
Högbo isn’t the only place asking these questions about food provenance. Over several days travelling through Gästrikland and neighbouring Hälsingland in eastern Sweden, I discover a network of millers, fishers, distillers, cheese makers and chefs connected by a shared idea: that food should reflect the place it comes from.
At Gammelstilla, an old ironworks has become a small whisky distillery. In the village of Gästrike-Hammarby, The Old Mill is now an award-winning restaurant run by Bogdan Ioan Gheorghe and Ellinor Andersson, with a tasting menu that features a roll-call of local producers alongside surprising ingredients such as the invasive species Japanese knotweed.
At Bergmans Fisk, in Norrsundet, low islands scatter across the bay and the Baltic stretches east towards Finland beyond the wooden smokehouses. The business is run by a seventh-generation fishing family whose connection to these waters stretches back more than a century. Inside the smokehouses, salmon hangs in neat rows, a slow process, refined over generations.
But for traditions – and the business – to survive, they have to evolve and diversify, Dennis Bergman explains. In 2020, the family opened a waterfront restaurant overlooking the bay where much of their fish is caught. We enjoy a smorgasbord of smoked salmon and böckling (hot smoked herring) piled on dark rye crispbreads. The family also operates a travelling fish van serving coastal communities and is planning a small hotel: new ventures that will help secure the future of old skills.
Driving north through the deep pine forests and lush fields of Hälsingland, I keep spotting hand-painted signs for potatoes, eggs and strawberries. Outside red-painted farm buildings, honesty boxes sit beside stacks of produce.
At Teve Kvarn, a mill south of Järvsö, I meet Anna Larsson, a seventh-generation miller. She sources grain from roughly a 150km (93-mile) radius, selling seed to farmers and then buying back the grain to ensure high-quality flour production. Only a handful of mills of this type remain in Sweden. Anna points out her newest machine – it was installed in 1930.
Beside the traditional wooden mill, shiny stills are visible in a tall glass building. This is the Tevsjö distillery run by Anna’s husband, Jonas, producing vodka, gin and aquavit using grain from the mill. The distillery runs on hydroelectric power generated from the nearby stream, and has already increased its production capacity more than 10 times on the strength of the products’ popularity – while creating 10 new local jobs.
At nearby Järvsö Lanthandel, I meet chef Tobias Annerhult who runs the general store and restaurant. For Annerhult, local sourcing isn’t just desirable, it’s his entire food philosophy. “I only buy salt, pepper, sugar and oil,” he tells me. “I don’t use stabilisers. Nothing gets thrown away; that feeds the creative process. Our philosophy is to grow through limitations.”
In a climate where vegetables arrive in abundance for only part of the year, preserving is essential. Annerhult pickles, cures and ferments local produce, including meat for charcuterie.
Tonight, we too have to work for our dinner, taking a cooking class that Tobias offers for private group bookings. We have brought produce collected across the region: flour from the centuries-old mill; cheese and potatoes from honesty boxes; fish from a family that has worked the same waters for generations; and vegetables from local greenhouses.
Together, we make fermented pea pancakes with sweet preserved apple and salty local goat’s cheese; bouncy fresh pasta using Anna’s wheat and eggs from Tobias’s chickens, served simply with burrata-style cheese, brown butter and garden herbs; and warm cake with the first of the season’s rhubarb.
It’s a meal that tastes all the better for knowing the stories and people behind it. Combining preserved and fermented ingredients with the season’s freshest produce harks back to traditional approaches to cooking and eating. Today’s chefs are reclaiming that philosophy, and the results are delicious.
It perhaps helps answer the question that changed Stefan’s career all those years ago. Why cook this food, in this place? Because when food truly belongs somewhere, it becomes a way of understanding that place too.
The trip was provided by Visit Sweden. For more information visit gastrikland.se and destinationhalsingland.se. Högbo Brukshotell has doubles from 1,995 Swedish kronor (£155) B&B

====================================================================================================

The AfD won a shock election in Germany. Elon Musk was thrilled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:00:01 UTC
15:00:01 KST

The Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party rattled European politics this week after a convincing victory in a German state election, which placed it only a few seats away from forming the country’s first state-level far right government since the second world war.
Elon Musk was thrilled.
“Gut gemacht!” Musk posted on X a week ago, using the German phrase for “well done” as he congratulated AfD party leader, Alice Weidel. It was one of at least a dozen posts the Tesla and SpaceX CEO made about the AfD following the result.
The AfD reciprocated Musk’s praise, with the party’s Saxony-Anhalt leader, Ulrich Siegmund, thanking the tech mogul for his support. Siegmund, who wants German schools to focus less on responsibility for the second world war and whose top staffers include four former members of a banned neo-Nazi youth group, called Musk a “visionary”.
Musk has become a central figure in the global far-right in recent years, using his support and influence to back anti-immigrant activists, illiberal leaders and nativist parties. Along with a preoccupation with race in the UK, much of that attention has been focused on the AfD, and the major results in the Saxony-Anhalt election, and Musk’s jubilation at their win, have revived scrutiny of his connections to it.
Musk’s ties to the AfD and German far-right predate the Saxony-Anhalt vote and coincide with the billionaire’s own public rightward drift. His views on immigration, politics and race, which he expresses relentlessly on X, have over the years become indistinguishable from many AfD policies. In boosting the AfD and receiving their adulation in return, Musk and the party have developed a symbiotic relationship to spread their far-right views both in Germany and the US.
Boosting the international far right
As Musk became more involved in politics in 2024, backing Donald Trump’s reelection with over $100m of his own money, he formed alliances with several other international far-right leaders who hold anti-immigration views and antipathy for democratic institutions.
Musk has appeared onstage with Argentina’s chainsaw-wielding Javier Milei, presented an award to Italy’s ultraconservative prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, then attacked Italian judges ruling on migrant rights and gave a livestreamed speech at UK anti-Islam activist Tommy Robinson’s rally where Musk claimed immigration was causing “the destruction of Britain”.
Musk also connected with Naomi Seibt, a German climate crisis skeptic and anti-immigration activist who frequently posts on X and was 24 years old at the time. Musk began personally messaging her after seeing her posts, Seibt told reporter Paul Ronzheimer of Axel Springer’s Global Reporters Network, and she promoted the AfD to him in their chats.
In late 2024, Musk wrote an opinion column for the German outlet Die Welt expressing his own support for the AfD. Musk’s op-ed claimed that Germany was on the brink of “economic and cultural collapse” that could only be solved by the AfD, which he called “the last spark of hope” for the country. He also argued that the party wasn’t extreme, giving the example that its leader Weidel has a same-sex partner who is from Sri Lanka.
“Does that sound like Hitler to you?” Musk wrote.
As Musk took a prominent role in the second Trump administration at the beginning of 2025, he used his platform and newfound political power to further boost the AfD. In early January of that year, Musk hosted a livestream for Weidel that researchers found gave her a huge boost on the platform as well as translated to a jump in German-language media coverage.
“Musk did in fact have an agenda-setting effect on traditional media in Germany,” said Jan Rau, a researcher at Research Institute Social Cohesion and Leibniz-Institute for Media Research. “You could very clearly see it. There was a huge spike of attention from traditional media for Weidel in that moment, and a lot of this attention was actually connected with Musk.”
Weeks after hosting the livestream with Weidel, Musk also appeared via livestream at an AfD rally. Only days after causing an uproar for delivering fascist-style salutes at a Trump inauguration rally, Musk told the AfD crowd in Germany that there was “too much focus on past guilt, and we need to move beyond that”. His remarks drew condemnations from Jewish leaders and accusations that he was attempting to normalize the far-right.
The limits of Musk’s influence
Musk’s close proximity to Trump and prominent role in the White House following the 2024 election magnified his political power, as well as fears from foreign governments that he was interfering in their national affairs.
After acquiring Twitter in 2022, Musk made several changes that helped boost the divisive, far-right politics of parties like the AfD. He reinstated previously banned far-right accounts, such as pro-AfD, anti-immigration Austrian activist Martin Sellner – who has taken credit for mainstreaming nativist “remigration” policies – and often promoted international right wing accounts through reposts.
“The changes Musk made to the platform has made it much easier for far-right communication,” Rau said. “That’s helpful for the AfD in many ways.”
But researchers including Rau also argue that the rightwing bubble Musk has created on X has its limits. Only around 5% of Germans use X to find news, according to a 2026 Reuters Institute survey, and many mainstream figures in the country have publicly given up on using the platform. While some of Musk’s backing of the AfD crossed over to mainstream attention, much of it in recent months has been confined to his captive audience on X.
Today, Musk is deeply unpopular in Germany, with a YouGov poll last year finding that only 19% of the country had a favorable view of the multibillionaire. Fewer still, only 13%, viewed his attempts to influence German politics acceptable. Even within the AfD, Musk is not an entirely welcome presence.
“Musk’s boosting, in some quarters, is not particularly helpful,” said Oliver Marsh, an independent researcher formerly at the nonprofit Algorithm Watch. “A lot of the party are traditional German nationalists and don’t really approve of an American billionaire weighing in on German politics”.
While the AfD’s ascendance has more to do with Germany’s domestic politics and social dynamics than it does with Musk, it did not stop him from taking some credit for their success. Musk reposted a claim from a Germany rightwing media commentator that the tech billionaire’s ownership of X had caused a “vibe shift” that led to the AfD’s victory.
Musk defends the ‘far center’ AfD
In the days after the AfD’s election success in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, Musk both celebrated the result and tried to claim that the party was not far-right at all but ideologically moderate. Musk posted that the party, which Germany’s own domestic intelligence agency last year labeled a rightwing extremist group, should be considered “far center”.
Musk also sought to reject American news media’s descriptions of the AfD being far-right, despite the party’s well-documented and extreme views on issues such as immigration, Islam and LGBTQ+ rights. Musk posted multiple replies to the Wall Street Journal and CBS News following the state election, attacking the outlets for using “far right” in their coverage.
“You are lying by calling AfD ‘far-right’,” Musk responded to a CBS News post on X, adding in another post that “‘far right’ is a propaganda term”.
The AfD party platform includes bans on public displays of Islamic beliefs; opposes same-sex marriage and adoption, despite Weidel’s long-term domestic partnership with a woman, which includes children; emphasizes ethnic-German identity and calls for mass deportations. AfD leaders also have received criticism over the years for downplaying the Holocaust and making provocative references to Nazism, with one of the party’s top members convicted in 2024 of using a Nazi paramilitary wing slogan during a rally.
Weidel has meanwhile claimed there is “a holy war against the German population” while calling for “remigration”, a term for mass expulsions once popular in far-right and white nationalist circles that has now been embraced by nativist parties as well as Musk and Donald Trump.
Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz responded to the AfD’s win this week by warning that the party’s true goals amounted to ethnic cleansing, a characterization which the far-right party denounced.
“If what is being advocated here, namely ‘remigration’, were to become reality, it would be nothing other than a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin colour,” Merz said.
Musk once again defended the AfD, reposting a user criticising Merz’s allegation to his more than 241m followers.
Musk’s views, which include a fixation on race and vocal opposition to immigration, have come to closely resemble those of Weidel and the AfD.
“Anyone who opposes remigration is a traitor,” he posted in July.

Tesco alerts police as supermarket becomes latest victim of scam ‘endorsement’ ads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Tesco has alerted City of London police after it became the latest in a string of companies and sports stars, including Barclays bank and Lewis Hamilton, to have its image hijacked in a “scam” by unlicensed casinos advertising via Facebook and Instagram.
The supermarket chain is among several household-name businesses to have been targeted in an apparent effort by casinos that cannot legally operate in Britain to capitalise on their brand recognition.
Their branding has featured in ads and websites, promoted via the US social media company Meta, that gave the false impression that the businesses had launched their own casinos.
Sports stars including Lewis Hamilton and Tyson Fury have also had their faces used without consent, while one offshore casino used a lookalike of the footballer Erling Haaland wearing a Norway shirt.
England’s Jude Bellingham and the Manchester United player Bruno Fernandes have also previously had their images used without consent by rogue gambling firms.
Both the Gambling Commission and the Advertising Standards Authority are aware of the problem, but appear to have had little success in preventing the spread of the ads.
A fake “Tesco casino” was advertised on Facebook and even had its own page on the platform until the Guardian sent questions to the social media site’s owner, Meta.
The ads were linked to a website, which is still accessible in the UK, that claims to be “the official Tesco casino”.
The site boasts that its slot machine games are “laid out as clearly as the aisles at a Tesco Extra” and claims that its casino is “built on the trust of Tesco, a FTSE 100 company with 107 years of UK trading history since 1919”.
However, it does not have a licence to provide gambling services in Great Britain, a legal requirement to operate.
Tesco declined to comment but the supermarket chain referred its concerns to the National Cyber Security Centre and Report Fraud service, run by City of London police. A spokesperson for City of London police said it had received the complaint but had not yet referred it to a police force for investigation “at this time”.
Barclays’ branding has been co-opted in promotional material that features the face of Lewis Hamilton.
In one Facebook advert for “Barclays Slots”, now taken down, an apparently AI-generated woman had her trousers pulled down to expose her buttocks. She then turned round to reveal that she was playing a Barclays casino game on her phone.
Barclays said it “does not endorse or have any involvement” with the material, and took appropriate action to protect customers from misleading use of its intellectual property.
Other ads that featured on Facebook and Instagram promoted fake casinos including Monzo slots, using the online bank’s imagery.
Monzo said this was an “AI-enabled scam where criminals take advantage of our much-loved brand to trick people”, and urged its customers to be alert to such material.
Meta said it had taken down the ads after the Guardian’s inquiries. But the company is understood to believe that advertisers – not its platforms – are responsible for complying with local regulations.
The boxer Tyson Fury responded to the appearance of an online casino bearing his name by filming a video for his Instagram followers, disavowing any involvement.
He said he had turned down “millions” offered by gambling companies in the past, and would never promote the industry. There is no suggestion the fake Tyson Fury casino was advertised on Meta platforms.
One cryptocurrency casino called Rainbet, which claims to be licensed by the Indian ocean island of Anjouan, uses an apparent lookalike of Manchester City and Norway striker Erling Haaland acting as a casino croupier, wearing a Norway top.
The site is not available to users in the UK, but was advertised via Meta.
Legitimate gambling companies, including Coral and Gala Bingo, have also fallen victim to the apparent deliberate impersonation by unlicensed casinos.
Bejay Patel, the managing director of UK and Ireland at Entain, which owns both brands, said any casino masquerading as a licensed operator was “exploiting British consumers and legitimate businesses alike and paying no taxes, while some of the world’s largest technology platforms continue to profit from hosting their adverts”.
He added: “Ofcom needs to take a harder line on the companies facilitating this activity.”
The Gambling Commission has previously criticised Meta’s failure to act on unlicensed casinos, as the regulator struggles to keep a lid on a surge in rogue casinos.
The commission said: “Illegal activity linked to gambling is a threat we take seriously, and using a trusted brand’s identity to funnel people towards unlicensed casino products is a particularly cynical version of it.”
It said it would act to take down unlicensed websites that target UK consumers and would be better able to do so from autumn, when it will get more powers as a result of the crime and policing bill.
The unauthorised use of intellectual property is outside the commission’s remit. The regulator said it was working with the ASA.
Several of the sites analysed by the Guardian claim to be licensed in Curacao, a Caribbean former Dutch colony that is known as a haven for online gambling companies that do not have a licence in big economies such as the UK or US.
That means that any which offer their services to British customers are doing so illegally.
The Tyson Fury-branded casino and Tesco casino appear to be targeting UK consumers, but link to a contact page did not work. In the case of the Tyson Fury casino, it led to a page that simply contained the text: “Silence is golden.”
The Guardian has approached representatives of Haaland and Hamilton for comment.

====================================================================================================

‘Cheap iPhone deal’: warning over scam sites selling latest Apple mobiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Apple has just launched a range of new iPhones, including a foldable handset, just as you decide it is time to replace your own ageing mobile. But you balk at the £1,199 price tag for the cheapest of the new options.
Searching online for a better price with the words “cheap”, “iPhone” and “deal”, you come across a website which offers an iPhone 18 Pro for a couple of hundred pounds less than the Apple site. You pay for the new phone via a bank transfer and wait for it to arrive.
But the website is a fraud - one of hundreds set up in the days before the new Apple phones were announced – and is designed to scam money out of people eager to get their hands on one of the new handsets.
Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo, the company’s first foldable phone, on Wednesday, as well as two new iPhone 18 Pro models.
At the same time, criminals were building up networks of fake sites. Security researchers found a large spike in the number of scam sites registered with “Apple” and “iPhone”, among other keywords, in their domain names.
It is expected that the number will proliferate into the hundreds.
Alexandre François, who investigates scams for the intelligence company WhoisXML API, says the days before and after the announcement of the phones typically see a glut of domain names being registered by criminals. Some are then developed into phishing sites in order to dupe people.
“Some are flagged as dangerous by dozens of security engines, yet they are still absent from the blocklists that browsers and security tools rely on, so for most people nothing stops the page from loading,” he says.
“In each of the last four iPhone launches, domain registrations referencing the new model peaked on ‘keynote day’ – the launch day itself: more than 200 new domains within 24 hours, against zero or one on a normal day.”
What it looks like
The domain names will often include words such as “Apple” and “iPhone 18”. The content of a developed site will look convincingly realistic as fraudsters frequently use AI to mimic genuine retailers.
One site found by François, an iPhone Pro Max, in three different colours, was advertised with claims of an “all-day battery”.
The release of technical specifications following the launch allows fraudsters to build more convincing websites. François says it then “becomes much easier to convince people that what they are looking at is a real iPhone”.
The sites may also claim to offer early access to the devices, as well as cheaper prices. The new iPhone 18 Pro starts at £1,199 officially, while the 18 Pro Max at £1,299, so expect the scam sites to quote prices substantially lower.
As with many scams, fraudsters may give people a deadline to buy – such as a few hours – to encourage them to abandon caution in a bid to land a bargain.
The sites will often only take payment via bank transfer to avoid giving people the protections available when you pay with a debit and credit card.
What to do
Remember what is on sale. So far, the iPhone Duo and the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have been announced – but not the standard iPhone 18. Pages which claim to be selling it now or taking deposits are fakes.
François says Apple does not operate lotteries and does not recruit people to test phones.
Legitimate websites will offer consumers a variety of ways to pay – debit and credit cards among them. Some fraudulent sites will insist payment is made using cryptocurrency, which should act as an immediate red flag.
Apple says its Safari browser has a warning for fraudulent websites that alerts users to phishing or malware sites.
If you find you have given out your financial details, contact your bank and Report Fraud. And then change your passwords.

Mapped: the £150bn megaproject that aims to protect Britain from energy shocks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Britain is embarking on one of the largest overhauls of its electricity grid in generations – a megaproject in which five times more infrastructure will be built by 2030 than was constructed during the previous three decades.
Tens of billions of pounds are being spent on new pylons, subsea cables and converter stations to connect a growing fleet of wind and solar farms and carry clean power to where it is needed.
It comes after successive global shocks – Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, then the Iran war – have exposed the vulnerability of the UK’s energy system to international market volatility and galvanised plans to bolster domestic low-carbon generation.
The cost of electricity in the UK has surged in recent years, far beyond that of comparable countries, largely because expensive gas-fired generation sets the price most of the time.
This volatility has accelerated efforts to transition away from fossil fuels, in the hope homegrown renewables can shield UK households from future shocks.
Yet that green drive is now being limited by Britain’s ageing grid, which, after decades of underinvestment, is often unable to transmit the new energy being generated.
“If we don’t have enough transmission network capacity, we won’t be able to make full use of renewable energy resources. We will then be more dependent on fossil fuels, with greater vulnerability to fossil fuel price shocks and higher CO2 emissions,” said Keith Bell, professor of electronic and electrical engineering at the University of Strathclyde.
Unblocking these bottlenecks will require well over 4,000 miles of new power lines by 2041, alongside significant improvements to cables already in place, Guardian analysis of official recommendations shows.
Much of that expansion will be visible, cutting across the countryside and bringing construction to rural communities along the way. It has prompted protests, with some residents claiming they face an “energy invasion” owing to the scale of the planned infrastructure.
Household energy bills are to rise in the short term to pay for the grid transformation, at a time when politicians are pledging cost-of-living support.
Britain’s National Energy System Operator (Neso) recently estimated that £64bn of investment will be needed for transmission projects by 2030 and a further £89bn beyond that – more than £150bn, which will be largely paid for by surcharges on household bills.
While these investments will eventually help lower costs by reducing reliance on expensive gas generation, on Friday the National Audit Office warned the government that dozens of grid projects risked delay, potentially placing further strain on consumers.
But a failure to build also has costs – as the below visual explainer sets out.
Grid upgrades will be largely paid for through household energy bills, coming on top of electricity prices that have risen sharply after global energy shocks.
The energy regulator Ofgem has announced that the energy bill price cap will rise by 4% from October to its highest level in three years, driven by increases in wholesale gas prices.
On the day of the price cap announcement, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, was challenged about whether “the drive towards net zero” was also costing people more. She replied: “Absolutely not.”
But Fahnbulleh went on to acknowledge that paying for upgrades would be unavoidable, saying: “For a decade and a half, under the last government, we didn’t invest in our energy system, we didn’t invest in the grid, and we’re going to have to deal with that. So for the grid to operate properly, we’ve got to upgrade it.”
Andy Burnham has attempted to reduce energy bills since entering Downing Street, with his first big policy announcement being a cut to VAT on them from 5% to 0%.
In the absence of further government intervention, rising network costs will soon add an extra £130 to a typical household’s energy bills by 2030, according to one forecast.
Ofgem has pointed out that households would still be paying more by 2030 if grid upgrades were not undertaken, due to the cost of curtailing renewables.
“While upgrades will require investment, failing to invest would also increase costs for consumers through higher constraint and balancing payments caused by grid bottlenecks,” a spokesperson said.
Many experts also agree that spending more on grid upgrades now alongside growing the UK’s low-carbon power capacity will lead to lower energy costs in the future.
Neso forecasts that full decarbonisation that meets the UK’s net zero targets could lead to energy spending falling from more than 10% of gross domestic product to less than 5% by 2050, owing to the wider use of cheaper renewables and lower waste.
Spending falls further than in a scenario with far less decarbonisation, in which the UK falls short its legally binding 2050 target, though it is initially higher because of the investment needed to increase renewable capacity.
Some argue there are ways to reduce the sharpness of this investment “hump” through a different approach to grid upgrades.
The Conservatives recently claimed transmission costs could be reduced by focusing on a smaller number of large nuclear and gas plants over many renewable sites, in turn reducing the number of new cables.
Others dispute those findings, pointing out that emissions would be higher – building nuclear sites requires large upfront costs and has proven to be difficult in recent years – and that gas prices are likely to exceed the assumptions used in their analysis.
Neso forecasts full decarbonisation would have a sizable benefit: shielding against energy shocks.
It has modelled the hypothetical impact of a 2022-style energy shock after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on a fully decarbonised energy system in the UK.
The original shock cost an extra 1.8% of GDP – equivalent to tens of billions of pounds. In a full net zero transition scenario it would have been closer to an extra 0.3%, more than six times smaller.
“Our analysis suggests that delivering net zero by 2050 could halve energy-related spending, whilst also providing greater protection from global price spikes in the process,” a Neso spokesperson said.
However, experts say getting to that point will require more than just new cabling projects.
“Transmission is only one piece of the puzzle, though – greater storage, demand flexibility, and potentially green hydrogen production would all help drive down curtailment costs and cut dependence on expensive gas,” said Collett-White.
“A better, not just bigger, grid should be the goal.”
With the geopolitical landscape looking increasingly turbulent, ministers may be convinced that making households pay for a better grid – and the protection it affords – will be worth it in the end.
A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Decades of underinvestment in the grid has left us overexposed to fossil fuel markets and unable to realise the full potential of clean, homegrown energy to lower bills for households.
“That’s why we’re building a decarbonised energy system that can bring down bills for good.”
A spokesperson for National Grid said: “Investment in upgrading the grid is supporting jobs, skills, and supply chains across Britain, while creating opportunities and benefits for local communities.
“We work closely with local people, consult extensively, and consider all technology options as we develop proposals for the infrastructure needed to support a secure energy future.”

Key Takeaways from the ISW:
- Ukrainian forces in late 2025 and throughout 2026 have successfully contested the initiative at both the strategic and operational levels for the first time since the August 2024 Kursk Offensive.
- Ukrainian successes in eliminating the Russian salient north of Lyman over the past several months have disrupted the Russian military command’s plans to conduct a wide encirclement of the Fortress Belt in Donetsk Oblast from the Lyman and Dobropillya areas.
- The Russian military command will likely need to reassess its campaign designs for the southern and northern flanks of the Fortress Belt given the elimination of its salient north of Lyman and particularly if Ukrainian forces are able to fully push Russian forces back to the Zherebets River and use the canalizing terrain to create a stable defensive line.
- Many Russian milbloggers are acknowledging that Ukrainian forces have largely eliminated the Russian salient north of Lyman and that fighting is mainly ongoing along the Zherebets River in the area.
- Russian generals have reportedly asked Russian President Vladimir Putin for an additional 800,000 troops to sustain and likely expand Russian offensive operations in the face of enormous Russian casualty rates.
- Russia does not have the training and administrative capabilities to absorb, integrate, and train 800,000 recruits at one time, particularly if Russian authorities try to do so alongside the semi-annual conscription cycle that normally starts in October.
- The increasing Russian casualty rates and declining recruitment rate will likely force Russia to conduct some form of mobilization in the near term, but the type and scope of mobilization Putin may choose is unclear at this time.
- The Russian General Staff likely wants to use the additional 800,000 troops to implement its offensive plans throughout the front rather than only in Donetsk, and the scope of any potential mobilization likely depends on what operations Putin authorizes.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky continues to support a future trilateral Ukrainian-Russian-US meeting and to suggest efforts to restart peace talks with Russia.
- Ukraine’s ongoing long-range strike campaign and Western sanctions are actively preventing the Russian oil industry from recovering its processing capacity and oil exports.
- Neither Russian nor Ukrainian forces advanced on September 11.

Indonesia, an archipelago of 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries as a key mode of transportation, with sea routes more affordable and readily available than air travel.
However, safety standards are not always rigorously enforced, resulting in a relatively high accident rate.

Rosh Hashanah 2026: The Jewish people must answer the shofar’s call to unity - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:52:58 UTC
14:52:58 KST

As we approach the upcoming Days of Awe, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur 5787, 2026, I find myself reflecting on the prayer of Unetaneh Tokef, the stirring and poetic liturgy we collectively recite during the Mussaf service:
On Rosh Hashanah it is written, and on Yom Kippur it is sealed: Who shall live, and who shall die. Who by water and who by fire. Who by famine and who by thirst. Who shall have rest, and who shall wander. Who shall be humbled, and who shall be exalted.
There are few passages in our prayer services that confront us so starkly with the uncertainty and unpredictability of human life. Unetaneh Tokef refuses to allow us to hide behind familiarity and comfort. In those short, searing lines, the illusions of certainty fall away. We stand before God vulnerable, humbled, and at God’s mercy. We confront our fragile state as human beings. We acknowledge how much is beyond our control, and we submit ourselves to God’s will.
While the prayer might leave us with a sense of trepidation, it also provides us with resolve and opportunity: U’teshuvah, u’tefillah, u’tzedakah – repentance, prayer, and charity – are the powers we possess to earn another year of life.
These are not abstractions from another time and place. They are guideposts that illuminate for us how to live our lives today. And their message is reinforced by the sound of the shofar.
The blast of the shofar is not a single note. Instead, we hear three distinct sounds: Tekiah, a whole sound. Shevarim, a broken sound. Teruah, a whimpering cry. These sounds, heard in succession, are gathered together into one unmistakable call.
We do not hear the voice of the shofar in solitude. An entire community stands together, on the same day, in the same room, awakened from the same slumber, summoned by the same ancient sound.
For me, this is a fundamental meaning of the Days of Awe. They begin with private reflection, examining our own actions, our own relationships, and our own responsibilities. But they cannot end there. Ultimately, we choose to stand together before God as one people, bound by one history, one destiny, and one eternal covenant.
This year has been particularly trying for the Jewish community, here in Detroit and around the world.
We have witnessed antisemitism creep from the margins of society toward its center – on our campuses, in our halls of government and on our very own streets. We have watched ancient hatred find new language and new audiences. We have felt, at times, that some of the allies we had counted upon chose to keep their distance and remain silent.
But what has touched me most deeply is something I will carry with me long after this year’s end.
Throughout this difficult year, I have witnessed the Jewish people step forward for one another with kindness and love. I have seen Jews reaching across communities and across continents to help their Jewish brethren.
I have seen individuals and organizations forge relationships that strengthen our community and uplift those around us. I have seen Jewish schools and day care centers, synagogues and Federations, community centers and campus Hillels, social service agencies and senior centers refuse to wait for someone else to come to their rescue, instead joining together to protect themselves and one another.
I saw this spirit of shared responsibility in Montreal, where 440 trained volunteers and a federation command center helped secure the Jewish institutions of their community. I saw it in Washington, where more than 400 community leaders from 41 states came together to advocate on Capitol Hill for the safety and security of Jewish life across America.
I have seen it in the extraordinary generosity of the North American Federation system, helping bring comfort, aid, and security to families and communities rebuilding their lives in Israel since October 7. And I have seen it in the foresight of the Israeli government, committing to help strengthen Jewish education throughout the Diaspora.
And in West Bloomfield, Michigan, we felt that same spirit deeply when the courageous Detroit community came together to support our brothers and sisters at Temple Israel during one of the darkest moments we have faced. The kindness, courage, and love shown by every facet of the Jewish community shone a powerful light that reminded us that when one part of our community is threatened, we all feel the pain, and we all share the responsibility to respond.
I have seen the Jewish people uplift Torah, uplift one another, and build strength and resolve together. That word – together – is not sentimental. It is vital. And it is sacred.
When our ancestors listened for the first time to the sound of the shofar at Mount Sinai, preparing to receive the Torah and enter into our eternal covenant with God, they stood as our sages described, k’ish echad b’lev echad – as one person with one heart.
Not because every Jew thought the same way. Not because every Jew saw the world the same way. And certainly not because disagreement had completely faded away.
Unity is not the absence of disagreement
We must remember that unity is not the absence of disagreement. Unity is the recognition that what binds us together is greater than what divides us. It is the understanding that despite our differences, despite the forces that attempt to pull us apart, we remain k’ish echad b’lev echad – one people, with one heart.
Rosh Hashanah is the birthday of the world. Throughout the prayer service, we are asked to imagine the world as the Almighty intended it to be: whole, just, unified, loving, and at peace, and we accept upon ourselves to proclaim God as King of the universe.
From Rosh Hashanah through Yom Kippur, we measure the distance between that vision and the world as it actually is. And we acknowledge that distance with complete honesty and humility – recognizing where we have fallen short, while trusting that our sincere prayers will be heard and accepted.
Repentance is always possible. For one person. For one community. And for an entire people.
This year, I pray that we meet this moment with clarity, faith, and resolve: that we remain clear-eyed about the threats confronting us, without allowing that reality to turn into fracture; that we remain vigilant without becoming fearful; and that we defend ourselves without forgetting who we are, what we stand for, and how deeply connected we are to one another.
In the end, we are one people. We serve the same God, who stands with us, who wants the best for us, and who asks us to become better – more compassionate, more kind, more loving, more unified and less afraid.
May every member of the Jewish people be written and sealed for a year of life, health, blessing and peace. May the prayers we offer during these sacred days not remain only words upon our lips, but deeply embedded in our hearts, resulting in commitments we will live by each and every day.
Shana Tova u’metukah. May you and your loved ones be inscribed and sealed for a good and sweet new year.
The writer is the chair of the Jewish Federations of North America (JFNA).

====================================================================================================

Giving surplus a second life, Jerusalem’s food rescuers are turning leftovers into a lifeline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:52:55 UTC
14:52:55 KST

Cast your minds back to those “halcyon” days of the COVID-19 mandatory vaccines, masks, lockdowns, and all manner of logistical nightmares. Chiefly among the latter was the ordinarily simple matter of ensuring you had all the necessities of keeping body and soul together, naturally including vittles.
“Food security” was a term bandied about with high regularity as supplies of staples such as plain old bread were often not guaranteed.
On my own moshav in the Jerusalem Hills, the arrival of the truck from Tnuva with its consignment of dairy products, or the appearance of the delivery man from the Angel bakery firm, were greeted with much glee and palpable relief.
Even if we are not visited by another pandemic anytime soon, in more normal circumstances we would do well to abide by the sagacious words of Britain’s favorite centenarian, iconic nature show frontman, and writer, Sir David Attenborough. When asked about the one thing he would like us all to remember with regard to Mother Earth, he simply replied: “Don’t waste.”
That sounds like a simple enough matter which can be applied in all sorts of quotidian areas. How about, for example, getting into the habit of arming ourselves with reusable bags the next time we pop along to our local makolet or supermarket, instead of merrily accruing plastic bags on offer at such enterprises.
Getting food to those who need it most
It is also a sentiment that sits particularly well with Daniella Seltzer. In fact, you could say it is her credo.
Seltzer is one of the movers and shakers behind the Jerusalem Food Rescuers initiative, which set up house at the Wholesale Market in Givat Shaul in 2019. The idea was to garner items from the crate loads of veggies and fruit coming into the vast market compound, pieces that were a little under- or overripe, bruised, or just might not look tempting to utopian TV commercial image-brainwashed shoppers.
As one can easily imagine, it wasn’t exactly smooth-going to begin with. The truck drivers hauling products from all over, site managers and supervisors, et al were used to getting the stuff through the gates, and duly apportioning it in accordance with their tried-and-tested, well-oiled procedure.
They weren’t about to let “an intruder” run their eyes and hands over the merchandise before it got to them. Or were they? Gradually, with due deference and persistence, Seltzer and her comrades in redemptive arms gained the trust and, eventually, respect and cooperation of the hard-nosed wholesale market folks.
Seltzer and the Rescuers team – almost all volunteers – are now the initial stop in the processing continuum and get to sift their way through the fruit and veggies first. The perceived inferior-quality products are subsequently sorted and find their way to various collection points, such as community centers, dotted around all areas of Jerusalem.
There, Jerusalemites of all walks of life, ages, and ethnic origins can then access healthy foodstuffs, gratis or at very affordable prices, that otherwise would probably not feature in their and their family’s daily diet.
Now Seltzer is taking the Jerusalem Food Rescuers’ work to another level by initiating the Jerusalem Urban Food Forum and a concomitant formula for leveraging efforts to make better use of food resources around the city.
The plan identifies approximately 2,200 food-based enterprise businesses in Jerusalem with potential relevance to food rescue. That includes restaurants and cafés, supermarkets, grocery stores, fruit and vegetable shops, bakeries, food producers, caterers, and institutional kitchens.
Coordinating all of that, and succeeding in gathering, pooling, and distributing the edible offloads from all those businesses, presumably, involves layered management dynamics.
“This points to the need for a citywide mechanism that can connect surplus food sources with community demand in real time,” the plan explanatory material notes. Seltzer reckons that, once up and running smoothly, that could yield around 7,000 tons of food a year.
She also cautions that municipal collaboration is the linchpin here. She says City Hall would need to invest in “coordination, business participation, logistics, digital tools, and community distribution capacity.”
Jerusalem commits to global urban food policy efforts
There appears to be goodwill coming from that direction, with Mayor Moshe Lion signing the Milan Urban Food Policy Pact in June, thereby adding Jerusalem to the ranks of over 300 cities worldwide committed to building and cultivating more efficient food systems that help to get healthier nutrition to folks who couldn’t ordinarily manage that. The local signatories of the Pact roster include Tel Aviv, Bethlehem, and Jericho.
That, of course, has all sorts of implications. As the World Health Organization (WHO) states – in case it wasn’t patently clear – in its healthy diet guidelines: “Diet plays a critical role in shaping the health and wellbeing of both individuals and populations, and unhealthy diets are a major risk factor for disease and disability.”
Interestingly, there wasn’t a lot of talk about that in the context of COVID when, besides all the emergency measures and constraints imposed on us, that might have been an opportune time to advise us to nurture our immune systems by, for example, steering clear of processed foods and sugar-rich products. In so doing, we would have improved our health and made our bodies more resilient to future pandemics or any potentially harmful bacteria that may come our way at some stage.
Doing our best to make fruit and vegetables – good natural sources of vitamins, iron, fibers, and potassium – available to all and sundry makes complete sense. Seltzer and the other members of the Food Rescuers gang are all for that, and spreading the word as far and wide as possible.
“The idea is to establish a network of cities, working individually and in tandem, to generate a system whereby there is greater accessibility to healthy food, with greater efficiency and enhanced connectivity between various municipal departments and personnel,” Selzer explains.
Cohesion is the name of the game
The plan aims to involve as many components of the human and economic urban fabric in the venture: “We need to take all the players in the city and get them to operate with greater synchronicity. That is a feature of the Milan Urban Food Policy.”
The global urban concept also calls for mutually beneficial cross-border dynamics. “The idea is for cities to work together, and to learn from each other through Best Practices, to see what works best.”
The initiative’s nonprofit core philosophy adds an endearing quality to the venture. “I believe it is all carried out voluntarily,” Seltzer notes. “It is wonderful. In Milan they created a [municipal] department that feeds off the [Milan Urban Food Policy Pact] website. That is amazing.”
There are various takes on how to make better use of available comestible resources. While the Italian unit’s purview includes overseeing the work of physical food rescue hubs, Greece’s Boroume model opts for a more streamlined, decentralized approach based on matching food donors directly with recipient organizations. That obviates the need for a central holding facility for collection and distribution.
Then there is the Canadian Second Harvest food recovery system, which facilitates the collection of surplus, healthy food from businesses and redirects it to charities to fight both hunger and environmental waste.
Addressing Jerusalem’s poverty woes
Back here, in sunny, socioeconomically disadvantaged Jerusalem, Seltzer says the plan offers a slew of benefits and sorely needed solutions in all sorts of practical areas. That includes a resounding financial bottom line.
“Jerusalem’s annual food loss may reach more than 200,000 tons, with an economic value approaching NIS 1.8 billion,” she says.
Those are simply stunning statistics made all the more egregious by another startling figure – around 40% of the capital’s residents live below the poverty line. That’s approximately twice the national average. However, that sorry state of affairs is somewhat offset by the Rescuers’ work.
To date, the nonprofit has salvaged 1,300 tons of food and has provided a similar number of local families with a regular supply of food. They are also doing their best to maintain food security efforts in the long run and have educated close to 10,000 school students about the ins and outs of food sustainability.
Lion’s signature on the Pact paper may have paved the way for Jerusalem to join hands with a global network of cities that understand food as a strategic urban issue, but there are plenty of facts on the ground to be addressed before the theory can become a health-inducing, nutrition-supportive local reality.
Seltzer would love to see our local purse string holders follow Milan’s lead.
“If we are going to make this plan work, we need to have a dedicated department set up in the municipality. The department should engage in food as an urban infrastructure, just like any other area [of municipal activity] which is critical [for life in Jerusalem].
“We have an education administration, and people who engage in transport, housing, etc., and we have food, the most basic need in life, which is ignored. It is so obvious that it is missed.”
Taking a food breather
The evidence of that is in full view on downtown and neighborhood streets, with hundreds of food outlets packed most hours of the day as many of us guzzle down portions that are way too generously proportioned for our health and are often simply not nutritious.
Contemporary lifestyles also come into the remedial equation, as technology makes deeper inroads into the natural order of things, encroaches on a gentler, healthier daily tempo, and screams out for eating on the fly.
How many of us, for example, other than, perhaps, on Shabbat, sit down together with family and friends to enjoy a relaxing, joyful, and possibly bonding repast?
I remember visiting a friend in Chicago many years ago, long before the advent of the Internet and smartphones, looking on in amazement as her siblings and parents, in turn, descended on the kitchen, secured their helping of dinner, and promptly disappeared into their bedrooms to chow down in front of their individual TV sets. Nowadays, there are, of course, even more entertainment and online information distractions that get in the way of harmonious mealtime intervals.
The Jerusalem Food Rescuers’ plan addresses that largely unnoted feature of daily 21st-century life.
A systematic umbrella review on family mealtimes, conducted by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in the United States in 2023, found that more frequent family meals are associated with protection against poorer diet, obesity, risk behaviors, poorer mental health and wellbeing, and weaker educational outcomes among children and adolescents.
That report followed a 2015 NIH document which found that frequent family meals were associated with better dietary and psychosocial outcomes for children and adolescents.
It stands to reason if we view the nuclear family group as an emotional and physical staple of individual and societal health. The Jerusalem paper soberly notes that “not every family has the time, space, money, kitchen, stability, or emotional bandwidth to eat together regularly.”
That’s where outside help can come in handy. “The policy question is how schools, communities, and cities can create more opportunities for shared, dignified eating,” it continues.
Hadar Lavi, director of the Social Sustainability Department of the Municipality of Jerusalem, says City Hall is right behind Seltzer and her co-workers’ efforts.
“Jerusalem is promoting urban food policy by joining the international Milan Urban Food Policy Pact, and establishing the Jerusalem Urban Food Forum, in conjunction with the Jerusalem Food Rescuers, and elements from academia and civil society,” her statement read.
The benefits offered by the citywide initiative resonate with Lavi. “The Forum addresses the development of urban food policy vision with a view to furthering a sustainable food system, reducing food waste, bolstering food security and promoting healthy nutrition in the city.”
Lavi also singles out the Rescuers’ sterling work in the field. “The Jerusalem Food Rescuers are playing a significant role in bringing the issue to the urban agenda, connecting different parties and leading professional dialogue. This is a joint process which is evolving, and which is designed to formulate practical measures for Jerusalem’s unique needs.”
That makes for a well-articulated official statement, and one can only hope that, with Seltzer and her team spearheading solutions for this ongoing pressing need, the financial wherewithal and political backing will be there to put it all into universal, personal, ecological, and financial practice.
“Food rescue should be understood as part of urban policy, not only charity,” Seltzer stresses in her Plan notes.
“It connects waste reduction, food security, climate action, business participation, community resilience, public health, and education. The Jerusalem Urban Food Forum can be the place where these pieces are finally coordinated into one practical citywide plan.”■
