Not your average Jewish mother: Lisa Edelstein on Hollywood, identity, and ‘Long Story Short'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:49:19 UTC
04:49:19 KST

When actress and artist Lisa Edelstein met her now-husband, artist Robert Russell, he came with a deep desire to rediscover his Jewish identity and pass it on to his sons from a former marriage, then three and five. He found the perfect partner for the job in Lisa.
In addition to being Jewish, Lisa has played numerous Jewish women, including Dr. Cuddy on House, the lead (and a producer) of Bravo’s Girlfriends’ Guide to Divorce, and the adult daughter of Alan Arkin’s character on Netflix’s The Kominsky Method.
Now she’s playing the matriarch anchoring Long Story Short, Netflix’s time-shifting adult animated series about three generations of a Jewish family.
The following is a blend of a written and a Zoom interview. She was warm, funny, and thoughtful.
Lisa grew up Conservative and kosher, building sukkahs and sitting through four-hour Seders, attending synagogue on Saturdays and Hebrew school until she was sixteen. Shabbat dinner was non-negotiable.
“My father would usually give a very simple Parsha,” she told me. “I didn’t know that’s what he was doing at the time. I just knew that every week he talked about the Torah portion. And that continued for my whole childhood.”
Edelstein's Jewish roots
HER GRANDPARENTS were immigrants, their first language Yiddish. Pogroms and war had scattered the family. Some cousins went to America, but many more ended up in Argentina and Israel.
Her father’s Aunt Leah founded Kibbutz Daliya in the early 1900s. “They turned the rocky, dry land into a forest and farm and hosted dance festivals once a year. That part of the family is still there, although some of their descendants have left the kibbutz.”
Other family members live in Tel Aviv, Herzliya, Nir Zvi, Haifa, and by the border of Lebanon. Her last visit was a few days after the last living Oct. 7 hostages came home.
“Israel is a beautiful, messy, complicated, diverse, loud, funny, tragic, amazing, gorgeous, powerful country, and I’m grateful for its existence.”
She drifted away from Jewish traditions in her young adulthood, but meeting her husband – and his own Jewish journey – pulled her back in.
“When we met, it was pretty apparent to both of us that we were going to stay together forever, and so we created a home. The boys were going back and forth 50/50 between our household and their mom’s, and we wanted to find a way to give them a joyous Jewish experience in this house.”
Their solution was a “hip-hop Shabbat” with dance lessons from an instructor followed by a big Shabbat dinner. When the boys outgrew hip-hop, it became Shabbat Dungeons & Dragons: friends over for dinner, then up half the night immersed in the fantasy tabletop game.
The boys have since graduated high school, but the joyous Shabbat dinner tradition continues at the Edelstein-Russell household, now with dozens of friends and family members.
ALTHOUGH SHE grew up in a Jewish neighborhood, Lisa got a taste of antisemitism and “otherism” at an early age. Her family moved to Wayne, a Jewish enclave in New Jersey, in 1967 – the same year the Civil Rights Act finally forced the town to take down the “No Negroes, no Jews, no dogs allowed” signs in shop and restaurant windows.
During a re-election campaign, the head of the school board claimed that the Jew running against him was going to cancel Christmas. In response to this outlandish charge, The New York Times dubbed the town “The Home of Antisemitism in the United States of America.”
“He won the election, by the way, and then he became mayor for 12 years. So that guy was running my town in one way or another during my entire childhood there,” Lisa said.
Her feelings of otherism, however, “weren’t because someone pointed at me and yelled JEW,” she explained. “It was our culture, in general, that somehow accepted the idea that Jewish women were spoiled princesses that only cared about Bloomingdale’s … that they had big noses and frizzy hair and were grating.”
I remember the jokes and the moniker Jewish American Princess, with its derisive acronym JAP. Jokes like, “What does a Jewish American Princess make for dinner? A reservation.” And, “How do you tickle a Jewish American Princess? Gucci, Gucci, goo.”
“I didn’t want to own that stereotype,” she continued. “And I guess on some level, I believed that that was true because that was what I was being told, and so I felt shame around my Jewish identity.”
When Lisa left home to study drama at New York University, she made a concerted effort to separate herself from that unpleasant association. “I felt like it was a part of myself I had to grow out of or away from, or somehow bury or erase.”
Edelstein's reinvention and journey of self-exploration
THAT REINVENTION, and an explosion of self-exploration, led her into the New York City club scene and a walk on the wild side. She became so well known in the clubs that famed journalist Maureen Dowd wrote a feature about her in The New York Times titled “Lisa in Wonderland.”
Dowd painted a colorful picture of the full-time drama student and celebutante: “She talks fast, walks fast, laughs often. Her stride is a fast-motion version of Marilyn Monroe’s bouncy gait. Everything about her, from her vivid alto to her mane of brown curls, seems to vibrate.”
Lisa immersed herself in a world of experimental theater and experimental human beings. “It was the most exciting and diverse group of creative people I’d ever seen,” she said of the club life.
“I couldn’t get enough of how weird and wonderful and psychedelic the city could be. I learned an enormous amount, met incredible people, and was immersed in a community bursting with imagination and juice. So it was more than just fun for me; it was me finding out what excited me, what surprised me, even what terrified me.”
In the club scene, she went by Lisa E, unsure how to “own a name like Edelstein out in the world without having to constantly battle with the preconceived idea of what that meant.” In time, she realized the stereotype had nothing to do with her.
Writing an AIDS-related musical, Positive Me, forced a decision: Lisa E, or Lisa Edelstein, on the poster? “Am I moving forward as myself, or am I moving forward as this creation?”
She decided she couldn’t leave herself behind. Changing her name felt like “Hitler would win. Like I was abandoning my people and my heritage and my ancestors. I started to realize, you have to find a way to carry yourself with you, despite what people might think.”
For decades, Jewish actors anglicized their names. Woody Allen was born Allan Stewart Konigsberg. Peter Coyote was Robert Peter Cohon. Winona Ryder changed her name from Winona Horowitz. And Albert Brooks was born Albert Einstein. Okay, you can’t blame him for that one.
JOINING THE Screen Actors Guild, Lisa said, marked another milestone. Was she worried about typecasting?
“The answer is yes, and for sure it got in my way. I had several experiences where producers would call me crying or tell me years later that they were not allowed to cast me because I was too Jewish. If I had changed my name, maybe that wouldn’t have happened. Who knows? I got jobs anyway, and a lot of those characters became Jewish without my trying, because people saw me that way, so that’s fine.”
That’s more than fine with me. The casting of non-Jewish actors in Jewish roles, a rare practice today for other marginalized groups, remains ubiquitous in Hollywood. I don’t love the idea of artificially restricting actors who can convincingly play other ethnicities, but if we are calling for authenticity for other minorities, we should do the same for Jews.
Lisa has also portrayed many Jewish mothers, so I asked her to describe her mother. “HA!” she playfully responded, “describe YOUR mother.” I didn’t, but Lisa did.
Bonnie Edelstein graduated high school at 16 and married at 19. She’s tough, critical, deeply opinionated, “confused by technology but offended by that confusion,” and loves playing solitaire on her phone.
Bonnie’s mother, Grandma Gertie, was one of Lisa’s favorite people – an unstoppable force of hilarity and attitude. “She smoked two packs of cigarettes for 70 years and then gave it up in a day. She was the president of the sisterhoods of five different synagogues in Coney Island and Brighton Beach.”
Both women fed directly into Lisa’s performance as the matriarch of Long Story Short, Naomi – a feisty, witty woman unafraid to pick a fight over something that matters to her. She loves her family the best way she knows how, but she still gets under the skin of her three kids.
Lisa admitted Naomi leans toward the stereotypical “cloying Jewish mom,” but believes it’s those very expectations that trick the audience into falling in love with her.
In a second-season twist, we learn, right alongside her children, that she’s beloved by the wider community and a heroine to many. It strikes me that in families, we’re all playing roles. Whether you’re the provider, the nurturer, the rebel, or the complainer, we get locked into those parts, and it keeps the people closest to us from ever fully knowing who we are.
Edelstein explores hidden histories in Little Bird
THAT THEME of hidden histories carries into another project of Lisa’s: Little Bird, a six-episode Canadian miniseries about the “Sixties Scoop,” when government policy tore Indigenous children from their families to be raised in foster care or adopted into non-Indigenous homes, cut off from their culture.
Adoptive parents believed they were rescuing abandoned children, not participating in a kidnapping scheme.
Lisa plays Golda Rosenbaum, a Holocaust survivor who immigrated from Poland to Montreal and adopted a young Saskatchewan girl, raising her as a Jew and renaming her Esther.
“Golda thinks she’s raising somebody who she shares the experience with of having lost their families,” Lisa explained. “She adopts her when she’s 5, and by the time her daughter is 25 and ready to get married, her daughter cannot move forward without finding out what actually happened to her.” So Esther sets off in search of her Indigenous family.
When a member of her Indigenous family dies, Esther processes her grief through both traditions. Lisa and I talked about how ritual and tradition help us process events and regulate our emotions.
“No one does mourning better than Jews,” Lisa opined. “We’ve got a guidebook like no other guidebook. There’s a written plan about how you walk through this tragedy in your life, and it’s beautiful.”
Jewish characters are rare in film and television outside stories with intrinsically Jewish storylines. Yet, Lisa made her Abby in Girlfriends’ Guide to Divorce, a show about a recent divorcee going through a common modern experience, a member of the tribe.
“That was a dream job. One that I’m so glad I got to experience while I could still wear really, really high heels for any length of time. To get to be funny and sexy, smart, and emotional all in one job was deeply fulfilling,” she said.
Edelstein's impulse to create
LISA STARTED PAINTING as an extension of a lifelong impulse to create, transforming what she once viewed as a private coping mechanism into an applauded second career.
“My husband gave me a painting on our second date, and asked me for a drawing in return,” she shared. Exchanging handmade gifts gradually became central to their relationship, helping her recognize that “that part of myself was valuable.”
The turning point came when COVID slowed the world. Looking for a subject for her artwork, Edelstein immersed herself in family photographs she inherited after helping her parents downsize. She discovered “so many stories, so many memories, so many things I didn’t remember,” and decided “to make myself a coloring book out of these images.”
What began with magic markers evolved into increasingly intricate works. When friends urged her to abandon markers for paint, she switched to watercolor, opening new creative possibilities.
She worked obsessively – sometimes “6 hours, 10 hours” – and found the experience exhilarating. Since then, she has moved into oils and mounted four exhibitions, with two works entering museum collections.
“It’s been a really magical journey,” she told me.
I was struck by the paintings’ vivid colors and dense patterns, which evoked their eras without overshadowing the people. Edelstein explained that her early reliance on markers naturally led her to seek photographs rich with pattern, making the 1970s of her youth “just a gift.”
Although her source material now spans about 100 years, she unifies work with a consistent palette.
“Mostly what I’m looking for in these images is narrative,” Edelstein said. She is drawn to photographs that “accidentally tell a story,” revealing something unexpected about a person’s character or life. Carefully posed family portraits rarely interest her.
One of my favorite paintings is Vampirella, a portrait of Lisa at eleven, in glasses and a nightgown, surrounded by the intimate clutter of her bedroom. Another painting that stays with me is Celebration, which bursts with affection and movement. Lisa believes the original photo was one of her grandparents’ wedding anniversaries.
What captivates her is not the event but the exuberant humanity within it: “There’s just so much momentum, there’s so many stories in that image.”
I am struck by the family dynamics – fathers and daughters, husbands and wives – and by the many yarmulkes. Edelstein explained that the visible Jewish identity in her work became an intentional artistic choice even before the Oct. 7, 2023 massacre of innocent Israelis and visitors by Hamas.
The impact of Oct. 7 on Edelstein's Jewish identity
When preparing for her first gallery show, she remembered being asked, “Are you sure you want to go this Jew-forward?”
“Well, yeah, it’s my family. We are also a minority,” she said, “and we have a rich culture in this country [USA].” After Oct. 7, that commitment deepened, and since then, she has made sure every exhibition includes work reflecting Jewish life and culture.
LIKE MOST JEWS, Lisa and Robert were devastated by the attack, but the reactions from friends were mixed.
“We have a few friends who cried with us, who checked in frequently, who never stopped wanting to talk about what happened and what we have all been going through,” she said.
On the other hand, “We had to end a few friendships completely because they were total dead ends. It has been painful and sad and also made us furious.”
While the hostages were still being held captive, Lisa wore a Star of David she bought during a visit to Israel in the 70s along with a yellow ribbon hostage pin. At work, a colleague referenced the star and pin, saying, “It seems like you’re making a very political statement. Are you sure you want to do that?”
“A Jewish person said this to me!” an exasperated Lisa told me.
“It doesn’t matter what statement people think I’m making by wearing this,” she told her colleague. “It matters that they know who they’re talking to, and edit accordingly.”
And then there was the silence.
“I confronted one of our friends post-Oct. 7. I felt she’d let her politics get in the way of her empathy when she didn’t even bother to check in with us after such a traumatizing event. Her excuse surprised me: she had no idea we would care about what was happening there. She had no idea that Jewish people feel connected to each other,” Lisa shared.
“She was shocked to be confronted, and I was shocked to realize that this was something completely unique to us. We are a people. We feel each other’s successes and failures, triumphs, and tragedies. Some of us are annoyed by ‘others of us,’ but we are still, somehow, an ‘Us.’ And that isn’t something most people experience or comprehend. It makes us incredibly special.” ■
The writer is an attorney and 20-year entertainment veteran, the CEO of Liberate Art, and the author of Artists Under Fire: The BDS War Against Celebrities, Jews, and Israel. From Australian judge to Israeli tour guide: David Parry's aliyah journey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:48:51 UTC
04:48:51 KST

"I felt the mission of my life was to get here,” says David Parry from his home in Zichron Ya’acov.
To fulfill that mission, the Sydney native took early retirement from his law career. He had worked his way up from specialist magistrate in administrative law to Australian District Court judge and deputy president of the State Administrative Tribunal in Perth, on Australia’s west coast.
“It was a tremendous privilege to uphold the rule of law and to resolve disputes between citizens and governmental authorities.
“I had a tenured position for another 15 years, but I resigned in favor of a lifelong dream to come to Israel. I always felt it was part of my life destiny,” David says. “My career enabled me to retire at the age of 55 with a pension that puts us in a position that we are truly blessed.”
To his baffled colleagues in Australia, he explained that he felt obligated to grab an opportunity that past generations had been denied “to make a contribution to the reestablishment of Jewish sovereignty and society in the ancestral homeland of the Jewish people.”
David, Sharon Parry join four kids, one grandchildren in Israel
Why Zichron Ya’acov? This bucolic Haifa district town is where David and Sharon Parry’s oldest daughter, Gabriella, who works in public relations for Israeli start-ups, lives with her husband, Joe, and their daughter – the Parrys’ only grandchild, with another on the way.
All four Parry kids made the move from Australia to Israel. Natalie and her husband, Yehuda, live in Jaffa; she is a senior data analyst. Mia is a Middle Eastern studies student at Shalem College in Jerusalem. Jacob, soon finishing his IDF service, has built up a 40k-strong social media presence (as @jakey_parry on Instagram) and is an actor in Michael Aloni’s new theater company, HaMakor.
“Sharon and I are incredibly proud that they all made the decision on their own to make aliyah and found their lives and communities and passions here,” says David, who’d happily spent his morning having breakfast with his granddaughter and then taking her to preschool.
“We were incredibly happy in Perth, and it was a great place to raise our children. But we always knew it was temporary.”
David and Sharon carve new path after arriving in Israel
BOTH DAVID and Sharon embarked on new careers after arriving.
David completed a tour-guiding course in English at the University of Haifa School of Tourism, received his license, and opened a website, TourWiseIsrael.com.
He is partnering with Israel Maven Tours in Jerusalem to offer three-day guided tour packages for English-speaking immigrants who want to explore their adopted land with peers: one to the Galilee and Golan in October and March (israelmaven.com/tzafonatour) and one to the Negev in January and February (israelmaven.com/negbatour).
David says he was always “an avid student of the extraordinary history, geography, and geopolitics of Israel and had visited many times. But after making aliyah, I finally had the time and space to tour and study this incredible land in depth.
“What a privilege it is to guide people in the country that has contributed to the world like no other and to help explain what is, perhaps, the most misunderstood place on the planet.”
He has discovered that the professional skills he developed as a judge are equally valuable as a tour guide: “mastery of facts, weighing different perspectives, clarity of expression, the ability to communicate complex issues to people from all backgrounds, and treating every person with respect.”
Sharon’s transition was more complicated. She has a doctorate in physiotherapy, with a specific interest in the deleterious health effects of desk-based work and how to mitigate them.
For the 18 years prior to aliyah, she was a university lecturer and researcher, and ultimately an adjunct professor of physiotherapy.
“The only negative aspect of our aliyah story is that the bureaucracy defeated her in converting her degree,” David says. “The Health Ministry decided that, although she was registered as a physiotherapist in Australia, because she was employed as a ‘lecturer’ and not a ‘physiotherapist’ for 18 years, she would have had to prove the number of hours she did in clinical training for her bachelor’s degree, which was 40 years ago. That was impossible.”
Therefore, Sharon decided to apply her expertise to a related endeavor: running workshops for companies, particularly hi-tech companies, on how to improve the workplace to prevent health problems of sedentary workers. Through her website, MoveWiseActive.com, she’s also offering workshops on fall prevention for seniors.
“She found something based on her experience that’s even more meaningful,” says David. “We’re hoping to do a bit of collaboration, combining her workshop with my tour.”
Though the couple has studied spoken Hebrew at ulpan, they work exclusively in English and have gained a close circle of friends in Zichron from English-speaking countries. Together, they take trips around Israel, play pickleball, and spend time at the beach.
David hopes for uptick in tourism
Of course, like all tour guides here, David is hoping for an uptick in foreign tourism.
“I’d ideally like to guide delegations and missions; I’m in touch with organizations from Australia and North America about that,” he says.
“There’s an incredible pent-up demand to come to Israel. There is a thirst to see the country. The second [that] flights open, tourists flock in.
“There’s simply no other place like Israel, no other place that was the crossroads of the world from the beginning. I would love to show not just its beauty and history, but the depth and meaning that lie beneath the surface.”
Married 35 years, the Parrys are happily starting over in Israel.
“It’s such an incredible blessing to be here. I really feel it was the mission of my life to facilitate my family’s return to Israel,” David emphasizes.
“Coming from the outside, we appreciate so much that we live here according to Jewish time; that the Jewish holidays and the rhythm of Jewish life are part of the culture of the country. I will never take that for granted.” ■

Type 31 schedule challenges being monitored

The Type 31 frigate programme continues to face schedule challenges linked to its ambitious build timeline and the integration, testing and assurance of ship systems, the Ministry of Defence has said.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard set out the position in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what challenges remained following references in the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority’s Major Projects Annual Report 2025 to 2026.
Pollard said the MOD was continuing to work with Babcock, the prime contractor for the five-ship Type 31 programme, to keep the build aligned with Royal Navy requirements and the planned delivery timetable.
He said: “The Ministry of Defence (MOD) continues to work closely with Babcock, the prime contractor, to ensure the Type 31 programme meets all user requirements to deliver a maritime security capability at a value for money price, in a timescale that is competitive with other international warship procurement programmes.”
The programme is based around an intentionally fast build schedule, with Babcock constructing the frigates at Rosyth using a repeatable production approach intended to support a steady flow of ships through assembly, integration and completion.
Pollard added: “Challenges can be expected when delivering a complex warship against an ambitious build timeline. Working closely with Babcock enables us to resolve any issues that may arise, alongside maturing the design and progressing construction, ensuring the build programme is stable and repeatable going forward.”
The minister also pointed to the complexity of bringing together the ship’s combat, communications, navigation, propulsion and other onboard systems while keeping testing and assurance aligned with the wider programme schedule. He added: “The complex nature of this work can present challenges, however all activities are subject to ongoing oversight by the MOD to ensure successful delivery to the RN.”
Readers should note that this answer does not identify a specific new delay or single integration issue affecting the programme, but confirms that schedule pressure remains tied to an ambitious construction plan and the need to complete ship-system integration, testing and assurance without disrupting the pathway into Royal Navy service.
Type 31 is intended to provide the Royal Navy with five general-purpose frigates, replacing part of the Type 23 fleet and increasing the number of modern surface combatants available for maritime security, presence and other tasks. The ships are being built by Babcock at Rosyth, with the programme also intended to demonstrate a more repeatable approach to warship production that can support future export opportunities and maintain shipbuilding activity across the yard.

Bahrain says it will not participate in Iran’s proposed Hormuz meeting
Iran tells Al Jazeera that Monday’s meeting is a sign of ‘good intentions’ towards neighbouring countries.
Bahrain says it will not be participating in a proposed meeting in Oman between Iran and other regional countries to discuss safe passage for shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has effectively blockaded the shipping channel throughout the war, stopping Gulf oil and gas exports worldwide, but Iran’s foreign ministry said a meeting is planned on Monday in Muscat for “consultations” on the strait’s future.

list of 4 items

“In light of what has been circulated … the Kingdom of Bahrain will not participate in it,” Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Saturday.
Pointing to attacks on infrastructure across the Gulf, Bahrain said that security and stability in the region “cannot be preserved through a policy of appeasement” and called for Hormuz to be open without “discrimination, fees or permits”.
Tehran has been pushing to formalise its control over the waterway, including potentially charging fees for passage, and has been in negotiations with Muscat, as Oman’s territorial waters also cover Hormuz.
The strait was free to use by shipping from all nations before the US and Israel attacked Iran late in February, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry said it maintains its commitment to dialogue, but “will not be a party to any collective meeting that includes Iran before the resumption of diplomatic relations between the two countries”.
Bahrain cut diplomatic ties with Iran in 2016 alongside Saudi Arabia during an earlier crisis between the regional rivals. While Riyadh restored ties in 2023, Manama is yet to do so.
‘We will talk to our neighbours’
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, told Al Jazeera on Saturday that the meeting is “a sign of Iran’s good intention because we have said all along that the security of the region must be guaranteed by the countries of the region, without intervention by the foreigners, without intervention by the outside powers”.
“This is a sign we will talk to our neighbours, despite the fact that their territories, their military bases or the military bases of the United States, were used to attack Iran,” he said.
Baghaei added that Tehran would “brief the delegations about the results of the Iran and Oman consultations regarding the safe passage of ships through the Strait of Hormuz”.
Reuters news agency quoted an unnamed senior Iranian official saying that the meeting in Oman will be a chance to discuss issues, but it is not expected to yield a signed agreement over the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported that an understanding between Iran and Oman would not provide for the immediate reopening of the strait but only establish the basis on which it could reopen.

====================================================================================================

The U.S. Is Having One of Its Most Active Wildfire Seasons. Here’s How the Costs Are Adding Up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:29:01 UTC
04:29:01 KST

The United States is on pace to see one of its most active wildfire seasons on record. According to a new AccuWeather report, large fires were active in at least 13 states as of Sept. 9, while more than 8.4 million acres had burned nationwide this year—about 1.3 million acres above the full-year annual average over the previous decade.
The extraordinarily active season is testing a recently overhauled federal wildfire-response system while placing mounting financial pressure on governments, taxpayers, insurers, and individual households.
How the U.S. changed its wildfire response after the Los Angeles fires
The Los Angeles fires in January 2025 were high-profile incidents that drew widespread attention to the nation’s risk. They were notable as sudden, highly concentrated, urban conflagration events—and they stand in contrast to the 2026 wildfire season, which has garnered less attention with the incidents geographically dispersed across the U.S.
However, almost twice as much land has burned so far in 2026 as had burned at the same point in 2025, according to AccuWeather.
The Palisades and Eaton fires in L.A. showcased just how costly massive wildfires are in terms of infrastructure damage, loss of life, and economic impact. Collectively, the fires burned about 37,500 acres and destroyed nearly 17,000 structures, killing at least 31 people. Munich Re estimated total damage at $53 billion, including $40 billion in insured losses—“by far the largest insured loss on record from a wildfire event,” according to the United Nations.
Read More: What Happens When the World Is on Fire
In response, President Donald Trump signed an executive order on June 12, 2025, calling for the consolidation of wildfire response resources within the Interior and Agriculture departments within 90 days. The U.S. Wildland Fire Service was formed as a result.
The order also directed agencies to review rules that might impede wildfire response, develop performance metrics, release relevant historical satellite data, and evaluate the sale of excess military aircraft for wildfire response. Those provisions carried deadlines ranging from 120 to 210 days.
Since then, the Administration has overhauled how the federal government fights fires. One of the largest shifts involves focusing on wildfire suppression. Since April, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has directed crews to presume a full-suppression strategy for every wildfire under the management of the Interior Department. While managers are instructed to select tactics according to on-the-ground conditions, the presumptive approach is suppression—a pursuit that is widely known to be expensive.
The move has drawn criticism as states compete for limited firefighting resources, and as federal forecasters expect above-normal significant-fire potential in parts of the West through September.
The financial toll of wildfires has dramatically escalated in recent years as fire seasons grow longer and fires become more severe.
Why wildfire costs are rising for federal and state governments
The National Multi-Agency Coordination Group (NMAC), composed of representatives from the federal and state agencies, establishes national preparedness levels ranging from 1 to 5. The country remained at Level 5 from July 18 through Sept. 4, meaning national resources were heavily committed and some regions had to take emergency measures to sustain operations. The level was lowered to 3 on Sept. 9.
During the Level 5 period, the National Multi-Agency Coordinating Group warned of “high competition” for firefighting resources nationally. It said the system lacked sufficient incident-management resources to meet every request, prompting concerns among lawmakers about whether resources could be exhausted before the season ended.
On Friday, five Democratic Senators—Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff of California, Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper of Colorado, and Ron Wyden of Oregon—released a letter to Burgum and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, expressing “serious concerns” about the departments’ preparedness and ability to adequately respond to the ongoing wildfire season.
The letter says the U.S. Forest Service and U.S. Wildland Fire Service had more than $6 billion in fire-suppression budget authority for fiscal year 2026 and had spent more than 70% by Aug. 31.
“Any wildfire that represents a threat to life, property, infrastructure or the environment should be extinguished as quickly as possible,” federal officials with the Wildland Fire Service said in a statement to the Associated Press in July when the policy was instituted. “Our experienced fire managers retain the authority to select the safest and most effective tactics based on conditions on the ground.”
Some experts argue, however, that full suppression is part of the issue that makes wildfires so large and expensive in the first place.
“These Western ecosystems are adapted to fire; they need fire, and they've burned for thousands of years. Roughly 150 years ago, we started suppressing fires, and in large swaths of the Western forests, that led to an accumulation of fuels,” Winslow Hansen, ecologist with the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies, tells TIME. Fuel can refer to any vegetation, twigs, branches, or organic soils that may be prone to catching fire—especially in the hot, dry conditions that are more prevalent nationwide due to climate change, he explains.
The combination leads to more fuel and drier fuel for fires, Hansen says, and “that leads to more intense fires, larger fires, and even faster fires.”
Federal suppression spending captures only one portion of wildfires’ broader economic toll. A Department of the Interior review estimated that wildfires impose between $87 billion and $424 billion in annual costs, measured in 2022 dollars, including property and health damages and other economic losses. The department cautioned, however, that significant gaps in the available data make the total difficult to calculate.
Separately, a 2018 Headwaters Economics review of existing research and five wildfire case studies estimated that suppression represented approximately 9% of the fires’ full community costs.
State governments are shouldering part of that broader economic burden. While no comprehensive national tally tracks their wildfire spending in real time, data within affected states illuminates the strain.
In Oregon, wildfires had burned 2.5 million acres and cost the state $236.2 million as of late August. Last week, the state approved nearly $123 million in additional funding and authorized $150 million in short-term Treasury borrowing to cover expenses while awaiting federal reimbursements. Officials project that the season’s total cost could reach $350 million, surpassing the state record of $318 million set in 2024.
In Utah, where more than 559,000 acres had burned as of Sept. 3, state wildfire costs had reached approximately $44.9 million and could approach $50 million. Federal costs associated with fires in Utah were estimated at approximately $216 million. Jamie Barnes, commissioner of the Utah Department of Natural Resources, said it could be a “record breaking” season by cost.
How rising wildfire costs affect Americans
While local, state, and federal governments are responsible for wildfire preparedness and suppression, these activities are funded primarily by taxpayers. For example, the four largest fires that plagued Colorado this year could cost taxpayers $266 million, according to a Colorado Drought Task Force meeting in July.
And the government does not bear the full burden of the fires; Americans shoulder it through property damage, skyrocketing insurance costs, supply chain disruptions, and lost business revenue. 
A study released in August analyzed data covering approximately 100,000 people and 50,000 homes inside wildfire burn areas. It found that occupants of destroyed homes experienced reduced earnings for three years after a fire, with cumulative losses equal to 26% of their pre-fire annual income. Within fire zones, lower-income households were more likely to lose their homes.
Wildfires also impose costs that are harder to quantify. A July study from the University of Southern California found that Los Angeles County residents who lived in evacuation zones during the 2025 fires reported elevated anxiety and depression nearly a year later, with the greatest effects among people already facing social and economic hardship.
These costs do not affect only people in communities directly touched by wildfires. In California, average homeowners-insurance premiums rose 84% between the end of 2020 and March 2026, according to Stanford researchers, who attributed the increase to a combination of wildfire risk, inflation and the state’s regulatory framework.
According to the 2026 Wildfire Risk Report by Cotality, a major real estate data and analytics company, more than 2.5 million properties across the 10 of the most exposed states face a moderate or greater risk of wildfire damage, with a combined reconstruction cost value approaching $1.4 trillion. The risk is concentrated in California, Colorado, and Texas. The report estimates that there are some 1.28 million at-risk properties in California alone.
No single figure can capture what the 2026 wildfire season will ultimately cost. The bills will emerge in different forms—from government spending and rebuilding expenses to higher insurance premiums and lost household income. The financial consequences typically persist long after the fires are contained.

Russian forces launched a mass drone attack on western Ukraine on Sept. 12, injuring at least five people in Volyn Oblast and causing power outages in neighboring Rivne Oblast, regional authorities said.
Both regions are located in Ukraine's northwest, far from the front lines, making them less frequent targets for Russian attacks.
The attack on Volyn Oblast lasted more than four hours, with more than 10 Russian unmanned aerial vehicles entering the region’s airspace, according to regional Governor Roman Romaniuk.
Most of the drones targeted the Kovel community, Romaniuk said. Five people were injured and received medical assistance. No deaths were reported.
Debris from one of the drones also struck a passenger train in Lutsk. Passengers had been evacuated before the impact, and no one aboard was injured, according to the governor.
In neighboring Rivne Oblast, Russian attacks caused power outages in parts of Dubno and in the Rivne district, according to regional Governor Oleksandr Koval. An unspecified enterprise in the Sarny district was also destroyed in the attack.
No casualties were reported, and energy crews were working to restore electricity, Koval said.
The attacks illustrate Russia's ability to strike deep into western Ukraine, far from the line of contact. Volyn borders Poland and Belarus, while Rivne lies immediately to its east.
Western Ukrainian regions have repeatedly come under long-range Russian drone and missile attacks targeting energy, transport, and other infrastructure. While these regions are targeted less frequently than Kyiv or Odesa — and far less frequently than front-line cities in Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts — they have increasingly been reached by Russian drones during large-scale nationwide attacks.
On Sept. 3, Russian drones hit several western regions during a nationwide attack that killed five people and injured dozens.
The attacks on Volyn and Rivne were part of a wider Russian drone assault across Ukraine on Sept. 12. According to President Volodymyr Zelensky, Russia launched nearly 500 strike drones at the country during the day.
"In essence, the Russians have expanded this war from the front lines, where they cannot achieve success, into the economic sphere, and their tactics are extremely primitive: to destroy every object that can help people endure the conditions of the war," Zelensky said.

Former Army secretary praises Ukraine in 1st public appearance since resigning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:24:12 UTC
04:24:12 KST

Former Army Secretary Driscoll praises Ukraine's warfare innovation in Kyiv during 1st public appearance since resigning
Kyiv - In his first public appearance since leaving the Trump administration, former Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll warned of "an inflection point in warfare," arguing that the world's largest militaries "have not adopted the speed and the innovation that they need."
Wearing a tie embroidered with a traditional Ukrainian pattern, Driscoll spoke alongside Eric Schmidt, the former Google CEO who now heads Perennial Autonomy, an American defense firm active in Ukraine. CNN's Fareed Zakaria moderated the discussion on the second day of the Yalta European Strategy forum, an annual conference organized by the Victor Pinchuk Foundation to discuss Ukraine's future in the West's security architecture.
Driscoll and Schmidt praised Kyiv's wartime innovations, in particular "DELTA," a Ukrainian software platform that allows military leaders to see a more complete picture of the battlefield by tying together data from radars, sensors and soldiers. The platform, Driscoll said, surpasses any technology the U.S. military currently possesses.
Driscoll said that as Ukraine obtains more processing power and expands its AI capabilities, it will have "an amazing opportunity for your nation to outrun the Russians, and out-innovate them, and out-partner so that you can crush them."
Driscoll, an Iraq War veteran and former venture capitalist, is a longtime friend of Vice President JD Vance, whom he met at Yale Law School. As Army secretary, he also took part in the administration's efforts to negotiate an end to Russia's war in Ukraine.
His resignation was announced on Aug. 31 amid reported clashes with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the removal of senior officers and the Army's modernization efforts. The White House did not give a reason for his departure.
During his 18 months as Army secretary, Driscoll pushed the U.S. military to apply lessons from the war in Ukraine. In January, the Army began rolling out procurement reforms aimed at getting new weapons into soldiers' hands more quickly.
The war with Iran has underscored this urgency. When Driscoll realized the U.S. lacked the defenses it needed against Iranian Shahed drones, help came not from America's largest defense contractors but from Schmidt's Perennial Autonomy. The company quickly supplied 13,000 "Merops" interceptor drones and 10,000 "Bumblebee" reconnaissance and strike drones — both widely used in Ukraine.
"He literally called me and I said, of course, yes," Schmidt said. "The question is, could the government have had a multi-year plan to anticipate this?"
Driscoll said that part of the key to answering those questions will be "to internalize these lessons that what you're doing here [in Ukraine] in a very scrappy, fast, iterative nature."
This found a receptive audience among the Ukrainian, European and American ministers, generals and legislators. When Zakaria, the moderator, noted the gap between the 300,000 drones the U.S. is likely to buy this year and the 7 million drones Ukraine will produce, former CIA Director David Petraeus shouted from the audience that Ukraine's projection is closer to 10 million drones.
But in recent months, the U.S. has seemed to turn away from the people and processes dedicated to learning lessons from the war in Ukraine. In August, the U.S. Army phased out a drone battalion tasked with studying lessons on Ukraine's drone warfare. Two of the unit's prominent backers, former Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George and the former commander of U.S. Army Europe and Africa, Gen. Christopher Donahue, were both fired or forced to retire early this year.
Driscoll did not address those departures. He defended the administration's commitment to Ukraine, while acknowledging that its support had fallen short of Kyiv's expectations.
"I believe the relationship that the U.S. has had with your country throughout this, has remained, not perhaps, as strong as you wanted, but from my position, it's been unflinching in the desire for you to be successful," he said.
But Driscoll had decided his own contribution would be greater outside government.
"My highest and best use to make the world a little bit safer at this very scary time was to do it on the outside," he said.

Journalist named successor as Uganda buries world's youngest king
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:11:58 UTC
04:11:58 KST

Hamza Kyeyune
12 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
The royal council chief of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom, Omujwera Musuuga Charles Kayondo Kamurasi, announced Saturday that journalist Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma is the next monarch, following the death of his cousin, King Oyo Rukidi IV.
Musuuga, the head of the Babiito royal clan from which the Tooro kings trace their lineage, made the announcement before mourners gathered to pay their final respects to the late king, who died at 34 on Aug. 27 in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment.
King Oyo was crowned at the age of 3 in 1995 after the death of his father. He earned a Guinness World Record as the world’s youngest reigning monarch. He led his people via regents appointed by the kingdom until he came of age at 18.
He died last month in the United States, where he was receiving treatment for cancer.
“I wish to inform Tooro and Uganda at large that Tooro has a new king. The council of the Babiito sat and elected Edward Rukidi. Whatever we’ve done is in accordance with Ugandan law, and we have put our Tooro culture and norms into consideration, let’s all maintain unity and always remember our culture,” Musuuga remarked.
Mixed reactions were heard from the congregation as Musuuga announced the successor, signaling a bitter royal succession dispute in the Tooro Kingdom.
Earlier, King Oyo’s immediate family, notably his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, and sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, publicly rejected the clan council's choice, insisting that King Oyo had left a will dictating that his hitherto unknown son should succeed him to the throne. Clan leaders said that a royal child must be officially introduced to elders in order to be considered for leadership.
Still unmarried at his death, he had no children known to the clan members or the public, plunging the kingdom into a rapid succession crisis.
King Oyo was the 13th monarch of the Tooro Kingdom, which was founded more than 200 years ago and ruled over more than two million people. He was laid to rest at the Karambi Royal Tombs in the western Ugandan city of Fort Portal on Saturday.
Traditional monarchs in Uganda
Uganda is a republic ruled by an elected president, but the country retains several traditional monarchies that still preside over their kingdoms. Their power is largely symbolic, but they wield considerable cultural and social influence. They are legally not allowed to engage in partisan politics and have no political authority.
Oyo Nyimba was arguably one of the most recognizable among them because of his unusual story, taking the throne at the age of 3.
His unusual status as a modern “boy king” led to considerable interest early in his reign, including from world leaders like former Libyan strongman Moammar Gadhafi, who repeatedly visited Tooro and supported Oyo and the queen mother for years before Gadhafi’s death in October 2011.
He spent time in the UK at Winchester University to complete his education. This time away from Uganda prompted a failed challenge to his position in 2015, when his cousin Prince David Kijanangoma declared himself the rightful king of Tooro, accusing Oyo of neglecting the region.

Quote: "Russian businesses that pay taxes into the war budget, and Russian oligarchs without whom Putin's system is impossible to imagine, must feel that there is no place in the world where they can live in peace and quiet for as long as this war continues.
When the Ukrainian economy is simply a target for Russia, this is certainly not the time for Europe to treat Russian oligarchs as friends. When Russia uses every euro and dollar to prolong the war, it is both immoral and suicidal to give Russian businesses opportunities to live their lives without feeling the consequences of the war."
Details: Zelenskyy said "Usmanov and Fridman are exactly the kind of Russian business figures who need to find the courage to take concrete steps against the war".
Quote: "With 500 Shaheds a day, this is certainly not the time to even begin the discussion about easing sanctions – especially sanctions against individuals about whom no one can say how exactly they have helped protect lives and reduce Putin's ability to continue the war.
We need to keep up comprehensive pressure on Russia for its war. Strengthen sanctions against Russia instead of weakening Ukraine!"
Background:
- On 11 September, EU ambassadors once again failed to agree on extending personal sanctions over Russia's aggression because of Slovakia and France's demands to change the list of sanctioned individuals.
- The deadline for extending these sanctions is 15 September.
- The restrictive measures targeting individuals were last extended on 14 March. On that occasion Slovakia also pushed until the last minute for Fridman and Usmanov to be removed from the list.

Could Iran’s regime collapse? Inside the Israeli assessment of Tehran’s future - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
19:12:40 UTC
04:12:40 KST

What is really happening behind the scenes in Tehran? How close is the collapse of the ayatollah regime, what is going through Mojtaba Khamenei’s mind, and why is Israel’s defense establishment on maximum alert?
Throughout January and February, intelligence agencies closely monitored the Iranian regime’s harsh campaign of retaliation against protesters across the country. Reports collected by officials in Washington and Jerusalem documented arrests, severe torture, and a widespread pattern of citizens disappearing without a trace.
Initially, Israeli and the United States had no plan to launch another operation after Operation Rising Lion. However, as reports emerged of mass killings carried out indiscriminately against men, women, children, and the elderly, Israel’s defense establishment delivered a firm message in closed forums: “The moment for another operation will come; it is inevitable.”
The motivation was not only the growing threat posed by Iran’s nuclear program and former supreme leader Ali Khamenei’s decision to produce thousands of ballistic missiles.
Israeli officials also cited a moral obligation not to stand aside in the face of mass killings. At the same time, they identified a strategic opportunity to advance a process that could ultimately lead to the collapse of the regime.
The White House meeting and the three pillars
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accepted the recommendation of the US administration and traveled to the White House for a critical meeting with US President Donald Trump, accompanied by senior security officials. The goal was to strengthen cooperation and approve a joint strategic plan.
During the closed-door meeting, no explicit commitment was made to overthrow the Iranian regime. One official clarified: “We are going to create the conditions for regime change.”
To advance that goal, the Israeli delegation presented three main pillars: alternative leadership, targeted influence campaigns, and ground operations. The approach was based on the clear understanding that airstrikes alone cannot topple a regime.
Six months after Operation Roaring Lion, Israeli security officials assess that the Iranian regime, despite the aggression it continues to display toward its neighbors, is moving along a path of internal deterioration. The process could take months or even years, but severe economic sanctions and international cooperation could accelerate it significantly.
At present, the regime is struggling to contain unrest in the streets and markets, as well as rising unemployment. Oil exports have been almost completely frozen, and the economic situation continues to worsen.
On the military front, Israeli officials assess that intelligence and operational gains have been preserved. According to security sources, Iran has not resumed uranium enrichment or transferred centrifuges, while most of its infrastructure remains buried deep underground.
“They carried out dilutions and various actions, but they did not transfer anything. Their defense industry has been destroyed,” a senior security official said.
The official added that the Pickaxe Mountain facility remains unchanged due to the lack of aerial munitions capable of destroying it.
The clock game: Fear in Tehran, pressure in Washington
The current situation is being managed under a “clock game,” with the American clock measured by fuel prices and Trump’s patience, and the Iranian clock growing more urgent by the day. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has already publicly recommended reaching a diplomatic agreement “while we are still standing on our feet,” amid growing tensions within the upper levels of the government.
For now, Iran is refusing to consider concessions and believes it can withstand the economic pressure. However, US statements regarding broad sanctions have placed Tehran under unprecedented pressure.
Washington is directing much of that pressure toward the United Arab Emirates and China, which serve as Iran’s main economic lifelines through their purchases of oil on the black market. The goal is to persuade them to stop helping Tehran circumvent sanctions.
Within Israel’s defense establishment, there is growing concern over the possibility of an unexpected Iranian move. The assessment is that Tehran may attempt to escape its economic pressure by attacking Israel in an effort to force limited negotiations and reach new understandings.
The Israeli message conveyed to Tehran has been clear: if Iran attacks, there will be no way back. Israel’s response, officials have indicated, would target critical national infrastructure that a collapsing regime would not be able to rebuild.
At the same time, Iranian officials remain concerned about the possibility of another surprise attack, and the heightened tensions continue to trouble senior figures in Tehran.

Former IDF chief Halutz: Netanyahu concealed warnings before Oct. 7, bears ultimate responsibility

2026-09-13

04:12:17 KST

Former IDF chief of staff Dan Halutz accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of knowing more than he disclosed ahead of the October 7 massacre and of concealing information, saying in an interview with 103FM that ultimate responsibility for the failure rests with the prime minister.
Halutz, speaking on 103FM, responded to the Haaretz report that Netanyahu received an explicit warning days before the October 7 massacre during a conversation with United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed.
Halutz first said he believed the conversation had indeed taken place.
"What could be simpler for the Emirati prince than to say there was no conversation if there was no conversation? That is why I believe there was one. But what I believe is irrelevant today. There are so many supporting reasons to understand that the man knew far more than he told those responsible for solving the problems afterward. Because he was incapable of solving the problems. He knew and concealed it."
Halutz then addressed the claim that Netanyahu had been warned but failed to act.
Halutz: Netanyahu received pre-Oct. 7 warnings but left security discussions without decisions
"I don't know how to get inside the mind of this psychopath. What goes through his head? Only he knows. And maybe the people who treat him.
"At the same time, the facts speak for themselves. You can keep asking 'why?' until the day after tomorrow. I don't know how to say why. I'm not a psychiatrist or a brain doctor. What I can say is that there are too many supporting reasons showing that there was information that the man concealed," he said.
"He did not imagine that it would reach that point," Halutz added.
"But he was prepared to absorb something. I am speculating here. It could be that, in certain circumstances, the man felt he was being blackmailed by the Qataris as a result of the entire system of money that flowed between Qatar and Hamas. And I don't know what was going through his mind when he didn't pass that information to the intelligence agencies. A primal fear that perhaps they would act and do something he did not want because it would set the region alight. At least that is what he said."
Halutz later responded to a report that Hamas had also conveyed a warning before the conversation with MBZ, and that no decision was made at the conclusion of a security discussion convened by Netanyahu.
"The bottom line of a discussion convened by the prime minister is the responsibility of the prime minister, not the other participants in the discussion. You can constantly level accusations at the supporting actors in the film. But in the end, if the film is bad, you blame the lead actor."
"He should have summed up the discussion if he thought the discussion warranted a conclusion," Halutz said. "Ask those who participated in discussions with Netanyahu, and many will tell you that one of the things he does not do is sum up discussions. He leaves them hanging in the air. Why? Because when you summarize, ultimately you say something definitive. You don't summarize with a foggy conclusion. When you do something definitive, you compel others, or yourself, to take action."
"I agree that the failure was total, broad, and included everyone," the former IDF chief said.
"But all the others have disappeared. They are no longer in the picture. One person remains on the table. Let the public decide and eat what he is cooking. I call on the public to understand: You must not elect a person who failed so totally in every respect."
Halutz continued, broadening his criticism beyond October 7.
"For a moment, I'm leaving aside the most terrible thing. Education: we have deteriorated to unimaginable places. Health: doctors are leaving the country. Should I keep listing things? Transportation, murders, and all of these things. There is one common denominator: The person responsible for everyone responsible is the prime minister."
Asked whether he was satisfied with the opposition leaders' campaign against Netanyahu ahead of the elections, Halutz replied: "There is a very high chance that the opposition will win. As for the campaign, I would try to be much more aggressive in this fight."

He spoke about how the Brics Network on Digital Agriculture will create new opportunities for farmers. “Through this initiative, AI, geospatial technology, and Digital Public Infrastructure will be connected to the real needs of farmers,” said the PM.On the theme of cooperation and friendship, Modi said this wasn’t limited to the government alone as India had sought to make entrepreneurs, farmers, researchers, women, youth, and ordinary citizens active participants in it.“Through Brics CONNECT, we have promoted skills, employability, women in the workforce, social security, and capacity building. To connect small enterprises with knowledge, finance, and new markets, we have initiated the Brics MSME Cooperation Portal,” he said.
The PM spoke about the need to strike a balance between human development and the environment, saying this was the foundation of sustainability. “It is also our responsibility towards future generations. For Smart Grids and Energy Storage, we have established the Brics Digital Centre of Excellence. This will help make our clean energy systems more reliable, efficient, and accessible,’ said Modi.

Ladakh begins reviving Tso Kar glacial lake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:57:10 UTC
03:57:10 KST

SRINAGAR: To revive the rapidly shrinking Tso Kar glacial lake, Ladakh administration has launched a project to divert an average of 132 cusecs (around 320 million litres) of untapped glacier water daily from Rupsho Kharnak stream in Changthang district to the lake. Officials expect the lake will be restored to its former glory within a year, calling it the first project of its scale in India to revive a high-altitude lake under such harsh climatic conditions.Situated at an altitude of nearly 15,000ft, the lake has lost nearly 70% of its water over the past decade, shrinking from around 11,000 acres to just 3,200 acres. Once a thriving habitat for migratory birds, including the black-necked crane, it now attracts far fewer birds.The project follows the successful diversion of 90 million litres of Stok glacier water into irrigation canals in Igoo-Phey and Chuchot villages near Leh. The administration described it as the region’s second major water-management initiative of its kind.The revival was conceived after Lt Governor VK Saxena visited Tso Kar on Aug 10. Villagers told him the lake once supported centuries-old salt trade and maintained a delicate ecological balance, but its decline had resulted in loss of grazing land and shrinking bird populations.
Saxena directed the public health engineering department to survey the area. Its report, submitted on Aug 30 after 15 days of groundwork, proposed an 11km RCC channel. Saxena, however, ruled out a new RCC structure and suggested first diverting the water to a depression through a simple earthen channel. Work began on Sept 2, ahead of the winter freeze.
Rupsho Kharnak stream, located about 11km from Tso Kar at an altitude of 18,000ft, has a peak summer discharge of around 132 cusecs. So far, 20 cusecs is being diverted to the first depression, which has filled by about 20% in four days using an earthen channel and a defunct concrete canal built in 1995.Before reaching Tso Kar, water will fill three natural depressions, creating freshwater wetlands of 270, 24 and 10 acres with a combined capacity of nearly 1,230 million litres. The wetlands will allow sediments to settle, ensuring cleaner water reaches the lake, while also creating new habitats for migratory birds and potential tourist attractions visible from Leh-Manali highway.
